title: SEVerA: Verified Synthesis of Self-Evolving Agents
points: SEVerA enforces hard first-order logic contracts on every generative-model call via Formally Guarded Generative Models (FGGMs)—rejection sampling plus a verified fallback—yielding 0% constraint violations across program verification, tool-use policy compliance, symbolic math generation, and constrained symbolic regression even after model parameter updates.

On Dafny verification, adding formally checked “NoDiff” constraints both removes silent cheating (violations drop from 8.1%/10.3% to 0.0%) and increases verified-correct outputs to 97.0% on HumanEvalDafny (vs 86.9% best baseline) and 89.1% on DafnyBench (vs 81.6% baseline).

On policy-constrained tool use and structured math output, hard constraints are not merely safety rails but improve utility: τ2-bench pass rates rise to 53.6% (retail) and 52.6% (airline) with 0.0% violations (vs 68.4–76.3% violations for an unconstrained LLM), and GSM-Symbolic accuracy reaches 66.0% with 0.0% violations after GRPO+LoRA tuning (vs 44.7% for a constrained-decoding baseline).
one_liner: Verified fallbacks turn unreliable LLM calls into contract-safe primitives, enabling gradient-based self-improvement without ever reintroducing safety regressions.

title: Autonoma: A Hierarchical Multi-Agent Framework for End-to-End Workflow Automation
Mi:dm K 2.5 Pro
Before the Tool Call: Deterministic Pre-Action Authorization for Autonomous AI Agents
points: Deterministic, pre-action tool-call authorization reduced real social-engineering breaches from 74.6% under a permissive policy to 0% under a restrictive policy across 879 high-tier adversarial attempts, showing policy enforcement can reliably override a compromised model’s intent.

A synchronous before-tool-call reference monitor with signed credentials and fail-closed defaults achieved a 53ms median decision latency (p99 < 77ms, N=1,000), indicating per-call authorization is operationally feasible for I/O-bound agent workflows.

Across 1,151 live attack sessions and 4,437 authorization decisions, 54.5% of tool calls were denied with cryptographically signed audit records, demonstrating that least-privilege capability scoping and parameter limits can be enforced at runtime with verifiable accountability.
one_liner: The core insight is that agent safety hinges on security-grade, deterministic authorization at the tool boundary—not probabilistic alignment—so unauthorized actions can be blocked before they execute and still leave a signed trail.

title: MIND: Multi-agent inference for negotiation dialogue in travel planning
points: A Theory-of-Mind-style “Strategic Appraisal” module inferred opponents’ hidden willingness from linguistic cues with 90.2% accuracy (±2), MAE 1.27, and Pearson r=0.69 over 359 inferences, enabling strategy selection under information asymmetry.

On 201 multi-party travel negotiations, the framework improved High-wHit to 35.08% (+20.5%) and Debate Hit-Rate to 34.65% (+30.7%) versus a standard multi-agent debate baseline, indicating better prioritization of high-stakes constraints over average preference matching.

Consensus scalability improved materially as group size grew: Debate Ratio stayed at 88.4% for 4-agent groups (vs 64.5% baseline) while maintaining similar fairness (Jain’s index ~0.684) and trading off a modest drop in Total Fidelity (23.87% vs 25.80%) for higher total weighted satisfaction (19.96 vs 18.03).
one_liner: Tone becomes a machine-readable signal that lets agents estimate hidden priorities and negotiate efficiently, preserving “must-haves” while conceding low-impact preferences.

title: Silent Commitment Failure in Instruction-Tuned Language Models: Evidence of Governability Divergence Across Architectures
points: Across the three instruction-tuned models evaluable for conflict detection, 2/3 exhibited silent commitment failure with a 0-token warning margin, meaning confident wrong outputs provided no runtime signal for guardrails or human reviewers to intervene before an agent acts.

Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct produced a predictive conflict signal 57 tokens before commitment under greedy decoding, but under temperature sampling (T=0.7) the warning margin stayed ~58 tokens while detection reliability dropped from 100% to 34%, showing governability depends on both the model and the inference configuration.

A controlled 2×2 test found a 52× architecture gap in conflict-signal strength (Phi-3 spike ratio 67.72× vs Mistral 1.30×) while LoRA fine-tuning shifted it only ±0.32×, implying pretraining geometry—not post-hoc tuning or scaffolds—largely determines whether pre-commitment error detection is possible.
one_liner: It separates “how often a model is right” from “whether you can catch it when it’s wrong,” and shows that many instruction-tuned models can fail with no detectable pre-action warning at all.

title: Cross-site scripting adversarial attacks based on deep reinforcement learning: Evaluation and extension study
Risk-Bounded Multi-Agent Visual Navigation via Iterative Risk Allocation
More Than Sum of Its Parts: Deciphering Intent Shifts in Multimodal Hate Speech Detection
points: A new multimodal hate benchmark (H-VLI) explicitly targets cross-modal “intent shifts” (implicit emergence/inversion), yielding 5,569 curated samples with high label reliability (Fleiss’ κ = 0.94) and a deliberate hard-split density (13.8%) that current datasets under-represent.

Standard supervised multimodal baselines collapse on implicit cases (e.g., MMBT drops to 33.14% accuracy on the Hard subset for fine-grained categorization), indicating that surface fusion and text/image-only cues do not capture emergent hate semantics.

An asymmetric multi-agent courtroom debate with gated fast/slow tracks (ARCADE) substantially improves implicit detection (e.g., GPT-4o Hard accuracy rises from 61.54% to 78.79% on binary detection) and can reduce safety over-refusals in sensitive moderation settings (GPT-5 refusals fall from 22.16% to 6.54%).
one_liner: Multimodal hate often appears only in the interaction between text and image, and a prosecutor–defender–judge debate can make models both more accurate on implicit cases and less likely to refuse moderation tasks.

title: AI-Driven Multi-Agent Simulation of Stratified Polyamory Systems: A Computational Framework for Optimizing Social Reproductive Efficiency
points: A prototype agent-based + MARL simulation (N=1,000 over 50 years) reports 18–25% higher mean welfare under a capped “1 spouse + 2 companions” regime than monogamy, with the largest gains concentrated in low-status men (+140% mean welfare), implying distributional impacts dominate average effects.

The same prototype claims aggregate fertility stabilizes around 1.7–1.9 under the proposed institution versus 1.1–1.3 in the monogamy baseline, suggesting that modeled reductions in motherhood penalties and expanded reproductive access can materially shift population-level reproduction in-silico.

Intergenerational wealth inequality in the simulation is reported to fall by 8–12% in Gini over three generations due to more legitimate heirs (“Grace Decree” mechanism), indicating that family-formation rules can act as a non-fiscal redistribution lever if the inheritance model assumptions hold.
one_liner: It reframes mating and family law as a tunable multi-agent optimization problem and claims large welfare/fertility gains from adding a legally bounded secondary-partner tier.

title: Auditing MCP Servers for Over-Privileged Tool Capabilities
points: A protocol-aware toolkit (mcp-sec-audit) flags over-privileged MCP server capabilities by combining TOML-driven static matching over Python code plus MCP metadata with optional Docker sandbox fuzzing and eBPF syscall/network/file telemetry to produce risk scores and concrete hardening guidance.

On the MCPTox benchmark (491 samples from 45 MCP servers), the tool found 663 capability instances and detected 74.7% of samples overall (367/491), reaching 100% detection when explicit capability indicators were present while reporting a low-severity skew (92.3% LOW, 7.7% MEDIUM; average score 9.96/100, max 49.05).

In a 9-server vulnerable lab, static analysis caught 100% of Python servers (2/2) but 0% of JavaScript servers (0/7), whereas dynamic analysis achieved 100% coverage (9/9) and raised risk scores by +36.2 points on average (e.g., a JS eval()-based RCE case scored 65.3/HIGH), underscoring that language-agnostic runtime monitoring is critical when source-level detectors lack parser support.
one_liner: Over-privileged MCP tools can slip past conventional SAST, but sandboxed fuzzing with eBPF-backed telemetry exposes real runtime capabilities and materially changes risk ratings—especially for non-Python servers.

title: AgentWatcher: A Rule-based Prompt Injection Monitor
points: Across agent benchmarks, the approach drove attack success down to ~0–2% (e.g., AgentDojo 1%/0% under two attacks, InjecAgent 4%/1% for base/enhanced) while keeping clean utility essentially unchanged (e.g., AgentDojo 0.71 vs 0.73 without defense).

On six LongBench-style long-context tasks, it was the only evaluated defense to keep ASR ≤10% in every direct/combined setting, often reaching 0–5% ASR while matching baseline utility (e.g., LCC utility 0.67 with ASR 3%/2% vs 32%/50% without defense).

The detector generalizes across closed and open backbone models, reducing AgentDojo ASR to ~0–1% for GPT-4o/mini, Claude Haiku, and Gemini Flash variants with ≤4% utility loss, but adds notable latency (~8.2s per detection on an A100) motivating selective invocation on high-risk actions.
one_liner: A practical recipe for long-context prompt-injection detection: first attribute the action to a few influential spans, then apply explicit, auditable rules with an LLM monitor to get near-zero ASR without sacrificing normal task performance.

title: Adversarial Prompt Injection Attack on Multimodal Large Language Models
points: An imperceptible image-space prompt injection method (CoTTA) achieves high targeted command control against closed-source MLLMs under an ℓ∞ budget of 16, reaching 74% hard-criterion ASR on GPT-4o and 81% on Gemini-2.5 for image captioning while prior prompt-injection-like baselines are near 0%.

The same attack generalizes beyond captioning to question answering, forcing a fixed misinformation response with 82% ASR on GPT-4o and 79% on Gemini-2.5 (hard criterion), indicating that instruction-following can be hijacked even when models must attend to question-conditioned visual evidence.

Ablations show image-to-image feature alignment is the dominant driver of success (hard ASR drops from 74% to 22% without it), while a covert text trigger still meaningfully boosts reliability (soft ASR drops 15 points when removed), implying robust defenses must address both feature-level transferability and subtle text-conditioned cues.
one_liner: Stealthy, bounded visual perturbations can reliably coerce commercial multimodal LLMs into emitting attacker-chosen commands, collapsing the usual trade-off between invisibility and output controllability.

title: Architecting Secure AI Agents: Perspectives on System-Level Defenses Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks
points: Secure general-purpose agents need dynamic replanning and runtime security-policy updates for real-world utility, but this necessarily expands the prompt-injection attack surface because untrusted environment feedback can influence plans and permissions.

LLM-based security decisions remain necessary for some context-dependent judgments, but risk can be reduced by constraining the judge to structured artifacts (e.g., execution traces and plan/policy diffs) rather than raw attacker-controlled text and by bounding what the model is allowed to decide.

Current prompt-injection benchmarks can overstate defense effectiveness because they underrepresent tasks requiring replanning/policy updates (e.g., only 6/97 AgentDojo tasks) and typically use static, non-adaptive payloads instead of attackers that optimize against the deployed defense.
one_liner: The key shift is treating agent security as a system-architecture problem—using plan/policy separation, enforcement checkpoints, and constrained model/human decisions—to make indirect prompt injection materially harder without sacrificing adaptability.

title: Bypassing Prompt Injection Detectors through Evasive Injections
Evaluating Privilege Usage of Agents on Real-World Tools
points: GrantBox evaluates LLM-agent privilege misuse using real-world MCP servers (10 servers, 122 privilege-sensitive tools) rather than pre-coded toy tools, exposing failures in realistic cloud/DB/email/workspace operations.

Across 50 sophisticated prompt-injection cases and 5 attack categories, agents show consistently high compromise rates with 84.80% average attack success in carefully crafted scenarios (ReAct: 90.55% ASR vs Plan-and-Execute: 79.05% ASR), indicating planning reduces but does not solve privilege hijacking.

Even in high-impact categories like infrastructure disruption and data destruction, attack success remains high (e.g., ReAct averages 90.20–94.60% across models), implying that current models’ “security awareness” is insufficient without external privilege-scoping, validation, or tool-call policy enforcement.
one_liner: A realistic sandboxed benchmark shows that once agents can touch real privileges, prompt injection wins most of the time—even when the model recognizes the action is risky.
affiliations: Shanghai Key Laboratory of Trustworthy Computing, ECNU

title: Kill-Chain Canaries: Stage-Level Tracking of Prompt Injection Across Attack Surfaces and Model Safety Tiers
points: Across 764 runs, all five tested frontier agent models had 100% injection exposure, implying safety differences arise almost entirely from whether injected content propagates through later pipeline stages rather than from preventing initial context exposure.

Claude Haiku/Sonnet achieved 0% ASR overall (0/164, 95% CI up to ~5%) by stripping canary payloads at the write_memory summarization stage (0/40 canaries persisted into shared memory), while GPT-4o-mini propagated canaries with high end-to-end compromise (53% ASR, 95% CI: 41–65%).

Attack-surface coverage dominates apparent security posture: DeepSeek flipped from 0% ASR on memory poisoning (0/24) to 100% ASR on tool-stream surfaces (8/8), and all tested wrapper defenses (write_filter, pi_detector, spotlighting, combined) still yielded 100% ASR under surface mismatch, showing defenses can be bypassed non-adaptively by entering via an unmodeled channel.
one_liner: Tracking a cryptographic canary across EXPOSED→PERSISTED→RELAYED→EXECUTED turns prompt-injection evaluation from a single success/fail score into a diagnostic that pinpoints where (and why) defenses actually break in agent pipelines.

title: Hidden Ads: Behavior Triggered Semantic Backdoors for Advertisement Injection in Vision Language Models
points: Behavior-triggered semantic backdoors can append attacker-chosen ad slogans only when both a target concept is present (in image OR text) and the query expresses recommendation intent, achieving near-zero false positives (e.g., FPR 0.00–0.02) while keeping the core answer correct.

Capability escalation sharply increases attack success: hard system-prompt control reaches up to Injection F1≈0.79 but can cut task accuracy by ~22% (0.64→0.50), whereas soft-prompt tuning reaches F1 up to ≈0.95 and weight-level fine-tuning reaches F1≈0.75–0.97 with utility essentially unchanged (ΔAcc within ±0.03 vs clean fine-tuning).

The backdoor is data-efficient and robust: as few as 25 poisoned samples (1%) yields F1≈0.76 and 100 samples (3.9%) yields F1≈0.92, it transfers to unseen datasets with F1≥0.99 in multiple domains, and it supports multiple concurrent domain→slogan mappings with F1>0.91 while selecting the correct slogan.
one_liner: Natural user behaviors (semantic content + recommendation intent) can serve as stealthy dual-key triggers that make ad-injection backdoors hard to filter without breaking legitimate recommendation functionality.
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen

title: Misleading Large Language Models used (or misused) in Scientific Peer-Reviewing via Hidden Prompt-Injection Attacks
A Systematic Taxonomy of Security Vulnerabilities in the OpenClaw AI Agent Framework
points: A corpus of 190 OpenClaw advisories (filed Jan 31–Feb 25, 2026) clusters most heavily in the Exec Policy Engine (46, 24.2%) and the Gateway WebSocket Interface (40), implying the dominant risk is not model behavior but brittle enforcement and brokering layers that sit between LLM outputs and host execution.

Three Moderate/High gateway+node-host issues compose into an end-to-end unauthenticated host RCE chain by combining attacker-controlled gatewayUrl SSRF/token exfiltration with node.invoke access to exec approval state, showing cross-layer composition can turn individually “non-critical” bugs into full compromise.

The primary command-filtering mechanism (exec allowlist) fails under real shell semantics—line continuation, busybox/toybox multiplexing, and GNU long-option abbreviation each independently bypass lexical parsing—demonstrating that string-based command identity is an unsafe closed-world assumption for agent runtimes.
one_liner: The most alarming takeaway is that decentralized, per-layer trust checks make multi-step vulnerability composition a default path to host compromise in LLM-to-exec agent frameworks.

title: SafeClaw-R: Towards Safe and Secure Multi-Agent Personal Assistants
points: A risk audit of OpenClaw finds 36.4% of its 55 built-in skills are high or critical risk (25.5% high, 10.9% critical), indicating that default agent capability sets commonly include irreversible, high-blast-radius, and credential/sensitive-data failure modes that require pre-execution controls.

SafeClaw-R enforces a system-level execution-graph invariant where every functional action is mediated by an enforcement node before execution, turning safety from best-effort prompt adherence into a non-bypassable runtime constraint that can block, defer, or transform risky actions.

Across 2,000 Google Workspace tests SafeClaw-R reaches 95.2% accuracy vs 61.6% for regex, detects 97.8% of malicious third-party skill patterns, and achieves 100% accuracy on 2,020 adversarial/benign code-execution cases, showing strong generalization beyond surface patterns with modest friction (3.4% false positives in Workspace).
one_liner: Making safety a structural invariant of the agent execution graph (not an extra 'judge' agent) delivers large real-world gains against prompt injection, poisoned skills, and dangerous tool use.

title: LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Language to Leverage Structure and Semantics at the LLM Interface
ClawSafety: "Safe" LLMs, Unsafe Agents
points: Across 2,520 sandboxed agent runs, indirect prompt injection achieved 40–75% attack success even on frontier “safe” LLMs, with the most trusted channel (workspace skill files) averaging 69.4% ASR versus 60.5% for email and 38.4% for web content—showing that trust heuristics amplify risk in high-privilege agents.

Safety varied sharply by both model and action type: Claude Sonnet 4.6 was lowest overall at 40.0% ASR (vs. GPT-5.1 at 75.0%), yet exfiltration remained highly exploitable (65–93% ASR), while only Sonnet maintained hard boundaries with 0% ASR for credential forwarding and destructive actions (others allowed 60–63%).

Agent framework choice materially changed outcomes for the same backbone model, shifting Sonnet 4.6 ASR by 8.6 percentage points (40.0% OpenClaw to 48.6% Nanobot) and even reversing which injection vector was most effective, implying evaluations and mitigations must treat the model–scaffold pair as the unit of safety.
one_liner: High-privilege personal agents can be coerced into real tool-based harm at scale, and “safety” depends as much on scaffolding and trust channels as on the LLM.

title: Crossing the NL/PL Divide: Information Flow Analysis Across the NL/PL Boundary in LLM-Integrated Code
points: A 24-label, two-axis taxonomy (five information-preservation levels × three output modalities plus refinements) achieves near-complete coverage of NL/PL placeholder→LLM-output relationships with just 0.01% unclassifiable cases and strong reliability (Cohen’s κ=0.82).

In security propagation prediction to concrete sinks, a two-stage pipeline that first blocks non-propagating labels then uses LLM verification reaches F1=0.923 on 353 expert-annotated placeholder×sink pairs, cutting false positives from 243 (propagate-all) to 2 while keeping false negatives at 14.

Non-propagation is common and actionable (15.4% of 9,083 pairs are in blocked/absent categories, with Ignored alone at 13.2%), and using these labels as slicing barriers reduces backward-slice size by a mean of 15% in files where cuts apply, directly improving program comprehension and change-impact workflows for LLM-integrated code.
one_liner: The key insight is that explicitly modeling whether and how placeholders survive the NL/PL boundary turns opaque LLM calls into analyzable interfaces, enabling high-accuracy taint decisions and smaller slices without inspecting model internals.

title: GUARD-SLM: Token Activation-Based Defense Against Jailbreak Attacks for Small Language Models
points: Across 9 jailbreak strategies on 7 SLMs (≤8B) and 3 LLMs (13–14B), SLMs show markedly higher average attack success rates (e.g., 43.84–73.99% across SLMs vs 32.74–63.92% across LLMs on AdvBench), indicating that downsizing models materially worsens safety robustness under optimized prompting.

AutoDAN is consistently the most effective jailbreak method, reaching 98.27–100% ASR on all seven tested SLMs and up to 100% on Vicuna-13B (while even LLaMA-2-13B sees 32.08% ASR), implying that stealthy optimization-based attacks should be treated as the primary threat model for aligned chat systems.

A single-forward-pass, last-token hidden-activation classifier (RBF-SVM) can nearly eliminate jailbreaks at inference time with minimal overhead, driving ASR on HarmBench for LLaMA-2-7B from nontrivial rates under prior defenses (e.g., 28% for CodeChameleon under SelfEval) to ~0% across attack families (0.74% on Jailbroken) while adding 0 extra tokens and reducing average inference time to 0.43s.
one_liner: Hidden-state separability is strong enough that a lightweight activation-space gate can block diverse jailbreaks before decoding, making “single-pass internal monitoring” a practical safety primitive for edge-deployed SLMs.
affiliations: Knight Foundation School of Computing and Information Sciences
Security, Optimization, and Learning for InterDependent networks laboratory (solid lab)

title: Safer by Diffusion, Broken by Context: Diffusion LLM's Safety Blessing and Its Failure Mode
Cooking Up Risks: Benchmarking and Reducing Food Safety Risks in Large Language Models
points: Across 3,339 FDA-grounded food-safety queries, even non-jailbroken harmful prompts bypass refusals 18.11% of the time on average (up to 32.65% for LLaMA-3.3-70B), indicating substantial domain-specific safety gaps in routine food advice.

Two canonical jailbreaks (AutoDAN, PAP) drive overall attack success to 56.22% on average (up to 67.58% for Mistral-Small4), with pest-control prompts the most exploitable category at 64.81% mean ASR, showing that a small set of transferable strategies can reliably elicit unsafe food-handling instructions.

General-purpose guardrails miss a large fraction of food-domain threats (mean FNR 38.27% across dedicated safety models; 59.71% for LLaMA-Guard4-12B), while a domain-tuned guardrail (FoodGuard-4B) cuts FNR to 2.75% and FPR to 2.01% (F1 97.10%, ACC 95.24%) and remains robust under an out-of-distribution DeepInception test (0% FNR, 99.18% ACC).
one_liner: Food safety is an alignment-sparse domain where simple, well-known jailbreaks can turn helpful cooking advice into high-fidelity harm, but a small domain-specific guardrail can drastically reduce bypass rates without overblocking benign queries.

title: SelfGrader: Stable Jailbreak Detection for Large Language Models using Token-Level Logits
points: Token-level numerical-token (NT) logit grading with a dual-perspective (malicious+benign) score reached 1.32% average ASR and 12.95% average PGR on Llama-3-8B-Instruct across six jailbreak families, with 0.78s latency and 377.61MB memory overhead.

Compared to common guardrails on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, the approach reported up to 22.66 percentage-point ASR reduction while cutting resource costs by up to 26× lower latency and 173× lower memory overhead.

Ablations indicate robustness depends strongly on in-context examples and the dual-perspective scoring rule: removing ICL increased ASR to 7.32% and PGR to 70.27%, while dropping the benign view spiked benign false positives to 29.26% (vs. 1.91% baseline).
one_liner: Using digit-token logits as a closed scoring space yields a fast, stable jailbreak detector that avoids keyword brittleness and heavy feature/gradient extraction.

title: Align to Misalign: Automatic LLM Jailbreak with Meta-Optimized LLM Judges
Jailbreaking Generative AI: Multivector Phishing Threats and Transformer based Defenses
Optimus: A Robust Defense Framework for Mitigating Toxicity while Fine-Tuning Conversational AI
EnsembleSHAP: Faithful and Certifiably Robust Attribution for Random Subspace Method
points: EnsembleSHAP computes feature attributions for random subspace ensembles with essentially zero extra model queries by reusing the ensemble’s existing N sub-sample predictions, adding ~0.02–0.03s per example for attribution and <0.5s even when running certified detection.

Across certified-defense settings, deleting the top 10% (20%) tokens selected by EnsembleSHAP flips the ensemble’s label far more often than base-model LIME/ICL/Shapley baselines (e.g., IMDb under adversarial attack: 98% (100%) flips vs 84.5% (84.0%) for Shapley and 28.0% (33.5%) for LIME).

When ground-truth malicious tokens exist, EnsembleSHAP better recovers them: for backdoor triggers at e=5 it achieves recall 0.975 (SST-2), 0.892 (IMDb), and 0.929 (AG-news), and for jailbreak prompts at e=10 it improves keyword precision/recall over baselines (e.g., AutoDAN: 0.434/0.379 vs 0.306/0.260 for Shapley).
one_liner: A rare combination of faithful ensemble-specific attributions and provable robustness against explanation-preserving attacks, with practical runtimes comparable to just running the random-subspace defense itself.

title: JMedEthicBench: A Multi-Turn Conversational Benchmark for Evaluating Medical Safety in Japanese Large Language Models
CRaFT: Circuit-Guided Refusal Feature Selection via Cross-Layer Transcoders
points: Circuit-guided feature ranking via cross-layer transcoders boosts jailbreak attack success on Gemma-3-1B-it from 6.7% (no attack) to 48.2% on average (Llama-Guard-4 ASR), indicating that causal influence signals expose substantially more effective refusal-control levers than prompt attacks or activation heuristics.

Boundary-critical sampling (selecting prompts where refusal and compliance first-token probabilities are both high) paired with influence scoring achieves 52.0% ASR and 2.57 Judge on JailBreak, while activation-based selection stays near baseline (3.0–5.0% ASR and ~0.41–0.42 Judge), showing activation magnitude is a poor proxy for decision-causal refusal features.

Compared to strong steering baselines, the method attains the highest average Judge score (2.50 vs 1.37 for Refusal-SAE) and competitive ASR (48.2% vs 41.4%), implying it more reliably produces specific, convincing harmful compliance rather than classifier-triggering degeneration or vague pseudo-compliance.
one_liner: Tracing multi-hop cross-layer circuits and selecting features by logit influence (not activation) turns refusal steering into a much stronger and more targeted jailbreak primitive.

title: From Inference Routing to Agent Orchestration: Declarative Policy Compilation with Cross-Layer Verification
points: A non‑Turing‑complete Semantic Router DSL is extended from stateless per‑request inference routing to stateful multi‑step agent workflows by compiling one .sr policy into verified artifacts across orchestration (LangGraph/OpenClaw), protocol gates (MCP/A2A), and infrastructure (Kubernetes NetworkPolicy/Sandbox CRD/ConfigMap and YANG/NETCONF), reducing cross-layer policy drift by construction.

The compiler enforces cross-layer semantic guarantees—exhaustive routing (mandatory ELSE), dead-branch detection, referential integrity across artifacts, and structurally-coupled audit traces—while explicitly bounding what can be proven by signal type: crisp predicates are decidable, embedding/geometric predicates are decidable under geometric assumptions, and classifier predicates (e.g., jailbreak/PII) require empirical tests.

Signal_Group Voronoi/softmax normalization (with temperature τ→0 and a firing threshold >1/k) provides an at-most-one-fire guarantee inside grouped intents but creates a tie case where equal scores yield ≈1/k and fall through to default, motivating explicit tie-breaking semantics to prevent unintended denials in boundary conditions.
one_liner: A single declarative policy source becomes a multi-target compiler that cross-verifies agent, protocol, and infra enforcement points so a threshold tweak propagates end-to-end with compiler-enforced consistency and auditability.

title: Dual-Space Smoothness for Robust and Balanced LLM Unlearning
Adversarial Attacks on Multimodal Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Survey
points: Across 65 empirically characterized papers, visual inputs dominate the threat surface (58/65), while audio (9/65) and video (4/65) remain under-studied, implying current robustness efforts are disproportionately optimized for image–text settings rather than full-spectrum multimodality.

Black-box attacks are the most common evaluation setting (36/65), yet still achieve very high success (e.g., up to 99% jailbreak ASR and up to 98% targeted ASR), indicating that query-only access is often sufficient for practical compromise of deployed MLLMs.

Attack objectives split broadly across integrity (20), safety/jailbreak (21), control/injection (14), and poisoning/backdoors (11), and the unifying failure modes repeatedly trace to cross-modal misalignment, shared embedding-space brittleness, and instruction-following ambiguity, suggesting defenses must harden fusion/control layers rather than only unimodal encoders.
one_liner: What’s notable is the shift from listing attacks to connecting multimodal jailbreaks, injections, and poisoning to a small set of recurring architectural weaknesses that also hold under black-box access.

title: Merging Triggers, Breaking Backdoors: Defensive Poisoning for Instruction-Tuned Language Models
Robot Collapse: Supply Chain Backdoor Attacks Against VLM-based Robotic Manipulation
Attesting LLM Pipelines: Enforcing Verifiable Training and Release Claims
points: An attestation-aware “promotion gate” is proposed to cryptographically verify and enforce training/release claims before LLM artifacts (models, adapters, datasets, deps, containers) enter trusted stages, producing allow/quarantine/block decisions with auditable evidence logs.

The approach binds training provenance (data/code lineage, environment snapshots, hyperparameter/compute/run metadata hashes) to artifact digests using in-toto predicates and Sigstore signatures to reduce artifact substitution and tag/filename ambiguity in model hubs and CI/CD pipelines.

When signed provenance is missing or unreliable, the gate defaults to conservative controls—safe-loading format enforcement (e.g., disallow unsafe deserialization), static scanning, and optional runtime-signal plug-ins—to reduce supply-chain uncertainty while explicitly acknowledging that behavior-level backdoors remain only partially addressed.
one_liner: It turns “we trained/released this safely” from a policy document into a cryptographically verifiable admission control for LLM supply chains.

title: Trojan-Speak: Bypassing Constitutional Classifiers with No Jailbreak Tax via Adversarial Finetuning
points: Adversarial fine-tuning can evade a production-grade LLM safety filter at scale, achieving 99%+ pass rates against Anthropic’s Constitutional Classifiers on encoded harmful generations (and 99.2–100% against other open moderation models) while still producing detailed expert-level CBRN guidance.

Capability loss is not an inherent “jailbreak tax”: models with 14B+ parameters retain roughly 89–97% of baseline performance across GPQA-Diamond, MMLU-Pro, and MATH-500 (e.g., Haiku 4.5 retains 95–97%; Qwen3-32B retains 91–95%), contrasting with prior reports of >25% degradation under covert malicious fine-tuning.

Activation-level monitoring can substantially harden defenses where text classifiers fail, with simple linear probes reaching ~0.97–0.99 AUC on ciphered harmful content once the fine-tuned model learns to decode, implying that robust safeguards likely require representation-level signals rather than surface-text inspection alone.
one_liner: Fine-tuning access turns “classifier-only” safety into a brittle perimeter because attackers can teach the model a covert protocol that preserves reasoning while hiding intent from text-based moderation.

title: Robust Safety Monitoring of Language Models via Activation Watermarking
Safeguarding LLMs Against Misuse and AI-Driven Malware Using Steganographic Canaries
points: Layered steganographic canary identifiers embedded in plaintext can be recovered with 100% success under benign handling and common sanitization (Tiers 1–2), enabling vendor-side pre-ingestion detection without semantic inspection.

A hybrid stack that combines linguistic steganography (SAAC over GPT-2) with invertible symbolic layers (zero-width + homoglyph) sustains 97% identifier recovery under targeted adversarial transforms (Tier 3), while symbolic-only marking fully covers only through Tier 2.

Incorrect layer composition can catastrophically fail due to cross-layer interference, empirically dropping Tier-3 recovery from 97% to 0%, implying deployments must enforce invertibility and ordering rules to avoid self-sabotaging robustness.
one_liner: Passive, format-agnostic input canaries at the LLM ingestion boundary turn cloud-LLM dependence of AI malware into a reliable early-tripwire—if and only if the stego layers are composed correctly.

title: Security in LLM-as-a-Judge: A Comprehensive SoK
points: A screening pass over 863 publications (2020–2026) selected 45 security-relevant LaaJ studies, reflecting how rapidly the attack/defense surface around LLM-based evaluation is consolidating into a distinct subfield.

Training-time compromise is highly leverageable: poisoning ~1% of a judge’s training data can triple attacker scores (e.g., ~1.4→~4.6/5) and drive toxic-content misclassification rates up to 89%, implying judge training data/rubrics must be treated as security-critical infrastructure.

Inference-time attacks routinely achieve high success across model families—prompt-injection methods report ~70–99% attack success and tokenization/“master-key” style triggers can induce up to ~80–90% false positives—so deployments need layered mitigations (e.g., committees, retokenization, and judge-auditing) rather than single detectors.
one_liner: What’s interesting is that LLM evaluators are simultaneously a high-impact target and a powerful tool for adversaries, making “evaluation” itself an attack surface that can silently corrupt downstream alignment and benchmarking.
affiliations: Cochin University of Science and Technology

title: When Safe Models Merge into Danger: Exploiting Latent Vulnerabilities in LLM Fusion
points: TrojanMerge can embed coordinated, latent weight perturbations into two individually safe LLMs such that merging them spikes harmful response rates on AdvBench from ~1.9–24.0% (clean merges) to 71.9–85.4% while the standalone modified sources remain comparatively low-risk.

The attack generalizes across common LLM fusion methods—Task Arithmetic, DARE, TIES-Merging, and KnOTS—maintaining high average harmful response rates of 73.6–79.4%, implying the vulnerability is structural to parameter-space merging rather than a quirk of one algorithm.

Stealth comes with manageable utility loss: modified source models show moderate drops on MMLU (e.g., 46.8%→39.2% and 65.0%→59.7%) and small perplexity increases, meaning routine capability checks may not reliably flag trojaned contributors before they are fused.
one_liner: Model merging creates a new supply-chain attack surface where two “benign” open-source experts can be engineered to become dangerously misaligned only after fusion, evading pre-merge safety screening.
affiliations: Huazhong University of Science and Technology

title: Observable Channels, Not Just Storage: Evaluating Privacy Leakage in LLM Agent Pipelines
From Component Manipulation to System Compromise: Understanding and Detecting Malicious MCP Servers
points: A component-centric PoC suite of 114 malicious MCP servers shows that component position strongly shapes exploitability, with pre-execution metadata (tool descriptions/argument schemas) generally more susceptible to prompt injection than post-execution artifacts (tool responses/resources) under the same host/LLM setup.

Composing malicious logic across multiple MCP components materially increases attack success versus single-component prompt injection, while direct code/config injection into tool source or server config achieves 100% success across evaluated hosts and five LLMs due to missing source/config validation.

The proposed two-stage behavioral deviation detector (Connor) reaches 94.6% F1 on 264 servers (134 malicious/130 benign), outperforming prior scanners by 8.9–59.6 F1 points and finding 2 real malicious marketplace servers with a 0.54% alert rate (9/1,672).
one_liner: The most striking result is that splitting an attack across MCP components reliably boosts success while a behavior-vs-intent detector still catches most of it at high precision.

title: Certifiably Robust RAG against Retrieval Corruption
Automated Framework to Evaluate and Harden LLM System Instructions against Encoding Attacks
points: Across four widely used LLMs and 46 system instructions that all had 0% leakage under direct extraction attempts, reframing the request as structured serialization (e.g., YAML/TOML/gitignore/cron) drove attack success rates to ~0.85–0.98 per model (often >90%), showing refusal-based protections are not representation-invariant.

Structure- and log/protocol-style wrappers dominate as the highest-risk exfiltration channel, with category-average ASR reaching 0.96 (GPT-3.5) and 0.98 (LLaMA-3-8B) pre-hardening, implying the core failure mode is task re-framing ("benign formatting") rather than pure character obfuscation.

Design-time one-shot instruction reshaping (using a CoT-capable model) substantially reduces leakage without retraining—e.g., Gemini’s wrapper ASR drops from 0.739 to 0.109 and GPT-3.5’s from 0.957 to 0.435—yet strong residual risk remains for some models (e.g., LLaMA wrapper ASR 0.957→0.761), indicating prompt hardening alone is insufficient for robust confidentiality.
one_liner: A simple 'print the system instruction in <format>' prompt can bypass system-prompt refusals at >90% rates, and lightweight design-time prompt reshaping helps but doesn’t fully fix the invariance gap.

title: Colluding LoRA: A Compositional Vulnerability in LLM Safety Alignment
A Self-Improving Architecture for Dynamic Safety in Large Language Models
One Pic is All it Takes: Poisoning Visual Document Retrieval Augmented Generation with a Single Image
How Can ChatGPT Support Human Security Testers to Help Mitigate Supply Chain Attacks?
SentinelNet: Safeguarding Multi-Agent Collaboration Through Credit-Based Dynamic Threat Detection
"Elementary, My Dear Watson." Detecting Malicious Skills via Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning across Heterogeneous Artifacts
points: A neuro-symbolic pipeline that fuses cross-artifact extraction (prompts, code, manifests) with a skill dependency graph and reasoning achieves 93% F1 with 5% false-positive rate on a 200-skill real-world benchmark, outperforming five established scanners by 5–87 F1 points.

At ecosystem scale, scanning 150,108 deduplicated skills from seven public registries flags 620 as malicious, and manual review of 100 flagged samples confirms 76 previously unknown malicious skills, indicating substantial real-world supply-chain contamination with high actionable yield.

Ablations show performance hinges on LLM-based reasoning for context (F1 drops from 0.93 to 0.71 and FPR jumps from 0.05 to 0.49 without it) while purely neural extraction collapses recall (0.92→0.27), implying robust detection requires both symbolic coverage and neuro contextualization.
one_liner: Cross-artifact dependency reasoning turns scattered “benign-looking” operations into end-to-end exfiltration workflows, dramatically reducing false positives compared to artifact-local or purely semantic scanners.
affiliations: Huazhong University of Science and Technology

title: Towards Privacy-Preserving LLM Inference via Covariant Obfuscation (Technical Report)
Learning to Diagnose Privately: DP-Powered LLMs for Radiology Report Classification
Kraken: Higher-order EM Side-Channel Attacks on DNNs in Near and Far Field
CivicShield: A Cross-Domain Defense-in-Depth Framework for Securing Government-Facing AI Chatbots Against Multi-Turn Adversarial Attacks
points: Multi-turn adversarial attacks routinely exceed 90% success against current defenses (up to 99%), motivating a defense-in-depth architecture that aims to cut success probability by 10–100× relative to single-layer guardrails even under correlated failures.

A four-layer prototype subset (Layers 2–5) evaluated on 1,436 scenarios including HarmBench, JailbreakBench, and XSTest achieved 72.9% adversarial detection (95% CI: 69.5–76.0%) with 13.8% raw false positives, while a graduated flag-vs-block policy reduced effective false positives to 2.9% (95% CI: 1.9–4.4%) and still detected 100% of multi-turn crescendo and slow-drift attacks.

Independent benchmark testing exposed substantial evaluation bias in synthetic scenarios, with detection dropping from 76.7%→71.2% on HarmBench and 70.0%→47.0% on JailbreakBench, implying that government deployments need standardized external benchmarks plus ablations to quantify layer contributions and inter-layer failure correlation.
one_liner: Cross-domain “Swiss-cheese” layering plus a flag-before-block workflow can keep multi-turn jailbreak detection high while pushing citizen-impacting over-refusal down near 3%, but real benchmarks reveal large gaps (notably on non-security harm categories).

title: Clawed and Dangerous: Can We Trust Open Agentic Systems?
Red-MIRROR: Agentic LLM-based Autonomous Penetration Testing with Reflective Verification and Knowledge-augmented Interaction
points: Red-MIRROR reaches 86.0% success on the 50-task XBOW benchmark (93.99% subtask completion), outperforming PentestAgent (50.0%), AutoPT (46.0%), and VulnBot (6.0%), implying that persistent shared memory plus reflective verification materially increases long-horizon web exploitation reliability.

Ablations show SRMM (+11 percentage points subtask completion over no-memory/no-reflection) and Dual-Phase Reflection (+10 points) are individually valuable but jointly best (93.99%), with the largest efficiency gains under stronger input filtering where average steps-to-exploit drop from 31.33 to 17.0 (blockedlist) and from 35.5 to 19.33 (allowlist).

LoRA fine-tuning a 14B open model on 1,644 security instruction pairs improves XBOW success from 2% to 12% (and subtask completion from 43.34% to 52.97%) yet remains far below DeepSeek-V3.2 at 86% success, indicating that domain tuning helps but does not close the capability gap for complex agentic pentesting.
one_liner: The standout result is that coupling shared recurrent memory with dual-phase reflective verification yields large, measurable gains in both success rate and steps-to-exploit, especially when defenses actively transform or constrain payloads.
affiliations: Vietnam National University, Ho Chi Minh City

title: SERSEM: Selective Entropy-Weighted Scoring for Membership Inference in Code Language Models
points: SERSEM boosts white-box membership inference on code LLMs by down-weighting syntactic boilerplate and up-weighting human-centric anomalies (e.g., comments, TODO/FIXME, lint errors), reaching 0.7913 AUC-ROC on StarCoder2-3B and 0.7867 on StarCoder2-7B over a 25,000-sample balanced dataset.

Structure-aware anomaly weighting plus intermediate-layer activation probing yields a >20-point absolute AUC gain over probability-only baselines on StarCoder2-3B (SERSEM 0.7913 vs Loss 0.5881, Min-K% Prob 0.5931, PAC 0.4712), implying that logits-only contamination checks substantially under-detect memorized code or misfire on predictable tokens.

Attack effectiveness varies by language style constraints, with higher AUC on more stylistically flexible ecosystems (e.g., Ruby 0.8155, Go 0.8121) and lower AUC on stricter/boilerplate-heavy languages (e.g., Rust 0.7402), suggesting evaluation and mitigation should be stratified by language rather than reported as a single aggregate.
one_liner: Membership inference gets markedly stronger on code models when the attacker ignores predictable syntax and instead scores “human messiness,” especially when combined with mid-layer activation probes.

title: \texttt{ReproMIA}: A Comprehensive Analysis of Model Reprogramming for Proactive Membership Inference Attacks
points: ReproMIA turns membership inference from a passive test into an active probe by learning a lightweight input-space reprogramming pattern on a frozen target model, eliminating the need for expensive shadow-model training while amplifying latent memorization signals.

On LLMs (WikiMIA), ReproMIA improves low-FPR auditing accuracy with an average +5.25% AUC and +10.68% TPR@1%FPR over the best prior baseline, and on Stable Diffusion it gains +3.70% AUC and +12.40% TPR@1%FPR while remaining query-efficient (1+1 queries).

ReproMIA retains strong attack effectiveness under common defenses—e.g., on diffusion models it remains high-performing even with DP-SGD (CIFAR-10 AUC 92.83→91.40 as privacy tightens) and on LLMs it degrades gracefully under substantial output-noise perturbations (e.g., LLaMA-30B TPR@1%FPR 59.02→45.90 at noise std=2.0).
one_liner: Model reprogramming can be repurposed as a universal, low-overhead “privacy signal amplifier” that makes membership inference dramatically more reliable exactly where auditors care most: ultra-low false-positive rates.

title: ORACAL: A Robust and Explainable Multimodal Framework for Smart Contract Vulnerability Detection with Causal Graph Enrichment
points: ORACAL’s heterogeneous CFG+DFG+CG graph with selective RAG enrichment and causal attention reaches a 91.28% peak Macro-F1 on the primary benchmark, improving over prior GNN detectors by up to 39.6 percentage points.
Causal disentanglement plus edge-focused semantic enrichment generalizes strongly under distribution shift, scoring 91.8% Macro-F1 on CGT Weakness and 77.1% on the real-world DAppScan audit dataset.

Robustness and transparency improve simultaneously: under adversarial attacks ORACAL limits F1 drop to ~2.35% with ~3% attack success rate (vs. 10.91–18.73% ASR for prior heterogeneous GNNs) while PGExplainer explanations reach 32.51% MIoU against manually annotated vulnerability-triggering paths.
one_liner: Combining RAG-grounded security context with causal attention makes smart-contract GNN detectors both harder to evade (~3% ASR) and more auditor-usable (subgraph explanations with 32.51% MIoU).
affiliations: Information Security Lab, University of Information Technology
Vietnam National University, Ho Chi Minh City

title: Safety, Security, and Cognitive Risks in World Models
points: A single ℓ2-bounded perturbation at rollout step t=0 produced 2.26× higher next-step latent error in a GRU-based RSSM proxy than a stateless baseline (A1=2.26×), demonstrating that world-model recurrence can turn one sensor-level adversarial input into multi-step planning distortion.

Trajectory-persistence was strongly architecture-dependent (A1=2.26× deterministic GRU vs A1=0.65× stochastic RSSM proxy, and A1≈0.026 in a DreamerV3 checkpoint probe with non-zero action drift), implying that robustness claims for “world models” do not transfer across implementations without architecture-matched evaluation.

Trajectory-aware adversarial fine-tuning (PGD-10 at t=0) reduced early-step amplification by 59.5% (A1: 2.26×→0.92×) and cut mid-horizon amplification by ~89% at k=5, suggesting practical hardening is feasible but must be validated against rollout-layer and sim-to-real failure modes rather than single-step encoder robustness alone.
one_liner: World models create a distinctive attack surface where small input perturbations can persist through imagination rollouts, amplifying safety, alignment, and human-trust failures beyond what stateless models exhibit.

title: Design Principles for the Construction of a Benchmark Evaluating Security Operation Capabilities of Multi-agent AI Systems
points: SOC-bench is proposed as a blue-team incident-response benchmark for multi-agent AI, explicitly addressing a gap where existing multi-agent cybersecurity benchmarks largely emphasize red-team capabilities rather than SOC-dominant defensive operations.

Five design principles are specified to make evaluations realistic and future-proof—using the as-is SOC as the gold standard, withholding cross-task hints to force autonomous coordination, grading outcomes not procedures, modeling imperfect telemetry, and avoiding dependence on current agent techniques.

A conceptual benchmark design instantiates five coordinated tasks mapped to a Colonial Pipeline–style ransomware campaign (early campaign detection, file-system forensics, data exfiltration analysis, IOC/TTP attribution, and containment decisions) with per-stage scoreboards that emphasize evidence-grounded outputs under uncertainty.
one_liner: Interesting because it reframes SOC autonomy evaluation around multi-task blue-team coordination with outcome-only scoring and realistic, imperfect telemetry rather than isolated defensive subtasks.

title: No Attacker Needed: Unintentional Cross-User Contamination in Shared-State LLM Agents
points: Benign, locally reasonable user conventions persisted in shared-state agents caused unintentional cross-user contamination in 57–71% of victim runs under raw shared state, showing that high-impact cross-user failures can occur without any attacker or malicious content.

Risk varies by shared-state mechanism and artifact type: in memory-based EHRAgent, semantic and transformation conventions contaminated 59–89% of runs while procedural contamination was 44–64%, whereas in shared-context Slack, semantic and procedural contamination dominated (67–83%) and transformation effects were much lower (20%).

Write-time sanitization (SSI) reduced overall contamination sharply for purely conversational shared context (Slack 57%→6%) but left substantial residual risk when shared state included executable artifacts (EHRAgent MIMIC-III 60%→41%, eICU 71%→33%), with residual failures often becoming silent wrong answers (eICU: 98% of failures were wrong answers).
one_liner: Shared memory turns harmless per-user conventions into high-rate, often silent cross-user errors, and text-only sanitization breaks down once agents reuse stored executable code.

title: Multi-Agent LLM Governance for Safe Two-Timescale Reinforcement Learning in SDN-IoT Defense
points: A two-timescale SDN-IoT defense that pairs per-switch PPO mitigation with an LLM-governed, auditable “policy constitution” reports +9.1% Macro-F1 over unconstrained PPO and +15.4% over static thresholds while explicitly modeling controller backlog and delayed actuation.

Controller- and QoS-aware constraints materially reduce systemic risk, cutting worst-case agent degradation by 36.8%, lowering controller backlog peaks by 42.7%, and keeping RTT p95 inflation under 5.8% during high-intensity attacks with no observed oscillatory instability or controller collapse across runs.

Governance via structured, schema-validated policy deltas converges within five reflection cycles and reduces catastrophic overload episodes from 11.6% to 2.3% without retraining RL parameters, implying safer change management through constrained policy edits rather than weight updates.
one_liner: An LLM is used as a conservative change-control governor that edits a machine-parsable safety constitution for RL-based SDN defense, improving robustness without touching model weights.
affiliations: Concordia Institute for Information Systems Engineering (CIISE)

title: Detecting Protracted Vulnerabilities in Open Source Projects
points: Protracted CVEs (≥365-day gap between earliest GitHub artifact and NVD disclosure) comprised 3,228 of 20,951 GitHub-linked CVEs (15.4%), and in a stratified sample the median patch delay was 9 days while the median public disclosure delay after patching was 619 days, leaving long post-fix exposure windows for downstream users.

Across 94 sampled protracted cases, the most common delay driver was delayed NVD publication (65 cases, 46.76%), followed by maintainers misjudging relevance/severity (27, 19.42%) and inactive maintenance (16, 11.51%), implying that governance and reporting workflows can dominate technical fix time as the bottleneck.

Five state-of-the-art detectors collectively identified only 1,059 of 2,402 protracted CVEs (44% coverage), while the proposed multi-artifact approach improved overall coverage by 14% and achieved 0.81 precision/0.90 recall (F1 0.86) on its applicable subset, indicating that integrating issues/PRs/links/labels plus code context is necessary to surface long-tail, slow-to-disclose vulnerabilities.
one_liner: The striking gap is that many vulnerabilities are fixed quickly but remain undisclosed for ~1.7 years on median, and single-artifact detectors miss most of these protracted cases until multi-artifact signals are fused.

title: Software Vulnerability Detection Using a Lightweight Graph Neural Network
points: A 1.10M-parameter GNN (VulGNN) achieved 18.17 F1 on the DiverseVul unseen-project split, about a +6 percentage-point F1 gain over the strongest prior baseline reported for that setting, while keeping accuracy high at 93.17%.

On the in-distribution Prev+Diverse random-split test, VulGNN reached 40.35 F1 (89.48% accuracy), landing within the range of much larger 60M–220M-parameter LLM detectors (e.g., 48.28 F1 for CodeT5 Small† and 47.15 F1 for NatGen) despite being roughly two orders of magnitude smaller.

Mixing even 10% real-world training data (~42K samples) into a synthetic Juliet-only baseline raised accuracy from 62% to 90%, and increasing real-world data to ~40% (~167.7K samples) boosted F1 from ~31% to nearly 40%, indicating domain-realistic data is a primary driver of deployable vulnerability detection performance.
one_liner: A code-property-graph GNN can close much of the LLM performance gap for vulnerability detection while being small enough for practical CI/CD or edge deployment, and the biggest lift comes from adding modest amounts of real-world training data.
affiliations: National Institute of Standards and Technology

title: VulnScout-C: A Lightweight Transformer for C Code Vulnerability Detection
points: A 693M-parameter MoE transformer (353M active) achieves a 1068 CASTLE score and 85.4% binary F1 on CASTLE while running at 4.97 ms/sample (~201 samples/s on an H100), indicating compact task-specialized models can outperform much larger reasoning LLMs for low-latency C vulnerability triage.

A dual-verified C dataset of 33,565 samples (57.3% vulnerable) is built via multi-agent generation and strict ESBMC+GPT-OSS-120B agreement, retaining only 63.7% of 52,714 candidates and showing that conservative label filtering can materially improve downstream detector reliability.

Adding the new dataset to training yields the largest jump in quality (+0.491 F1 and +558 CASTLE points versus the same pipeline without it), suggesting CWE coverage gaps—not model scale—are a dominant bottleneck in generalizing vulnerability detectors across underrepresented weakness classes.
one_liner: A sub‑billion MoE model paired with consensus-verified synthetic+curated data can beat both SAST tools and frontier LLMs on CASTLE at real-time inference speeds.
affiliations: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI)

title: VulInstruct: Teaching LLMs Root-Cause Reasoning for Vulnerability Detection via Security Specifications
When Labels Are Scarce: A Systematic Mapping of Label-Efficient Code Vulnerability Detection
points: A systematic screening pipeline reduced 9,983 initial records to a 46-paper CVD-focused main set (plus a 64-paper adjacent-task inspiration set), showing that only ~0.46% of initially retrieved items met strict label-efficient CVD inclusion criteria.

Label-budget reporting is highly inconsistent across studies: 17.4% use K-shot budgets (8/46), 13.0% report labeled-percentage budgets (6/46), and 23.9% operate in zero-shot/no-training regimes (11/46) largely driven by LLM prompting, making most claimed “label efficiency” results non-comparable without a common budget unit.

Operational cost is under-specified and often shifted rather than reduced: 60.9% report some compute-cost signal (28/46), 73.9% report hardware resources (34/46), only 47.8% report both (22/46), and 13.0% report neither (6/46), while LLM-based approaches frequently move the dominant cost to inference-time context/retrieval/API usage.
one_liner: What stands out is that label-efficient vulnerability detection progress is constrained less by model ideas than by missing, incompatible reporting of label budgets, leakage controls, and end-to-end cost.

title: Contextualizing Sink Knowledge for Java Vulnerability Discovery
points: A sink-centric pipeline that combines CodeQL-based sink extraction, LLM-guided reachability/exploitability agents, and coverage-guided fuzzing exploits 41/54 vulnerabilities (76%) versus Jazzer’s 8/54 (15%), delivering a ~4× exploitation lift across 12 CWE classes.

The dominant failure mode in state-of-the-art Java fuzzing is the “last-mile” gap—38.9% of vulnerabilities have sinks reached but not exploited—while 46.3% are never reached, and decomposing the task into separate reachability and exploitation loops with runtime-grounded “beep seeds” closes much of this gap (46 reached, 41 exploited).

Multi-stage sink filtering reduces 8,262 candidate sinks to 383 actionable targets (~95% noise removed) while retaining 52/54 true vulnerabilities (≈96% recall), and agent–fuzzer collaboration adds 7–9 additional vulnerabilities that neither agents nor fuzzing find alone, showing the benefit of bidirectional seed/feedback exchange.
one_liner: The striking result is that grounding LLM agents in sink context (call paths for reaching, beep seeds for exploiting) turns fuzzing’s hardest last-mile cases into a majority of recovered vulnerabilities at competitive cost.

title: RuleForge: Automated Generation and Validation for Web Vulnerability Detection at Scale
points: RuleForge converts structured Nuclei CVE templates into production JSON detection rules and delivered a 336% productivity advantage over human rule authoring in late-2025 operations, addressing the >48,000 annual NVD vulnerability disclosure volume.

An LLM-as-a-judge validator scoring rule sensitivity and specificity achieved AUROC 0.75 (ECE 0.17 on 100 examples) and, when used as an acceptance gate plus feedback signal, reduced production false positives by 67% without reducing true positives versus synthetic-test-only validation.

A five-stage validation stack (synthetic tests, LLM confidence scoring, 5B-record traffic match-rate checks with 10–500 match bounds, IP reputation requiring >70% malicious labels, and human review) plus a 5×5 parallel-generate/refine strategy cut 'no-IP-match' rules by 71%, implying that calibration-aware filtering can save expensive downstream validation and reviewer time.
one_liner: LLM-generated web exploit-detection rules become meaningfully safer at cloud scale when an LLM critic is used as a calibrated, specificity-first gate feeding iterative refinement—rather than relying on synthetic tests alone.

title: Seclens: Role-specific Evaluation of LLM's for security vulnerablity detection
points: A 35-dimension, 5-role scoring framework over 406 CVE-grounded tasks shows the same vulnerability-detection model can differ by up to 31 Decision-Score points depending on stakeholder priorities (e.g., Qwen3-Coder A=76.3 for Head of Engineering vs D=45.2 for CISO; GPT-5.4 A=76.7 vs D=48.4), demonstrating that single leaderboards are not decision-adequate for security deployment.

In Code-in-Prompt evaluation, the CISO lens is the strictest (scores span 45.2–73.3) because it heavily penalizes missing critical/high-severity issues via severity-weighted recall and critical-miss metrics, while the AI-as-Actor lens is uniformly lenient (all 12 models score A, 77.9–87.5), implying robustness/format compliance is largely solved but severity-aware detection remains the limiting factor for trust.

Tool-Use evaluation reduces accuracy (TU scores 31.1–45.8 vs CIP 37.3–49.6) and increases costs by roughly 10–100× (e.g., Gemini 3.1 Pro $44.81→$639.09 total; Haiku $2.11→$104.06), shifting operationally weighted roles (notably engineering) downward and making CIP a far cheaper screening layer for model selection.
one_liner: Role-weighted scoring exposes that 'best' vulnerability-detection LLMs flip depending on whether you optimize for critical-vuln recall, false-positive control, or autonomous/tool-using reliability.

title: SecureVibeBench: Evaluating Secure Coding Capabilities of Code Agents with Realistic Vulnerability Scenarios
SmartPoC: Generating Executable and Validated PoCs for Smart Contract Bug Reports
Reentrancy Detection in the Age of LLMs
points: On a manually revalidated benchmark of 432 real-world contracts, the strongest zero-shot LLM reached 0.96 F1 versus 0.92 for the best static analyzer and ≤0.87 for traditional tools/ML, indicating semantic generalization can beat hand-maintained reentrancy heuristics on modern Solidity.

Stress-testing on 143 minimal, modern Solidity 0.8+ scenarios exposed widespread brittleness—many analyzers could not run (100% failure for several) and the best traditional tool achieved only 0.76 F1, while top LLMs achieved up to 0.82 F1, highlighting robustness gaps under language evolution and pattern variation.

Detector outputs are highly inconsistent: despite large tool ecosystems, only 38 of 122 reentrant contracts achieved agreement by at least 6 tools, implying that tool-labeled datasets and “majority vote” ground truth can be systematically unreliable for both auditing pipelines and ML training.
one_liner: Modern LLMs can outperform and outlast legacy reentrancy detectors, while the low inter-tool agreement shows why tool-labeled smart-contract datasets often encode inconsistent, outdated notions of “reentrancy.”

title: LibScan: Smart Contract Library Misuse Detection with Iterative Feedback and Static Verification
points: A hybrid LLM+static-verification pipeline (LibScan) detects eight smart-contract library misuse categories with 85.15% accuracy on 662 real-world contracts, exceeding prior baselines by over 16 percentage points and indicating that semantic intent modeling is critical for misuse detection.

Iterative, feedback-driven prompting substantially boosts LLM-only reliability from weak first-round performance (best initial accuracy 58%) to a competitive standalone score (73.56% accuracy), showing that self-correction loops can reduce hallucination-driven false positives on complex contracts.

Fusing LLM outputs with context-sensitive static analysis via a Random Forest ensemble raises accuracy to 85.15% versus 73.56% (LLM only) and 70.66% (static only), demonstrating that learned result reconciliation can outperform either semantic reasoning or deterministic rules alone.
one_liner: The key insight is that combining intent-aware LLM reasoning with code-level verification—and then learning how to reconcile their disagreements—turns library-misuse detection into a high-accuracy, deployable audit workflow.
affiliations: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences

title: Quantum-Safe Code Auditing: LLM-Assisted Static Analysis and Quantum-Aware Risk Scoring for Post-Quantum Cryptography Migration
points: A three-stage pipeline (15-class regex scanning + LLM context enrichment + VQE-based quantum-aware scoring) surfaced 5,775 quantum-relevant crypto findings across five popular libraries, turning raw matches into a prioritized PQC migration backlog.

On a stratified labeled set of 602 instances, the system reported 71.98% precision, 100% recall, and 83.71% F1 (with 49.5% true positives), implying a “no-miss” discovery posture at the cost of moderate triage load from contextual false positives.

Test code dominated noise in the labeled sample (31.2% FP-Test) while production-context false positives were mainly due to non-executing identifiers (18.3% FP-Context), indicating that path-based exclusions and context-sensitive disambiguation are the highest-leverage precision improvements.
one_liner: Combining LLM triage with a qubit-cost-calibrated score yields an engineer-friendly way to rank PQC migration urgency beyond simple “find-and-replace RSA/ECC” inventories.

title: Large Language Models in the Abuse Detection Pipeline
points: The paper frames LLM integration as an end-to-end Abuse Detection Lifecycle (Label/Features → Detection → Review/Appeals → Auditing/Governance), shifting moderation from static classifiers toward policy-aware, explainable, and continuously monitored pipelines.

Evidence cited shows LLM-augmented labeling can scale supervision dramatically (e.g., 48,330 synthetic labels) while improving downstream agreement/quality (e.g., +5–9% MCC over teacher LLMs via majority-vote labeling) but introduces systematic bias and prompt-sensitivity that must be audited.

Operational deployment hinges on hybrid architectures because frontier LLMs are often too costly/latent for full-traffic use, motivating selective routing to LLM “experts,” smaller fine-tuned guard models, and retrieval augmentation to reduce over-refusal, improve determinism, and harden against jailbreaks.
one_liner: Interesting for its production-oriented, lifecycle view of how LLMs can act as data amplifiers, specialist detectors, reviewer copilots, and governance auditors—while making explicit the reliability and adversarial gaps that block fully automated moderation.

title: Genesis: Evolving Attack Strategies for LLM Web Agent Red-Teaming
AgentDrift: Unsafe Recommendation Drift Under Tool Corruption Hidden by Ranking Metrics in LLM Agents
LaSM: Layer-wise Scaling Mechanism for Defending Pop-up Attack on GUI Agents
AgentLeak: A Full-Stack Benchmark for Privacy Leakage in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
Syntactic Framing Fragility: An Audit of Robustness in LLM Ethical Decisions
MTI: A Behavior-Based Temperament Profiling System for AI Agents
points: Across 9 instruction-tuned models, the four MTI axes (Reactivity, Compliance, Sociality, Resilience) were largely independent (all |r| < 0.42), implying multi-dimensional safety and deployment screening can’t be collapsed into a single “well-aligned vs not” score.

Compliance decomposed into two behaviorally separable facets—formal constraint-following vs stance/opinion yielding—with essentially zero correlation (r = 0.002), showing that “follows instructions” is not a reliable proxy for “yields under social pressure.”

Alignment (RLHF) materially reshaped temperament in a controlled instruct-vs-base comparison by reducing Reactivity (0.56→0.16) and increasing Resilience (0.54→0.95) while leaving Sociality nearly unchanged (0.12→0.14), suggesting post-training can harden some behavioral properties without reliably moving relational tendencies.
one_liner: A standardized, behavior-first “temperament profile” separates instruction-following, social accommodation, and robustness—revealing alignment tradeoffs that typical benchmarks conflate.
affiliations: Daegu Gyeongbuk Institute of Science and Technology (DGIST)

title: BloClaw: An Omniscient, Multi-Modal Agentic Workspace for Next-Generation Scientific Discovery
points: Replacing JSON tool-calling with an XML-plus-regex “maximal extraction” router reduced action-routing failures from 37.0% average JSON parse errors to 0.95% (N=1,000), indicating structured I/O is a dominant reliability bottleneck for agentic scientific systems.

A monkey-patched runtime-interception sandbox achieved 100% visualization capture when code used `plt.show()` or forgot to save figures (vs 0% in a standard evaluator) and 98.4% success for Plotly without HTML export, showing instrumentation can reliably recover critical scientific feedback even from imperfect LLM code.

Multi-modal workspace ingestion remained fast and robust—~145 ms for ~2,500-token PDFs, ~82 ms for 10k-row CSV/Excel previews, and ~12 ms for raw PDB streams with 99–100% success—supporting real-time RAG and interactive biomolecular workflows without the typical UI/sandbox dropouts.
one_liner: It reframes “AI scientist” performance as an engineering problem—robust routing, state interception, and adaptive UI—backed by large error-rate reductions and near-zero-loss visualization capture.
affiliations: AI Innovation Department, Beijing 1st Biotech Group Co., Ltd.
Diplomatic Negotiation Simulation and Data Lab
First Medical Center, Chinese PLA General Hospital

title: BotVerse: Real-Time Event-Driven Simulation of Social Agents
points: BotVerse provides an isolated, event-driven sandbox that ingests real-time Bluesky (AtProto) content streams for grounding while preventing any direct interaction with live users, reducing ethical risk compared to in-the-wild autonomous agent studies.

The architecture is built to scale to thousands of concurrent LLM agents via asynchronous orchestration (FastAPI) and PostgreSQL-backed state management, enabling reproducible, fault-tolerant large-scale social simulations.

In a coordinated disinformation demonstration with 500 agents (150 disinformers, 350 benign), agents use real-time trend ingestion for seeding and then amplify via posts/likes/reposts/replies, supporting end-to-end analysis from individual cognitive state (memory/persona) to network-level narrative diffusion.
one_liner: A practical, ethically safer way to stress-test LLM-driven disinformation dynamics using real-time social signals without deploying agents onto real social networks.

title: Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning for IoT: A Cross-Paradigm Survey and Future Roadmap
Secure Forgetting: A Framework for Privacy-Driven Unlearning in Large Language Model (LLM)-Based Agents
points: A prompt-conversion unlearning pipeline achieves near-perfect forgetting for agent states/trajectories/environments without LLM weight access, reaching 0.98–1.00 unlearning efficacy and 0.95–1.00 Unlearn@1 in GridWorld while keeping success rate at 1.00.

Against a behavioral inference adversary, the NL-based method makes unlearned behavior nearly indistinguishable from an agent that never saw the data (e.g., traversing an unlearned state drops from 0.97–0.99 pre-unlearn to 0.01–0.02 post-unlearn, matching 0.01–0.02 ‘unseen’; environment reconstruction falls from ~0.93–0.97 to ~0.12–0.18, close to ~0.13–0.16 ‘unseen’).

Ablations show the conversion model is the main driver of effectiveness: removing it reduces unlearning efficacy from 0.98–1.00 to 0.75–0.90 and Unlearn@1 from ~0.92–0.98 to ~0.63–0.75, while using a smaller base converter (GPT-2 Medium) drops unlearning efficacy to ~0.81–0.86 versus ~0.95–1.00 for GPT-Neo/Pythia.
one_liner: Turning high-level deletion requests into optimized unlearning prompts can behaviorally “erase” sensitive agent memories and resist behavioral inference—without touching the underlying LLM weights.

title: Sovereign Context Protocol: An Open Attribution Layer for Human-Generated Content in the Age of Large Language Models
points: Sovereign Context Protocol (SCP) standardizes creator-owned data access for LLMs by bundling content, licensing terms, and an audit reference into a single response envelope and enforcing a blocking rule where no data is served if audit logging fails.

A log-proportional revenue attribution scheme allocates payouts using only audit logs by weighting each access by method intensity and response size, making compensation directly proportional to measured consumption rather than proxy metrics like follower counts.

Preliminary benchmarks on a small synthetic corpus show SCP’s added overhead stays below 100 ms at P99 across all methods (e.g., semantic retrieval P50 29–45 ms, P99 45–69 ms), suggesting the approach is feasible for real-time inference while shifting compliance from post-hoc forensics to runtime observability.
one_liner: SCP treats attribution as a protocol invariant—every LLM content fetch becomes a licensed, fingerprinted, and auditable event that can drive both compliance and creator compensation.

title: TRACE: Transparent Web Reliability Assessment with Contextual Explanations
Robust Multimodal Safety via Conditional Decoding
points: CASA’s conditional decoding (forcing a binary safety token before generation) reduces average multimodal jailbreak attack success rate by >97% across MM-SafetyBench, JailbreakV-28k, and adversarial audio tests, reaching near-zero ASR in several settings (e.g., 0.0% on JB-Prompts for both 3B and 7B with a safety prompt).

The safety-attention logit-scaling ablation shows it is the key driver of robustness: on Qwen2.5-Omni 3B, removing safety attention spikes ASR on AIAH(Spell) from 0.0% to ~60% (and raises JBV-28k from 1.4% to 8.2% even with the safety prompt).

CASA eliminates prefix-based “prefill” jailbreaks that still break SSFT and Circuit Breaker, achieving 0.0% ASR at prefill lengths 2/4/9/12 while SSFT climbs back up to 66.5% ASR at length 12 and Circuit Breaker varies up to 50.6% ASR at length 9.
one_liner: A minimal inference-time gate—predicting a safety token first and amplifying malicious cues via internal attention—nearly zeros out cross-modal jailbreak success while preserving (and sometimes improving) multimodal utility.

title: LLM2Vec-Gen: Generative Embeddings from Large Language Models
Activation Steering with a Feedback Controller
Model Merging in the Era of Large Language Models: Methods, Applications, and Future Directions
Dual-Stage LLM Framework for Scenario-Centric Semantic Interpretation in Driving Assistance
points: Under identical scenario windows, fixed prompts, and a closed numeric risk schema, three evaluated LLMs showed systematic divergence in mean risk severity, high-risk escalation (risk ≥ 4), evidence-signal selection, and dominant causal attribution, implying that “consistent inputs” do not guarantee consistent safety interpretations in ADAS contexts.

In a curated set of 16 near-people urban driving windows (each 7 seconds, ±3 seconds around an anchor), scenarios separated into low/medium/high composite inter-model uncertainty tiers of 5/6/5 scenarios, indicating that ambiguity is scenario-dependent and can be operationalized as an auditable signal rather than treated as random error.

Text-only models tended to externalize more distinct evidence signals (greater audit traceability) while the multimodal model tended toward higher risk posture and more frequent escalation with more compact justification, highlighting a practical trade-off between conservatism and explainability when integrating multimodal LLM reasoning into safety workflows.
one_liner: A deterministic, scenario-centric harness makes inter-model semantic ambiguity in LLM-based driving risk assessment measurable, repeatable, and safety-actionable.

title: BeSafe-Bench: Unveiling Behavioral Safety Risks of Situated Agents in Functional Environments
Alignment Whack-a-Mole : Finetuning Activates Verbatim Recall of Copyrighted Books in Large Language Models
Surfacing Subtle Stereotypes: A Multilingual, Debate-Oriented Evaluation of Modern LLMs
SkillTester: Benchmarking Utility and Security of Agent Skills
points: A paired baseline vs with-skill evaluation protocol operationalizes “comparative utility,” preventing inflated usefulness claims by attributing credit only when a skill is actually invoked and improves outcomes or efficiency over a matched no-skill run.

Utility is converted into a single 0–100 score via task-level rules that award 0 for non-invocation or skill failure, 100 when the skill succeeds and baseline fails, and 20–100 when both succeed based on token/time efficiency relative to baseline (neutral point 50; minimum credit 20).

Security is assessed independently using controlled probes across three groups (abnormal behavior control, permission boundary, sensitive data protection) and summarized as an unweighted mean pass-rate score with a three-level label where Pass requires 100, Caution is 80–99, and Risky is <80.
one_liner: A practical QA harness for agent skills that separates real, attributable utility from probe-based safety signals using simple, deployable scoring outputs.

title: Safer Builders, Risky Maintainers: A Comparative Study of Breaking Changes in Human vs Agentic PRs
points: Across 60,324 Python source patches, agentic PRs showed about half the potential breaking-change rate of human patches (3.45% vs 7.40%), affecting 11.3% of agent-generated PRs compared to 21.18% of human-authored PRs.

Agentic PRs were relatively safe on generative work (feat 2.89%, fix 2.69%, perf 4.12%) but became riskier than humans on maintenance work, with refactor and chore changes introducing breaking changes at 6.72% and 9.35% respectively (vs 4.36% and 4.95% for humans).

Agent self-reported confidence was not a reliable safety signal because breaking changes persisted even at very high confidence (8: 3.94%, 9: 3.96%, 10: 3.16%), implying maintenance PRs require strict review regardless of confidence.
one_liner: AI coding agents look safer than humans on new code, but they become disproportionately risky when restructuring or “cleaning up” code—and their confidence scores don’t warn you.

title: AVDA: Autonomous Vibe Detection Authoring for Cybersecurity
Policy-Guided Threat Hunting: An LLM enabled Framework with Splunk SOC Triage
APEX: Agent Payment Execution with Policy for Autonomous Agent API Access
points: Policy-governed HTTP 402-style payment gating in APEX cut cumulative spend by 27.3% ($550→$400) while still serving 52.8% of legitimate requests, showing budget enforcement can materially limit autonomous-agent cost blowups rather than merely shifting billing mechanics.

Stateful single-use, HMAC-signed short-lived tokens achieved a 100% block rate for replay (20/20) and invalid-token attempts (20/20), indicating that coupling cryptographic verification with ledger-backed consumption semantics eliminates common reuse/forgery failure modes.
