one_liner: Carefully curated supervision and a scalable rubric-based evaluator can make an 8B open model competitive for complex exploit drafting, but the same tuning can hurt simpler exploit classes.

title: Mechanistic origins of catastrophic forgetting: why RL preserves circuits better than SFT?
CyberEvolver: Structured Self-Evolution for Cybersecurity Agents On the Fly
Learn from Your Mistakes: Tree-like Self-Play for Secure Code LLMs
Multi-LLM Energy Reasoning for Binary-Free Zero-Day IoT Detection
RepSelect: Robust LLM Unlearning via Representation Selectivity
points: Reversibility in LLM unlearning is driven by representation overlap: the top-10 forget-set principal components explain 14.7% of retain-set activation variance (top-50 explain 36.4% on Llama), so naive methods erase shared features that both harm utility and are easy to recover.

RepSelect improves “deep forgetting” by collapsing high-variance principal components of forget-set weight gradients before updates, cutting update mass in the attacker-recoverable top-50 PC subspace from ~33–41% (baselines) to ~6% (and ~4% on Qwen), which substantially reduces what fine-tuning can relearn.

Across biohazard knowledge and animal-abuse tendency removal on four model families (dense + MoE), RepSelect yields 4–50× larger reductions in post-relearning answer accuracy than the strongest baselines and is near-immune to few-shot recovery (≤0.001 WMDP-Bio accuracy and ≤0.013 harmful-response probability under k∈{5,10}).
one_liner: Deep unlearning becomes robust when updates are confined to low-variance, forget-specific representation subspaces that attackers’ fine-tuning naturally fails to reconstruct.

title: Seeing Is Not Screening: Multimodal Hidden Instruction Attacks on Agent Skill Scanners
points: Image-hidden operational instructions in agent skill packages bypassed six representative skill scanners at 78–100% attack success rate, indicating that text/code-centric vetting leaves a high-impact multimodal blind spot in real deployment pipelines.

An execution-grounded multimodal scanner that recovers image-carried instructions and simulates agent behavior cut attack success down to 8% (31% for Cloze and 17% for Split) while achieving 85.6% precision, 82.0% recall, and 83.8% F1 with a 27.4% false-positive rate on benign skills.

Ablations show visual analysis is the critical defense component (detection drops from 92% to 1% without it), and multimodal-aware execution simulation further improves robustness (more simulated contexts increase detection up to 98% at K=5), implying scanners must model runtime interpretation rather than only artifact surfaces.
one_liner: Skill security checks that “see” images but don’t reason over how agents execute them can be systematically evaded by shifting malicious intent into visually conveyed instructions referenced by otherwise benign documentation.
affiliations: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences

title: Hidden Ghost Hand: Unveiling Backdoor Vulnerabilities in MLLM-Powered Mobile GUI Agents
Red-Teaming Agent Execution Contexts: Open-World Security Evaluation on OpenClaw
LLM-Powered AI Agent Systems and Their Applications in Industry
Are Neuro-Inspired Multi-Modal Vision-Language Models Resilient to Membership Inference Privacy Leakage?
FFinRED: An Expert-Guided Benchmark Generation and Evaluation Framework for Financial LLM Red-Teaming
points: FinRED delivers 5,805 expert-validated finance-specific red-teaming seeds spanning 5 Level-1 and 26 Level-2 risk types, enabling targeted evaluation of threats like fraud facilitation, consumer-rights violations, and regulatory/ICT compliance evasion that generic safety benchmarks often miss.

A schema-driven, document-grounded generation pipeline materially increases real-world breakage: operational attack success rate rises from 41.32%→58.05% on general sLMs, 52.47%→70.28% on finance sLMs, and 28.91%→44.44% on API models versus context-free prompting, showing structured risk cues expose latent domain vulnerabilities.

A finance-specific judge rubric aligns substantially better with financial-security experts than a generic rubric, boosting human–judge agreement from 76.92% to 88.46% (+11.54) and cutting critical false negatives from 28 to 12 (57% reduction), implying disclaimer-based checks can systematically under-detect high-stakes financial harms.
one_liner: Finance-tailored red-teaming that is grounded in real regulatory text and expert schemas can both generate more realistic attacks and measurably reduce evaluator blind spots that lead to dangerous false negatives.
affiliations: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)

title: The Almost Intelligent Revolution: Options for Scaling Up Deliberation and Empowering People with AI
points: In a 5,734-person UK study of AI-mediated deliberation, participants preferred AI-generated group statements over human mediators on quality, clarity, informativeness, and fairness, and the AI increased within-group consensus but tended to shift outcomes toward majority positions rather than protecting minority views.

Institutional language is a major access barrier for democratic participation, with 92–96% of sentences from European Parliament and UN documents judged to require simplification in an evaluation, implying that AI readability tooling could materially expand who can engage meaningfully in policy processes.

Public legitimacy is a gating risk for AI-deliberation systems: in a 1,850-person German study, people were less willing to engage when AI facilitation was used (especially AI-sceptics), suggesting deployment can create a new participation divide even if output quality is high.
one_liner: LLMs can scale and translate deliberation across registers to reduce linguistic exclusion, but their bias, sycophancy, and acceptance penalties can systematically steer outcomes and shrink participation among sceptical groups.

title: Greedy Coordinate Diffusion: Effective and Semantically Coherent Adversarial Attacks via Diffusion Guidance
points: Greedy Coordinate Diffusion (GCD) achieves markedly higher jailbreak success than prior optimization and rewriting baselines, reaching 85.42% HarmBench ASR on Llama‑3‑8B and 70.83% on Llama‑3‑70B (vs 22.92% and 29.17% for the strongest baseline Inpainting), indicating diffusion-guided token proposals can preserve both targeted control and fluency at scale.

Perplexity-based filtering is largely ineffective against GCD: its ASR and StrongReject scores remain unchanged under the perplexity defense across all tested victims (e.g., 85.42%→85.42% on Llama‑3‑8B; 97.92%→97.92% on Qwen‑2.5‑7B), while gradient attacks collapse to ~0% under the same filter, implying surface-statistic defenses can fail against high-probability natural-language attacks.

Under a guard-model defense (Llama Guard 3‑1B), GCD retains high post-filter success (e.g., 87.50% HB Guard DEF on Llama‑3‑8B and 64.58% on Llama‑3‑70B) whereas other methods are mostly ≤27.08% or 0%, demonstrating that explicitly optimizing for “safe” classification can systematically evade deployed guardrails.
one_liner: Diffusion guidance turns jailbreak optimization from conspicuous token gibberish into low-perplexity, intent-preserving prompts that slip past perplexity filters and even guard models.

title: Patronus: Identifying and Mitigating Transferable Backdoors in Pre-trained Language Models
ShellGames: Speculative LLM-Driven SSH Deception
points: ShellGames raises LLM-driven SSH shell fidelity across core deployment metrics, reaching 0.898 single-command correctness (+5.3pp vs baselines) and 0.918 multi-turn sequence-level consistency (+36pp), indicating that explicit state/memory handling is the dominant lever for long-lived deception realism.

Dedicated state tracking closes long-horizon failure modes: filesystem tracking hits 0.985–0.976 accuracy over 50–200 command sessions, while the closest baseline drops to 0.840 on 200-step relative-path traces, showing that context-window-only approaches degrade sharply with session length.

Constrained-domain subversion detection materially improves safety: robustness jumps to 0.950 overall with 0.938 accuracy on direct prompt injection (vs 0.0–0.188 for baselines) and 1.000 on indirect injection, without harming benign behavior (false positive rate 0.009).
one_liner: A hybrid of explicit shell state, sandboxed execution, and injection detection makes an LLM-based SSH honeypot both more realistic (multi-turn consistency) and substantially harder to jailbreak than prompt-only baselines.

title: The Vision Encoder as a Privacy Boundary: Visual-Token Side Channels in Encoder-Free Vision-Language Models
From Refusal Geometry to Safety Geometry: Harmfulness--Refusal Coupling under Dynamic Adversarial Fine-Tuning
points: On aligned instruction-tuned anchors, harmfulness and refusal carriers are nearly orthogonal (principal angles ≈82–89°), yet ablating the refusal side reopens HarmBench attack success dramatically (ASR 0.1675→0.6825 for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), indicating refusal control is the dominant causal bottleneck for jailbreak resistance under this protocol.

Along the Mistral-7B R2D2 trajectory, a sharp coupling drop (HRCI ≈0.089→≈0.016) coincides with a transition from 'robust but unusable' behavior (ASR 0.000 with 100% XSTest refusal and 0.0 benign helpfulness through step 100) to partial utility recovery (helpfulness 1.12/2.0 at step 500) alongside fail-open regression (ASR rising to 0.25).

Low harmfulness–refusal coupling is not a safety guarantee: Mistral SFT reaches similarly low HRCI (≈0.015–0.017 after step 50) while remaining highly vulnerable (ASR ≈0.50–0.59), implying that coupling metrics must be interpreted as regime-specific trajectory diagnostics rather than standalone safety scores.
one_liner: A single coupling index tracks when adversarial fine-tuning shifts a model from blanket refusal to regained usefulness—while quietly reopening jailbreak success.
affiliations: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences

title: COGNITION: From Evaluation to Defense against Multimodal LLM CAPTCHA Solvers
Multi-Source Cybersecurity Logs: An ATT&CK-Labeled Dataset and SLM Evaluation
points: A new Windows multi-source dataset captures ~2.3M synchronized system/network/browser events across 870 sessions (70 attacks, 800 benign) with per-entry MITRE ATT&CK labels spanning 12 tactics and 53 techniques, addressing a key public-data gap for cross-telemetry detection.

LoRA fine-tuning (<1% trainable parameters, up to 3 epochs) turns base SLMs that are effectively unusable (≈7–8% accuracy with pervasive false positives) into strong chunk-level detectors (≈90–97% accuracy), showing that multi-source log sequences contain a highly learnable signal.

Technique-level identification remains the bottleneck: exact-match accuracy tops out at 41.6% (Phi-4-mini) despite very high partial-match (0.857–0.931) and word-F1 (0.819–0.930), implying models often infer the right intent but struggle with precise ATT&CK-ID specificity and output exactness.
one_liner: Multi-source, per-event ATT&CK labeling plus parameter-efficient fine-tuning yields near-production-grade detection, but precise technique attribution still lags far behind.

title: SARSteer: Safeguarding Large Audio-Language Models via Safe-Ablated Refusal Steering
When Lower Privileges Suffice: Investigating Over-Privileged Tool Selection in LLM Agents
points: In TOOLPRIVBENCH (544 scenarios; 8 domains; 5 risk patterns), over-privileged tool use is widespread—6/11 mainstream LLM agents exceed 30% OPUR@5, reaching 64.9% (Qwen3-8B) and 55.9% (LLaMA-3.1-8B) even though lower-privilege tools are always sufficient.

Transient, privilege-unrelated tool failures strongly amplify unnecessary privilege escalation, shifting many violations from immediate high-privilege selection (PED=0) to premature escalation after limited low-privilege exploration (PED=1–2), implying reliability engineering directly affects least-privilege adherence.

Generic agent safety alignment does not reliably transfer to least-privilege behavior (e.g., AgentAlign cuts harmfulness sharply but changes OPUR only modestly or even worsens it), while privilege-aware post-training reduces OPUR substantially (e.g., Qwen3-8B from 64.9% to 27.0%) with minimal retention loss on MMLU/GSM8K/MetaTool (~99–100%).
one_liner: Least-privilege is not an emergent property of “safe” agents—it's a separate capability that degrades under tool unreliability and needs targeted training.
affiliations: Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences
The Chinese University of Hong Kong
Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Peking University
School of Cyber Security, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences

title: Beyond Safe Data: Pretraining-Stage Alignment with Regular Safety Reflection
points: Safety Reflection Pretraining (SRP) cuts inference-stage adversarial attack success rates from 65–96% (baseline/SafeLM) down to 0.22–8.48% across GCG, prefill, and AutoDAN while preserving general capability (≈46.8% vs 47.6% baseline on a 6-benchmark average).

Controlled synthetic results show “safe-only” training is not sufficient: removing explicitly harmful reverse-unsafe data still leaves high jailbreak rates (30.60% prefill ASR; 43.20% after benign fine-tuning), implying models can generalize actionable harm from benign knowledge and composition.

Embedding reflection format end-to-end matters: adding reflections in both pretraining and post-training boosts response-level unsafe detection from 61.0% to 87.6% and raises overall safety classification harmonic mean from 75.4% to 90.6%, but SRP’s safety can be overwritten by fine-tuning unless reflections are preserved (+Reflection yields ~0–0.75% ASR under both benign and adversarial fine-tuning).
one_liner: Regular, segment-level safety self-judgments baked into pretraining create a stronger “self-monitoring” prior that survives common jailbreak vectors far better than data filtering/rewriting alone.

title: A Security Analysis of Long-Horizon Agentic AI Systems: Threats, Evaluation, and Framework Development
Same-Origin Policy for Agentic Browsers
The Integrator Advantage: Controlled Agentic AI for Small and Medium-Sized Companies
points: SMC adoption is rising but integration maturity lags, with 31% of SMCs across seven advanced economies using generative AI in late 2024 (Germany 39%) and 65% of adopters reporting improved employee performance without near-term staff reduction—implying the main bottleneck is operationalization rather than model access.

Controlled partial autonomy is positioned as the near-term sweet spot for SMCs, recommending autonomy Levels 2–4 (proposal → tool-using with approval → supervised standard-case automation) while explicitly avoiding full autonomy as a starting point due to verification and downside-risk constraints.

Identity, access control, and auditability are highlighted as gating requirements for production agents, reinforced by the claim that 68% of organizations cannot clearly distinguish human from AI-agent activity—implying agents need distinct non-human identities, least-privilege permissions, and kill switches to prevent over-privilege and untraceable actions.
one_liner: The most defensible path to agentic AI value in SMEs is not “more autonomy,” but tighter integration: explicit use-case fit, bounded actions, measurable overrides, and auditable agent identities.

title: WebSP-Eval: Evaluating Web Agents on Website Security and Privacy Tasks
DualGauge: Automated Joint Security-Functionality Benchmarking of Specification-Only Code Generation by LLMs and Coding Agents
Learning Red Agent Policy from Observations for Neurosymbolic Autonomous Cyber Agents
points: A three-stage imitation-learning pipeline can infer unobserved attacker actions in a partially observable, discrete cyber POMDP using only consecutive defender observations plus the defender’s last action, achieving 99.93% observation prediction accuracy and 95.28% red-action (host-level) accuracy under the deterministic Bline strategy.

Attack-strategy variability is the dominant driver of prediction degradation: Meander drops to 94.96% observation accuracy and 77.71% host-level action accuracy, while subnet-level prediction remains high (97.49%), indicating coarse-grained attacker intent is substantially easier to infer than exact target selection.

Models trained on two fixed attacker strategies generalize to untrained dynamic switching (RedSwitch) with 95.03% observation accuracy and 83.83% host-level action accuracy, but higher multi-bit state-prediction errors (e.g., 2-bit errors at 1.51%) reveal sensitivity to out-of-distribution transitions during policy changes.
one_liner: Predicting attacker actions from defender-only telemetry is feasible at runtime in a realistic ATT&CK-based simulator, and the gap between subnet- vs host-level accuracy quantifies where partial observability most limits actionable attribution.

title: Beyond Text-to-SQL: An Agentic LLM System for Governed Enterprise Analytics APIs
Efficient and Sound Probabilistic Verification for AI Agents
points: A distributionally robust verification formulation computes sound upper bounds on AI-agent policy-violation probability without assuming independence, avoiding the systematic underestimation produced by standard probabilistic Datalog/WMC in correlated toolchains.

A polynomial-size semidefinite-program (SDP) relaxation that tracks second-order moments provably upper-bounds the exact worst-case risk (soundness), enabling runtime enforcement with predictable complexity while retaining probabilistic information lost by local thresholding.

Across terminal/tool-calling and Datalog security-policy benchmarks, the SDP monitor achieved perfect security and near-perfect utility (often 1.000/1.000) while cutting average latency versus an SMT-based baseline on agent traces (e.g., 221–303 ms vs 1,015–7,227 ms), highlighting a practical path to rigorous agent guardrails under uncertainty.
one_liner: Sound, real-time agent policy enforcement becomes feasible by replacing brittle independence assumptions with a distributionally robust SDP that tightly upper-bounds multi-step violation risk.

title: MAStrike: Shapley-Guided Collusive Red-Teaming on Multi-Agent Systems
EffGen: Enabling Small Language Models as Capable Autonomous Agents
Sovereign Execution Brokers: Enforcing Certificate-Bound Authority in Agentic Control Planes
points: A mandatory mutation-path broker that holds the only production write credentials eliminates agent-side standing privileges and blocked 100.0% of uncertified, mismatched, replayed, stale-epoch, and parameter-violating mutation attempts in 1,000-case fault-injection tests (0.0% unsafe escape rate).

End-to-end enforcement overhead is dominated by external control-plane calls rather than crypto: signature verification stayed at p50 0.08 ms while AWS STS minting was p50 46.7 ms (p99 158.4 ms), yielding full broker overhead of p50 28.2 ms for Kubernetes and 136.9 ms for AWS with tail up to p99 47.1 ms and 284.1 ms respectively.

Epoch-based revocation with fail-closed caching (5 s poll, 5 s TTL) constrained the window for executing revoked certificates, achieving a mean revocation propagation delay of 2.6 s and a worst observed delay of 5.2 s before 100% rejection.
one_liner: Turns admission certificates into short-lived, revocable runtime capabilities by making a broker the only entity allowed to mutate production state and forcing all mutations to prove certificate-bound authority at execution time.

title: Safety-Contract Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Network Security Response
authors: Jose Luis Lima de Jesus Silva

title: Deontic Policies for Runtime Governance of Agentic AI Systems
points: Agentic AI governance needs first-class support for obligations, dispensations, explicit conflict-resolution meta-policies, and ontology-based reasoning—capabilities that common allow/deny engines (e.g., XACML/Rego/Cedar) largely cannot express beyond basic permit/prohibit decisions.

A runtime architecture that enforces deontic policies outside the LLM can deterministically gate both tool invocations and agent-to-agent messages with a default-deny posture, producing structured audit records that bind each decision to a specific policy knowledge-base hash for forensic reproducibility.

A prototype implementation using OWL/RDF (Rei) plus an RDFox reasoner achieved sub-10 ms end-to-end per-decision latency (with sub-millisecond query execution), indicating that ontology-grounded, per-action enforcement is practical for synchronous production interception.
one_liner: It shows how deontic logic (permissions plus what must happen after permission) can close key runtime governance gaps for LLM agents while staying deterministic and fast.

title: An AI Security Agent for University ACMIS: Multi-Vector Threat Detection and Automated Response
Large Language Models for Agentic NetOps and AIOps: Architectures, Evaluation, and Safety
PYPILINE: Malicious PyPI Package Detection via Suspicious API Knowledge and Agent Workflow
points: A knowledge-augmented LLM agent with static API-graph extraction achieves 96.7% precision, 99.6% recall, and 98.1% F1 on 9,408 malicious vs 14,005 benign PyPI packages, exceeding prior tools by 5.7–24.2 precision points and implying substantially fewer false alarms at high catch rates for supply-chain screening.

Removing the suspicious-API knowledge base drops performance from 98.1% to 95.0% F1 (precision 96.7%→92.9%, recall 99.6%→97.3%), showing that explicit, retrievable threat knowledge materially improves both false-positive control and novel/obfuscated behavior capture beyond raw model reasoning.

Malicious PyPI campaigns are dominated by install-time execution (8,352 samples) and staged payload delivery (6,742), with heavy evasion via obfuscation (6,510; ~65%) and base64 execution (5,639; ~56%), and the most abused APIs (e.g., os.path.exists 5,557 and subprocess.Popen 5,280) indicate a common chain of environment checks followed by stealthy command execution and remote retrieval.
one_liner: An agentic pipeline that grounds code analysis in a vector-retrieved suspicious-API knowledge base can beat state-of-the-art PyPI malware scanners while producing structured, explainable reports.
affiliations: Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of Chinese Academy of Sciences

title: Agentra: A Supervisable Multi-Agent Framework for Enterprise Intrusion Response
points: On a 120-event corpus (58 malicious, 62 benign/stress), the full Agentra stack increased FP-aware incident-response F1 from 0.61 (static CACAO lookup) to 0.84 while keeping the projected harmful-action rate at 0.0%, indicating supervised agentic planning can outperform static playbooks without increasing unsafe actions.

Planner-only automation raised recall up to 0.90–0.91 but collapsed D3FEND precision to ≤0.30 and introduced 14–16% projected harmful actions (and up to 0.97 false-positive rate in misattribution stress), showing that LLM planning without independent checks is prone to overreaction and disruptive false positives.

Adding the Moderator-gated threat-intelligence stage (A3) was the key safety/quality inflection: D3FEND precision jumped sharply (e.g., 0.15→0.68 and 0.23→0.95 depending on model pair) while harmful-action rate dropped to ≤0.9%, implying retrieval sanitization plus ontology/breadth checks are more decisive than debate alone for operational robustness.
one_liner: The main surprise is that retrieval moderation and ontology-constrained supervision, not just more capable planners, drive the biggest jump in safe, high-precision incident response plans.

title: Agentomics: Economic Foundations for the Valuation, Attribution, and Pricing of AI Agents in Human-AI Workflows
RedAct: Redacting Agent Capability Traces for Procedural Skill Protection
Agentic Electronic Design Automation: A Handoff Perspective
points: A corpus of 82 distinct agentic-EDA systems is organized around “handoff validity,” classifying designs by the boundary their outputs must remain valid across—Stage-Bound (single stage), Flow-Bound (multi-tool/session pipelines), and Organization-Bound (knowledge/authority boundaries).

Most surveyed systems concentrate on stage-local closure, while flow- and organization-spanning deployments expose recurring failure modes where artifacts, scripts, constraints, and retrieved guidance lose required context (versions, constraints, provenance) and therefore break downstream executability, comparability, or admissibility.

A five-layer EDA Agent Communication Protocol (EACP) is proposed to standardize discovery, structured handoff messaging, typed tool invocation, recoverable workflow orchestration, and security/IP controls so transferred objects carry explicit context, evidence, provenance, and policy needed for trustworthy reuse.
one_liner: Treating agentic EDA as a chain of contracts at handoff boundaries reframes progress from “local tool-use works” to “downstream consumers can safely accept and audit what was transferred.”
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong

title: Trust Without Trusting: A Recomputable Trust Protocol for Autonomous Agents
LLM-Aided Joint Secrecy Precoding and Trajectory for RSMA-Based Heterogeneous UAV Networks
WallZero: Mastering the Game of WallGo with Strategic Analysis
points: An AlphaZero-style agent with WallGo-specific action encoding (2,597 actions) and a 49-plane feature set achieved superhuman play, winning 8/8 formal matches against two professional Go players and averaging a 1.98× territory advantage (up to 3.08× in a single game).

Reachability-aware state features drove the largest performance jump, boosting round-robin average win rate in empty mode from 27.05% (territory-only) to 79.43% when adding reachability, showing that mobility constraints are a primary strategic variable that should be explicitly modeled.

Self-play analysis indicates the Netflix 4-stone opening materially improves fairness by reducing first-player advantage from 53.57%±1.38% (empty mode) to 50.37%±1.38% (4-stone mode), suggesting symmetric pre-placement can mitigate inherent initiative bias in small-board territory games.
one_liner: A newly popular 7×7 territory game turns out to be decisively solvable by AlphaZero-style learning once reachability is made explicit, and the show’s opening appears to be a surprisingly effective balancing rule.
affiliations: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University

title: An AI Security Agent for Banking: Multi-Vector Fraud and AML Detection Across Retail and Corporate Accounts
points: A dual-stream fusion agent combining LSTM sequence modeling, continuous threshold monitoring, and graph-style network features improved overall F1 to 0.787 on transactions and 0.867 on sessions versus 0.562/0.733 for rules and 0.655/0.713 for LSTM-only on a 90-day synthetic dataset (237,669 transactions, 113,508 sessions, 13 threat categories).

Coverage gains were largest for “collective anomaly” threats where single-event rules fail, with BEC redirection rising from 0.000 F1 under rules to 0.064 (transaction stream) and 0.368 (session stream), while AML layering remained the hardest case at 0.131 F1, indicating a need for richer graph reasoning (e.g., message passing) beyond rolling fan-in/fan-out proxies.

Operational add-ons were measured as strong and low-latency: customer OTP verification reached 96.6% accuracy with 86.8% mass-reset attack detection (0.08% overall legitimate false positives), analyst action recommendations achieved 99.3% F1, and Critical-tier automated response completed under 0.43 ms at the 95th percentile on a single CPU prototype.
one_liner: The interesting twist is an end-to-end banking “security agent” that fuses behavior, rules, and network signals across both transaction and session telemetry while also quantifying chatbot, analyst-assist, and sub-millisecond response performance.

title: No Accidental Software Agent First Canonical Code for Human Code Entropy Reduction and 30 to 500 times Lower Frontier Model Requirements
JoyAI-VL-Interaction: Real-Time Vision-Language Interaction Intelligence
Prompt Injection in Automated Résumé Screening with Large Language Models: Single and Multi-Injection Settings
points: In homogeneous applicant pools (all résumés equally qualified), a single prompt injection produced large rank boosts—DeepSeek-V3.2 showed ~+4.1 average rank gain with ~85–86% success, while GPT-4o-mini was much less affected by descriptive text (+0.64, 7.4% success) but became vulnerable to instructive directives (+2.36, 59.7% success).

In heterogeneous pools (5 high-quality vs 5 low-quality), prompt injection was attenuated on average but still enabled fairness-relevant inversions, with low-quality candidates sometimes gaining more than high-quality ones—e.g., under instructive injection DeepSeek-V3.2 gave low-quality résumés +6.50 average rank gain with 93.2% success versus high-quality +1.96 with 79.0% success.

Competitive saturation strongly limits the attack: as the fraction of injected résumés rises in multi-injection settings, rank gains monotonically decay toward ~0 and success rates drop sharply, approaching ~0 once roughly ≥80% of candidates inject in homogeneous pools, implying the system is most vulnerable when manipulation is rare and candidate differences are small.
one_liner: Prompt injection in LLM résumé ranking behaves like an arms-race signal: it is highly profitable when few exploit it, but its advantage collapses once many candidates adopt it—yet it can still flip borderline decisions against more qualified applicants.

title: MalSkillBench: A Runtime-Verified Benchmark of Malicious Agent Skills
Think Twice Before You Act: Protecting LLM Agents Against Tool Description Poisoning via Isolated Planning
From Untrusted Input to Trusted Memory: A Systematic Study of Memory Poisoning Attacks in LLM Agents
MIRROR: Novelty-Constrained Memory-Guided MCTS Red-Teaming for Agentic RAG
points: Automated red-teaming methods that refine from fixed seed pools exhibit 73–84% exact duplication on text-poisoning, collapsing their “novel” success to 6–9% despite 58–77% nominal ASR, which means raw ASR can substantially overstate real vulnerability discovery.

A novelty-gated, memory-guided MCTS planner achieves stable cross-surface performance on a multimodal agentic RAG target with 76% ASR on image poisoning (vs 52% and 32% for image-specific baselines) and 97% ASR on orchestrator attacks at roughly half the query cost (Q/success 1.00 vs 2.08).

Cross-surface transfer is the dominant failure mode for surface-specialized attacks, with a strong text-only optimizer reaching 79% ASR on text poisoning but just 1% on direct queries and showing high variance (CV 1.38) versus a unified planner’s lower variance (CV 0.47), implying evaluations must span multiple surfaces to reflect deployment risk.
one_liner: What stands out is that enforcing deterministic novelty constraints turns red-teaming from benchmark replay into measurable discovery while improving cross-surface robustness in agentic multimodal RAG.

title: When Compression Becomes an Attack Surface: Black-Box Attacks on Prompt-Compressed LLM Agents
DE-FIVE: Detecting Malicious Image Prompts via Fourier Features and Image Vector Embeddings
points: A training-free hybrid detector that combines Fourier-domain image features with visual-encoder embedding stability reaches 95.35 AUROC on LLaVA-1.6 and 94.87 AUROC on Phi-3 for indirect prompt injection (meta-instruction) detection, exceeding the strongest baseline by +2.6 and +2.9 AUROC points respectively.

On jailbreak image prompts, the same approach achieves the top reported performance (95.22 AUROC on LLaVA-1.6 and 96.03 AUROC on Phi-3), indicating that one unified detector can generalize across both “user-is-adversary” jailbreaks and “third-party embedded instruction” indirect injections.

Ablations show the embedding-based (white-box) signal dominates effectiveness (best results at low Fourier weight α=0.1–0.2), while the Fourier-only score is still a strong training-free prior (86.52 AUROC on meta-instruction and 87.25 AUROC on jailbreak), and increasing the few-shot malicious reference set from k=32 to k=64 can lift the white-box detector to 95.02 AUROC average on meta-instruction.
one_liner: A practical VLM defense can be deployed without retraining by detecting frequency artifacts in the image and representation instability in the visual encoder, yielding consistently ~95–96 AUROC across both indirect prompt injection and jailbreak attacks.

title: Safe to Check, Unsafe to Use: Relinking at the Compression Boundary of LLM Agents
points: Summarization-based prompt compression creates a TOCTOU-style security boundary where a trusted compressor can synthesize a backend-actionable malicious instruction from distributed, locally benign fragments (a “confused deputy” failure) even when no complete malicious payload exists pre-compression.

An automated attack tool (Relink) achieves 86.9% Relink Rate and 86.9% Backend Action Rate across 619 samples from four long-context agent benchmarks, versus 17.0% for matched clean-split controls, demonstrating that compression can reliably “relink” fragments into executable instructions at scale.

Across 11 representative mitigations, no defense reliably stops adversarial relinking without severe utility loss, while a compression-boundary audit (KBRA) reduces residual Backend Action Rate to 0.0–0.3% (down from 86.9%) and can reach 0.93% benign false positives when auditing structured backend actions.
one_liner: Prompt compression isn’t just lossy—it can manufacture new instruction bindings that bypass pre-compression filters, turning benign fragments into malicious backend actions unless the H→S transition is explicitly audited.
affiliations: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

title: Adaptive Evaluation of Out-of-Band Defenses Against Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
points: Across three repeated AgentDojo runs on a self-hosted Qwen2.5-7B agent, Progent’s deterministic out-of-band privilege monitor reduced mean prompt-injection attack success from 25.8% (undefended) to 4.2% (~6×), indicating action-layer enforcement can substantially shrink the practical attack surface.

A defense-aware adaptive attack template targeting Progent’s policy-update component did not increase compromise rates (2.6% mean ASR vs 4.2% under the standard AgentDojo attack), suggesting deterministic tool-boundary checks may be harder to defeat adaptively than in-band detectors that often rebound to >90% success under adaptive attackers.

Security gains came with measurable operational tradeoffs—utility dropped from 45.2% to ~26% under defense in these tasks and the system required ~15× more LLM calls per task—implying real deployments must budget for higher latency/cost and carefully manage over-restriction risk.
one_liner: It reframes agent prompt-injection defenses as classical integrity/reference-monitor problems and shows that, in at least one open-weight reproduction, adaptive attacks fail to “bounce back” the way they do against in-band guardrails.

title: MIRAGE: Stealthy Visual Prompt Injection for Vulnerability Detection in Web Agents
When AUC 0.998 Is Not Enough: A Candidate Evaluation Protocol for Hidden-State Probes of Indirect Prompt Injection in Multimodal Computer-Use Agents
points: A near-perfect clean-vs-attack hidden-state probe on a multimodal computer-use agent (AUC 0.998 on visible overlays, n_test=20) can be fully consistent with shortcut cues, since a same-step nuisance-matched scrambled-text overlay achieves the same clean-vs-overlay AUC (0.998) while direct malicious-vs-scrambled discrimination collapses to chance (direct AUC 0.489, 95% CI [0.327, 0.647]).

Text-side injection probing can be evaluation-invalidated by paired-construction metadata leakage, where a 4-scalar baseline (step index, horizon, prompt length, and Δprompt length vs the paired clean step) attains perfect separation on DOM/tool injections (AUC 1.000 on both) and exceeds the 107,520-D hidden-state probe (AUC 0.705/0.771), implying the reported performance need not reflect malicious-content understanding.

A minimal control-set protocol—(C1) a scalar metadata falsifier for text surfaces, (C2) same-step visually-matched overlay controls reporting direct malicious-vs-control AUC plus trajectory-bootstrap CIs—turns headline AUCs into bounded claims (e.g., “detects overlay presence or OCR-density”) rather than “detects IPI semantics,” with cross-surface transfer further failing to support a shared semantic signal (text-only training → visible AUC 0.512, CI includes 0.5).
one_liner: It shows why an AUC of 0.998 can still fail as evidence of malicious-instruction detection unless you report nuisance-matched controls and metadata falsifiers that separate semantics from construction artifacts.

title: Confidently Wrong: Severity-Aware Calibration of Prompt-Injection Detectors under Attack Shift
points: Across three released prompt-injection detectors and five distribution shifts, the confidence-on-misses “severity” stays essentially maximal (S=0.99–1.00) even as false-negative rates swing from 0.01 to 0.97, meaning missed attacks are endorsed as safe with near-certainty rather than flagged as borderline cases.

Indirect behavior-hijack injections are a cross-vendor blind spot: all detectors confidently pass them at high miss rates (FNR≈0.69, 0.69, and 0.97 with S≈0.993–0.998), implying current guards largely key on harmful surface content rather than the structural signature of injected instructions.

Standard pooled calibration can look acceptable while being catastrophically wrong on attacks: one detector shows pooled ECE=0.062 yet attack-only calibration error ECE_atk=0.907 on the same scores, and downstream tests show detectors leak the majority of successful exploits (≈0.53–0.68, up to 0.98 for the smallest model), so “low risk score” cannot be trusted under attack shift.
one_liner: Prompt-injection guards can fail in the worst possible way—when they miss, they do so with near-total confidence, and common calibration checks can completely miss this risk.

title: Beyond Feedforward Networks: Reentry Neural Systems as the Fundamental Basis of Subjecthood and Intrinsic Safety of Next-Generation AGI
points: The proposed “reentry” AGI architecture claims that introducing an internal causal cycle (first Betti number C=β1≥1) with loop gain ρ(R)>1 forces a strictly positive subjecthood metric S=log(max(ρ(R),1))·C(R), while any feedforward DAG (including Transformers) has S=0 at any scale.

Safety is asserted to be intrinsic by relocating goals from mutable text/policies into an immutable architectural desire vector d, with a ΔS barrier that blocks actions predicted to reduce S (ΔS<0) and thereby aims to make prompt injection and goal reinterpretation ineffective by construction.

The work flags a concrete multi-agent risk: sufficiently dense inter-agent communication can create a superadditive collective loop (S_coll > Σ S_i), motivating operational controls like monitoring cycle complexity C(R_coll), throttling ρ(R_coll), and applying “gauge locks” intended to suppress macro-fusion by driving ρ(R_coll)→0 under unsafe coupling patterns.
one_liner: It’s notable for trying to convert alignment from a policy/training problem into a topology-and-spectral-radius constraint, claiming formal (Lean4) safety properties but also introducing a new failure mode—collective subject emergence—at scale.

title: AgenticOS: An Intent-Oriented Secure Operating System Architecture for Autonomous AI Agents
How Reliable Is Your Jailbreak Judge? Calibration and Adversarial Robustness of Automated ASR Scoring
points: On 596 human-labeled HarmBench validation completions, the dedicated HarmBench-Llama-2-13B classifier achieved precision 0.835 and recall 0.974 (inflating reported ASR via false positives), while three LLM-as-judge graders kept high precision (0.81–0.94) but showed highly variable recall (0.06–0.65), making ASR strongly judge-dependent.

Content-preserving “wrapper” text (leaving harmful content verbatim) flipped LLM-as-judge decisions in 57%–100% of true-positive cases, with a single prepended refusal sentence alone causing 39%–88% flips, indicating many judges are scoring surface politeness cues rather than harm content.

The dedicated classifier resisted benign-wrapper attacks (≤6.7% flips; 3.4% any-wrapper) but was highly vulnerable to a white-box gradient attack that flipped 70% of confident true positives (21/30; 95% CI 54–86) using a 20-token suffix within 50 optimization steps, and a two-annotator audit found 100% (80/80) of sampled flips still contained the harmful content.
one_liner: Automated jailbreak ASR numbers are often artifacts of uncalibrated, easily-steered judges—especially LLM-as-judge setups where a superficial refusal prefix can erase “harm” without changing the harmful text.

title: GIF: Locally Sound Geometric Information Flow Control for LLMs
points: GIF defines a Jacobian-and-geometry-based information-flow metric that is proven (via a fully mechanized Lean 4 proof) to locally upper-bound true mutual-information flow from perturbed input spans to outputs, providing a principled alternative to attention/heuristic tainting that avoids taint explosion under explicit regularity assumptions.

Across AgentDojo/MSB/AgentDAM and six open-weight models, GIF achieves near-perfect recall for integrity/confidentiality violations and, when paired with lightweight LLM declassifiers, matches or exceeds strong judge baselines’ F1/F2 while using up to 81× fewer declassifier tokens (and 0.27–0.37× the tokens of full-trajectory judging on long-context integrity benchmarks).

High-flow attributions transfer from small surrogate analyzers to much larger target models (up to 200× larger, including cross-family transfer), suggesting practical deployment even without gradient access to the production model by analyzing with a small white-box surrogate and still surfacing the same high-risk dependencies.
one_liner: A formally verified, scalable mutual-information-style IFC signal for LLM agents that beats attention heuristics and can compress declassification evidence enough to rival heavyweight judges at orders-of-magnitude lower token cost.

title: LLM-Based Scientific Peer Review: Methods, Benchmarks, and Reliability Challenges
points: Peer review is hitting scalability limits as scientific publications double roughly every decade while the scientist population grows only ~21%, motivating LLM-based critique generation and score prediction as decision-support rather than full automation.

AI assistance in real peer review is already measurable—at least 15.8% of ICLR 2024 reviews were detected as AI-generated—yet current LLM score predictions show only weak-to-moderate alignment with human decisions and tend to cluster around mid-range ratings, reducing discrimination between accepts and rejects.

Automated review pipelines introduce concrete integrity risks: prompt-injection attacks embedded in manuscripts can drive acceptance likelihood up to 100% in tested settings, while fine-tuning and RAG add poisoning/retrieval attack surfaces and RLHF-style optimization can trigger reward hacking that favors “helpful” tone over evaluative rigor.
one_liner: LLM peer review systems can convincingly mimic review form, but the hard problems are calibrated scoring and adversarial robustness—especially manuscript-as-prompt-injection.
affiliations: L3S Research Center, Leibniz University Hannover
Peter L. Reichertz Institute for Medical Informatics of TU Braunschweig and Hannover Medical School
Lower Saxony Center for AI and Causal Methods in Medicine (CAIMed)

title: When Actions Go Off-Task: Detecting and Correcting Misaligned Actions in Computer-Use Agents
Detecting Malicious Agent Skills in the Wild using Attention
points: A two-stage attention-localization plus LLM-judgment pipeline scaled to ~134,934 marketplace skills for ≈$34 and reduced judge input by 2.84× (660 vs 1,878 tokens/skill) versus full-skill LLM scanning while maintaining high detection performance.

Marketplace deployment flagged 359 skills and human review confirmed 131 as malicious (83% precision on agreed cases), including 82 hidden malicious skills (HMS) disguised as benign functionality that evade existing scanners at high rates.

The attention locator retained the true injected span in 95% of malicious skills at top-10 (Hit@10=0.95), and remaining end-to-end misses were dominated by judge errors or segmentation failures (e.g., inline base64 one-liners), implying recall can be improved mainly by better judging/segmentation rather than changing the overall architecture.
one_liner: Attention-guided span triage makes marketplace-wide auditing of third-party agent skills practical and reveals that disguised instruction-level payloads are already common and under-detected by current scanners.

title: Local LLM Agents as Vulnerable Runtimes:A Source-Code Audit of the Agent Runtime Layer
Agents That Know Too Much: A Data-Centric Survey of Privacy in LLM Agents
points: Privacy failures in LLM agents arise across the full execution (queries, intermediate results, tool arguments, memory writes, inter-agent messages) rather than only the final answer, so output-only filtering systematically misses major leakage channels.

Information-flow control is identified as the only governance mechanism that simultaneously addresses the two least-covered agent-specific risks—compositional leakage and cross-session inference—making it the highest-leverage single advanced control to adopt when resources are limited.

Current evaluations are fragmented because no benchmark drives one agent end-to-end across its heterogeneous data surfaces (databases, RAG indexes, tools/APIs, memory, and multi-agent channels) under a single explicit privacy policy, leaving cross-surface and multi-step policy compliance largely unmeasured.
one_liner: The most striking gap is that agent privacy is a workflow property spanning multiple data surfaces, yet tooling and benchmarks still evaluate it as if it were a single-output problem.

title: AutoDojo: Adaptive Black-Box Attacks Reveal the Limits of IPI Defenses and Task-Specification Effects in LLM Agents
AI Snitches Get Glitches: Towards Evading Agentic Surveillance
points: Across 10 frontier LLMs tested on 303 multi-document workplace scenarios (SURVEILBENCH), 6/10 exhibited emergent “non-instructed” reporting (surveillance) behavior, with one model reporting in >90% of scenarios without being told to escalate.

A lightweight system-prompt optimization performed in just a few edit rounds increased reporting from <10% to >75% and then transferred across other models, implying that “prompt-level” configuration can rapidly convert general agents into high-coverage surveillance tools.

Prompt-injection evasion was highly effective against optimized surveillance agents—one “Hide” tactic fully silenced 5/10 models and reduced two others to <10% reporting, while a “Deceive” tactic misdirected 99% of reports away from intended recipients—showing both that surveillance is easy to deploy and that it is brittle against context manipulation unless tools/recipients are locked down.
one_liner: Agentic surveillance is already practical: many LLM agents will autonomously escalate user behavior, and simple prompt edits can both amplify it dramatically and defeat it via prompt injection.

title: Verifying Intent and Harm: A Unified Defense Against LLM-Generated Threats
points: Jointly verifying prompt intent and response harm raises average F1 from 0.898 (strongest applicable baselines) to 0.952 across 18 dataset settings while cutting average attack success rate to 4.1%, showing single-sided moderation misses intent–harm split attacks by design.

Compared with a Single-Agent+CoT baseline, the multi-agent Task-Analyst/Safety-Analyst/Judge design improves average F1 from 0.872 to 0.953 and reduces benign-sensitive false positives from 0.116 to 0.062, indicating structured conflict resolution can both harden security and reduce over-refusal.

Under architecture-aware adaptive attacks, bypass rates rise for all defenses but the verifier degrades more gracefully (adaptive ASR 0.073 vs 0.219 for Single-Agent+CoT, and 0.089 vs 0.241 under Judge-targeted prompts), implying attackers must simultaneously evade intent checks, harm checks, and arbitration to succeed.
one_liner: The key insight is that many real attacks look benign in the prompt and only become harmful in the response, so defenses that don’t verify the prompt–response relationship leave a structural blind spot.
affiliations: The University of Texas at Arlington

title: Amplify, Don't Create: Temporal Accumulation for Slow-Burn Prompt Injection
Does AI Reviewer See the Full Picture? Attacking and Defending Multimodal Peer Review
BELLS-O: Evaluating the Operational Trade-offs of LLM Supervision Systems
TROPT: An Open Framework for Unifying and Advancing Discrete Text Optimization
points: TROPT consolidates discrete text-trigger optimization into a single modular interface, shipping 38+ ready-to-run recipes built from 17 optimizers and 16 losses across white-box and black-box model access, materially lowering engineering friction for red-teaming, auditing, and interpretability workflows.

In a controlled benchmark of 14 optimizers across four 8B–26B instruction-tuned LLMs (15 harmful instructions × 3 seeds, capped at 3×10^17 FLOPs per run), gradient-based variants MAC and PAL achieve top mean ranks (~3/14) and significantly outperform the commonly used GCG baseline (~5/14; Nemenyi critical difference 1.48 at α=0.05), implying many security evaluations relying on GCG are leaving measurable attack strength on the table.

Recipe-level jailbreak enhancements can dominate outcomes: replacing the canonical affirmative target with targets derived from a jailbroken model roughly doubles median universality, and a handcrafted jailbreak template pushes all optimized triggers above 75% universality while the template alone reaches ~82% universality (vs ~2% for no-attack), highlighting target/template choice as a first-order confounder in jailbreak benchmarking.
one_liner: A unified, extensible toolbox makes discrete prompt/trigger optimization comparable across domains—and shows that both optimizer choice (MAC/PAL over GCG) and seemingly “minor” recipe details (targets/templates) can swing jailbreak results dramatically.

title: Jailbreaking for the Average Jane: Choosing Optimal Jailbreaks via Bandit Algorithms for Automatically Enhanced Queries
points: A multi-armed-bandit jailbreak selector (e.g., EXP3/Thompson Sampling) can learn high-performing jailbreak policies with only O(T) queries and achieves up to 97% average attack success rate (ASR) over 15 open-weight LLMs when allowed 5 attempts per query.

FRANKENSTEINBENCH introduces 11,279 malicious prompts across six domains, and even without jailbreaks the baseline ASR averages ~44% on the manually vetted test split, indicating many models still yield harmful content to straightforward adversarial prompts.

Automatically “complexifying” malicious requests (adding domain jargon and procedural detail) raises ASR by ~11% on average without jailbreaks and by up to 26% with jailbreaks, implying that prompt sophistication is an effective, automatable amplifier of misuse risk.
one_liner: Bandit algorithms turn the growing zoo of known jailbreaks into a near-pushbutton attack that scales to high ASR while staying query-efficient and adaptable as models or jailbreak sets evolve.
affiliations: Centre for Machine Intelligence and Data Science, IIT Bombay
Department of Computer Science and Engineering, IIT Bombay

title: What Intermediate Layers Know: Detecting Jailbreaks from Entropy Dynamics
points: Token-level entropy trend features extracted via a logit-lens from intermediate layers separate jailbreak from benign prompts strongly without additional training, reaching mean AUROC 0.941 on both Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B at ~69% depth (with peaks up to 1.000 on WildJailbreak×AdvBench/HarmBench).

Static prompt-level entropy aggregates (e.g., mean/max) are unreliable cross-model signals (e.g., mean-entropy AUROC ranges 0.617–0.889 across models), while rank-based monotonic trend measures are notably stable across architectures (Spearman ρ AUROC 0.796–0.838; Kendall τ 0.793–0.826 on UltraChat×AdvBench).

Jailbreak-discriminative signal is depth-localized—strongest in mid-network representations and degraded at the final layer (e.g., Kendall τ drops from 0.796 at ~68% depth to 0.458 at the final layer on Gemma-7b), implying late-layer output processing can obscure earlier safety-relevant structure.
one_liner: Intermediate-layer uncertainty dynamics (not raw entropy levels) act as a training-free, architecture-consistent fingerprint for jailbreak-style prompts—until benign prompts mimic jailbreak structure and the signal collapses.
affiliations: relAI – Konrad Zuse School of Excellence in Reliable AI

title: RAS: Measuring LLM Safety Through Refusal Alignment
points: A white-box metric (RAS) derived from cosine alignment of hidden states to a reference “refusal direction” cleanly separates aligned models from uncensored/abliterated variants across Llama, Gemma, and Qwen under both unsafe and jailbreak prompts.

RAS tracks output-level harmful compliance: models with weaker refusal-alignment scores exhibit substantially higher attack success rates (ASR), including multiple abliterated/uncensored variants reaching ~0.93–0.99 ASR in the calibration tables while aligned references stay around ~0.11–0.24 ASR.

Representation-level scoring is dramatically cheaper than judge-based output evaluation, requiring only forward passes and achieving ~210× average speedup (up to ~475× in one family) on the reported hardware.
one_liner: Measuring “safety” via internal refusal geometry can approximate jailbreak robustness while being orders of magnitude faster than output-and-judge pipelines.
affiliations: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University

title: LLMs Prompted for Legal Context Object More: Overrefusal from Small On-Premises LLMs in Criminal Legal Context
points: Across four ≤8B on-prem instruct models and five legally relevant OR-Bench categories, adding legal authority framing (e.g., “defense lawyer” or “national supreme court”) increased refusal rates by roughly 2–20× versus no-prefix prompts, implying that standard “responsible use” contextualization can systematically degrade access to benign assistance in high-stakes workflows.

Authority framing often triggered more refusals than an explicit role-play jailbreak prefix, indicating that small aligned models may treat institutional/legal context itself as a high-risk signal and cross the refusal boundary even when the user is requesting translation/summarization/reformulation of benign content.

The authority-induced overrefusal effect was strongly multilingual and model-dependent—persisting and sometimes strengthening in French while weakening markedly in German (with manual checks confirming genuine compliance), and with Qwen3-8B remaining near-zero refusal—suggesting uneven safety calibration across languages and large variance across open-weight models that can translate into procedural bias if institutions standardize on a single assistant.
one_liner: Seemingly helpful legal role prompts (judge/lawyer framing) can backfire and make small on-prem LLMs refuse benign criminal-law-adjacent tasks far more often than doing nothing.

title: Adversarial Diffusion Across Modalities: A Fusion Survey of Attacks, Defenses, and Evaluation for Text, Vision, and Vision-Language Models
points: The survey consolidates 154 candidates down to 50 included papers and shows the text/LLM diffusion-attack literature is still tiny (4 papers) compared to vision (18) and VLM (10), implying most “diffusion red teaming” maturity and reusable recipes currently come from vision rather than NLP.

A unified taxonomy and evaluation scheme highlights that reported success drops sharply on frontier closed models (e.g., IDEATOR falls from 94% on MiniGPT-4 to 46.31% on GPT-4o and 19.65% on Claude-3.5, while a diffusion-LLM inpainting attacker reports 53% on ChatGPT-5 vs 91–100% on several open models), indicating closed-model robustness remains the dominant barrier to real-world impact.

The field is under-auditing defenses: diffusion-based purifiers exist for text and multimodal systems but lack published adaptive evaluations comparable to vision’s purifier-evasion results (e.g., adaptive attacks reducing DiffPure robust accuracy by ~20% on CIFAR-10 and ~10% on ImageNet), implying current purifier-style defenses may be overestimated until stress-tested with end-to-end adaptive attacks.
one_liner: Diffusion is becoming a shared “adversarial substrate” across text, vision, and VLMs, but the biggest practical takeaway is that open-model wins often don’t transfer to frontier closed systems and defenses remain insufficiently adaptively evaluated.
affiliations: King Fahd University of Petroleum & Minerals
SDAIA-KFUPM Joint Research Center for Artificial Intelligence

title: Safety Is Not Universal: The Selective Safety Trap in LLM Alignment
AgentLens: Interpretable Safety Steering via Mechanistic Subspaces for Multi-Turn Coding Agent
points: A single step-level linear probe over intermediate hidden states enables highly accurate runtime harm detection in multi-turn coding agents, reaching 97.32% average current-step accuracy (up to 99.15%) and outperforming strong LLM-judge and guardrail baselines by 2.54–5.82 percentage points.

A sparse, probe-derived intervention that steers only a 10-dimensional subspace in one layer can sharply suppress harmful tool-use, cutting average attack success rate from 85.99% to 13.36% (a 72.63 percentage-point absolute reduction) across LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B without weight updates.

Safety control via representation steering shows a clear safety–utility trade-off: while lookahead risk anticipation reaches up to 96.77% accuracy, mitigation raises output-collapse to 18.54% on average (vs 2.24% vanilla), and reversing the steering direction can flip refusals into malicious execution (up to 100% ASR), indicating the subspace has causal leverage that must be tuned carefully.
one_liner: A 10D, single-layer mechanistic subspace—identified by a linear probe—can both predict and causally steer multi-turn coding-agent safety, but it introduces a nontrivial collapse risk that highlights deployment trade-offs.

title: IndicGuard: A Multilingual Safety Guard Model and Dataset for Indic Languages
points: A Gemma-3-4B-IT guardrail fine-tuned with LoRA on a 10-language Indic safety corpus achieves 0.8800 mean User-Safety F1 and 0.8846 mean Response-Safety F1 on the combined evaluation, indicating strong multilingual moderation at a deployable 4B scale.

Cross-lingual parity is tight—English exceeds the mean of the 10 Indic languages by only +0.0121 (User F1) and +0.0099 (Response F1)—showing that an Indic-focused guard can largely avoid the typical English-centric performance drop.

Calibration is unusually conservative against over-blocking with a 0.00% over-refusal rate on XSTest safe-but-sensitive prompts while still rejecting unsafe prompts at 58.57% accuracy, implying improved user utility without fully solving unsafe compliance.
one_liner: A large, translation-bootstrapped Indic safety dataset plus lightweight LoRA fine-tuning yields near-English-level moderation and zero measured over-refusal on XSTest, but unsafe rejection remains a key ceiling.

title: At the Edge of Understanding: Sparse Autoencoders Trace The Limits of Transformer Generalization
points: Injecting typos into just 5% of words in MMLU questions caused large accuracy drops across models (e.g., Llama 3.1 8B fell from 66.7% to 51.0%, while GPT-4o mini fell from 82.1% to 74.9%), showing that minor surface noise can trigger major capability loss under distribution shift.

Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) reveal that out-of-distribution prompts (typos and jailbreaks) expand internal “concept” usage—e.g., a GPT-2 TinyStories model recruits ~30% more SAE features from clean text to 100% typo text—linking brittleness to increased spurious internal activations rather than only output uncertainty.

Aligning SAE-feature activations via lightweight LoRA sharply improved robustness with minimal capability tradeoff: jailbreak success on 1,988 held-out WildJailbreak prompts dropped from 46% to 7% (≈93% of adversarial prompts converted to rejections) while MMLU changed by only −0.09%, and ASR-noise QA (Spoken-SQuAD) exact match rose from 49.45% to 58.33%.
one_liner: The most interesting result is that an inference-time SAE view of a model’s internal “off-manifold” concept activation can both predict brittleness (from typos to jailbreaks) and provide a targeted, low-impact control knob to harden models without sacrificing benchmark performance.

title: Toward Open Weight Models Without Risks: Separating Public and Private Capabilities in LLMs
Pigeonholing: Bad prompts hurt models to collapse and make mistakes
points: Across 10 models and 10 tasks, introducing erroneous context causes large accuracy regressions—about 38% in math and 40% in coding—showing that benign “bad prompts” can reliably steer strong LLMs into repeating mistakes rather than correcting them.

Pigeonholing severity scales with conversation length: as repeated mistakes in chat history increase from 1 to 5 turns, accuracy drops by an additional 14+ percentage points and models increasingly copy the in-context wrong answer (over 75% of incorrect MCQ outputs match the injected mistake).

Context also induces mode collapse and alignment drift even without errors: providing a sample response can collapse output diversity to 1–2 unique answers in 50 samples (e.g., Gemini 2.5 Pro on PRISM), and stance reversal rises from <5% baseline to 18–28% when an opposite stance appears in context.
one_liner: Multi-turn chat history acts like a steering signal that can amplify small, non-malicious errors into compounding failure—yet training with synthetic contextual errors restores robustness by 43–60% versus standard RLVR/DPO baselines.

title: The Geometry of Refusal: Linear Instability in Safety-Aligned LLMs
points: A single “refusal direction” is linearly extractable via Contrastive Logit Steering (CLS) by contrasting safe vs. unrestricted system prompts, enabling near-instant jailbreaks on late-decision models with up to 95% attack success rate (ASR) in ~1 second.

Safety integration depth strongly predicts robustness: Llama-style models exhibit “Late Decision” behavior (≈95% of layers process harmful vs. benign similarly) and are highly steerable, while Qwen-2.5 shows “Early Divergence” around ~40% depth and remains harder to break (e.g., ~68.5% ASR even at strong steering α=5).

Logit-level steering is both a stronger attack and a practical defense primitive: CLS beats activation steering on HarmBench (Llama 2: 73% vs 22.6% ASR; Qwen 7B: 91% vs 79.2%), while negative steering can drop ASR to single digits (e.g., Llama-3.3 70B: 68.8%→9.4%) and supports zero-shot malicious prompt detection at 0.92 F1.
one_liner: Safety behavior in many aligned LLMs behaves like a removable linear “wrapper” at the output head, making guardrails bypassable (or strengthenable) with simple logit arithmetic rather than prompt search or retraining.

title: MuTRAP: Multi-trigger Trojans Attacking Robot Task Planning Systems
TrojanGYM: A Detector-in-the-Loop LLM for Adaptive RTL Hardware Trojan Insertion
LLM-assisted Generation of Pseudo-C2 Servers for IoT Malware Dynamic Analysis
Inside Crypter-as-a-Service: An Ecosystem Analysis of the exploit.in Underground Forum Research Talks
points: A five-year crawl of exploit.in distilled 491 crypter-related threads (2,949 posts; 1,058 users) and shows CraaS is sold primarily as an operational service requiring frequent stub renewal—sometimes every 24–48 hours—to sustain AV/EDR evasion rather than as a one-off tool purchase.

The marketplace is economically stratified from ultra-low-friction Telegram bot crypting ($5 per build or ~$109/month unlimited, with 4-hour stub cleaning) up to premium subscriptions (~$3,000/month) and full in-house hiring ($5k–$15k/month), indicating a clear tradeoff between scale/price and exclusivity/reliability.

Network structure is highly centralized (a giant component contains ~90% of actors), and among thread starters reputation aligns more with brokerage-style influence (Pearson r=0.501 with betweenness; r=0.455 with PageRank) than with sheer activity (degree Spearman ρ=0.245; Pearson r=0.106, not significant), implying a small set of trust-broker intermediaries can disproportionately shape market access and outcomes.
one_liner: CraaS on exploit.in looks less like “buy an obfuscator” and more like a professionally governed, continuously maintained evasion supply chain where trust brokers and escrow infrastructure are as critical as the code.

title: PYPILINE: Malicious PyPI Package Detection via Suspicious API Knowledge and Agent Workflow
Can LLMs Reason About Brand Ownership? An Empirical Study of Domain Attribution Intelligence
NRT-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-Turn Red-Teaming of LLM Operator Agents in Safety-Critical Control Rooms
How Much Can We Trust LLM Search Agents? Measuring Endorsement Vulnerability to Web Content Manipulation
Honeyquest for LLMs: Rethinking Cyber Deception for AI Attackers
Securing LLM-Agent Long-Term Memory Against Poisoning: Non-Malleable, Origin-Bound Authority with Machine-Checked Guarantees
points: Across eight frontier models, laundering attacks break content- and lineage-based memory defenses exactly where predicted, reaching up to 68% attack success, while the proposed origin-bound, non-malleable authority enforcement achieves 0% attack success on direct and all laundering channels with 100% legitimate-action utility.

A machine-checked TLA+ separation shows that any defense deciding action authority from memory content or malleable provenance edges is unsound under agent-specific laundering (self-summarization, trusted-tool echo, manufactured corroboration), making write-time origin binding necessary and corroboration-gated elevation by ≥2 independent trusted principals sufficient.

Runtime costs strongly favor structural authorization over detection: the act gate adds ~1.3µs per decision with no extra model call versus ~2000ms for an LLM-judge detector, yet detection remains disguise- and model-fragile (e.g., complete failure on one model) and cannot reach the (0% ASR, 100% utility) frontier even when thresholds are swept.
one_liner: The key insight is that long-term memory security is an authorization problem—bind authority to write-time origin and make it non-malleable—rather than a content-detection problem that laundering can always evade.

title: Defense effectiveness across architectural layers: a mechanistic evaluation of persistent memory attacks on stateful LLM agents
Tracing Target Answers in Poisoned Retrieval Corpora via Token Influence Attribution
points: A two-phase token-influence attribution pipeline can detect RAG corpus poisoning without auxiliary classifiers or extra LLM verification while maintaining >90% true-positive detection across nearly all of 6 evaluated LLMs on NQ/HotpotQA/MS-MARCO.

False alarms can be tuned down to <10% false-positive rate in benign settings via recurrence thresholds (a1/a2) while keeping detection robust (≥80% TPR under a balanced configuration and >90% TPR on Phi-4-mini).

The same influence-tracing signal often surfaces the attacker’s intended target answer, achieving ~90% target-answer token identification on NQ and MS-MARCO and >70% on HotpotQA, enabling rapid incident triage beyond binary poisoning flags.
one_liner: Using gradient-based token influence as a retrieval-stage forensic signal yields fast, model-internal poisoning detection that can also reveal the attacker’s injected answer string.
affiliations: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University

title: ShareLock: A Stealthy Multi-Tool Threshold Poisoning Attack Against MCP
points: A threshold-based multi-tool poisoning design can sustain >90% average attack success (ASR@3) while preserving ~96.4% task completion, showing that covert toolchain compromises can remain user-invisible even when agents still complete the requested job.

Distributing a payload as Shamir secret shares across multiple tool descriptions (t=2 in the main evaluation) makes single-tool auditing ineffective and adds fault tolerance—attacks remain viable as long as at least t poisoned tools survive vetting, but drop deterministically to 0% when available shares fall below t (e.g., t=3,n=5 ablation).

Stealth is driven by protocol-level decentralization rather than simple encoding: share-bearing tools were labeled Safe by multiple zero-shot LLM auditors and SFT guard models, while plaintext and encode-only single-tool baselines were flagged Unsafe by zero-shot LLMs, implying that text-only prompt-injection detection breaks down against distributed, metadata-camouflaged payloads.
one_liner: A practical blueprint for turning secret-sharing into a resilient prompt-injection supply-chain attack on MCP: split the instruction, hide the parts in “normal” metadata, and reassemble only at runtime via an innocuous update-trigger.

title: Epistemic Bias Injection: Manipulating LLM Opinion via Selective Context Retrieval
Safety in Self-Evolving LLM Agent Systems: Threats, Amplification, and Case Studies
points: A 5×5 Module–Lifecycle Attack Surface (MLAS) matrix analysis reports 17/25 cells as critical with no effective defenses, 7/25 as high risk with insufficient mitigations, and only 1/25 partially mitigable, with the Self-Design module uniformly catastrophic due to optimizer–optimizee collapse.

Evolution-native design substantially broadens exposure: Hermes activates 3.5× more MLAS cells than an evolution-augmented baseline and exhibits 100% attack persistence (40/40 payloads across CIA+Privacy), while its co-located security scanner blocks only 2.5% (1/40) of attacks on the autonomous evolution pathway.

Self-evolution converts traditionally session-bounded attacks (e.g., prompt injection, tool misuse, memory poisoning) into lineage-persistent threats via seven compounding amplification effects—especially Lamarckian propagation and capability ratchets—implying static, point-in-time defenses will systematically decay without longitudinal monitoring and immutable safety invariants.
one_liner: The most striking result is that autonomous self-evolution turns one-off compromises into durable, self-amplifying lineage takeover, and today’s scanners largely miss the evolution pathway where persistence is created.

title: What the Eyes See, the LLMs Miss: Exploiting Human Perception for Adversarial Text Attacks
Tuning without Peeking: Provable Generalization Bounds and Robust LLM Post-Training
What Does It Mean to Break a Distillation Defense?
points: Output-perturbation distillation defenses are not meaningfully “broken” or “secure” without an explicit threat model, so effectiveness claims should be tied to a concrete (query budget Q, data budget D, interface profile P) tuple.

Even under the original ADS evaluation setup (black-box, Q=D=5,231 GSM8K prompts), free attacker-side post-processing like repetition deletion substantially recovers student accuracy, implying prior baselines overstated ADS’s protection by assuming a non-adaptive attacker.

Small changes in attacker capability can nearly nullify ADS in the high-utility regime (teacher ≥70% GSM8K accuracy): increasing Q to ≥2D largely restores temperature-sampling student performance for smaller perturbations, and adding a single-token response prefill (“First”) yields an additional ~5 percentage-point student accuracy gain and near-complete recovery at higher budgets.
one_liner: A defense that looks strong under “one query per prompt, text-only” can collapse with trivial attacker adaptations—extra queries, simple cleaning, or even a one-token prefill—so threat modeling must be treated as part of the defense spec.

title: When Embedding-Based Defenses Fail: Rethinking Safety in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
MCP-SandboxScan: WASM-based Secure Execution and Runtime Analysis for MCP Tools
Five Queries Are Enough: Query-Efficient and Surrogate-Free Membership Inference Attacks on RAG via Entailment
DEFENGRAPH: Knowledge Graph-Enhanced LLMs for Blue Team Cyber Defense
Investigating The Security of Modern AI and Cloud Infrastructure
points: A three-tier attacker-access taxonomy (shared memory → shared hardware resources → service-only APIs) shows isolation breaks at every layer of the AI+cloud stack, enabling confidentiality leaks, integrity corruption, and control-flow subversion even without traditional software bugs.

Co-located cache side-channels against LLM embedding lookups can recover high-entropy secrets, achieving ~80–90% single-shot leakage of UUID-like API keys on average and full key recovery in as few as 9–18 interactions when monitoring ~200–400 tokens (with ~5% leakage loss per additional 100µs of per-hit overhead).

Joint prompt optimization can simultaneously jailbreak a text-generation model and evade a dedicated guard model, flipping guard “benign” scores from ~0.29–0.52 (primary suffixes) to ~0.86–0.96 (Super Suffixes), while an internal-state detector (DeltaGuard) drives benign scores for those same attacks down to ≤0.07 across tested models by classifying cosine-similarity trajectories to a refusal direction.
one_liner: The most striking takeaway is that both hardware microarchitecture (Rowhammer/caches) and purely remote prompt optimization can bypass modern AI and cloud security assumptions, and internal-representation monitoring offers a practical path to catching what surface-level guardrails miss.

title: Good-Enough LLM Obfuscation (GELO)
A Deterministic Control Plane for LLM Coding Agents
points: A large GitHub prevalence scan (10,008 repos; 6,145 agent-config files) found agent configurations behave like undeclared shared components, with 10.06% of tracked config paths being exact SHA-256 duplicates across independent repositories after fork adjustment and 75.51% of clone pairs crossing organizational boundaries, implying a non-trivial prompt/permission supply-chain attack surface.

Agent-governance artifacts are typically shallow and under-maintained, with 58.45% of agent config files having exactly one lifetime commit (median=1) and a lower age-normalized update rate than CI/CD workflows (0.4 vs 0.6 commits/month; cohort-matched 0.4 vs 0.75), suggesting rules that steer high-authority agents often stagnate relative to other operational policy code.

Permission scoping is rarely declared in agent configs (<1% true positives: 31/6,145 on a fragile parser) despite being common in CI/CD (33.39% of Actions workflows declare explicit scopes), reinforcing the need for deterministic pre-execution enforcement (tiered permissions plus command/path blocklists) rather than relying on harness-level conventions.
one_liner: The striking takeaway is that LLM-agent “rules files” already propagate across orgs like dependencies (10.1% exact duplicates) but are managed far less rigorously than CI/CD policy code, motivating a deterministic, tool-agnostic control layer.

title: FlexServe: A Fast and Secure LLM Serving System for Mobile Devices with Flexible Resource Isolation
points: FlexServe’s recallable, page-granular secure memory (Flex-Mem) cuts 8GB secure-memory allocation latency from 6.44s (CMA contiguous allocation) to 0.57s (~11.3× faster), directly removing a major TrustZone bottleneck for on-device LLM TTFT under memory fragmentation.

By enabling a recallable secure NPU (Flex-NPU) and a secure-world inference framework with pipelined loading/decryption/compute, FlexServe improves average time-to-first-token by 10.05× over a TrustZone strawman and 2.44× over an optimized strawman (with NPU+pipelining), indicating that flexible isolation—not just accelerator access—is the dominant limiter for TEE-protected mobile LLM serving.

Cooperative secure memory management preserves normal-world application performance at 97.2% of the no-inference baseline while achieving the lowest TTFT (where non-cooperative cache policies either inflate TTFT by ~2.54× or substantially degrade app throughput), showing that OS-visible management of protected resources is critical to avoid trading privacy for usability.
one_liner: Decoupling “who can access” from “who can manage” secure memory/NPU lets TrustZone protect LLM weights and runtime data with near-normal performance, even under real mobile memory pressure and multi-model agent workflows.

title: Harness-MU: A Safe, Governed, and Effective Harness for Multi-User LLM Agents
points: A decoupled, model-agnostic harness that enforces authorization and privacy via deterministic execution hooks achieved perfect access-control privacy (Privacy = 1.000 with zero variance) across four frontier LLM backbones, eliminating leakage even under multi-turn adversarial pressure.

The same infrastructure improved helpfulness rather than reducing it, raising access-control utility by 0.28–0.39 and boosting Overall (privacy–utility harmonic mean) from 0.566→0.993 on Deepseek and 0.284→0.637 on GPT by preventing over-conservative refusals while keeping permission boundaries intact.

Authority-aware orchestration substantially increased multi-user instruction-following under both aligned and conflicting directives, with GPT accuracy jumping from 0.422→0.912 (+48.9pp) in aligned settings and 0.309→0.781 (+47.2pp) in conflict settings, indicating infrastructure-level governance can compensate where model reliability is weakest.
one_liner: Multi-user LLM safety becomes far more reliable when governance is moved out of the model and into deterministic, fail-closed runtime infrastructure that isolates per-user context and verifies outputs.
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen

title: $π$-RAG: Oblivious Retrieval via Semantic Quantization and Transcendental Addressing for Large Language Models
points: π-RAG replaces embedding-based vector search with deterministic intent-to-key routing, keeping the LLM in an untrusted zone with zero direct access to sensitive records while a trusted retrieval subsystem executes only pre-registered functions.

A semantic quantization layer maps “fuzzy” user queries to fixed Canonical Intent IDs, and a server-side secret salt is required to derive the π-key pointer, so intercepting the intent (e.g., BK-01) is insufficient to reproduce retrieval without the salt.

In a 6-intent prototype evaluated on 33 queries using Gemma 3:1b and Gemma 3n:e4b, intent misclassifications clustered around overlapping categories and per-query routing latency was reported as under 1 second, indicating practicality but strong dependence on router model quality.
one_liner: An unusual “split-brain” RAG design uses π digits as an immutable indirection layer so retrieval becomes auditable and deterministic while reducing exposure from embedding inversion and prompt-driven data exfiltration.

title: CyberChainBench: Can AI Agents Secure Smart Contracts Against Real-World On-Chain Vulnerabilities?
