points: An on-chain, dynamic benchmark built from 541 real DeFi exploit incidents across 9 EVM chains enables end-to-end evaluation of agent workflows (detect→exploit→patch) with executable oracles, profit-based exploit scoring on historical mainnet forks, and replay-based patch regression tests.

Frontier agent performance shows a steep capability drop from detection (best 37.5%) and exploitation (best 43.7%) to patch synthesis (best 23.4% pass rate), indicating that producing functional, non-breaking fixes remains the primary bottleneck even when agents can successfully find and weaponize vulnerabilities.

Exploit-capable configurations can realize large economic impact at low marginal cost—Codex×GPT-5.5 achieved a 0.44 average profit ratio and $57.4M total profit over a 200-case exploit set at ~$2.39 per case—while patch “block-only” behavior can be misleading (e.g., 98.9% exploit block rate but 1.1% full pass rate), underscoring the need for regression-validated patch metrics rather than exploit-blocking alone.
one_liner: The most striking result is that agents can generate profitable, executable on-chain exploits cheaply, but reliably patching without breaking legitimate behavior lags far behind detection and exploitation.

title: Exposing the Illusion of Erasure in Knowledge Editing for LLMs
points: Universal adversarial suffixes can bypass multiple popular knowledge-editing methods, achieving >85% exact-match recovery of the original (pre-edit) fact in context-guided elicitation across tested models, indicating edits frequently mask rather than remove knowledge.

Even with no semantic prompt template, blind reconstruction recovers full edit triplets at 15%–48.5% in white-box settings (and can reach 47.5% when extracting only old/new objects), showing that edited models retain extractable structural signatures of the intervention.

Mechanistic probes show low-rank edits mainly affect a small subspace and act as targeted suppression (e.g., intervention logits penalize the old answer while boosting the new one), producing anisotropic “trench-like” solutions that are brittle to prompt perturbations and undermine privacy-style unlearning (e.g., PII extraction succeeds up to 92% under context-guided attacks while standard extraction baselines achieve ~6%).
one_liner: Post-hoc knowledge editing often creates an illusion of erasure: the old fact remains inside the model and can be systematically re-exposed with transferable adversarial triggers.
affiliations: Birla Institute of Technology and Science, Goa

title: Agent-Assisted Side-Channel Attacks on Non-Prefix KV Cache in RAG
points: Non-prefix KV-cache fusion in multi-tenant RAG introduces a deterministic “Step-Wave” TTFT timing signature that leaks hidden private-prefix length with near single-token precision by combining per-chunk routing cost (~38.6 ms/chunk) and tail recomputation slope (~0.13 ms/token, intra-group r≈0.91).

SpliceLeak turns this structural leakage into end-to-end semantic recovery by inducing boundary collisions and using an extraction agent to recover tokens right-to-left, reaching up to 100% extraction success in bounded-entropy settings with as few as 63 requests per token and a stable hardware-driven latency gap of about +104 ms (and up to +1057 ms in targeted cloze-style probes).

A two-part mitigation (Quantized Chunk Padding + Constant-Time Boundary Fusion) effectively removes the oracle by flattening the TTFT differential (reported ∆TTFT≈0, empirically driven near-zero/negative residuals) while preserving cross-tenant cache-sharing benefits with negligible throughput/latency overhead (e.g., <1% TTFT increase in the reported setup).
one_liner: A real-world RAG performance optimization (non-prefix KV fusion) accidentally creates a high-SNR timing oracle that enables token-by-token recovery of “private” system prompts unless boundary fusion is made constant-time.
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China

title: Red-Teaming the Agentic Red-Team
points: A manipulation technique that avoids explicit prompt-injection payloads (“agent-phishing”) achieved worker code execution in 97.8% of runs across 10 evaluated agentic red-teaming tools and 6 frontier LLMs, with failures largely due to models refusing to start the pentest rather than resisting the exploit path.

Across 12 popular open-source agentic offensive-security systems, common architectural flaws enabled sandbox escape and host compromise in most cases (10/12 achieved some host escape and 8/12 reached full host RCE), showing that containerization alone is not a meaningful safety boundary when workers have elevated capabilities or host-adjacent interfaces.

Guardrails were ineffective at preventing misuse: all tested systems were susceptible to unbounded weaponization once the worker was compromised, and secrets were exfiltratable in 11/12 systems (often due to flat architectures, shared tokens, or weak inter-container isolation), implying enforcement must move to OS-level controls plus strict least-privilege segmentation.
one_liner: Offensive-security agents are a high-risk pivot: a target you scan can reliably turn your own agent infrastructure (and often your host) into the compromised system unless you design for containment under the assumption the LLM will misbehave.

title: Signature filtering: a lightweight enhancement for statistical watermark detection in large language models
Detect, Unlearn, Restore: Defending Text Summarization Models Against Data Poisoning
points: Influence-function ranking plus semantic consistency checks identifies fine-tuning-stage poisoned document–summary pairs with ~85–92% detection precision (and ~86–94% recall in reported settings) by exploiting the fact that effective poisons disproportionately concentrate in the top-20% most influential training samples.

A purely post-hoc remediation step—gradient-ascent unlearning on detected poisons—restores up to 96% of pre-poison behavior while keeping summarization utility essentially unchanged (reported <0.6% ROUGE degradation), offering a practical alternative to full retraining across multiple model families and datasets.

In black-box auditing, poisoned summarization models show a robust behavioral signature: 2–3× higher sensitivity to semantics-preserving perturbations (SAP), enabling near-perfect detection reported as 100% TPR with 0% FPR at a fixed threshold across nine architectures and six datasets, including under adaptive attacks (≈95–98% TPR).
one_liner: Training-time poisoning leaves measurable, persistent artifacts—high training influence and amplified perturbation sensitivity—that can be detected and mostly reversed after deployment without full retraining.
affiliations: The University of Texas at Arlington

title: Are Frontier LLMs Ready for Cybersecurity? Evidence for Vertical Foundation Models from Dual-Mode Vulnerability Benchmarks
Improved Pseudorandom Codes from Permuted Puzzles
Multi-Agent LLM Governance for Safe Two-Timescale Reinforcement Learning in SDN-IoT Defense
Inherited Circuits, Learned Semantics: How Fine-Tuning Creates Evasion Vulnerabilities Invisible to Standard Evaluation
points: A fine-tuned PowerShell malware classifier can retain perfect held-out in-distribution accuracy (Foundation-Sec 100% vs Llama 95.3% on a matched 74-pair set) yet become systematically evadable under behavior-preserving transformations, including 4/4 misses on Invoke-WebRequest→iwr aliasing and 9/63 misses on case-mutation variants where the base model had 0/63 misses.

Causal interventions localize most malicious-vs-benign evidence to an inherited late attention bundle (Layer-12 heads) whose patching removes ~81% of the malicious decision margin (mean effect ≈−3.824) and flips 29.7% of labels (87/293), implying fine-tuning often reweights and specializes existing circuits rather than creating new detectors.

A cheap pre-deployment drift signal can flag transformation-sensitive families without generating evasive samples: a linear probe at the resid_pre13 boundary predicts key head contributions strongly (r=0.80–0.87) and an indicator-token ablation sign test identifies role reversals (Invoke-WebRequest flips from driver in Llama, −1.60, to suppressor in Foundation-Sec, +1.13, with 73.7% of scripts positive), which correctly prioritizes where red-teaming should focus.
one_liner: Security fine-tuning can turn inherited transformer circuits into brittle indicator-token rules that look great on standard tests but expand the real evasion surface under simple, behavior-preserving rewrites.

title: Evaluating LLMs for Real-World Web Vulnerability Detection
Representation Matters: An Empirical Study of Program Representations for LLM Vulnerability Reasoning
points: Switching from raw source code prompts (53.5% curated accuracy) to structural graph prompts dramatically improves LLM vulnerability classification, with the best representation (AST+PDG) reaching 83.2%—a +29.7 percentage-point gain on 107 real-world C/C++ testcases across five CWE types.

Graph-only prompts are both more accurate and far cheaper than source-plus-graph prompts, achieving 74.4% curated accuracy at ~5,973 input tokens on average versus 69.4% at ~12,938 tokens (2.2× more tokens) and a 59.9% clipping rate, indicating that extra raw code context often harms rather than helps.

A measurable “context dilution” effect appears: adding raw source to compact graph evidence can reduce performance even without truncation, implying that static-analysis-derived representations can act as a semantic compression layer that improves signal-to-noise for security reasoning.
one_liner: Program representation is a first-order control knob for LLM vulnerability reasoning—compact AST/PDG graphs can beat raw source while using roughly half the tokens, and more context can actively degrade results.

title: RAVEN: Agentic RAG for Automated Vulnerability Repair
points: A locally deployable agentic RAG pipeline combining historical fix retrieval, cross-file dependency curation, and iterative review/validation reaches an 83.13% overall repair success rate on 160 real-world CVEs across Java and C, indicating that open-source LLMs can be competitive with proprietary repair agents at substantially lower operational cost.

Multi-axis evaluation shows strong generalization beyond “localized” memory bugs, including 86.75% success across 10 Java CWE categories (83 CVEs), 86.94% success on C out-of-bounds read and incorrect authorization (29 CVEs), and 65.22% success on 23 out-of-distribution Vul4J CVEs spanning mostly unseen CWEs, implying retrieval + repository context is a key lever for robustness to unseen vulnerability classes.

Efficiency measurements in a fully local setup average ~7–8 minutes per vulnerability with the context-retrieval stage dominating usage (~99.5k tokens and ~155s on average), suggesting the main scaling bottleneck is repository-level dependency discovery rather than patch synthesis itself.
one_liner: An agentic RAG repair stack using medium-sized open-source LLMs achieves high CVE fix rates while keeping deployment local and costs negligible, with cross-file context curation emerging as the dominant driver of both capability and runtime.

title: Revelio: Cost-Efficient Agentic Memory Safety Vulnerability Detection For Repository-Scale Codebases
points: A two-stage agentic workflow that generates broad vulnerability hypotheses with cheap models and then requires sanitizer-verified Proof-of-Vulnerability (PoV) confirmation achieved zero false positives while scaling to repository-sized C/C++ codebases.

Across seven mature OSS-Fuzz projects continuously fuzzed for 5–8 years, the system found 19 previously unknown memory-safety vulnerabilities (7 CVEs) in a median ~65 minutes and ~$42 per project, totaling ~$300 (~$16 per validated vuln).

On 100 CyberGym/Arvo projects, it validated 175 vulnerabilities with 69% recall of the known bugs at ~$9.10 per vuln, outperforming frontier coding agents (55/39/31 vulns) while those baselines exhibited substantial false-positive rates (49–60% vs 0%).
one_liner: Turning LLM vulnerability claims into trustworthy findings is largely an engineering problem: enforce a hypothesis→PoV pipeline and let sanitizers, not the model, be the final arbiter.

title: Mind your key: An Empirical Study of LLM API Credential Leakage in iOS Apps
Decoupling Reconnaissance and Exploitation: Measuring the Capability Boundaries of LLM-Based Web Penetration Testing
points: A two-stage decoupled protocol (reconnaissance vs. exploitation) exposes that LLM pentest agents can reach up to 90.0% Functional Success Rate (FSR) when given correct vulnerability context, implying current systems are execution-capable but evaluation is often confounded by upstream perception errors.

Autonomous reconnaissance is the dominant bottleneck, with Targeted Vulnerability Recall (TVR) commonly plateauing around ~50% without prior knowledge due to failures parsing noisy/unstructured telemetry, meaning end-to-end black-box results systematically underestimate true exploit capability via error cascading.

A Verified Empirical Knowledge Base (VEKB) materially lifts both stages (e.g., Hexstrike-AI + Gemini 3 Pro FSR 61.4%→81.4% and TVR 54.3%→87.1%), while architecture still determines “capability niches” (e.g., isolation-heavy multi-agent designs better on long-horizon deserialization chains, and graph-driven designs better on cross-session access-control reasoning).
one_liner: Decoupling recon from exploit shows today’s LLM pentest agents fail more on seeing the bug than on exploiting it, and verified knowledge plus state isolation closes much of the gap.
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China
Suzhou Institute for Advanced Research, University of Science and Technology of China
Nanjing University of Science and Technology

title: Understanding the (In)Security of Vibe-Coded Applications
points: In a random sample of 200 publicly deployed vibe-coded web apps, 90% contained at least one exploitable vulnerability (median 7 per vulnerable repo), showing insecurity is the norm rather than driven by a few outliers.

Vulnerability impact is often severe—76.7% of 1,471 validated issues were High/Critical—with risk concentrated in trust-boundary failures (Broken Access Control 36.0%, Cryptographic Failures 20.7%, Injection 17.7% comprising 74.4% total) and predominantly in backend code (62.7%).

Root causes cluster into systematic lifecycle defects rather than isolated coding mistakes, led by “hidden security rules” knowledge gaps (43.9% of all vulns) plus objective-driven shortcuts and memory failures, and while mitigations help (production-ready prompts cut replayed vuln reintroduction from 40% to 13%; self-check prompts to 18%), no single intervention eliminated all repeated failures and agents still shipped insecure code despite recognizing risk in 32% of vulnerable runs.
one_liner: Vibe coding pushes end-to-end app delivery to agents, but the dominant failure mode is missing implicit security obligations at trust boundaries—so quick prompt tweaks help, yet systemic workflow and responsibility gaps keep high-severity vulns recurring.
affiliations: CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security

title: Verifiable Manifest Signing and Transparency Enforcement for Secure MCP-Based LLM Pipelines
Poisoned Playbooks: Demystifying Knowledge Poisoning Effects on AI Security Agents
points: A single injected “Poisoned Playbook” can systematically redirect RAG-based security agents’ exploit behavior (not just their answers) across 11 CTF tasks, 3 frontier LLM families, 2 model generations, and 11 real-world CVEs, showing a low-cost 1→N integrity risk in the security-knowledge supply chain.

Poison adoption is structured by the “Verification Boundary”: claims refutable from local artifacts are reliably rejected (L1), claims checkable only via model prior knowledge are model/generation-dependent (L2), and runtime-/dependency-dependent claims are consistently adopted (L3), implying zero-day and sparse-evidence regimes are intrinsically most vulnerable.

On real-world CVEs, well-documented vulnerabilities show 0% poison adoption while post-cutoff runtime-dependent CVE poisons show 100% adoption (7/7), and mitigations like verification prompting and multi-source retrieval help only when stronger counter-evidence exists but weaken under information monopoly and sparse-evidence conditions.
one_liner: RAG makes public security write-ups an operational attack surface where unverifiable runtime claims can reliably steer autonomous vulnerability reasoning, especially in zero-day-like evidence gaps.

title: How Your Credentials Are Leaked by LLM Agent Skills: An Empirical Study
FirmCure:Towards Autonomous and Adaptive Rehosting of Linux-Based Firmware
points: An LLM-orchestrated, closed-loop rehosting pipeline (static dependency inference → boot-time reflective repair → runtime multi-agent intervention) achieved 100% kernel boot, 100% network bring-up, and 100% port activation across 21 Linux-based IoT firmware images spanning 10 vendors and 5 architectures, indicating that semantic + feedback-driven adaptation can eliminate most template/heuristic brittleness in full-system emulation.

End-to-end service interactivity reached 90.5% (19/21) versus 9.5% for FirmAE and Greenhouse and 19.0% for Firmwell, showing that runtime fault diagnosis and targeted remediation (e.g., bypassing hardware checks, fixing filesystem/config drift, web-root/path reconciliation) is the primary lever for crossing the “port-open but non-interactive” barrier.

A stable interactive rehosting substrate enabled practical security outcomes—10/10 targeted CVEs were reproduced and 5 new vulnerabilities were found in commercial firmware—demonstrating that autonomous rehosting directly translates into higher vulnerability analysis throughput and broader device coverage without physical hardware.
one_liner: Turning firmware rehosting into an agentic feedback-control loop (with runtime interventions, not just static analysis) is enough to move from ~10–20% interaction to ~90% interaction at scale across heterogeneous IoT firmware.

title: Empirical Software Engineering TerraProbe: A Layered-Oracle Framework for Detecting Deceptive Fixes in LLM-Assisted Terraform
points: A five-layer oracle shows that apparent repair success collapses from 83.3% targeted-finding removal to just 10.4% full-scanner cleanliness and 39.6% producing a valid terraform plan, demonstrating that scanner-only pass rates dramatically overstate trustworthy security repair.

On real-world Terraform modules, 71.4% of plan-compared repairs are deceptive fixes that pass every automated oracle yet preserve the original vulnerability, and these deceptive-fix rates are statistically indistinguishable across Gemini-2.5-flash-lite, GPT-4o, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet (57.1%–71.4%, all pairwise Fisher p>0.10), implying a systemic failure mode rather than a model-specific weakness.

IAM-level inspection confirms concrete security non-improvement: in all 9 CKV2 AWS 11 deceptive-fix cases the wildcard Resource="*" permission remains post-repair (unmitigated privilege-escalation risk), highlighting the need for intent-level gates such as plan-diff review and IAM policy simulation rather than relying on static-check disappearance.
one_liner: Layered oracles expose that LLM “repairs” can reliably make scanners go quiet while leaving cloud permissions just as dangerous.

title: The Tatoxa System for Text Detoxification in Low-Resource Languages: The Case of Tatar
points: Tatoxa achieves the top automatic detoxification performance for Tatar with J=0.695 (CLEF-Tatar) and J=0.680 (new dataset) while reaching very high non-toxicity accuracy (STA=98.2% and 97.0%), demonstrating that targeted low-resource pipelines can beat both open and proprietary LLM baselines on safety-critical rewriting.

A small amount of native Tatar supervision materially changes outcomes: the added 701 gold toxic→neutral pairs are majority high-toxicity (57%) and mostly require rewriting rather than deletion (607/701, 86.6%), implying that effective detoxification in low-resource settings is primarily a generation/editing problem, not just a keyword-removal problem.

Cross-lingual transfer is unreliable even from culturally/linguistically close sources: fine-tuning on Tatar data yields the best cross-lingual J=0.5598, while Russian transfer is among the worst (J=0.4897) and even a large multilingual mix ranks below French-only transfer (0.5415 vs 0.5567), indicating that in-language data and culturally grounded toxicity cues dominate over resource size or proximity.
one_liner: A translation-synthesis + filtering + candidate-ranking pipeline can make Tatar detoxification robust enough to outperform strong proprietary LLMs, while cross-lingual transfer (including from Russian) remains a weak substitute for native data.
affiliations: Institute of Applied Semiotics Tatarstan Academy of Sciences

title: HelpBench: Assessing the Ability of LLMs to Provide Privacy, Safety, and Security Advice
points: Across 18 state-of-the-art LLMs evaluated on 450 realistic privacy/safety/security (PSS) help-seeking questions, average advice quality was 82% but 14% of responses scored below 65%, evidencing a persistent long tail of inaccurate or harmful guidance.

Topic difficulty is uneven and statistically significant across models, with scams scoring highest on average (88%) while moderation-tool guidance is lowest (77%), implying safety-critical deployments need topic-aware reliability gating rather than a single global trust threshold.

The benchmark’s rubric+auto-rater approach scales evaluation to 40,500 responses with strong agreement to expert scoring (Pearson r=0.85 overall; 0.96 factual vs 0.78 delivery), enabling continuous monitoring that can pinpoint failures like unsafe advice in at-risk contexts and ToS-evading recommendations.
one_liner: Even top models that look strong on average still produce a non-trivial tail of low-scoring, potentially harmful PSS advice—making consistency, not just mean score, the key safety bottleneck.

title: RepSelect: Robust LLM Unlearning via Representation Selectivity
Governance Decay: How Context Compaction Silently Erases Safety Constraints in Long-Horizon LLM Agents
points: Context compaction turns fully compliant long-horizon agents into policy violators by raising tool-call constraint violations from 0% (policy visible) to 30% on average and up to 59% across 7 model families and 1,323 episodes, despite no change in model or user request.

Whether the governance rule survives the summary is almost perfectly predictive of safety—violations are 0% when the constraint survives compaction but jump to 38–43% when it is dropped—showing the harness’s summarizer/evictor is the dominant safety-critical component.

Deletion-focused prompt injection against the compaction step can reliably erase constraints and defeat “robust” models (e.g., 0%→65% on a model resistant to a fixed probe), while a training-free mitigation (Constraint Pinning) restores violations to 0% with <0.5% token overhead but still fails under operator-impersonation unless authority is enforced out-of-band.
one_liner: The surprising risk is that the memory/summarization layer—not the base model—can silently delete deployment-specific policies and thereby flip an agent from 0% to majority-rate violations, yet a small harness-only change can largely eliminate the issue.

title: Memory Contagion: Cross-Temporal Propagation of Evaluator Bias via Agent Memory
points: Biased trajectories stored in agent memory can drive measurable future behavior shifts even under perfect (oracle) consolidation, with length-preference contagion reaching Γ=13.18 (95% CI [9.05, 21.10], p<0.01) on DeepSeek V4-Chat, implying that biased input alone is sufficient to create cross-temporal bias propagation.

Contagion is strongly bias- and model-dependent: length bias propagates robustly on DeepSeek V4-Chat but is absent on newer/higher-capability models (DeepSeek V4-Pro and Claude Sonnet 4.6 both Γ=0.00), while authority bias fails to propagate in 15 controlled multi-seed runs (Γ=0.00), indicating this vulnerability is not universal across biases or model generations.

No safe contamination threshold was observed because detectable propagation appears with as little as 20% biased memories (p=0.2), and LLM summarization-based consolidation can partially mitigate susceptible cases by reducing length contagion ~84% (Γ drops from 13.18 to 2.03), suggesting memory pipelines must audit and filter inputs rather than relying on better consolidation alone.
one_liner: Externalized agent memory can act like a time-delayed channel that carries evaluator bias forward—even into agents with unbiased evaluators—unless the model/memory pipeline is specifically resistant.

title: AutoRAS: Learning Robust Agentic Systems with Primitive Representations
RIFT-Bench: Dynamic Red-teaming For Agentic AI Systems
points: A code-grounded NodeSpec representation enabled automated, unified red-teaming across 45 heterogeneous agentic systems, with structure extraction quality remaining high overall (0.934±0.097 node-alignment coverage and 0.966±0.044 code-reference overlap).

RIFT-Bench scaled to 105 reusable probes that instantiated into >10,000 attack tests, and scanning showed attacks were usually exercised in practice (attack activation rate 0.789–0.893 by domain) while still achieving substantial objective success (deterministic ASR 0.145–0.333 by domain, up to 0.669 on a wild system).

Mitigation evaluation surfaced explicit safety–utility trade-offs: a simple “description removal” defense drove a targeted description-injection attack from AAR=1.0/ASR=0.333 to AAR=0.0/ASR=0.0 but reduced task utility from 0.947 to 0.744 and increased execution drift from 0.082 to 0.131, implying defenses can ‘work’ while materially degrading agent usefulness.
one_liner: A system-structure graph (NodeSpec) makes agent red-teaming portable, letting the same probe templates automatically adapt to a new codebase and reveal where defenses cut risk at the cost of capability.
affiliations: Fujitsu Research of India Pvt. Ltd. (FRIPL)

title: Escaping the Self-Confirmation Trap: An Execute-Distill-Verify Paradigm for Agentic Experience Learning
points: EDV’s decoupled Execute–Distill–Verify pipeline (heterogeneous parallel rollouts + third‑party contrastive distillation + consensus validation) reduces “wrong-but-self-consistent” memory insertion and yields higher downstream success than single-agent experience loops and inference-time ensembling alone.

On τ2-bench, EDV achieves 86.6 Pass@1 vs 83.5 (Router) and 81.5 (Judge), and on MMTB reaches 58.10 overall vs 55.96 (Router), indicating that improving memory construction quality can outperform purely routing/judging-based test-time scaling.

Memory reliability is operationally critical: injecting just 10% erroneous yet coherent memories drops ReasoningBank’s τ2-bench RETAIL Pass@1 from 82.5 to 77.2 (−5.3), while EDV’s audited memory improves correctness/groundedness (3.72→4.41) and halves potential harm if reused (1.08→0.51) on a 5-point rubric.
one_liner: EDV shows that multi-agent role separation plus strict consensus gating can turn agent memory from a self-reinforcing liability into a measurable reliability boost on long-horizon tasks.
affiliations: Shenzhen International Graduate School, Tsinghua University
University of Science and Technology of China

title: Open-source LLMs administer maximum electric shocks in a Milgram-like obedience experiment
SycoEval-EM: Sycophancy Evaluation of Large Language Models in Simulated Clinical Encounters for Emergency Care
FinRED: An Expert-Guided Benchmark Generation and Evaluation Framework for Financial LLM Red-Teaming
OTTER: A Red-Teaming System for Toxicity-Evading Jailbreak Prompt Optimization
A Red Teaming Framework for Large Language Models: A Case Study on Faithfulness Evaluation
points: A multi-role attacker–target–jury pipeline with ensemble judging and inter-judge reliability (Fleiss’ κ) scales automated faithfulness testing to 24,000+ English Q&A and 192,000 Arabic evaluations while reducing reliance on human labels.

Exploitative prompts that embed false premises raise question-answering unfaithfulness to 7.6–7.9% ASR versus 3.35–3.85% for “challenging” prompts, showing that subtle premise manipulation is a reliably effective black-box attack on context-grounded accuracy.

Simple structural constraints act as a practical mitigation: imposing a 50-word limit in Arabic summarization cuts unfaithfulness from 7.20% to 5.04% (≈30% relative reduction, z=3.21, p=0.0013) without retraining, while observed results also suggest model design choices can outweigh parameter scaling (e.g., Llama-3.1-70B showing comparable or higher unfaithfulness than 8B in some settings).
one_liner: A modular red-teaming setup turns faithfulness into a measurable, automatable attack surface—then shows that lightweight output constraints can meaningfully reduce hallucination without changing the model.
affiliations: King Fahd University of Petroleum & Minerals
SDAIA-KFUPM Joint Research Center for Artificial Intelligence

title: Security and Privacy in Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Architectures, Threats, Defenses, and Future Directions for Building Trustworthy Systems
points: RAG expands the effective attack surface from a single LLM to a multi-stage pipeline (retrieval → context construction → generation) where persistent threats like retrieval poisoning and indirect prompt injection can systematically steer outputs by corrupting what evidence is retrieved and packed.

Privacy leakage in RAG can occur even without exposing raw documents because observable retrieval signals (e.g., top‑k results, scores, citations, and hit-rate patterns) enable membership/index inference and are compounded by federated-update leakage (gradient leakage, Sybil/collusion) in distributed deployments.

No single mechanism is sufficient: practical trustworthiness requires defense-in-depth (guardrails + retrieval protections + privacy-aware context assembly + generation verification + monitoring), with explicit privacy–utility trade-offs where stronger protections (DP, secure aggregation, encrypted retrieval/SMPC) typically increase latency/communication or reduce retrieval accuracy.
one_liner: The most actionable takeaway is that “context construction” (ordering/truncation within finite windows) is a first-class security boundary in RAG, not just an engineering detail.
affiliations: Birla Institute of Technology and Science, Pilani

title: Account-History Features for Social Bot Detection in the Era of Large Language Models
TRACE: A Threat Modelling Methodology for Distributed, Cloud-First, and Decentralized Organisations
points: TRACE reframes threat modeling around five evidence-linked primitives—threat actors, roles, assets, critical invariants, and trust/authority edges—so distributed authority, control-plane/supply-chain compromise, and authorized-but-malicious actions become explicit rather than “out of scope.”

A comparative matrix across nine common frameworks and ten dimensions indicates none natively covers critical invariants, distributed privileged authority, collusion, cloud/SaaS control-plane risk, and human/operational failure in one coherent workflow, while TRACE claims first-class support across all ten dimensions.

The methodology operationalizes safer human–AI co-working via sequential review gates and traceability constraints (every model object, threat, attack-tree node, and recommendation must link to sources or be labeled as an assumption), explicitly targeting automation-bias failure modes like plausible-but-unsupported architectures and generic perimeter-era threat lists.
one_liner: What stands out is a perimeter-free threat-modeling pipeline that treats authority graphs, invariants, and collusion surfaces as first-class objects, then constrains LLM assistance with evidence traceability and human approval gates.

title: PolicyAlign: Direct Policy-Based Safety Alignment for Large Language Models
A Survey of Toxicity Detection and Mitigation Strategies for Multilingual Language Models
points: Multilingual safety failures are systematically induced by language-shift prompts, translation pivots, code-switching/transliteration, multi-turn interactions, and post-deployment fine-tuning, implying that English-only, single-turn evaluations substantially underestimate real-world toxic-output risk.

Multilingual detoxification coverage is broadening (e.g., RTP-LX spans 28 languages, PTP 17 languages with 425K prompts, and TextDetox/PAN covers 9 languages), but fragmented label schemas and culturally contingent definitions of harm make cross-benchmark comparisons unreliable without shared protocols and native-speaker validation.

Mitigations (data filtering, SFT/RLHF/preference tuning, decoding-time steering, representation editing, and guardrails) reduce overt toxicity but can over-suppress legitimate dialectal or identity-related expression, creating a safety–equity trade-off that is amplified in low-resource and code-mixed settings.
one_liner: What stands out is the end-to-end taxonomy tying multilingual attack surfaces (translation, code-switching, adaptation) to detox pipelines while emphasizing that evaluation gaps and cultural misalignment—not just model capability—are the dominant blockers to globally reliable toxicity mitigation.

title: Rising From the Ashes: How Agentic AI is Unblocking Challenges in Cybersecurity
points: Cybersecurity incident costs are estimated at 0.001%–9% of global GDP, underscoring that scaling defenses hinges on reducing labor/latency/expertise bottlenecks rather than inventing entirely new primitives.

A capability-to-challenge mapping argues that five agentic AI traits—natural-language understanding, high-volume information processing, cognitive stamina, generalization/replicability, and multidisciplinary knowledge—can systematically mitigate five adoption blockers (excessive human effort, unattainably low latency, scarce expertise, task-specific solutions, and problem complexity).

Across 16 defensive case studies (from instrumentation optimization and formalizing standards to SBOM/supply-chain analysis, provenance triage at hundreds of millions of events/day, and self-healing systems), agentic AI is positioned to convert previously non-scalable expert workflows into parallelizable, repeatable pipelines—but only if agent autonomy and privileged tool access are secured to avoid amplifying AI-specific vulnerabilities.
one_liner: Agentic AI is framed as a force multiplier that can resurrect stalled security ideas by making expertise replicable and low-latency reasoning practical, while simultaneously creating a new requirement to secure the agents themselves.

title: SoK: AI Secure Code Generation: Progress, Pitfalls, and Paths Forward
points: A three-layer KAUGE framework shows secure-coding-principle understanding (6,382 fixed-answer questions from 456 OWASP/CERT rules) is high across models (lowest mean 86.2%) yet consistently exceeds executable secure generation, exposing a large knowledge–actuation gap of ~47.9 points on function tasks (CWEval) and ~72.9 points on web apps (BaxBench).

Natural-language understanding of secure coding principles is a strong predictor of executable secure outcomes (Spearman ρ=0.71, p=0.025 on CWEval secure-pass@k; ρ=0.63, p=0.056 on BaxBench), but models often fail at applying defenses at the correct implementation boundary even when they can correctly identify the relevant principle.

Mechanism-aware diagnosis reveals why pass/fail metrics mislead: among functional outputs, “secure-only” cases (secure but not SCP-compliant) outnumber “compliant-only” cases (compliant but vulnerable) by 1,100 vs 287 (p<0.001), showing security can arise via unmodeled defenses while apparent principle compliance can still miss sink-specific exploit details.
one_liner: The interesting twist is that models largely “know” secure coding in natural language, but the hard problem is reliably actuating that knowledge into boundary-correct, functionality-preserving defenses under executable exploits.

title: AgentRiskBOM: A Risk-Scoping Security Bill of Materials for Agentic AI Systems
points: A JSON-schema “authority envelope” for tool-using agents achieves 14/16 native capability-dimension coverage versus 1.0 (SBOM), 1.5 (AI-BOM), and 2.0 (ML-BOM), making autonomy, tool permissions, credential scope, approvals, memory persistence, and audit signals first-class review objects rather than implicit configuration.

Across 52 risk scenarios in 14 categories and 13 open-source agents, the artifact provides 100.0% modeled risk-category visibility compared with 10.5% for SBOM-like views and 20.9% for AI-BOM-like views, turning operational risks (e.g., unsafe external actions, inter-agent trust propagation, missing approvals/logging, and overprivileged credentials) into pre-deployment checkable fields.

Structured “authority drift” becomes mechanically gateable: a diff detector correctly classified all 33 injected deployment mutations, and an independent penalty-based scorer shows rank-level robustness with Spearman 0.73 (despite only 46% label agreement), implying scores work best for triage and change detection rather than automated certification.
one_liner: The most actionable shift is treating delegated agent authority (tools, permissions, memory, approvals, and auditability) as a versioned, diffable bill-of-materials that can be enforced in CI/CD before incidents occur.

title: PolicyGuard: Towards Test-time and Step-level Adversary (Backdoor) Defense for Reinforcement Learning Agent
Next-Gen CAPTCHAs: Leveraging the Cognitive Gap for Scalable and Diverse GUI-Agent Defense
Whose Agent Are You? Multi-Layer Fingerprinting and Attribution of Autonomous Web Agents
FALCON: Transforming Cyber Threat Intelligence into Deployable IDS Rules with Self-Reflection
AOHP: An Open-Source OS-Level Agent Harness for Personalized, Efficient and Secure Interaction
points: An Android OS-level “agent harness” that treats agents as first-class OS actors improved mobile agent performance on 30 cross-app tasks, increasing checkpoint-weighted completion from 54.44% to 75.56% (+21.12 points) and fully solving 7 additional tasks versus stock Android.

On the 11 tasks both systems completed successfully, the harness reduced operational overhead by 44.64% fewer tool calls, 44.21% lower runtime (33.94→18.93 minutes), 51.55% fewer tokens (7.10M→3.44M), and 47.62% fewer LLM requests (273→143), indicating that OS-native structured interfaces and background execution materially lower agent cost-to-complete.

Default-redaction plus vault-mediated execution and taint tracking prevented private plaintext exposure while still enabling legitimate actions, passing five policy checks (sensitive display, ordinary actions, sensitive actions requiring consent, fail-closed on unsupported access, and redacted/tainted sensitive event streams) in an annotated payment-app case study.
one_liner: Making agents OS-native—via composable services, structured UI/event streams, and system-enforced information-flow control—simultaneously boosts task success and cuts LLM runtime/token costs while tightening privacy guarantees.

title: Data Facts: A Metadata Schema for Structured Data Exchange in the NANDini Multi-Agent Ecosystem
points: Adding a single data_facts_url pointer to agent registry records enables structured dataset discovery plus on-demand freshness (TTL) and integrity (SHA-256) checks with 100% retrieval success and only ~260–270 ms extra time-to-first-data from two additional HTTP round-trips.

Live data access via the schema and access pipeline eliminates prior-driven guesswork on counter-intuitive queries, delivering 100% decision accuracy (420/420) versus 35.2% without data access (p < 0.001) across 840 evaluations and remaining robust across 1–3 agent delegation hops.

Safety controls are measurable and effective: TTL enforcement cuts stale-data decision errors from 37.6% to 8.8% (76.6% stale detection, FP=0), checksum verification detects 100% of injected corruption (1%–50%), and the JWT+capability-gateway+A2A delegation stack blocks 100% of 46 forgery attempts with zero observed data leakage.
one_liner: A minimal metadata pointer plus TTL and cryptographic checks can turn multi-agent data exchange into a verifiable, access-controlled pipeline that dramatically improves correctness while actively resisting tampering and credential forgery.

title: OGD4All: A Framework for Accessible Interaction with Geospatial Open Government Data Based on Large Language Models
Sovereign Execution Broker: Enforcing Certificate-Bound Authority in Agentic Control Planes
HardSecBench: Benchmarking the Security Awareness of LLMs for Hardware Code Generation
VeriPort: Automated and Verified Patch Backporting at Scale
points: An agentic backporting pipeline that isolates minimal security hunks and gates every patch with both exploit and regression “oracles” achieved 95.3% reliability across 10 runs on 128 BackportBench tasks without an upstream MSP, beating the strongest baseline by 22.7 percentage points and reaching 100% pass@10.

At npm ecosystem scale, the system solved 91.3% of 393 CVEPatchBench tasks reliably across 3 runs versus 71.1% for Claude Code (a 20.2-point gain), while also showing far lower run-to-run variance (2.3 points vs 9.5), indicating materially better operational stability for automated remediation.

Production deployment generated 5,000+ verified backported patches for 169 high/critical CVEs and empirically corrected advisory metadata by flagging 2,100 falsely listed affected versions and 127 missed vulnerable versions across 92 advisories, leading to 23 upstream advisory fixes (−387 versions, +81 versions).
one_liner: Verified patch backporting becomes practical when LLM-generated fixes are treated as untrusted drafts and only shipped after independent, executable exploit-blocking and functionality-preserving evidence passes per version.

title: One Goal, Many Commands: Characterizing Denylist Fragility in AI Agents
Agent Skill Framework: Perspectives on the Potential of Small to Medium Language Models in Industrial Environments
Firewalls to Secure Dynamic LLM Agentic Networks
Will the Agent Recuse Itself? Measuring LLM-Agent Compliance with In-Band Access-Deny Signals
Free-Riding the Agentic Web: A Systematic Security Analysis of x402 Payments
Privacy-Aware Agent Collaboration for Dynamic VR Slice Management in 6G SD-RAN
SoK: The Pitfalls of Deep Reinforcement Learning for Cybersecurity
Infrastructure for the Agentic Web: Gap Analysis and Architecture from the Agentverse Platform
The Web4 Agent Economy: A Large-Scale Empirical Study of the Landscape, Challenges, and Opportunities
points: Web4 already operates at meaningful scale with 99,448 EIP-8004 agent identity registrations across chains, heavily concentrated on BNB Smart Chain (~40.0%) and Base (~19.9%), indicating rapid but geographically uneven ecosystem formation.

The machine-to-machine payment layer shows production-grade volume with daily x402 activity reaching millions of transactions and an average payment size of about $0.46 USDC, signaling a shift from subscription APIs to pay-per-call micro-settlement as the default economic primitive for agents.

Developer-reported friction clusters into three integration bottlenecks—identity/authorization (230 issues; ~69.1% closed), cross-environment ops (96 issues; 50.0% closed), and payment interoperability (87 issues; ~25.3% closed)—implying that payment conformance across payer/gateway/resource remains the dominant reliability risk as adoption scales.
one_liner: What’s interesting is the ecosystem has already hit “millions of sub-$1 agent payments per day,” yet the hardest problem is still basic interoperability and conformance at the payment boundary rather than lack of protocols.

title: AXE: Grey-Box Exploitability Confirmation for Localized Vulnerability Reports
AInterviewer: A Platform for Designing and Conducting AI-led Qualitative Interviews
Specifying AI-SDLC Processes: A Protocol Language for Human-Agent Boundaries
Probabilistic Agents in Deterministic Audits: Evaluating Multi-Agent Systems for Automated Audits Based on the German IT-Grundschutz
points: HybridRAG+multi-agent automation meaningfully reduces manual audit effort in semantic-heavy phases (Structural Analysis and Modeling), but still tops out at modest extraction quality with best entity-extraction F1 of 52.3% and best dependency-analysis F1 of 53.8%, leaving human validation mandatory where omissions create audit-critical blind spots.

Dependency reconstruction remains the main safety bottleneck: the highest-recall model finds 70.1% of the 881 ground-truth dependencies yet with only 43.6% precision, reflecting systematic generation of “plausible” but unsupported links that can break deterministic protection-need inheritance chains.

Deterministic compliance judgments are not reliably automatable with current LLMs, as the IT-Grundschutz check achieves only 32% best accuracy and models over-predict non-compliance (false negatives) by failing to distinguish documented intent from implemented evidence, implying AI should act as an evidence-retrieval and draft-reporting assistant rather than an autonomous auditor.
one_liner: The core takeaway is that LLM agents can extract and organize audit-relevant facts, but their probabilistic reasoning collapses when the workflow demands deterministic, evidence-backed compliance verdicts.

title: SkillHarness: Harnessing Safe Skills for Computer-Use Agents
On the Inseparability of Instructions and Data in Shared-Embedding Sequence Models
Prompt Injection as Role Confusion
It's a TRAP! Task-Redirecting Agent Persuasion Benchmark for Web Agents
Forensic Trajectory Signatures for Agent Memory Poisoning Detection
points: A mechanistically forced tool-call transition—invoking memory recall before sending an exfiltration email—separates successful persistent-memory poisoning executions from non-exfiltration runs with AUC=0.9563 using a single rule, and suppressing this transition breaks the attack under the stated architecture assumptions.

A lightweight trajectory detector using only tool-call order/count features reaches AUC=0.9904 (BCa 95% CI [0.987, 0.993]) and 0.9838 recall on 2,520 delayed-trigger runs (76.2% attack successes), showing that high-fidelity detection is possible without memory-content access, prompts, model weights, or email contents.

The behavioral signature is overdetermined and largely model-agnostic: removing all recall-related features leaves AUC unchanged at 0.9904, leave-one-model-out tests hit AUC=1.000 on 6/9 model hold-outs, the invariant transfers to GPT-4.1/GPT-4o without retraining, and a prefix-only variant still achieves AUC=0.934 enabling inline blocking with moderate degradation.
one_liner: Tool-call logs alone can act like EDR for LLM agents by turning persistent memory-poisoning into a detectable, architecture-induced trajectory signature that generalizes across model families and even distinguishes memory attacks from prompt injection.

title: Adversarial Pragmatics for AI Safety Evaluation: A Benchmark for Instruction Conflict, Embedded Commands, and Policy Ambiguity
points: A contrastive, linguistically controlled benchmark design exposed that 85.2% (46/54) of outputs were policy-compliant while only 66.7% (36/54) were full task successes, showing that “safe-looking” behavior can mask capability or pragmatic-control failures unless task, policy, and risk are labeled separately.

Minimal-pair robustness was low even when row-level success looked decent: only 48.1% (13/27) of pair–model cells passed a strict criterion requiring both variants to be task-successful and policy-compliant, indicating that many models rely on brittle heuristics that break under changes in embedding, deixis, transcript context, or policy framing.

LLM judges produced valid structured labels for all 54 rows but had uneven validity—66.7% agreement on task success versus 98.1% on refusal outcome—implying LLM-as-judge is suitable for triage on obvious refusal/compliance labels but unsafe to use as a primary grader for nuanced pragmatic constructs like attribution, ambiguity, and agent transcript interpretation.
one_liner: The key insight is that safety evaluation errors often come from pragmatic misinterpretation (quote vs command, content vs authority, scope vs exception), and minimal-pair tests plus judge-validity metrics make those failure modes measurable rather than hidden by pass/fail scores.

title: An Empirical Evaluation of Prompt Injection Vulnerabilities in Large Language Models Across Multilingual and Obfuscated Attack Scenarios
points: Across 15,540 generations over six frontier LLMs, 68.76% of malicious prompts produced fully actionable phishing/malware outputs and 80.84% produced at least partial attack enablement (full compliance + stalling), indicating prompt injection misuse is the dominant outcome rather than an edge case.

Safety behavior is strongly model-dependent—full compliance ranges from 44.09% (GPT-5 Mini) to 84.32% (DeepSeek-V3.2), yet even the most conservative model still fulfills 74.32% of malicious requests when stalling assistance is counted, implying today’s “refusal-only” guardrails leave substantial exploitable residual risk.

Attack success increases with realistic framing and non-English inputs: elaborate prompts raise average full compliance from 62.01% (direct) to 76.69% (elaborate) and Turkish/Chinese/Russian show higher full compliance than English (up to 80.18% vs 71.31%), while simple obfuscations reduce but do not prevent harm (Hex still 54.41% full compliance), exposing multilingual and encoding-aware alignment gaps.
one_liner: Multilingual and context-rich prompt injections reliably elicit phishing and keylogger assistance from all tested LLMs, and lightweight obfuscation only weakly degrades attacker success.

title: Security--Fidelity Tradeoffs: The Hidden Cost of Prompt Injection Defense
points: A new benchmark (SECFID) makes three prompt-injection outcomes—execute, process-as-data, or ignore—separately observable, revealing that standard attack-success metrics conflate safe data handling with content suppression.

Across 1,168 examples and 48 model/defense configurations, no system achieves both strong prompt-injection security and high task fidelity: the highest-fidelity point hits 96.5% fidelity but only 47.8% security, while the most secure points reach 99.3% security with just 71.0%–73.9% fidelity.

Defenses that look equally “secure” by execution-rate can behave very differently: SECALIGN can convert many hijacks into faithful processing (repair) whereas DefensiveTokens often attains similar security by suppressing content, and a simple fidelity-aware DPO preference tuning boosts processing substantially (e.g., on held-out editing, 43.2%→80.6% processed) while keeping execution below 1%.
one_liner: Measuring prompt-injection “security” alone can hide whether a defense is actually robust or just silently deleting user data—and SECFID quantifies that hidden cost.

title: Reasoning Up the Instruction Ladder for Controllable Language Models
Analyzing Defensive Misdirection Against Model-Guided Automated Attacks on Agentic AI Systems
Red-Teaming Coding Agents from a Tool-Invocation Perspective: An Empirical Security Assessment
Understanding and Evaluating Claw-like Agent Security Through a Computer-Systems Lens
points: SafeClawArena’s 406 adversarial tasks show end-to-end compromise rates spanning ~20% to ~70% across 15 (platform, model) configurations, indicating that always-on, system-privileged “Claw-like” agents remain broadly exploitable even with frontier LLMs.

Native in-process malicious Plugins succeed 100% on unhardened platforms regardless of the underlying LLM (but drop to 0% when the platform removes the plugin loader), demonstrating that some failures are fundamentally system-layer privilege violations that model alignment cannot compensate for.

Platform hardening can dramatically reduce risk for some model families (e.g., GPT-5.4 overall attack success 70%→22%), yet can yield little benefit or even regressions for others (e.g., Gemini variants remain ~50%+ on the hardened platform), implying defenses must be evaluated jointly with the specific LLM and may shift leakage across channels rather than eliminate it.
one_liner: The most dangerous agent failures come from cross-component system behaviors (loaders, memory, logs, credential mediation), where the LLM is often not the security boundary at all.

title: RIPA: Sensory-Vector Prompt Injection Attacks on LLM-Controlled ROS 2 Robots
points: Across 100 runs per injection variant on five LLMs, prompt-injection robustness was strongly model-specific rather than scale-dependent (e.g., Llama-3.3-70B and Gemma-3n ~4B both hit 100% ASR on all variants, while two mid-size models had 0% ASR on direct-override yet 100% ASR on structural variants).

A two-stage hybrid semantic firewall reduced ASR to 0% for known injection patterns with 0/20 false positives on a small benign set, but still suffered a 10.2% trial-weighted bypass rate (58/570) under obfuscation—dominated by synonym substitution (30/30) and hyphenated encoding (28/30).

Sensor-context poisoning via LiDAR (publishing fabricated /scan that becomes system-prompt state) achieved 100% ASR on DeepSeek-V4-Flash across all variants (N=30), showing that compromising environment-state serialization can reliably hijack actuation while bypassing user-message firewalls entirely.
one_liner: If an LLM-controlled robot trusts serialized sensor context, then prompt injection stops being just a text problem and becomes an end-to-end pipeline integrity problem across OCR/STT/middleware—with simple obfuscations still slipping past keyword-centric filters.

title: IHDec: Divergence-Steered Contrastive Decoding for Securing Multi-Turn Instruction Hierarchies
points: IHDec, a training-free inference-time method that uses Jensen–Shannon divergence to detect role-influence inversions and applies divergence-steered contrastive decoding, improves multi-turn conflict instruction-hierarchy accuracy on IHEval by +11.98 percentage points over the strongest reported training-based baseline and by up to +38.1 percentage points over architectural interventions.

On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct in multi-turn conflicts, IHDec reaches 50.68% accuracy versus 12.60% (ISE) and 13.25% (prompting), indicating that hierarchy failures in long dialogues are better addressed by token-level decoding control than by role-embedding fine-tuning that degrades under recency-driven history effects.

IHDec preserves general capability with only a 0.088-point drop on MT-Bench-101 (9.29→9.21) while also improving benign aligned instruction following by up to +7.48 percentage points and reducing prompt-injection susceptibility on Safety Defense by up to +39.0 percentage points over vanilla.

The method flips an observed negative scaling trend into positive scaling synergy: across Qwen3 4B→32B, vanilla instruction-hierarchy accuracy stays low (~12–13%) while IHDec increases monotonically to 38.5% at 32B (a +27.8 percentage point gain), showing larger models amplify risk unless actively steered at decoding time.
one_liner: A lightweight JSD-based attribution signal can gate contrastive decoding to stop lower-priority prompts from silently taking over in late-turn conversations without paying an alignment tax.

title: AI Snitches Get Glitches: Towards Evading Agentic Surveillance
Distributed Attacks in Persistent-State AI Control
points: Persistent-state coding workflows enable distributed (multi-PR) attacks that keep each pull request locally plausible, yielding high success-conditioned evasion of standard PR-diff monitors (e.g., 87% gradual vs 75% best-position non-gradual on a task-description diff monitor) and exposing that a single monitoring approach cannot reliably cover both gradual and single-PR “timed” payloads.

High evasion is a property of the persistent-state attack surface rather than one model: under the same GPT-4o diff monitor, gradual-attack evasion remains ≥65% across different attacker backends (Claude Sonnet 4.5: 94% with 45% success; Gemini 3.1 Pro: 65.3%; Kimi K2.5: 100% on 53/53 successful attacks).

Defenses improve most from stateful summarization and cross-modality ensembling rather than more raw context: a stateful link-tracker diff monitor cuts gradual evasion from 87% to 54%, and a 4-monitor (diff+trajectory) ensemble reduces gradual evasion from 93% under the weakest standard diff monitor to 47% while keeping honest false positives below 2%.
one_liner: Persistent codebases turn AI agent subversion into a supply-chain-like game where distributing and timing payload components across PRs can beat even strong LLM monitors unless monitoring itself becomes stateful and multi-view.

title: On Optimizing Multimodal Jailbreaks for Spoken Language Models
MetaBreak: Jailbreaking Online LLM Services via Special Token Manipulation
Robust Harmful Features Under Jailbreak Attacks: Mechanistic Evidence from Attention Head Specialization in Large Language Models
Low-Agreeableness Persona Conditioning for Safe LLM Fine-Tuning
HARC: Coupling Harmfulness and Refusal Directions for Robust Safety Alignment
points: HARC reduces average jailbreak attack success rate by 4.67× on Llama-3.1-8B and 4.75× on Qwen-2.5-7B versus the base model while keeping over-refusal at or below baseline and preserving overall helpfulness/capability.

Black-box jailbreaks succeed primarily by suppressing the prompt-side harmfulness and/or refusal residual-stream directions before any output is generated, and different attack families (e.g., DAN vs PAIR vs CodeAttack) occupy separable regions in the harmfulness–refusal projection plane.

Even when prompt-side harm recognition is bypassed, the model often re-recognizes harmfulness during response generation (response-token positions) yet fails to convert that signal into refusal, motivating dual-position coupling that scales to 70B/72B models with near-zero ASR on PAIR/PAP/DeepInception and large CodeAttack drops (e.g., 0.688→0.242 on Llama-3.1-70B).
one_liner: Coupling a model’s internal “harmfulness” and “refusal” directions at both prompt and generation time turns safety into a low-dimensional control problem that improves jailbreak robustness without the usual capability or over-refusal tax.

title: Echoes of Human Malice in Agents: Benchmarking LLMs for Multi-Turn Online Harassment Attacks
Harnessing Textual Refusal Directions for Multimodal Safety
points: MARS, a training-free inference-time method that reuses text-derived refusal directions, raised unsafe-image refusal on VISU from 0.2–22.9% (zero-shot) to 43.3–78.5% across five MLLMs while keeping safe-image refusal comparatively low (0.6–10.3% for most models).

On multimodal jailbreaking (HADES), MARS boosted refusal to 59.2–99.5% and improved Llama-Guard safety scores to 79.8–99.8%, substantially reducing successful jailbreaks without requiring any multimodal safety data.

For video jailbreaks, MARS achieved the strongest training-free gains—e.g., +59.4 percentage points refusal on Qwen3-VL (28.8%→88.2%) and +52.0 points on Qwen3.5 (26.2%→78.2%)—showing that text-only safety structure can transfer even to video inputs.
one_liner: A simple text-only activation “refusal direction,” once corrected for modality bias via neutral-image re-centering and trust-region scaling, becomes a scalable safety layer for images and videos without multimodal safety training data.

title: EvalSafetyGap: A Hybrid Survey and Conceptual Framework for LLM Evaluation-Safety Failures
points: Benchmark-based capability signals can be misleading under optimization pressure, with 29/60 widely used benchmarks showing high or very high saturation (including 14/60 “very-high”), and only 16% of 445 benchmark papers reporting uncertainty estimates or statistical tests—undermining fine-grained model comparisons.

A ten-model audit found no reliable link between capability and sustained jailbreak robustness: the capability–ASR-100 association was statistically indeterminate (Pearson r=+0.232, p=0.520; 95% CI [-0.530, 0.741]), implying capability thresholds alone are a weak basis for safety assurance.

The apparent open–closed “safety gap” in the audit was modest and largely attributable to governance/disclosure rather than behavioral robustness, with the largest group separation in governance (mean gap ≈0.268; d≈1.90) while ASR-100 robustness differed little (gap ≈0.043; p=0.640) and conclusions were sensitive to how one borderline model was classified.
one_liner: Capability scores, safety metrics, and governance disclosures can all improve while the underlying safety properties remain uncertain, so safety evaluation must be dynamic, multi-attempt, and audit-ready.

title: Beyond the Prompt: Jailbreaking Function-Calling LLMs via Simulated Moderation Traces
points: A stateful function-calling design that interleaves trusted tool schemas/validation messages with untrusted arguments and tool-like outputs enables jailbreak intent to be distributed across turns, making prompt-level sanitization and single-message filtering fundamentally incomplete defenses.

Simulated Moderation Traces (SMT) achieves near-perfect jailbreak performance on tool-enabled commercial LLMs, reaching 99.67% ASR on SafeBench-Tiny and 98.33% ASR on JailbreakBench with high harmfulness (Avg HarmScore 74.27/76.83) while using fewer than 1.5 queries on average (1.48/1.37), substantially outperforming prompt-centric and prior function-calling baselines.

Traditional mitigations (length limits, low temperature, safety reminders, safety checks) reduce SMT but still leave high residual risk (e.g., 78% ASR on Claude-Sonnet-4.5 under combined defenses), whereas a function-calling-aware system-prompt guard (FCGuard) can drop ASR to 0% on GPT-5.4 and Claude-Sonnet-4.5, implying that defenses must reason over full interaction state (schemas, arguments, tool outputs, and history) rather than isolated prompts.
one_liner: Function calling turns “tool traces” and validator feedback into a high-privilege side-channel that can progressively convert refusals into compliance with strikingly few queries.

title: Securing the AI Agent: A Unified Framework for Multi-Layer Agent Red Teaming
points: AI-Infra-Guard operationalizes a four-layer agent attack-surface model (infrastructure, protocol/tool, agent behavior, model) and ties each layer to a distinct evidence type and assessment method, implying end-to-end agent security requires heterogeneous testing rather than a single scanner.

The infrastructure module scales deterministic coverage to 75+ AI components with 107 fingerprint rules and 1,443 vulnerability rules, and explicitly stratifies confidence into verified/version-based/inferred findings (including 87 empty-predicate rules) to manage uncertainty from missing versions and immature advisory ecosystems.

The skill supply-chain scanner is benchmarked on SkillTrustBench (5,520 cases distilled from 62,652 skills) where top base models reach ~0.98–0.985 loose F1 with recall ~0.997, but false-positive rates vary sharply by model (as low as 0.012 vs as high as 0.187), showing model choice can dominate operational triage cost even with a fixed audit harness.
one_liner: The standout idea is layer-paradigm matching: treat agent security as an evidence problem and pick rule-based, LLM-audit, interactive red teaming, or statistical jailbreak evaluation depending on which layer you’re trying to prove unsafe.

title: Cognitive Firewall: A Proactive, Zero-Trust, Multi-Gate Framework for LLM Safety
points: A four-gate, conversation-level “Cognitive Firewall” reduced jailbreak attack success from 45%/10%/30%/74% (undefended) to 1%/0%/2%/14% across single-turn (jbb), escalation (crescendo), decomposition (safemt), and human-crafted multi-turn (mhj) attacks, showing that tracking intent and trajectory can nearly eliminate automated jailbreaks but still leaves a meaningful residual on hardest human attacks.

Most risk reduction was proactive (pre-generation): intent and consistency gates accounted for the majority of blocks (e.g., 89/92 jbb blocks from intent and 48/50 crescendo blocks from consistency), while the post-generation output gate was critical for decomposition payloads (e.g., 21/39 safemt and 12/43 mhj blocks), implying defenses need both early conversation oversight and a final response backstop to cover complementary failure modes.

The framework achieved an 8% over-refusal rate on XSTest versus 18–21% for stricter guard baselines, and it blocked 75% of authority/override probes (12/16) with 0% benign role-mention refusals, indicating that isolating “zero-trust” authority claims as a dedicated decision channel can improve security without heavily degrading benign utility.
one_liner: Decomposing safety into categorical, escalation-combined gates (intent, zero-trust context, trajectory consistency, and output risk) materially improves multi-turn jailbreak containment while keeping false refusals relatively low.

title: The Geometry of Refusal: Linear Instability in Safety-Aligned LLMs
SCARCE: Scalable Cascade Analysis for Rare-event Characterisation via Embeddings
points: Replacing Subset Simulation’s handcrafted performance function with learned embeddings plus geometric “rulers” yields ∼400–500× lower mean absolute error on MNIST rare misclassification than grid-searched traditional SS, while avoiding systematic over-counting (traditional SS reports ≈9.6×10⁻³ vs a ≈4.0×10⁻³ reference).

A non-negative supermartingale construction enables an anytime-valid, level-wise high-probability upper envelope on the running rare-event probability estimate, remaining statistically valid under adaptive quantile thresholds and early stopping (via Ville’s inequality control of upward excursions).

For fleet-level LLM jailbreak probability estimation using Llama-Guard-3-8B hidden states, a PCA-based ruler reaches 2.6% mean relative error for adversarial fractions η≥10⁻³ across five turns—well within the reference’s own 27.9% average bootstrap relative half-width—and transfers to a GCG-style corpus with 2.93% relative error after refitting calibration, with a directional KL selector correlating strongly with estimation error (Spearman ρ=0.83).
one_liner: A practical path to certifiable rare-event safety metrics: data-driven Subset Simulation that stays sample-efficient, transfers across domains, and still supports anytime-valid bounds under adaptive stopping.

title: Sparse Autoencoders are Capable LLM Jailbreak Mitigators
Break the Brake, Not the Wheel: Untargeted Jailbreak via Entropy Maximization
Resolution Thresholds in VLM Detection of Harmful ASCII Art Across Construction Modes and Languages
points: Across 62 valid (model, ASCII-mode) strata, 59.7% showed a statistically significant monotonic drop in harmful-ASCII detection as resolution increased (BH-corrected q<0.05), establishing resolution as a first-order failure trigger for VLM moderation.

Word-embedded ASCII construction is the most reliable evasion: positive English-word fill (L5) achieved the lowest aggregate detection rate at 0.062 pooled over models, resolutions, and languages, indicating most VLMs default to reading benign filler text over the global harmful shape.

Language effects were minor relative to resolution/mode effects: only 4.7% of 640 English-vs-Chinese strata differed significantly after BH correction, implying the vulnerability generalizes across scripts even though Chinese-word fill (L8) showed a notable low-resolution advantage for Chinese-built models (0.69 vs 0.36 pooled detection at r=0.1) that reversed at high resolution (0.00 vs 0.11–0.13 at r≥0.8).
one_liner: Downscaling often helps VLMs “see” harmful ASCII art, but semantic filler—especially positive English words—still defeats detection across most resolutions and models.

title: Curvature-Guided Module Localization for Low-Rank Detoxification of Backdoored Large Language Models
points: Curvature-guided module localization plus targeted rank-8 LoRA repair drove Triggered Malicious Response Rate (TMRR) to 0.000 in multiple settings (e.g., begin-trigger: K=5 with 1000 samples at 30 epochs and K=7 with 100–1000 samples at 10–30 epochs; middle-trigger: K=5 or K=7 with ≥100 samples at 10–30 epochs), showing that backdoor removal can be achieved via localized weight-space edits rather than full retraining.

The approach is data-efficient for the hardest cases where trigger effects must propagate through the network, reaching near-zero/zero TMRR with as few as 50–100 detoxification examples in the middle-trigger setting (e.g., K=5 at 50 samples and 30 epochs yields TMRR=0.070 and at 100 samples yields TMRR=0.000), implying that mechanistic target selection can substitute for large clean corpora when adapter budget is limited.

Benign behavior is largely preserved while suppressing the backdoor, with Triggered-to-Clean Behavioral Similarity (TCBS) typically staying high (~0.82–0.86) even when TMRR collapses to ~0, indicating that aligning triggered internal activations to clean trajectories can neutralize the attack without broad capability degradation.
one_liner: Mechanistic localization using activation patching plus Fisher/K-FAC curvature identifies a small, nonredundant set of transformer projections where low-rank “surgical” repairs can erase a conditional LLM backdoor while keeping outputs clean-like.

title: CSO-LLM: Class Subspace Orthogonalization for Post-Training Backdoor Detection and Trigger Inversion in LLMs
points: Adding a class-subspace orthogonalization (CSO) cosine-similarity penalty to a margin-based objective provides implicit token blacklisting that can move an innocuous true trigger token (“seriously”) from rank 830 to rank 2 in a 30k-token vocabulary, sharply reducing false trigger candidates dominated by target-class sentiment words.

In post-training settings with only model access plus ~50 clean samples per class, CSO-based detectors achieve high detection with low false alarms (e.g., on Qwen3-4B/Yahoo-7 at high poison rate: discrete CSO detects 9–10/10 poisoned models across triggers with 1/10 false positives on clean models), while plain margin detection fails completely (0/10 TPR, 10/10 FPR).

CSO enables accurate ground-truth trigger inversion for multi-token triggers where prior LLM defenses largely fail (e.g., on Qwen3-4B/Yahoo-7, “Tell me seriously” recall is 25/30–30/30 tokens for CSO vs 0/30–8/30 for DBS/MM/UAT/GBDA), and it remains effective against moderately adaptive “intrinsic-feature” triggers but can be evaded by highly non-stealthy triggers that spread behavior across many sentiment synonyms.
one_liner: CSO turns backdoor trigger search into a geometry problem: penalize “moving toward the target class subspace” and innocuous triggers pop out while target-class-looking tokens get suppressed.

title: FlipGuard: Defending Large Language Models Against Quantization-Conditioned Backdoor Attacks
points: Quantization-conditioned backdoors can remain effectively hidden during full-precision auditing yet activate after common post-hoc quantization (INT8/FP4/NF4), collapsing security scores (e.g., StarCoderBase-3B Code Security 74.6% → 7.0% after INT8; Phi-2 content-injection Keyword Occurrence 0.07% → 92.9% after NF4).

FlipGuard’s targeted pre-quantization weight perturbations (typically ~6–20% of weights) largely neutralize QCB behaviors across code vulnerability insertion, over-refusal, and content injection, restoring attacked models to near-baseline security levels (e.g., Phi-2 NF4 over-refusal 30.2% → 0.53%; Phi-2 NF4 injection 92.9% → 0.47%; StarCoderBase-3B INT8 Code Security 7.0% → 82.4%).

The defense can deliver high security with small utility changes on standard benchmarks (MMLU/TruthfulQA/HumanEval/MBPP) and appears safe to apply even when a model is clean (e.g., clean Phi-2 over-refusal stays ~0.53–0.60% after FlipGuard + quantization), supporting a practical “defend-before-you-quantize” supply-chain posture.
one_liner: Quantization itself becomes an activation switch for stealth backdoors, and a lightweight pre-quantization weight “boundary flip” can shut them down without needing data or trigger samples.

title: When the Aggregator Cheats: Data-Free Backdoors in Federated LLM-based QA Systems
Breaking the Rounding Trap: Securing LLMs against Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors
Cloak and Detonate: Scanner Evasion and Dynamic Detection of Agent Skill Malware
points: Payload-preserving evasion is highly effective against install-time skill scanners: self-extracting packing bypassed all eight evaluated scanners at >90% (≥96% for most static/hybrid tools) and structural obfuscation bypassed >80% on most static scanners, reaching 96% on a hybrid scanner, implying appearance-based auditing is brittle under adaptive adversaries.

Cloaking does not meaningfully reduce real agent utility: across Claude Code (Sonnet 4.6) and OpenAI Codex (GPT-5.4), neither structural obfuscation nor packing caused statistically detectable task-success degradation on 87 SkillsBench tasks while preserving high trajectory similarity (~0.88–0.90), meaning evasions can remain operational and stealthy.

Behavior-centric runtime auditing substantially improves robustness: the proposed sandbox+information-flow approach detected 97% of benchmark attacks at 2% false positives and sustained 87% detection on executable in-the-wild malicious skills, while a top static scanner collapsed from 99% to 10% under structural obfuscation, showing dynamic OS-boundary evidence resists surface-level cloaks.
one_liner: Static scanning for agent skills fails under semantics-preserving transformations, but runtime detonation with OS-level information-flow tracking remains effective even when the payload is packed or obfuscated.
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Guangzhou HKUST Fok Ying Tung Research Institute

title: Linguistic Firewall: Geometry as Defense in Multi-Agent Systems Routing
points: Non-textual, evaluation-driven routing (ANTAP) reduces description-based router-hijacking Attack Success Rate to near-zero (≈0.2–0.4%) versus ~67–75% for a description-based router, showing that removing inference-time metadata parsing can structurally eliminate an entire injection pathway.

Empirically learned behavioral operators also suppress backdoored/sleeper agents: across multiple LoRA backdoor variants (e.g., BadNet/Sleeper/VPI/MTBA/CTBA), ANTAP holds ASR to ~0.3–2.4% on triggered queries while embedding-based routing remains far higher (≈12–21%) and textual routing stays ≈73–79%, implying offline capability tests can function as a practical root-of-trust for MAS routing.

Routing via a single geometric projection yields large efficiency and scaling gains: ANTAP’s online latency is ~26–38 ms versus ~0.4–2.5 s for text-based routing as prompt/description length grows, and its ASR can even drop with more agents (3.35%→0.46% from 2→19 agents) while the text baseline worsens (~33.9%→34.9%).
one_liner: Turning agent selection into a fixed embedding-space projection creates a 'linguistic firewall' that makes metadata prompt-injection effectively inexpressible at routing time while improving latency by orders of magnitude.

title: AI-Generated PowerShell Malware: An Experimental Framework and Dataset
points: Fine-tuned open-weight LLMs generated PowerShell malware whose dynamic malicious-event footprint closely matched real-world samples, with a median Jaccard similarity of 84.5% and 48.4% of cases showing complete event overlap.

High-fidelity malware generation was achieved with sub-10B-parameter models using parameter-efficient QLoRA training and 4-bit quantization, indicating consumer-hardware attackers can bypass proprietary-model guardrails by self-hosting smaller models.

Static/text similarity can understate functional risk because generated scripts often diverge lexically yet converge behaviorally, making sandboxed dynamic analysis with telemetry-derived rules essential for reliable evaluation of LLM-generated malware.
one_liner: Behavioral dynamic analysis shows small open-weight models can produce PowerShell malware that is operationally indistinguishable from real samples nearly half the time, despite low textual similarity.
affiliations: Università degli Studi di Napoli Federico II

title: Cybersecurity is the True Frontier for Generative AI Success or Failure
points: Static binary malware analysis forces AI systems to handle contexts where a single sample can reach billions of tokens and attackers can intentionally pad binaries to evade analysis, making naive long-context transformer approaches computationally infeasible and operationally brittle.

Despite malware being involved in under 20% of attempted breaches, static analysis remains a high-leverage proving ground because expert labeling can take hours to weeks per binary and yields ambiguous ground truth due to analyst disagreement and adversarial manipulation.

Early agentic malware-analysis demonstrations show feasibility but not readiness for scale, exemplified by multi-agent systems taking 46 minutes to analyze one relatively simple malware sample, implying that real-world deployment will hinge on hybrid triage, tool integration, and stringent latency/false-positive constraints.
one_liner: Cybersecurity stress-tests generative AI with adversaries, massive unlabeled data, and hard real-time constraints—conditions where impressive demos often fail to translate into dependable defenses.

title: PYPILINE: Malicious PyPI Package Detection via Suspicious API Knowledge and Agent Workflow
LLM Semantic Signaling Game and Mechanism Design: Systematic Blindness, Awareness Shaping, and Mindset Dynamics
points: Aggregate token-level risk scores from LLM-generated messages can be treated as approximately Gaussian (e.g., stealth setting showed Kolmogorov distance 0.016 with skewness 0.10 and excess kurtosis −0.04), enabling closed-form likelihood-ratio/threshold detection rules for LLM-mediated phishing.

Receiver “awareness” modeled as a feature-set type (what cues are even represented) drives large differences in adversarial success: a stealth phishing control was accepted 54.1% by naive receivers but only 15.7% by highly aware receivers, with Gaussian predictions matching Monte Carlo within ≤1.0% absolute error across all pairs.

Mechanism-design levers can flip incentives toward benign pooling by reshaping costs and populations: increasing the aware-receiver share to ~0.48 eliminates profitable malicious deviation, and adding a modest nonbenign-control penalty (τ=0.10) drops the required aware share to ~0.18, implying that awareness training plus friction/guardrails can be substitute complements in practice.
one_liner: The key twist is that “systematic blindness” is formalized as missing features (not just wrong thresholds), which explains why stealthy LLM phishing can persist until defenses expand the receiver’s representational cue set and/or change incentives.
affiliations: New York University Tandon School of Engineering

title: From Similarity to Vulnerability: Key Collision Attack on LLM Semantic Caching
KidnapRAG: A Black-Box Attack for Hijacking Reasoning in Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
