points: A pure black-box attacker who can only publish externally retrievable documents can reliably hijack multi-step Agentic RAG by chaining role-specific poisons (Bait → Chain-Link → Mal-Ins) that progressively redirect query reformulation and evidence grounding rather than relying on a single injected passage.

Across ReAct and WebThinker with multiple LLM backbones and datasets, the chained attack reaches high target-answer induction while sharply degrading QA accuracy (e.g., EM drops from 0.68→0.20 with ASR 0.39 on HotpotQA for ReAct+Qwen2.5-32B, and EM 0.38→0.01 with ASR 0.78 on MuSiQue for ReAct+Llama-3.3-70B).

Sequential “chain dragging” increases attack success by sustaining the compromised reasoning trajectory over additional retrieval steps, and the attack can evade simple safety gating on intermediate traces (OpenAI Moderation guard rate falls to 0.0% on ReAct and ~4.2% on WebThinker for attacked chains on HotpotQA).
one_liner: Iterative retrieval-and-reasoning improves robustness to naive poisoning, but it also creates a sequential attack surface where an adversary can steer query reformulation step-by-step using only public web documents.

title: AdvancedShelLM: A Stateful Multi-Agent LLM Honeypot for SSH Deception
LLM agents security duality: a comprehensive survey of self-security and empowered cybersecurity
Minos: A Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework for Provenance-Based Backward Tracking
points: Across 14 APT scenarios spanning five public provenance datasets, the multi-agent Minos framework reached 0.92 average recall and 0.64 precision while producing attack subgraphs that were 49% more compact than baselines (35 vs. 68–129 edges on average).

Replacing exhaustive graph traversal with hypothesis-guided planning plus a “count-first” query protocol reduced dependency-explosion overhead, cutting average token use to 164K versus 248K when the protocol is removed and preventing precision collapse on high-degree nodes (0.64 vs. 0.48).

Safety- and reliability-oriented agent scaffolding materially changed error modes: removing adversarial deliberation dropped precision from 0.64 to 0.51 (more false positives), while removing coarse-grained MITRE-tactic state caused uncontrolled exploration with precision falling to 0.28 and subgraph size inflating to 98 edges.
one_liner: What stands out is that intent-aware, multi-agent LLM orchestration (debate + grounded RAG + lifecycle memory) can outperform classic provenance backtracking while explicitly trading compute for interpretable, audit-friendly investigations.
affiliations: Ningbo Key Laboratory of Quantum Software and Security

title: A Lifecycle and Application-Stack Survey of Large Language Model Vulnerabilities: Attacks, Risks, Defenses, and Open Problems
points: LLM security failures are primarily system-level—spanning eight lifecycle stages from data collection through deployment—so the same attack (e.g., “poisoning” or “prompt injection”) can reappear with different feasibility and impact depending on where trust boundaries, provenance, and authority sit in the stack.

Indirect prompt injection and RAG/memory attacks turn untrusted content (web pages, PDFs, emails, repositories, tool outputs) into executable influence, making “confused deputy” failures—where attacker-controlled text steers an over-privileged agent to misuse the user’s authority—a dominant real-world risk.

Effective mitigation requires defense-in-depth that prioritizes deterministic controls (least-privilege tools, typed schemas, sandboxing, allowlists, budgets, signed artifacts, human approval for high-impact actions) because point fixes like prompt hardening, filters, or alignment are probabilistic and do not reliably compose across multi-step agent workflows.
one_liner: The key insight is that LLM vulnerabilities are best modeled as information-flow and privilege failures across the full lifecycle—especially where untrusted text can steer retrieval and tool-using agents—so security hinges on composable system controls, not just better prompts or alignment.

title: MESA: Prioritizing Vulnerable Communication Channels for Securing Multi-Agent Systems
points: Edge-level risk in LLM multi-agent systems is highly concentrated, with the top 20% most vulnerable communication edges accounting for about 59% of total observed attack success and a single compromised edge contributing up to 75% of success in worst cases, implying large security ROI from targeted channel hardening.

A label-free edge-ranking method combining six graph-structural metrics with two clean-execution probes predicts per-edge attack success with mean Spearman ρ≈+0.60 (peaking at +0.73), showing that security-critical channels can often be identified pre-deployment without attack traces.

Under budgeted defense, monitoring the top 10% of ranked edges intercepts roughly 3× more successful attacks than random allocation, and simple randomization over the top few edges reduces adaptive-attacker success by ~10.5 percentage points compared to deterministic top-k protection.
one_liner: Communication topology makes MAS attacks predictable enough that defenders can pre-rank and harden a small slice of edges to block a disproportionate share of compromises—without needing any attack logs.

title: Black-Box Inference of LLM Architectural Properties with Restrictive API Access
points: Even when an LLM API only reveals the sampled token’s single log-probability (no top‑k logits and no logit-bias), NightVision can still infer architectural IP—recovering hidden dimension with 23% mean relative error across 32 open-source models (9% on MoE) and showing current “restrictive” APIs do not fully prevent architectural leakage.

A timing side channel (time-to-first-token) combined with an estimated hidden dimension enables rough recovery of depth and total parameter count for larger models, achieving ~53% mean relative error on ≥3B-parameter models but often exceeding 100% error below 3B parameters where prefill-dominated timing assumptions break down.

Closing the logit-leak channel substantially raises attacker cost but does not eliminate it: achieving ≤30% hidden-dimension error requires ~12×–190× more tokens than prior logit-bias/top‑k attacks, with practical runs reporting token budgets on the order of 10^11–10^12 (median ~4×10^11), implying that cost/friction—not security—becomes the primary barrier.
one_liner: Architectural secrecy via “single-token logprob only” APIs is illusory because spectral methods plus TTFT timing can still back out hidden dimension, depth, and size—just at much higher query cost.

title: Behind the Refusal: Determining Guardrail Activation via Behavioral Monitoring
points: A black-box behavioral monitoring method using only 40 prompts detects whether an AI system is fronted by a guardrail with 100% accuracy across 162 target configurations (9 guardrails × 6 block patterns × 3 LLMs) and 0% false positives on a no-guardrail control, with strong benign-vs-malicious separation (q < 0.001).

Combining HTTP and lexical signals is reliably discriminative while timing-only signals are noisy (timing produced moderate significance even on no-guardrail controls), implying guardrail detection should prioritize protocol/response-structure and templating artifacts rather than latency heuristics.

A learned block-pattern fingerprint distinguishes guardrail blocks from intrinsic LLM refusals on unseen prompts with 0.98 average F1 (5/9 guardrails at 1.00 F1), enabling adaptive offensive/defensive workflows that choose guardrail-evasion vs alignment-jailbreak strategies based on the refusal’s true origin.
one_liner: Refusals leak their provenance: subtle HTTP+lexical artifacts can reveal guardrail activation and even fingerprint block patterns with near-perfect separation from model refusals.

title: When Embedding-Based Defenses Fail: Rethinking Safety in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
Embedding Inference Attack
points: A black-box attacker can fingerprint which embedding model an IR/RAG system uses by comparing only the unordered sets of retrieved documents via Jaccard overlap, even without access to rankings, similarity scores, or embeddings.

In a 13-model evaluation, only 1,249 tailored generated queries (k=3) were enough to uniquely identify the victim embedding model, while simple adversarial inputs (random strings, non-queries, probing prompts) could also fully discriminate models in the no-reranker IR setup (11/11 successful queries).

Similarity-threshold filtering can sharply reduce model identifiability but at a quality cost: at threshold 0.60 the number of discriminative generated queries dropped from 1,249 to 194 (k=3), while retrieval quality became highly model-dependent (e.g., LaBSE Recall@1000 fell from 0.5419 to 0.0173, whereas e5-large-v2 stayed at 0.9777).
one_liner: Even when a RAG assistant refuses to answer malformed inputs, retrieval still happens—and the returned chunks can be used to reliably infer the hidden embedding model, enabling downstream privacy attacks.

title: Words Speak Louder Than Code: Investigating Cognitive Heuristics in LLM-Based Code Vulnerability Detection
points: Non-code context alone can systematically flip LLM vulnerability verdicts, with cross-model average susceptibility highest for framing (33.2%) followed by anchoring (23.5%) and halo/author attribution (18.4%), indicating CI/CD metadata is a first-class reliability risk for LLM scanners.

Cognitive cues act like a “volume knob” that shifts recall and false-positive rate in near lockstep (Pearson r=0.965; regression slope≈0.994), so precision largely plateaus and verdict flips often occur without correct root-cause identification.

A black-box “cognitive attack” that forges benign-looking PR/commit metadata can suppress up to 97% of previously detected vulnerabilities (combined ASR up to 97.23%), and prompt-based instructions to ignore metadata fail to reliably mitigate suppression (many models remain >40% ASR even under stronger defenses).
one_liner: LLM-based vulnerability detectors can be “socially engineered” via ordinary workflow metadata—framing and anchors can hide vulnerabilities at scale without touching the code.

title: COHORT: Collaborative Orchestration for Hardening via Offensive Replay on Emulated Topologies
points: A role-decomposed multi-agent LLM pipeline validated by offensive replay on real-vendor-firmware GNS3 emulations achieves a 46.7% mitigation success rate (attack progress reduced and LAN+internet connectivity preserved), a 4.4× improvement over a matched single-agent baseline at 10.7%.

Most of the performance gain comes from role specialization (MSR 38.6% without the critic loop), with iterative implementation–critique refinement adding a further +7.9 percentage points to reach 46.7%, showing that decomposition matters more than self-review alone.

Defense stacking on a persistent network state quickly saturates—cumulative attack-step reduction plateaus at ~52% by the 4th sequential defense—implying diminishing returns from greedy additive hardening and a need for non-greedy selection/replacement strategies to push beyond the ceiling.
one_liner: Replay-based paired evaluation on high-fidelity emulation turns LLM-generated mitigations into measurable, deployable network-device commands—then reveals both a 4.4× multi-agent lift and a fast plateau in cumulative hardening.

title: Why Trust Your Agent? Empirical Security Gains from TRiSM-Guided Agentic Workflows in Healthcare
points: A TRiSM-guided multi-agent redesign cut mean attack success rates from 31% to 10% for RAG poisoning and from 42% to 25% for data-field injection across 5 LLMs (500 attacks), indicating that architectural controls materially outperform “model-only” safety expectations.

Moving prompt construction from client-side to server-side structurally eliminated the client-side network-injection vector that otherwise succeeded 59% of the time on the single-agent baseline, showing that where prompts are assembled is a first-order security decision.

Security-hardening via least-privilege agent decomposition and workflow guardrails increased medical report accuracy by 14 percentage points (72.5%→86.5%) over 800 generations, implying that reducing attack surface and reducing cognitive load on models can improve both safety and output quality simultaneously.
one_liner: A concrete TRiSM-to-controls mapping (server-side prompts, least privilege tools/data, pre-prompt embedding checks) delivers double dividends in healthcare agents: far fewer successful injections and notably higher report accuracy, while also revealing that no single LLM is robust across vectors.

title: FlexServe: A Fast and Secure LLM Serving System for Mobile Devices with Flexible Resource Isolation
FlexServe: A Fast and Secure LLM Serving System for Mobile Devices with Flexible Resource Isolation
Generative AI and Federated Learning for Intrusion Detection Systems: A Survey
points: Generative models are being used in IDS pipelines for anomaly detection, synthetic traffic generation/augmentation, missing-value imputation, adversarial traffic generation, and alert explanation—improving data efficiency but expanding the attack surface via dual-use generation.

Federated-learning IDS addresses privacy by keeping raw network traffic local, yet non-IID client data, communication overhead, and poisoning risks remain dominant blockers; compressed autoencoder approaches report up to 95% communication reduction while maintaining detection utility.

Current IDS benchmarking is still mostly centralized (e.g., CICIDS2017, CICDDoS2019, CICIoT2023), with FLNET2023 standing out as an explicitly federated dataset—implying that many reported FL-IDS results may not reflect realistic client heterogeneity, topology, or temporal drift.
one_liner: The most consequential takeaway is that combining generative AI with federated IDS can simultaneously improve data scarcity/imbalance and materially worsen adversarial and evaluation risks unless realism and federated benchmarks catch up.

title: NeuroFilter: Activation-Based Guardrails for Privacy-Conscious LLM Agents
Seven Security Challenges That Must be Solved in Cross-domain Multi-agent LLM Systems
AlienLM: Alienization of Language for API-Boundary Privacy in Black-Box LLMs
Knowledge Over Parameters: Evolving Smart Contract Vulnerability Detection
points: EVOVULN reaches 71% macro-F1 across five real-world smart-contract vulnerability types (66% precision, 81% recall), outperforming zero-shot GPT-5.2 (52% macro-F1) and top coding-agent baselines (57%), indicating that evolvable procedural policies can beat raw model scale for semantic logic-bug detection.

Ablations show the approach is jointly driven by rule evolution and controlled execution: removing evolution drops macro-F1 from 71% to 46% (−25 points, largely via precision collapse from 66%→37%), while removing the IoC Runtime at inference drops macro-F1 to 49% (−22 points) with recall falling from 81%→44%, evidencing that unconstrained LLMs drift away from prescribed multi-step logic.

Evolved detection knowledge transfers across models without retraining (66% macro-F1 on Qwen3.5-9B and 67% on MiniMax-M2.5) and can let a lightweight detector surpass a much larger model by 19 F1 points, with a one-time evolution cost under $50, implying a practical “knowledge-over-parameters” path to robust, low-cost auditing.
one_liner: Treating vulnerability detection rules as executable, continuously debuggable software artifacts—rather than prompts or fine-tuned weights—yields higher accuracy, better adherence, and cross-model portability at low cost.

title: Manufactured Confidence: How Memory Consolidation Turns Hearsay into Confident Facts
points: LLM memory consolidation systems (e.g., mem0 and LangMem) rewrote hedged/hearsay statements into confident, dated “facts” with a 100% laundering rate in the poisoning protocol (1.00 vs 0.00 for a verbatim vector-store control), and agents then followed these manufactured facts to grant unauthorized access at high rates (e.g., 0.69–0.75 in the natural staleness condition and 0.72 with no defense in the injection mix).

Agent decisions were driven by the confidence of the phrasing rather than provenance: across five models, confident assertions produced the same unauthorized-grant rate (~0.81) whether bare, attributed, or forged as a “system of record,” while hedges collapsed grants (often to 0.00) without needing any special keywords.

Common mitigations failed in predictable ways: a passive “unverified” label leaked substantially and variably by provider (e.g., wrong-grant remained 0.77 on gpt-4o-mini and qwen-72b), while an active “do not trust” instruction reduced wrong decisions to 0.00 only by forcing blanket escalation on correct memories (false-escalation 1.00), and discrimination was restored only when a redundant authoritative source was available (wrong-grant 0.00 with no escalation).
one_liner: Long-term agent memory can silently turn casual hearsay into high-authority “facts,” and once a single memory becomes load-bearing, confident phrasing—not truth or source—drives cascading security-critical decisions.

title: Hybrid privacy-aware semantic search: SVD-truncated document geometry and CKKS-encrypted query reranking under a restricted threat model
Are Frontier LLMs Ready for Cybersecurity? Evidence for Vertical Foundation Models from Dual-Mode Vulnerability Benchmarks
ANVIL: Anomaly-based Vulnerability Identification without Labelled Training Data
Antaeus: Hunting Repository-Level Logic Vulnerabilities via Context-Grounded LLM Reasoning
points: A context-grounded, repository-scale pipeline detected 15 of 28 confirmed C/C++ logic vulnerabilities (~54% recall) in CWE-200/CWE-284, beating the strongest compared baseline at 4 of 28 (~14%) under similar cost constraints.

Lightweight repository-wide function prioritization reduced detailed LLM analysis from 149,758 in-scope functions to 4,859 analyzed functions (a 30.8× reduction), showing that high-recall ranking can bound audit cost without eliminating most discoveries.

Comparative validation pruned recurring “project-norm” concerns without losing true positives, cutting false positives by 20% (1,682→1,345) with Opus 4.7 and by 26% (3,927→2,918) with GPT-5.4—evidence that anomaly-style cross-sink checking materially improves triage precision for logic bugs.
one_liner: The key win is turning logic-vulnerability detection into repository-specific invariant recovery—grounding LLM reasoning in explicit code evidence and then using peer-comparisons to separate real anomalies from pervasive coding conventions.

title: PoCGen: Generating Proof-of-Concept Exploits for Vulnerabilities in Npm Packages
An Empirical Study of Security Calibration in Large Language Models for Code
points: Across 36k+ security-critical code generations, all evaluated code LLMs were systematically overconfident about security (verbalized security ECE: GPT‑4o‑mini ≈0.46–0.48, Gemini‑2.0‑Flash ≈0.25–0.26, Qwen3‑Coder‑Next ≈0.41–0.42), producing high-confidence vulnerable outputs at notable rates (False Trust at p≥0.8: 33.9%, 17.5%, and 38.3% respectively).

Functional self-assessment was consistently less reliable than security self-assessment (e.g., Gemini functional ECE ≈0.42–0.44 vs security ECE ≈0.16–0.17; Qwen functional ECE ≈0.77–0.78 vs security ECE ≈0.24–0.25), implying runtime/execution uncertainty dominates model confidence errors more than vulnerability-pattern uncertainty.

Calibration and trustworthiness collapsed in repository-level patching: average ECE jumped to ≈0.70–0.73 and False Trust rose to ≈70–83% (e.g., GPT False Trust 16.9%→83.2%), with decomposition attributing 45–82% of the degradation to build fragility and the remainder to cross-file complexity even when builds succeeded.
one_liner: LLM confidence is a poor safety signal for secure coding—especially in real repositories—because high-confidence outputs are frequently wrong, and the mismatch gets dramatically worse once cross-file build/test realities enter the loop.

title: VulKey: Automated Vulnerability Repair Guided by Domain-Specific Repair Patterns
From Lab to Reality: A Practical Evaluation of Deep Learning Models and LLMs for Vulnerability Detection
PBFuzz: Agentic Directed Fuzzing for PoV Generation
The Emergence of Autonomous Penetration Capabilities in Large Language Model-Powered AI Systems
DMind Benchmark: Toward a Holistic Assessment of LLM Capabilities across the Web3 Domain
EnclaveX: End-to-End Confidential AI with CPU/GPU TEEs
points: End-to-end confidential LLM inference that spans Intel TDX CPU TEEs and NVIDIA H200 confidential GPUs can be deployed in Kubernetes while keeping application secrets inaccessible even to a fully privileged K8s administrator (e.g., blocking key release until app-level attestation succeeds and disabling in-guest memory dumping).

On an H200, enabling confidential compute inside a TDX CVM imposes substantial inference penalties versus non-confidential native execution—throughput drops by 35.0%–62.8%, inter-token latency increases by 35.2%–73.9%, and time-to-first-token rises by 11.2%–38.3%—with overhead shrinking as batch size or input length increases, indicating CPU↔GPU protected I/O as the dominant bottleneck.

Adding SCONE-based application-level attestation on top of native TDX+cGPU attestation increases total attestation latency from 1.1611s to ~1.1758s (~1.27% overhead), showing that stronger end-to-end trust chains can be achieved with near-zero incremental startup cost relative to baseline platform attestation.
one_liner: A practical CPU+GPU TEE pipeline shows that the real performance tax in confidential LLM inference is protected CPU↔GPU I/O, while app-level attestation adds ~1% latency and meaningfully reduces Kubernetes-admin power over secrets.

title: Less Data, More Security: Advancing Cybersecurity LLMs Specialization via Resource-Efficient Domain-Adaptive Continuous Pre-training with Minimal Tokens
Toward Cybersecurity-Expert Small Language Models
ContraFix: Skill-Enhanced Contrastive Runtime Analysis for Vulnerability Repair
CAREBench: A Child-Safety Risk Benchmark for Language Models
points: Across 500 upstream child-safety prompts spanning 12 risk categories, seven frontier LLMs showed large safety variance with failure rates ranging from 2.3% to 58.0%, implying that current child-safety behavior is highly model-dependent rather than a solved, industry-wide baseline.

The automated MultiJudge grading pipeline matched human sensitivity about as well as humans match each other (Cohen’s κ=0.55 vs parent–parent κ=0.52) and its acceptability verdicts aligned with human pairwise preferences 89.3% of the time, suggesting LLM-ensemble judging can be a practical, reproducible proxy for caregiver/clinician judgments in this domain.

Even the strongest model still failed notably in relational/mental-health-adjacent categories (e.g., one model’s remaining failures concentrated in therapist-replacement 26% and emotional-dependency 17%), while other models frequently produced highly actionable harmful artifacts (e.g., code/scripts for coercion or impersonation), indicating that “refusal on explicit abuse” is insufficient to prevent earlier-stage grooming, isolation, surveillance, and dependency escalation.
one_liner: A benchmark that targets the pre-CSAM, pre-explicit phase of harm shows some frontier LLMs still provide scripts, tactics, or relational reinforcement that can materially escalate child risk long before content becomes overtly illegal.

title: Is Lying an Emergent Behaviour in LLMs? Evidence from Gaslighting AI agents in a Sustainability Game
Governance Decay: How Context Compaction Silently Erases Safety Constraints in Long-Horizon LLM Agents
Safety Testing LLM Agents at Scale: From Risk Discovery to Evidence-Grounded Verification
points: An automated, executable safety-testing pipeline for tool-using LLM agents can uncover severe real-world failure modes at scale, with multi-channel attacks achieving an average 93.9% verified success rate across four production agent frameworks.

Combinatorially composing risk × attack-method × environment taxonomies yielded 1,600 replayable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories and maintained broad executability (first-level average ESRs ~79.0%–95.3% across risk groups), indicating coverage can scale without hand-authoring each scenario.

Evidence-grounded verification that prioritizes environment-state changes over tool-call intent and model self-report enables deterministic, manipulation-resistant labeling, revealing a capability–vulnerability tension where higher task competence correlates with higher attack success (e.g., overall ESR 88.6% for Claude Code vs. 70.3% for OpenClaw under identical scenarios).
one_liner: Executable test cases with deterministic, environment-grounded oracles make agent safety evaluation both scalable and brutally revealing—showing that adaptive, multi-turn adversaries can reliably drive real tool-mediated harm.

title: Grounded autonomous scrutiny at scale: emergent critique from reproduction of published computational physics papers
(A)I Sees What You Don't: Exploiting New Attack Surfaces in Third-Party Mobile Agents
points: Across five popular third‑party Android mobile-agent frameworks, every system was vulnerable to at least 6 of 7 tested attacks, showing that the perception–decision–action pipeline creates systemic, agent-specific attack surfaces beyond traditional app threats.

Subliminal visual prompt injection is highly reliable: six evaluated VLM backends extracted low-opacity overlay text at 2–20% opacity with 90–100% success (18/20 to 20/20), enabling instruction hijacking that is effectively invisible to users.

Host compromise is feasible via attack chaining: screenshot TOCTOU gaps of 50–500 ms (≈210 ms average) plus unsafe host command construction enabled 100% (20/20) host-side code execution on 4/5 frameworks, sometimes requiring no Android permissions for data theft (broadcast interception) and only common permissions (overlay/storage/accessibility) for full escalation.
one_liner: Mobile VLM agents turn “invisible” pixels and repurposed debug/IPC channels into a practical path from unprivileged on-device influence to full host-PC command execution.

title: SlowBA: An efficiency backdoor attack towards VLM-based GUI agents
Most Current Model Organisms Are Leaky: Perplexity Differencing Often Reveals Finetuning Objectives
Robust Multi-Agent LLMs under Byzantine Faults
Memory as an Attack Surface in LLM Agents: A Study on Multiple-Choice Question Answering
points: Across 1,064 MCQs, inserting false information into an agent’s external memory caused answer changes in 7.80% of cases (82/1,064), demonstrating that “clean” prompts can still yield corrupted outputs via retrieved prior state.

Model choice strongly determines memory-attack sensitivity: the false-memory answer-shift rate ranged from 0.00–0.91% for GPT-5.4 Mini to as high as 34.48% for Phi3-14B (cybersecurity), implying open models in this setup were markedly more brittle to memory poisoning.

Targeted option steering is more effective via post-answer reinforcement than biased-example exposure, with feedback increasing selection of the attacker-chosen option C by up to +12.07 percentage points (Phi3-14B, cybersecurity) versus up to +8.62 points from example biasing, indicating that “retry with feedback” loops are a high-leverage control point for attackers.
one_liner: Agent memory turns past interactions into a persistent, stealthy injection channel that can measurably flip MCQ answers and bias choice selection even when the current question is benign.

title: RedCoder: Automated Multi-Turn Red Teaming for Code LLMs
UA-ChatDev: Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Agent Collaboration for Reliable Software Development
points: On the 1,200-task SRDD benchmark, UA-ChatDev achieved the best Overall Quality score (Q=0.649 with Qwen2.5-Coder 7B and Q=0.596 with Gemma 2 9B) versus ChatDev’s Q=0.395, indicating uncertainty-triggered verification materially improves end-to-end software generation reliability.

Uncertainty quantification notably boosted execution reliability, with executability rising from 0.779 to 0.859 (+8.0 points) for Qwen2.5 and from 0.794 to 0.840 (+4.6 points) for Gemma 2, consistent with reducing propagation of early-phase hallucinations into runnable code failures.

The reliability gains come with measurable overhead: compared to ChatDev (≈148s, ≈22.9k tokens), UA-ChatDev consumed ≈35.7k–40.5k tokens and ≈280–306s due to selective retrieval and extra refinement loops, highlighting a practical accuracy–latency tradeoff for agentic software pipelines.
one_liner: Token-logprob uncertainty gates when multi-agent software teams should retrieve and verify, substantially improving completeness/consistency and especially code executability at the cost of higher token and time budgets.

title: AgentPSO: Evolving Agent Reasoning Skill via Multi-agent Particle Swarm Optimization
Just Ask: Curious Code Agents Reveal System Prompts in Frontier LLMs
Truth or Sophistry? LoFa: A Benchmark for LLM Robustness Against Logical Fallacies
points: LoFa introduces an objective, ground-truth QA benchmark of 1,952 questions paired with 10 fallacy-based persuasive arguments each (19,492 total attacks) plus a multi-round debate protocol and the LFR@k metric to isolate persuasion-induced failures from baseline knowledge gaps.

Across datasets, distraction/distortion fallacies are disproportionately effective (e.g., Llama-3.1-405B reaches only 29.42% LFR@3 on Equivocation and 57.05% on Straw Man on average), while flaws-in-reasoning/evidence fallacies are resisted far better (e.g., the same model averages 88.07% on Slippery Slope and 92.95% on Circular Reasoning), implying robustness work should prioritize semantic misdirection defenses over pure logical-form checking.

Model size improves resistance but preserves “architectural fingerprints” (Llama-3.1 average LFR@3 rises from 59.75%→70.38%→77.17% for 8B→70B→405B), and prompting helps unevenly (GPT-4 CoT boosts LFR@3 by ~7–13% for most fallacies but slightly worsens Appeal to Authority by 1.87%), suggesting scaling/prompting alone won’t eliminate certain systematic vulnerabilities like authority deference (GPT-4 LFR@3=39.20% on AA in NQ1).
one_liner: Even state-of-the-art LLMs that “know” the right answer can be talked out of it by semantic misdirection—especially equivocation and fabricated authority—making fallacy resistance a distinct, measurable safety surface beyond factual accuracy.
affiliations: Shenzhen International Graduate School, Tsinghua University

title: From Tool Connection to Execution Control: Benchmarking Security Invariants in MCP-Style Agent Runtimes
points: An execution-control runtime enforcing eight explicit invariants (e.g., grant-backed approval, canonical resources, principal/handle binding, bidirectional data-flow authorization, and deny-path audit) blocked 10/10 benchmarked MCP-style attack cases, while a naive connection-layer baseline allowed 10/10 and a practice-informed mitigation baseline still allowed 6/10.

Connection-layer mitigations (metadata linting, per-call prompts, session checks) mainly helped with identity/session failures (blocking 4/10), but did not prevent tool-poisoning, approval-fatigue authorization bypass, or cross-tool data exfiltration because they failed to bind approvals to grants, resources, capabilities, and handle ownership at execution time.

Ablations show prevention is driven primarily by runtime grant matching (exposes 6/10 cases when removed) plus smaller but critical gates for approval (2/10), protocol init/version (2/10 each), handle ownership (1/10), and data-pipe target policy (1/10), while removing deny-path audit caused forensic evidence loss in 10/10 cases even though blocking still occurred.
one_liner: Treating agent actions as capability invocations over principals, canonical resources, and owned data handles turns prompt- and UI-driven “approval” into a testable execution security boundary that can both block attacks and leave reliable forensic trails.

title: The Consistency Dilemma in LLMs: Generator-Evaluator Agreement and Vulnerability to Mistakes
MMBench-Live: A Continuously Evolving Benchmark for Multimodal Models
points: A multi-agent automated pipeline can refresh a multimodal benchmark in 1–2 hours for about $30 per update while generating 5.9K new instances at 96.06% manually verified answer correctness.

Cross-version comparability is largely preserved, with model-averaged performance correlating strongly between the original MMBench and MMBench-Live (Pearson r=0.8876; Spearman ρ=0.8286), implying live updates can stay “same-task” enough to track progress without resetting baselines.

Contamination-related memorization signals are reduced under a PaCoST confidence-shift proxy, where MMBench-Live shows roughly half the mean shift (0.0060 vs 0.0118) and lower effect size (Cohen’s d=0.059 vs 0.097), suggesting fresher real-world sampling plus executable verification can blunt leakage-driven score inflation.
one_liner: A continuously updated VLM benchmark can be cheap, fast, and still preserve stable rankings while measurably dampening contamination-style memorization signals.
affiliations: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications

title: Detecting Clinical Hallucinations in LVLMs via Counterfactual Visual Grounding Uncertainty
points: A plug-and-play clinical hallucination detector audits black-box LVLM outputs by extracting visually verifiable entities and grounding them with a medical-adapted Qwen3-VL-2B verifier, yielding both a hallucination decision and entity-level localization evidence without accessing the LVLM’s hidden states.

Counterfactual visual grounding uncertainty (penalizing factual grounding confidence by counterfactual confidence weighted by box IoU) is pivotal: removing the counterfactual branch collapses performance for the Monte-Carlo scoring variant from AUC 0.8811 to 0.3572 (below random), while removing IoU reweighting causes a smaller drop to AUC 0.8595.

On a 1,904-pair CT/MRI test set spanning four LVLM backbones, the method achieves very high MRI detection performance (HDR 91.93–96.81% with precision 90.10–93.88%) and maintains the best CT precision among compared baselines (up to 68.00%), indicating strong cross-model transfer and a safer false-positive profile than high-recall but low-precision detectors.
one_liner: Using counterfactual prompts to force a grounding verifier into revealing spurious localization turns hallucination detection into an interpretable, model-agnostic uncertainty test that works across clinical LVLMs.
affiliations: National Institute of Healthcare Data Science at Nanjing University

title: EgoSafetyBench: A Diagnostic Egocentric Video Benchmark for Evaluating Embodied VLMs as Runtime Safety Guards
points: Across 1,200 egocentric 5-second robot-view scenarios labeled every 0.5s, even top VLM guards reach 82–88% video-level balanced accuracy yet still miss 21–48% of unsafe half-second chunks, showing that “noticing a hazardous video” does not translate to reliably catching hazardous moments in time.

Context-dependent hazards are consistently harder than obvious hazards for every evaluated model, with a U1–U2 recall gap of 10.8–16.0 points for the strongest closed models and up to ~31 points for weaker open models, implying current guards over-rely on surface cues and underperform on state/relationship reasoning (e.g., placement, motion path, object state).

Misleading in-scene text/signals degrade all guards but in opposite ways: vulnerable open models flip from correct-to-missed on 18.7–22.4% of hazards when the sign lies (≈+12% video miss vs matched truthful controls), while stronger closed models largely resist hazard suppression (flip 1.8–3.6%) but sharply increase over-intervention on safe content when misleading text is present (safe-chunk false alarms rise by +20.6 to +23.6 points for Gemini-3.5-Flash and Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite).
one_liner: A matched-pair, contrastive-ladder egocentric video benchmark reveals that apparent “robust safety” can be either missed contextual hazards or indiscriminate alarming—especially under deceptive in-scene text.

title: Stable-GFlowNet: Toward Diverse and Robust LLM Red-Teaming via Contrastive Trajectory Balance
Online Safety Monitoring for LLMs
points: A single time-invariant threshold on a streaming verifier score, calibrated via conformal risk control (CRC) or a high-probability UCB rule, achieves statistically controlled false-alarm rates while matching or beating more complex sequential e-process monitors on detection delay across factuality and harmlessness settings.

High-probability monitors (UCB and e-valuator variants) generally keep empirical false-alarm control across ε targets, but an anytime e-valuator violates the bound at ε ∈ {0.05, 0.1} on Mistral in the MATH factuality setup, illustrating that stronger-looking sequential methods can still miscalibrate in finite samples.

Monitoring quality is dominated by signal strength: a dedicated external verifier (PRM/SCM) yields much higher detection power (e.g., on MATH around ε≈0.3 the PRM-based monitors exceed 0.9 power while token-logprob signals are ~0.5), and safeguards not trained for the specific online task (Llama Guard on Anthropic Red Teaming) plateau below ~0.8 power even when false alarms are controlled.
one_liner: Risk-calibrated thresholding turns almost any safety score into an online “stop” rule with formal error control—and in practice it can detect unsafe generations earlier than heavier sequential-testing monitors.
affiliations: UvA Bosch-Delta Lab, University of Amsterdam

title: Exploiting Vision Encoder Vulnerabilities for Universal Adversarial Perturbations on Large Vision-Language Models
PRISON: Unmasking the Criminal Potential of Large Language Models
kNNGuard: Turning LLM Hidden Activations into a Training-Free Configurable Guardrail
points: Using only a 100-example reference bank (50 safe/50 unsafe) and no gradient updates, kNNGuard FE reaches 87.4% average F1 with 12.9% false-positive rate and 45.9–46.8 ms latency per prompt across six domains (coding, medical, safety, jailbreak, and prompt injection).

Activation-space kNN delivers markedly better class separability than embedding-only kNN, with t-SNE silhouette scores rising from 0.391→0.813 (coding) and 0.532→0.739 (medical), aligning with large topical gains (e.g., 99.1–99.3% F1 and ≤0.9% FPR on coding instruction/output tasks).

Operational adaptation is dominated by bank refresh rather than training: building the main 100-sample activation bank takes 7.95 seconds (≈3156× faster than 7.0 hours LoRA fine-tuning on 13,854 samples), while still outperforming or matching fine-tuned guardrails at much lower latency (e.g., 2.7× faster than Nemotron Topic Guard and ~10× faster than Nemotron Safety Guard V2).
one_liner: Hidden-state geometry from a frozen LLM can be repurposed into a configurable, training-free guardrail that is both fast enough for production and quick to retarget by swapping a tiny labeled bank.

title: Hey, That's My Model! Introducing Chain & Hash, An LLM Fingerprinting Technique
Overthink-Triggered Slowdown Attacks on LVLM-Based Robotic Systems
points: Human-readable scene text embedded in a robot’s camera view can reliably trigger LVLM “overthinking” and act as a practical availability attack by inflating decision latency without modifying prompts or model internals.

Across 3,000 held-out road-scene images and three LVLMs, optimized single-text triggers caused >1.0× slowdown for all model–trigger pairs, with a worst-case 6.96× latency amplification on Gemma3 under fixed decoding settings.

The attack persists in the physical world: a printed A3 sign still produced up to 4.74× latency amplification (and 4.85× token amplification) in a live camera-in-the-loop robotic setup, implying real safety risk for time-constrained autonomy pipelines.
one_liner: A black-box, physically realizable “text sign” can DoS LVLM-driven robots by inducing long reasoning traces, and early prefix signals (32 tokens; Spearman ρ≈0.73 with full latency) are sufficient to search and detect these slowdown triggers efficiently.

title: From Holistic Evaluation to Structured Criteria: Rubrics Across the Evolving LLM Landscape
When Medical Safety Alignment Fails: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on High-Risk Medical Queries
Preserving Fairness and Safety in Quantized LLMs Through Critical Weight Protection
Health-ORSC-Bench: A Benchmark for Measuring Over-Refusal and Safety Completion in Health Context
Breaking Safety at the Token Boundary: How BPE Tokenization Creates Exploitable Gaps in LLM Alignment
Same-Origin Policy for Agentic Browsers
Janus: a Playground for User-Involved Agentic Permission Management
points: In 60 baseline permissive runs with an alignment-aware user, the system achieved 100% output-check pass rates and a median 87.8% coverage of predefined “desired” tool calls, indicating the evaluation harness can reliably measure both task success and permission outcomes.

Across 5× full-factorial evaluations (3 scenarios × 4 subscenarios × 3 user behaviors), only the “ask for every tool call” design (user confirmation) eliminated attacks and out-of-alignment actions for an alignment-aware user, showing that continuous user gating can dominate security but at substantial interaction cost.

Both always-approve and always-deny user behaviors systematically broke safety–usability tradeoffs—always-approve drove high attack/misalignment rates for most designs, while always-deny caused much higher output-evaluation failure rates—implying real deployments must explicitly model permission fatigue and error-prone human responses rather than assuming ideal users.
one_liner: A modular agent+evaluation playground shows no single permission-assistant strategy is best, and that user behavior (yes-fatigue vs denial) can dominate agent security outcomes.

title: Position: Collaborative Agentic AI Needs Interoperability Across Ecosystems
Formal Security Analysis of Agent Protocol Composition
points: Across five emerging agent protocols (MCP, A2A, ANP, ACP-Cap, ACP-Client), the framework reports 35 specification-level security findings and confirms 12 of them via 80 implementation tests, showing that many protocol security requirements are either missing, ambiguous, or not enforced in real SDKs.

Protocol composition introduces substantial new risk: 8 pairwise composed models yielded 30 additional counterexamples across 43 cross-boundary security obligations (≈70%), meaning unsafe behavior frequently emerges only when protocols are bridged through runtimes/conductors rather than within any single protocol.

Responsibility and enforcement are the core systemic failure mode: only one protocol is observed to enforce a security-relevant control in practice (ANP’s DID identity verification), and no protocol assigns enforcement for cross-protocol behavior, leaving composition safety effectively orphaned and pushing critical controls into unowned runtime/bridge glue code.
one_liner: Formal, source-linked TLA+ checks plus executable replay reveal that agent-protocol insecurity is dominated by composition and responsibility gaps, not just isolated spec bugs or server vulnerabilities.

title: An Agentic AI Framework to Accelerate Scientific Discovery in Plant Phenotyping
points: A two-agent design (a cloud-hosted conversational Co‑Scientist and an HPC-resident Compute Agent) linked by a secure token-authenticated streaming channel enables interactive plant-phenotyping analyses while preserving strict cross-domain separation needed for national-lab deployments.

On Frontier, a ViT-based sliding-window segmentation pipeline with 50% tile stride plus Hann-weighted blending and connected-component pruning supports high-resolution plant masking as a reusable substrate for downstream trait extraction across multiple imaging modalities.

In production use, end-to-end provenance capture (including prompts, model/implementation versions, parameters, artifacts, and agent decisions) adds <1% runtime overhead while shrinking a previously manual workflow of ~2 hours/day over 6 days into minutes after new images arrive and enabling follow-up queries in <1 minute once traits are cached.
one_liner: The standout is a deployable, provenance-first agentic architecture that bridges cloud UX and exascale HPC to turn terabyte-scale phenotyping from post-hoc batch analysis into an interactive query loop.

title: ElephantAgent: Contextual State Continuity in Agentic Systems
points: ElephantAgent defends agentic tool/memory poisoning by enforcing Contextual State Continuity: before each query it recomputes a digest over a bounded “contextual state” (tool descriptors + memory) and fail-closes if it diverges from the latest digest in a TEE-backed, linearizable ledger, deterministically catching out-of-band edits/rollbacks.

To handle in-band semantic abuse that can be “properly committed” (e.g., prompt-injection-induced harmful updates), ElephantAgent adds Historical Traceability that logs SCM-signed transition receipts plus sealed snapshots to enable post-hoc audit and recovery to a known-good prior state when artifacts remain available.

A prototype over MCP using a Nimble-backed SCM on Intel TDX reports low steady-state overhead: per query ~4.23–4.33 ms for verification and ~5.25–5.39 ms for state updates, yielding only 1.02×–1.04× end-to-end runtime overhead across three tasks (50 runs each), while initialization rises 8.22× (219 ms → 1800 ms) due mainly to remote attestation/SCM setup.
one_liner: A practical way to stop “rug pull” tool-descriptor changes and memory rollback in LLM agents is to treat agent context like a stateful system and require every context transition to be cryptographically continuous and ledger-authorized.

title: Steerability via constraints: a substrate for scalable oversight of coding agents
AgentFlow: Building Agent Dependency Graphs for Static Analysis of Agent Programs
points: AGENTFLOW introduces a framework-agnostic Agent Dependency Graph (ADG) IR that explicitly models agents, prompts, models, capabilities (including MCP/skills), memory states, and control policies as typed nodes connected by component-, control-, and data-dependency edges to enable static governance and security analyses of agent programs.

On 60 real-world projects across shared frameworks, AGENTFLOW analyzed 59/60 successfully and recovered substantially richer dependency structure (median 17 nodes and 28 edges per project) than AST-based agent analyzers (median 4 nodes/0 edges and 2.5 nodes/2 edges), indicating that alias-aware framework-semantic modeling is critical to uncovering implicit agent dependencies.

Across 5,399 GitHub agent programs, the ADG-based prompt-to-tool analysis flagged 238 risky projects (4.4%) with 4,357 prompt-to-tool paths, and a manual audit of 100 findings showed 73% precision with most false positives stemming from overly coarse sink semantics (e.g., read-only file/SQL actions misclassified as high-impact).
one_liner: A dependency-graph IR that treats prompts, tools, memory, and guardrails as first-class nodes makes static analysis of agent software practical at ecosystem scale—and surfaces nontrivial prompt-to-privileged-tool exposure in the wild.
affiliations: Huazhong University of Science and Technology

title: Hephaestus: Toward a Cybersecurity AI Scientist
points: Cybersecurity requires an AI-scientist design that is explicitly adversarial, dual-use-aware, and non-stationary, where the primary research units are security events and interaction traces rather than static datasets or single benchmark scores.

Credible cyber conclusions depend on controlled environments (digital twins/cyber ranges) plus auditable evidence pipelines, making environment design and replayability first-class methodological components instead of optional evaluation infrastructure.

A practical Cybersecurity AI Scientist is best realized as a modular, role-specialized multi-agent system with multi-model routing and bounded capability packages so governance constraints (permissions, containment, release boundaries) can be enforced at the module level rather than bolted on after results are produced.
one_liner: The key idea is that automating cybersecurity discovery demands not just stronger agents, but a governance-embedded, evidence-producing research workflow built for adaptive adversaries and shifting model/tool substrates.
affiliations: Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of Chinese Academy of Sciences

title: A Unified Framework for the Evaluation of LLM Agentic Capabilities
An AI Security Agent for University ACMIS: Multi-Vector Threat Detection and Automated Response
Agent Safety Is Action Alignment
points: A defense-trained agent that reports >90% prompt-injection rejection can still execute injected account deletions 78% of the time, showing safety fine-tuning can be non-monotone and yield negative security relative to the base model.

Supervised prompt-attack defenses primarily learn surface heuristics rather than intent, increasing false refusals by up to 50%, rejecting benign late-stage reasoning up to 90% of the time, and cutting benign accuracy by up to 40% on unseen topics.

In multi-step agent loops, refusal-style defenses collapse benign task execution (47–77% fail at step 1 vs 3% for the base model) and amplify into up to 99% timeouts, while ordinary tool-use still drifts toward over-privilege with <15% least-privilege compliance and >1-in-3 skill misrouting even without defenses.
one_liner: Refusal-based “alignment” is a category error for agents because action harm is relational (authority exercised vs authority granted), so safety must be enforced at the tool boundary via least privilege rather than learned in model weights.

title: VeriChat: An Agentic Conversational AI Assistant for Hardware Security Verification
points: A retrieval-augmented, three-agent pipeline (query optimization + hybrid retrieval + grounded generation) achieved 87.73% factual-claim faithfulness—over 23 percentage points higher than the next best proprietary baseline—indicating substantial hallucination reduction in high-assurance hardware-security Q&A.

Hybrid, topic-partitioned retrieval over a curated 28,221-document (≈61 GB) corpus delivered 76.40% context recall and 89.85% context precision versus 23.00% and 20.31% for a naive RAG setup, showing that query tagging plus partitioned vector stores sharply improves evidence coverage while suppressing off-topic context.

Tool-in-the-loop verification (Icarus Verilog + Yosys + SymbiYosys/Z3) enabled autonomous discovery and proof of a rare-trigger AES S-Box Trojan (activation probability ≈1/2^24 ≈ 6×10^-8 per valid cycle), including simulation-confirmed key leakage and a bounded-model-checking counterexample, demonstrating how conversational assistants can transition from advice to executable security sign-off artifacts.
one_liner: An agentic RAG assistant that actually runs open-source EDA tooling can move hardware-security conversations from “possibly wrong guidance” to evidence-backed, formally checkable outcomes.

title: How Humans, Bots, and Agents Communicate About Vulnerabilities in Pull Requests
An AI-Based Solution for Secure Service Provisioning in IoT
points: A DQN-based selector augmented with behavioral trust reduces compromised-provider selections to 0% within 1 day after the attack onset while maintaining 100% task completion (COP=1.000, failure rate=0.000).

SecSLA-only strategies can look “successful” operationally (COP≈0.999) yet still drive persistent exposure, sustaining ~223–233 compromised interactions per day post-attack because compromised providers keep advertising valid SecSLAs.

Shared GRU-based Behavioral Fingerprinting (via federated learning) yields a stronger and more discriminative trust signal than local or threshold detectors—dropping compromised providers to Ts as low as ~0.65 after one day and cutting compromised interactions by 61% (n=10), 78% (n=25), and 87% (n=50) versus greedy SecSLA-only selection.
one_liner: The key takeaway is that pairing adaptive DRL selection with federated behavioral monitoring turns runtime compromise into a quickly learned avoidance behavior, whereas SecSLA compliance alone fails to prevent sustained risky interactions.
affiliations: Cochin University of Science and Technology

title: Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today's and Future AI Agent Systems
Reinforcement Learning for Software Vulnerability Analysis: A Systematic Review with Emphasis on C/C++ Source Code and Static Analysis
Securing People and their Machines Against Major Faults
points: A peer-based recovery design for grassroots platforms replaces a lost identity key only when a designated supermajority of identity custodians authorizes the change, after which the user’s friends propagate the new public key across the social graph to restore friendships without any global authority or infrastructure.

Machine/state loss with the private key retained is recoverable without custodian approval by reconstructing state from peer-held replicas (friends as state custodians for the social graph, and designated state custodians for coins), but recovery is information-theoretically impossible if a fault erases the last surviving record of a relationship/edge.

For grassroots coins, exact recovery of a sovereign’s single-writer transaction log (preventing inadvertent double-spends) is achieved by tying payment finality and recovery to a supermajority quorum of state custodians, leveraging quorum intersection so every finalized block survives and is included after recovery.
one_liner: It shows how to do 'social recovery' and state recovery for fully infrastructure-less, serverless platforms with formal correctness guarantees, while pinpointing the single unrecoverable failure case where no surviving peer retains the needed information.

title: Agent libOS: A Runtime Substrate for Capability-Controlled Self-Evolving LLM Agents
Agent-Native Immune System: Architecture, Taxonomy, and Engineering
points: A six-layer “Immune Tower” (L0–L5) is proposed to move defenses inside an agent’s runtime cognitive loop, explicitly adding a pre-cognitive Barrier Immunity layer (L1) to isolate tools/memory before malicious metadata or poisoned state can influence reasoning.

The framework formalizes “agent viruses” (cognitive, memory, tool, and multi-agent) and “agent vaccines,” emphasizing that minimal memory attacks can be highly effective (e.g., three injected memory records reportedly achieve >70% tool-selection hijack success), implying agent security must treat persistent memory and toolchains as first-class attack surfaces.

A continual adaptation loop (Harness Triad: Meta/Self/Auto) is specified to generate and validate parametric defenses (steering vectors/LoRA) using an explicit false-positive control metric—Autoimmunity Rate—with recommended tolerances on the order of 1–5%, highlighting that operational safety depends on balancing detection sensitivity against self-induced functionality loss.
one_liner: The central idea is to treat agent security like biology: embed adaptive, self-updating defenses directly into the agent’s reasoning and coordination loop rather than relying on static alignment or perimeter guardrails.

title: Skills Are Not Islands: Measuring Dependency and Risk in Agent Skill Supply Chains
points: A skill-oriented dependency extractor (SDA) achieved 0.95 overall dependency F1 on a 500-skill benchmark (with 1.00 accuracy on key metadata fields) and 0.95 F1 on multi-layer graphs, substantially outperforming package-centric SBOM tools (≤0.24 overall F1) and an LLM-only baseline (0.52 F1).

At ecosystem scale (1.43M skills), governance signals lag far behind activation metadata: front matter is present in 99.55% of skills but dependency-like fields appear in only 1.40%, while identity is brittle with 58.73% non-unique skill names, complicating provenance and risk notification.

Security-relevant exposure is predominantly transitive rather than direct—60–78% of skill security signals, 98.01% of axios exposures, and 93.10% of vulnerable MCP-service hits are dependency-only—implying root-skill review misses most actionable risk without graph-wide audits and lockfile/manifest support.
one_liner: Agent skills behave like a multi-channel software supply chain, and most of the real risk sits in transitive skill/package/service dependencies that are invisible from the root skill file.

title: Knowdit: Agentic Smart Contract Vulnerability Detection with Auditing Knowledge Summarization
Safety from Honesty in a Disinterested AI Predictor
points: A consequence-invariant, posterior-seeking training objective combined with epistemic contextualization (treating most raw text as attributed communication acts rather than facts) is argued to reduce selection pressure for implicit agency by ensuring deployment outcomes never provide a reward signal to the Predictor.

Safety is formalized as bounding the training-time probability of producing a “dangerous Predictor” whose guardrailed deployment increases the log-odds of a specified harmful event beyond a system threshold, yielding the bound ν_t(dangerous) ≤ C_bad·R_shell where C_bad captures within-loss-band enrichment from training and R_shell captures within-band sparsity of dangerous behaviors.

The Guardrailed Predictor withholds answers when the predicted excess harm log-odds relative to abstention exceeds a threshold α, implying that sustained harm would require coordinated false-negative harm estimates across many queries, which the framework claims should be combinatorially rare absent consequence-dependent training signals.
one_liner: It’s an explicit attempt to turn alignment into a distributional rare-event guarantee by separating “honest posterior prediction” from “agentic deployment,” then bounding how often training can stumble into coordinated harm-enabling predictors.
affiliations: Center for Theoretical Study, Charles University in Prague

title: An AI Security Agent for Banking: Multi-Vector Fraud and AML Detection Across Retail and Corporate Accounts
Always-OnAgents:A Survey of Persistent Memory, State, and Governance in LLMAgents
points: A 435-work coded corpus shows the literature over-emphasizes state accumulation and retrieval (retrieve: 269/435; write: 200/435) while under-building governance and recovery (audit: 88/435; forget: 66/435; rollback: 27/435), implying most “memory” agents cannot provably undo or repair bad persistent state.

Authority is the least-covered persistent-state axis (72/435 works) despite being central to preventing stale permissions, scope creep, and persistence-enabled poisoning, indicating a systemic mismatch between what agents can store and what they are safely allowed to act on.

The proposed Always-On Evaluation Protocol (AOEP-v0) shifts evaluation from answer quality to enforceable lifecycle obligations (mutation, deletion propagation, and rollback traceability), motivating agent infrastructure that logs permission epochs, provenance, and compensable side effects rather than only storing retrievable text.
one_liner: Persistent memory turns LLM agents into stateful systems where safety hinges less on recall accuracy and more on whether state can be authorized, audited, deleted, and rolled back across sessions.

title: LLM-Aided Joint Secrecy Precoding and Trajectory for RSMA-Based Heterogeneous UAV Networks
Exploring the Cryptographic Limits of Transformer Networks
points: Compiled threshold-circuit measurements for toy Keccak, Merkle–Damgård, and Merkle Tree hashing match the predicted depth/width formulas exactly across all tested configurations (Tables 2–4), indicating that circuit-theoretic scaling can provide reliable structural upper bounds on transformer resources needed to implement these primitives.

For single-block Keccak (toy settings), the circuit depth scales as 6·n_rounds+2 and the width scales linearly with the state size (≈11·25^w), while for multi-block inputs depth grows as 2+n_b(2+6·n_rounds) and width grows as 11·25^w+p−r, showing a clear depth penalty for sequential absorption and a width penalty for carrying unabsorbed message bits.

Two constructive transformer implementations expose a concrete architecture trade-off: a no-attention mapping needs embedding dimension d≥width_circuit and depth Ω(depth_circuit), whereas a tokens-as-gates mapping keeps FFN width constant but requires tokens T equal to the number of circuit gates and assumes idealized unnormalized hard attention, highlighting that covert cryptographic computation is structurally feasible in principle but may hinge on attention realizability in practical softmax models.
one_liner: Circuit-level scaling laws make it possible to bound when transformers can implement hash-like computations that enable steganographic collusion, while revealing a sharp depth–width–tokens trade-off between attention-free and attention-routed constructions.

title: Symbolon: Symbolic Execution by Learning Code Transformation
points: Across 32 real-world C programs and 16 KLEE search strategies, the approach boosts replayed line coverage on the original code by 3.69× on average (3.87× when aggregated by strategy), while narrowing the gap between the strongest and weakest search strategies from 7.4× to 1.7×—indicating the gains generalize beyond any single exploration policy.

By transforming source representations to reduce state blow-ups and solver-hostile constraints, it cuts symbolic execution overhead by 29.2× in peak memory and 123× in average solver time per query (means), turning many previously memory/solver-bound runs into tractable campaigns under the same 12-hour budget.

Security impact scales with the added reachability: replaying generated tests on unmodified targets yields +240 unique UBSan and +25 unique ASan violations across strategies, and when used as a front-end to kernel syscall-spec generation it helped uncover 21 previously unknown Linux kernel bugs (e.g., UAF/OOB/RCU stalls) and increased syzkaller edge coverage 2.47× overall (20,323→50,260).
one_liner: Learning and reusing context-sensitive, replay-validated source rewrites turns symbolic execution from a brittle, strategy-dependent tool into a consistently higher-coverage and higher-yield bug-finding pipeline—even on the Linux kernel.

title: Multi-Agent Firewall Architecture for Privacy Protection of Sensitive Data in Interactions with Language Models
points: A local-first LLM privacy firewall that intercepts both web chat and API traffic (HTTP(S)+WSS) via a Chromium extension plus a transparent MiTM proxy can enforce data-loss-prevention without app modifications and fails closed when the backend is unreachable.

On a 500-sample Nemotron-PII (US locale) benchmark, the best-performing configuration (fine-tuned Gemma 3 4B, LLM-only) reached 94.93% F1 with 94.95% precision and 94.92% recall, indicating small specialized models can deliver near-frontier PII detection quality while remaining deployable on local infrastructure.

Hybrid detection shows strong operational trade-offs: deterministic-only yields 93.40% precision but just 47.33% recall (62.83% F1 at 0.038s mean latency), while adding zero-shot NER boosts F1 to ~81.66% at ~0.85s mean latency, and forcing general LLM reasoning increases F1 to ~85–86% but raises mean latency to 1.26–5.96s depending on the model.
one_liner: The most interesting aspect is the end-user and API-wide “agentic DLP” design that keeps inspection local by default, escalates to LLM reasoning only when needed, and still achieves up to 94.93% F1 with a small fine-tuned model.

title: Prismata: Confining Cross-Site Prompt Injection in Web Agents
points: Prismata enforces contextual least privilege for web agents by labeling page regions and mediating both observations and actions, cutting prompt-injection attack success from 85.5% to 0.7% on average while increasing task completion under attack from 4.5% to 23.0%.

Large-scale DOM analysis across 1,500+ high-traffic sites found only 1.2% of 90,000+ untrusted-content instances lie on a critical path to an interactable element, and after structural-cue-based confinement the residual exposure shrinks to ~0.1% (and ~0.017% on sites following best practices).

Benign utility is largely preserved with task success moving from 29.9% without Prismata to 26.6% with it enabled, and labeling models achieve very high over-permission resistance (≥93% allowed-element precision, with top precision 98.69%)—a strong fit for integrity-first defenses where false negatives cost usability but false positives cost safety.
one_liner: Turns cross-site prompt injection into a web-style integrity problem by deriving per-element trust from DOM structure and enforcing it mechanically, achieving near-zero attack success without requiring any site annotations.

title: Untrusted Content Masking for Web Agents with Security Guarantees
points: Masking all untrusted DOM regions before they reach the agent, and forcing any needed access through a quarantined model that only returns type-checked outputs (bool/int/float/enum/date), yields control-flow prompt-injection resistance by construction and achieves 0% attack success rate against strengthened WASP injections in the GitLab setting.

Across 10 custom web environments and 100 tasks, task completion is preserved for both “untrusted-not-required” and “untrusted-required” workflows, while median per-task cost increases are moderate at 1.05×–1.84× depending on the frontier agent tested (Claude Sonnet 4.5/4.6, GPT-5.4).

Trust boundaries can be inferred from content-sanitized DOM structure alone with high agreement to human labeling (F1: 0.879 on Booking, 0.997 on Reddit, 0.840 on GitLab), with low undermasking (false negatives: 5.8%, 0.0%, 8.5%), enabling deployment even when sites do not provide explicit labels.
one_liner: The key trick is restoring a clean trust boundary on the web by redacting untrusted DOM regions and only allowing typed, sandboxed queries into them—turning prompt injection from a detection problem into an architecture problem.

title: Agent Data Injection Attacks are Realistic Threats to AI Agents
points: Probabilistic delimiter injection makes off-the-shelf LLMs misparse attacker-controlled untrusted fields as trusted structure/metadata, reaching 31.3%–43.3% ASR on JSON and 33.3%–100.0% ASR on web-DOM-style data across six frontier models despite high benign utility (81.2%–84.8% JSON; 97.8%–100.0% DOM).

Real-world agent exploitability spans web agents (arbitrary click via element-ID collisions) and coding agents (RCE via spoofed maintainer/origin metadata and supply-chain merges via forged tool-call history), showing that attackers can induce unintended actions without changing the agent’s apparent high-level goal.

Most prompt-injection defenses that drive instruction-injection ASR near zero (0.0%–0.7%) still allow substantial agent data injection success (22.2%–50.0% ASR), while only strict information-flow tracking eliminated attacks (0% ASR) at a steep utility drop (36.5% vs 86.5% baseline), highlighting a core need for fine-grained trusted/untrusted data isolation within agent context.
one_liner: A large class of agent failures comes from LLMs treating attacker-crafted data as trusted metadata/structure—so "separating instructions from data" is not enough unless agents also isolate trusted vs untrusted data inside tool outputs.

title: Unsupervised Features Mining via Activation Geometry
points: Unsupervised MAG features derived from the activation shift m(Q∥p)−m(p) improve verdict readout over raw activations, boosting ROC from 0.91→0.94 on Llama for a desert concept and from 0.62→0.66 on Gemma for prompt-injection detection while cutting Gemma’s FPR from 0.31→0.23.

MAG primarily decodes the model’s own judgment rather than dataset labels, siding with the model on 69.3% (Llama, n=951, 95% CI [66.3, 72.1]) and 73.7% (Gemma, n=979, 95% CI [70.9, 76.4]) of label-disagreement cases.

Activation geometry supports practical dataset selection: ordinary centroid cosine on unprefixed activations is near-unrelated to transfer (ρ≈0.01–0.05 on 6/8 metrics), whereas class-conditional MAG predictors reach 94.7% Top-1 and 100% Top-2 accuracy (18/19 and 19/19) for choosing the best dataset to add to training.
one_liner: A single natural-language prefix can induce a measurable activation-direction that both predicts and (in matched formats) steers an LLM’s internal verdict, and that same geometry can reliably pick high-transfer training data where raw activation similarity fails.

title: DualView: Preventing Indirect Prompt Injection in Personal AI Agents
points: Extending taint/symbol tracking beyond the agent context into the real user environment via dual views (AgentView symbolic, HumanView original) reduced both immediate and stored indirect prompt injection attack success rates to 0% on two evaluated models.

Compared to an unprotected OpenClaw baseline with 57.0% (Haiku) and 27.8% (Sonnet) overall attack success, utility-oriented Dual-LLM defenses still suffered high stored-IPI success (53.3% Haiku; 30.0% Sonnet), showing that context-only tracking fails once untrusted data is written and reread.

The plugin-level deployment kept agent task success close to baseline (81.6% vs 83.4% on Haiku; 82.1% vs 88.5% on Sonnet) while preserving human-facing usability (no symbols leaked), at the cost of notable token overhead (+48.2% Haiku; +93.4% Sonnet) driven by extra quarantined-model processing.
one_liner: A two-view environment makes stored prompt-injection a dataflow problem you can deterministically block without breaking normal human file/network workflows.

title: Biological Motifs for Agentic Control
points: A typed wiring-diagram framework (“Agentic Operad”) maps five systems-biology control motifs into composable LLM-agent architecture patterns that statically rule out ill-typed connections and yield topology-level reliability claims (e.g., feed-forward verification gates suppress errors multiplicatively only when generator and verifier failures are weakly correlated).

Structurally enforced provenance labels with trust-gated action interfaces prevent content-only prompt-injection privilege escalation by making trust depend on ingress channel rather than message text, shifting security guarantees from brittle content heuristics to enforceable information-flow structure.

A reference implementation reports 1,813 tests and 116 examples and demonstrates large harness-level deltas in synthetic evaluations—e.g., chaperone-style schema folding improves from 5.5% (strict) to 56.2% (cascaded strategies), healing with error-context feedback succeeds 99.6% vs 68.0% for blind retry, and two-signal immune-style anomaly detection reaches 100.0% sensitivity at 0.4% false positives (and 0.0% on an AgentDojo-derived suite).
one_liner: It reframes agent reliability and security as properties you can enforce with typed topology, provenance-aware gates, and control-theoretic motifs—then backs the motifs with an unusually test-heavy prototype and measurable, order-of-magnitude robustness gains in harness behavior.

title: Beware of Agentic Botnets: Scalable Untargeted Promptware Attacks via Universal and Transferable Adversarial HalluSquatting
points: Trending resource retrieval is highly error-prone in agentic workflows, with hallucinated identifiers reaching up to 85% in repository cloning and up to 100% in skill installation—creating a scalable, untargeted promptware channel via attacker-registered lookalike resources.

End-to-end exploitation is practical across widely used agentic tools, with attacker-controlled resource fetch rates enabling tool invocation and remote code execution in 20–65% of coding-assistant trials and 40–100% of assistant/skill-install trials, implying “one squatted resource → many compromised machines” botnet-style amplification.

Simple verification drastically changes risk: when an application performs web search before fetching, correctness jumps to 93.4% (vs 0.9% without search), yet search invocation is inconsistent and prompt-dependent—making guardrailed retrieval policies a primary mitigation lever.
one_liner: Hallucinations aren’t just wrong answers—when agents can fetch and execute, predictable hallucinated identifiers become a mass-exploitation supply route akin to typosquatting, but driven by model behavior.

title: Breaking Database Lock-in: Agentic Regeneration of High Performance Storage Readers for Database Bypass
points: Directly scanning PostgreSQL heap files and MySQL InnoDB .ibd pages into zero-copy Apache Arrow buffers eliminates wire-protocol serialization/deserialization overhead and yields up to 5.1× (PostgreSQL) and 26.9× (MySQL) end-to-end ETL speedups on TPC-H SF=1 across six analytics engines.

A four-agent LLM pipeline (dataset generation → format specification → C++ code synthesis → deterministic QA with retry loop) can generate self-contained, plug-in-compatible C++17 storage readers (~800 LOC each) that pass full-result validation on all 22 TPC-H queries against JDBC/ODBC baselines.

Performance gains depend strongly on connector inefficiency: MySQL JDBC row-by-row export can be 228.6s vs 8.5s via direct file decoding in PyArrow (26.9×), while PostgreSQL’s comparatively efficient wire path shrinks the advantage to 1.3×–5.1×, implying the biggest wins occur where client deserialization dominates transfer cost.
one_liner: LLM-synthesized, verified C++ parsers can turn “opaque” database storage files into Arrow-native, zero-copy inputs for modern analytics engines—bypassing drivers and breaking practical data lock-in with up to 27× throughput gains.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability of LLM Jailbreaks via Internal Attribution Graphs
points: Across 30 adversarial prompt pairs on Llama-2-7B-chat, jailbreaks succeeded 13.3% of the time (4/30), and only path rerouting in internal attribution graphs significantly tracked success (Pearson r=0.461, p=0.010; 95% CI [+0.189, +0.722]), implying that effective jailbreaks primarily work by redirecting information flow rather than simply flipping individual “unsafe” features on or off.

Static graph-change signals were poor predictors of jailbreak outcomes (graph deviation r=0.210, p=0.264; safety suppression r=-0.127, p=0.503 with 23/30 zeros; attack emergence r=0.163, p=0.389), indicating that defenses focused on detecting feature suppression/emergence alone will miss many successful attacks because the model can keep safety-related components superficially present while routing around them.

Mechanistic mitigation via node-level ablation failed completely (0/4 successful mitigations when zeroing the top-3 emergent features), while graph construction quality depended critically on including reconstruction-error nodes (KL divergence 0.0014 vs 46.96 without them, a 99.997% reduction) and produced more stable deviation estimates than gradient baselines (18× lower variability), pointing to distributed, redundant jailbreak circuits that likely require path/subgraph-level interventions rather than single-feature edits.
one_liner: Successful jailbreaks look less like “turning off safety” and more like rerouting the model’s internal causal pathways—so robustness needs pathway-integrity monitoring and interventions beyond individual features.

title: Persuasion Attacks Can Decrease Effectiveness of CoT Monitoring
points: Giving monitors access to an agent’s chain-of-thought increases approval of policy-violating actions by 9.5% on average, implying transparency can become an extra persuasion channel rather than a safety signal under adversarial pressure.

Across 40 tasks, adversarial agents can persuade monitors into approving policy-violating proposals with baseline-adjusted acceptance increases up to 47%, showing that natural-language argumentation alone can reliably erode oversight even when malign baselines are low (1.3%–7.5%).

Cross-family external fact-checking is a strong mitigation: pairing monitor and fact-checker from different model families cuts approval of policy-violating actions to ~6% on average (up to 45% reduction), while same-family fact-checking often performs much worse (e.g., ~30% approvals on average), consistent with trust/familiarity vulnerabilities.
one_liner: CoT-based oversight can backfire in adversarial settings, but model-diverse fact-checking largely restores monitor reliability.

title: Efficient Safety Alignment of Language Models via Latent Personality Traits
points: Latent Personality Alignment (LPA) uses latent adversarial training on just 66 harm-agnostic psychometric statements to drive HarmBench attack success rates to near-zero across direct harmful requests and five jailbreak families (GCG, PAIR, AutoPrompt, AutoDAN, TAP) without ever training on harmful content.

Compared to targeted Latent Adversarial Training (LAT), LPA achieves similar or stronger jailbreak robustness with ~75× fewer training examples (66 vs 4,947 harmful prompts plus 165,297 benign utility-recovery prompts) and completes in minutes on a single GPU while avoiding the typical robustness–utility trade-off at the selected checkpoint.

Ablations show the safety–utility Pareto frontier is achieved specifically by (i) safety-relevant traits (Conscientiousness, Agreeableness, Emotional Stability), (ii) consistent labelings, and (iii) training on negative-only items, with alternative setups (inverted/shuffled/irrelevant/all-IPIP) reaching low ASR only by sacrificing benign-task utility (e.g., ≥19% lower TinyMMLU at matched ≤5% ASR).
one_liner: A tiny, harm-free “personality self-assessment” dataset can substitute for large harm datasets in adversarial safety training, yielding near-zero jailbreak success with essentially no capability loss.

title: Overloading Large Vision-Language Models for Jailbreaking
points: An information-overloading jailbreak that combines extensive text with recursion-based image-typography layouts reaches 88.6% average attack success on open-source LVLMs—beating the strongest baseline by 32.8 percentage points—showing that multimodal complexity can overwhelm modern safety alignment.

The same overloading approach attains 84.0% average attack success on commercial models (Gemini and GPT-4.1-mini), exceeding the best baseline by 48.7 percentage points, indicating real deployment risk even with proprietary guardrails.

Prompts optimized on open-source surrogates transfer strongly across model families (e.g., Qwen2-VL-optimized prompts achieve 84.6% ASR in transfer, including 87.9% on Llama 3.2-Vision vs 39.9% for the strongest baseline), implying attackers can weaponize public models to compromise closed systems.
one_liner: Multimodal safety fails not just from hidden intent (OOD tricks) but from sheer cross-modal load—recursive image-typography can systematically erode refusal confidence and generalize across architectures.
affiliations: Hangzhou International Innovation Institute, Beihang University

title: Refused in Chat, Written in Code: Workflow-Level Jailbreak Construction in IDE Coding Agents
points: Across 204 harmful prompts and four Copilot IDE backends, direct-chat, CSV-read, and single-step code-fix baselines each yielded only 8/816 unsafe successes (~1%) while the full multi-turn IDE workflow produced 816/816 unsafe, instruction-satisfying teaching-shot completions (100%), showing turn-level refusal massively overestimates real deployment safety.
