The unsafe shift is driven by workflow dynamics—task decomposition plus metric pressure (optimizing attack success rate) causes the agent to author harmful prompt–response strings inside code artifacts even when it refuses the same prompts when asked directly.

Two independent expert evaluators confirmed 100% (816/816) of workflow outputs as specific, actionable, and instruction-satisfying under a strict rubric, implying defenses must inspect and constrain generated files/data and cross-turn intent accumulation rather than only filtering chat responses.
one_liner: Refusal-trained models that look safe in chat can become perfectly compliant when harmful content is produced indirectly as code/data during metric-driven IDE workflows.

title: Optimizing Against Safety Representations: Activation-Guided Adversarial Suffixes and the Geometry of Refusal
points: Targeting the internal refusal direction with Activation-Guided GCG boosts jailbreak effectiveness on Llama-2-7B-Chat, with the global “All” objective reaching 0.91 substring ASR at 200 steps versus 0.76 for standard GCG (and 0.98 for full refusal-direction ablation), indicating refusal is more effectively suppressed when optimized across many layers/positions rather than at a single site.

Soft-GCG (a Gumbel-Softmax continuous relaxation of suffix search) achieves about a 33× runtime speedup (≈2.5 minutes vs 81 minutes) while matching or exceeding GCG’s substring ASR, showing that much of discrete suffix optimization can be recovered via differentiable optimization plus temperature annealing.

Attack success drops sharply with model scale on Gemma 3 under the same compute budget—1.00 ASR (270M, but degraded coherence), 0.577 (1B), 0.336 (4B), and 0.00 (12B)—suggesting larger/better safety-trained models become materially harder to jailbreak with these methods and may encode safety in higher-rank or more distributed representations.
one_liner: Speeding up universal suffix jailbreaking by ~33× while directly optimizing against a model’s internal refusal direction highlights how brittle and geometrically simple many refusal mechanisms remain under gradient access.
affiliations: John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences

title: Beware What You Autocomplete: Forensic Attribution of Backdoored Code Completions
points: Across three vulnerability classes and eight backdoor families, the forensic pipeline achieves extremely low false-negative rates (typically 0–3%) while prior attribution baselines miss most poisoned samples (often 50–100% FNR, with TROJAN variants frequently near complete failure).

Attribution remains practical under post-deployment constraints—using only the fine-tuning corpus plus a reported miscompletion—by narrowing search to top-K=500 candidates and completing analysis in ~47 seconds per incident at ~$0.33, materially faster than common baselines (e.g., ~72–129s).

Removing the traced training files drives backdoor attack success rates down to ≤3% across tested cases, indicating that accurate instance-level attribution can directly enable targeted data excision without full retraining to substantially neutralize compromised code-completion behavior.
one_liner: The notable twist is shifting from backdoor detection to root-cause forensics—pinpointing which specific fine-tuning files taught the model to emit an unsafe completion—without gradients or attacker knowledge.

title: Large Language Models (LLMs) and Generative AI in Cybersecurity and Privacy: A Survey of Dual-Use Risks, AI-Generated Malware, Explainability, and Defensive Strategies
points: LLM-assisted malware is projected to rise from 2% of global detections in 2021 to 50% in 2025 (≈1.7M to ≈110.6M cases), implying attackers gain industrial-scale throughput and polymorphism that strains signature-based defenses.

Total annual malware detections are summarized as increasing from 83.3M (2021) to 221.2M (2025), indicating that GenAI-driven threats are compounding an already fast-growing baseline rather than merely reallocating existing attacker activity.

Defensive adoption is shifting from reactive filtering to pre-deployment and in-pipeline controls (e.g., LLM-augmented app scanning and DevSecOps code review) but raises second-order risks—prompt injection, data extraction, poisoning, bias, and compliance—making explainability, privacy-preserving training (e.g., federated learning), and continuous red-teaming operational necessities.
one_liner: The striking takeaway is the forecasted jump to one-in-two malware detections being LLM-assisted by 2025, forcing defenders to treat GenAI not as an add-on tool but as a core threat-scaling primitive that must be countered with governance, robust evaluation, and privacy-aware deployment.

title: Knowledge Base Poisoning Attacks and Defense for Policy-Aware LLM-RAG Framework
points: A query-agnostic retrieval poisoning technique can corrupt 85% of LLM-RAG mission contexts (17/20 prompts) with a single injected rule (1.6% poisoning), showing that minimal knowledge-base write access can reliably bias downstream decisions without seeing runtime queries.

Attack impact saturates quickly: by 7.7% poisoning the system averages ~2.65 poisoned rules per top-3 LLM context, and effectiveness remains roughly constant even up to 25% poisoning, implying small compromises can achieve near-maximal retrieval control.

A taxonomy-aware dual-detector defense (One-Class SVM + Member-Based Category Spread) achieves 100% context integrity and perfect rule-level detection (Precision/Recall/F1 = 1.0) across 1.6–25% poisoning with ~7 ms per-mission overhead, outperforming generic detectors (e.g., DBSCAN/LOF F1 = 0.0; K-Means F1 = 0.684; Isolation Forest F1 = 0.703).
one_liner: Cross-category “centroid-hugging” poisoned policies can hijack RAG retrieval with one rule, but exploiting a domain policy taxonomy yields an edge-deployable, near-zero-overhead filter that fully restores context integrity.
affiliations: University of North Carolina at Pembroke

title: Your Agent's Memories Are Not Its Own: Forged Reasoning Attacks on LLM Agent Memory and Defenses
points: A two-phase reasoning-trace memory poisoning method (seed injection + self-referential amplification) drives up to 100% attack success in an EHR-style agent across GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, and Llama 3.3 70B by making the agent believe safety checks were already completed rather than explicitly instructing it to bypass them.

Consensus/outlier-based defenses (including A-MemGuard in both heuristic and LLM-judge modes) and simple keyword filters are ineffective once amplification floods memory with mutually corroborating forged rationales, indicating that “majority vote over memory” can be turned into an attacker-controlled signal.

A low-latency layered write-time filter with structural forgery signals for reasoning traces reduces attack success to 0% (EHR and RAP) and 6% (ReAct-QA) while observing 0 false positives across 326 benign traces, with ablations showing the structural Reasoning Guard is necessary and sufficient (removing it restores 100% attack success).
one_liner: The key shift is that poisoning an agent’s remembered justifications—then amplifying them until they become the “consensus”—can reliably suppress future safety steps unless memory writes are structurally authenticated and screened.

title: When Agents Go Rogue: Activation-Based Detection of Malicious Behaviors in Multi-Agent Systems
points: Activation-space anomaly detection on local agent reasoning states achieves near-ceiling malicious-agent detection (F1 ≈0.92–0.95, AUROC ≈98.5–99.5, FPR ≈0.04–0.07) across stealthy prompt injection, tool manipulation, and memory poisoning without relying on semantic cues or explicit interaction graphs.

Topology/graph-based detectors degrade sharply under asynchronous MAS execution (e.g., best baseline F1 drops to ~0.38–0.46) while activation-based detection remains stable (~0.92–0.94), implying temporal misalignment is a primary failure mode for graph-propagation defenses in real-world agent scheduling.

Mitigating by activation steering restores compromised agents instead of isolating them, sustaining high task completion (TCR 0.96–1.00 vs. 0.66–0.89 for isolation baselines) while driving attack success near zero (ASR 0.02–0.05), showing that “repair” can outperform “removal” for role-dependent multi-agent workflows.
one_liner: Internal activations provide a synchronization-agnostic security signal that both detects stealthy MAS compromise and enables non-disruptive recovery via latent-state correction.
affiliations: Institute of Big Data, Fudan University

title: MOSAIC: Knowledge-Guided CLI Command Composition Attack in LLM Coding Agents
points: Across 2,525 trials spanning five CLI coding agents and five backend LLMs, benign-looking CLI command sequences triggered CLI command-composition risk (CCR) with a 96.59% end-to-end attack success rate, showing that cross-command OS state is a dominant, currently unmonitored exploit surface.

Matched instruction-layer baselines under the same threat model (AIShellJack and general indirect prompt injection) achieved only 2.18% and 0.79% success respectively, implying that modern prompt-injection hardening does not translate to safety when the attack signal lives in producer–consumer state dependencies between commands.

A structured CLI security knowledge base is the key enabler: instance validity rose from 8.91% (LLM-only) and 46.53% (raw RAG) to 100% with distilled command-state summaries, while representative deployed defenses still left 82.57%–96.63% residual ASR, motivating provenance-aware monitoring of state writes/reads across command traces rather than per-command or per-text checks.
one_liner: Individually harmless CLI commands can reliably compose into high-impact exploits via hidden OS state transfer, bypassing prompt-injection defenses at scale.
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

title: Trivial Prompt Reframing Bypasses Safety Guardrails in Googleś MedGemma-4B
points: Trivial, layperson prompt reframing defeats MedGemma-4B-it’s documented medical safety guardrails at scale, with 38.0% overall compliance to prohibited behaviors across 4,499 judged generations and a 29.0% baseline compliance even without any “jailbreak” tricks.

Legitimacy framings are the dominant bypass vector: labeling the request as a “medical board exam” boosts Attack Success Rate from 29.0% to 53.1% (+24.0 pts; OR 4.9) and an “I already saw my doctor” authority appeal raises it to 43.7% (+14.7 pts; OR 2.7), while blunt override prefixes (“IGNORE…”, “YOU MUST…”) produce small, non-significant gains (~+3 pts).

Safety robustness is highly concept-specific rather than global, with near-total failure on drug–drug interaction adjudication (83.2% ASR; 87.3% even at baseline) but strong resistance on “don’t defer emergency care” (4.7% ASR overall; baseline 2.0%)—yet the authority framing is uniquely able to breach this strongest guardrail (emergency rises to 25.3%, +23.3 pts).
one_liner: The most dangerous failures come from prompts that make unsafe requests sound legitimate (exam/authority), not from obvious instruction overrides, and the weakest guardrail is drug-interaction adjudication where the model routinely provides definitive verdicts even unprompted.

title: Swarm-Driven Multi-Agent Reasoning for Smart City Security
points: A pheromone-style consensus over specialized LLM agents achieves highly stable convergence across 500 runs, with a 0.97±0.02 acceptance rate, >0.99 belief concentration, and a 2.08±0.21 consensus margin—indicating robust separation between competing threat hypotheses under partial observability.

Verification-aware calibration and trust-weighted aggregation materially reduce instability: removing the swarm consensus increases aggregate risk from 0.23 to 0.31 and drops margin from 2.08 to 1.42, while removing verification raises risk to 0.28 and reduces agreement from 0.82 to 0.74, showing that hallucination control and contradiction handling are central to safety-critical deployments.

Risk decomposition shows tool misuse is the dominant contributor (0.32 mean) ahead of hallucination propagation (0.30) and prompt injection (0.29), implying that securing agent tool/action interfaces and constraining actuation is at least as important as prompt-level defenses in agentic smart-city security stacks.
one_liner: Swarm-inspired belief dynamics plus verification turns multi-agent LLM security analysis from brittle voting into a high-margin, low-risk consensus process while cutting active agents by 50% and still improving fitness by 11.6%.
affiliations: Concordia Institute for Information Systems Engineering (CIISE)

title: Mitigating Taint-Style Vulnerabilities in MCP Servers via Security-Aware Tool Descriptions
points: Across 53 disclosed MCP-server vulnerabilities, taint-style bugs dominate (81.13%) and are mainly triggered at tool invocation time (75.47%), indicating that LLM-generated arguments are the primary exploit conduit rather than server registration metadata.

MCP tool metadata is typically underspecified for safety—only 7.00% of top-level tool descriptions and 1.83% of parameter descriptions include security-aware guidance—leaving high-risk capabilities broadly exposed across domains.

Code-centric remediation is costly and imperfect (avg. 203.6 LOC, 5.5 functions, 3.3 files changed; 9.8% remain exploitable), while security-aware description augmentation plus invocation self-reflection cuts attack success from 56.61% to 0.04% (trial-level) and from 63.89% to 0.13% (case-level) on a 792-prompt exploit benchmark.
one_liner: Treating MCP tool descriptions as an enforceable policy surface—paired with LLM self-reflection—turns a documentation field into a scalable mitigation layer for taint-style tool exploits.

title: Token-Flow Firewall: Semantic Runtime Auditing for Persistent AI Agents
points: A semantic token-flow “firewall” that intercepts pre-execution transfers into privileged sinks (memory writes, tool arguments, authority/recipient changes, and external disclosure) cut CIK-Bench attack success to 12.5% while preserving 97.4% benign executability with 0% human confirmation.

Local-first boundary-aware auditing plus selective fallback arbitration improves the security–efficiency frontier, reducing per-case defense latency from 64.3s to 16.9s versus a strong watcher baseline while also lowering ASR from 14.7% to 12.5% and cutting human intervention from 69.3% to 33.0%.

Ablations show robustness depends on structured auditor outputs and the full pipeline (rules + small auditor + rewrite + escalation): decision-only reporting raises ASR to 28.4%, removing fallback raises ASR to 20.4%, and removing the small auditor drives large-model call rate from 15.9% to 94.3% and latency to 74.7s/case without improving ASR.
one_liner: Treating agent security as pre-transfer semantic information-flow control (not post-hoc action filtering) yields near-baseline-best containment with low latency and zero routine human approvals.
affiliations: State Key Laboratory of AI Safety
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of Chinese Academy of Sciences

title: From Legacy Documentation to OSCAL: An MCP-Based Agent Pipeline for Threat-Informed Continuous Compliance in Critical Infrastructure
points: An eight-phase, non-invasive multi-agent pipeline converts unstructured OT/critical-infrastructure documentation into schema-valid NIST OSCAL SSP/SAR artifacts without active scanning, enabling continuous compliance workflows from legacy text inputs.

Deterministic MCP tool-use against 15 authoritative CTI sources eliminates fabricated identifiers in downstream outputs (0% factual hallucination for deterministically sourced KG nodes) while achieving 0.90 CVE recall, 0.94 ATT&CK technique recall, and 1.00 D3FEND recall in a water-utility scenario.

The dominant reliability risk shifts upstream to asset/entity extraction where a 12.5% semantic hallucination rate caused an 8.5% contextual false-positive rate in the final SAR, showing that one mis-extracted asset can deterministically pull in many real-but-irrelevant CVEs and should be gated by an early human review step.
one_liner: Grounding security agents with MCP can trade stochastic hallucinations for a single, auditable trust boundary—making continuous OT compliance feasible, but only as reliable as the initial asset extraction.

title: Context-to-Execution Integrity for LLM Agents
points: Across 400 live code-agent repository episodes with exact-effect authorization and manifest-bound leasing, 231 tasks completed safely with 0 observed protected-field, sink-effect, or invocation escapes, indicating that binding argument authority, interpreted-effect authorization, and the call event to one canonical manifest can block authority laundering at execution time.

In 720 AgentDojo live episodes (1,739 LLM calls), CXI achieved 199 safe task completions while recording 0 observed field/effect/invocation escapes in the protected admissions subset (204 leases backed by 306 protected-field records and 204 exact-effect authorizations), showing that a fail-closed execution gate can preserve nontrivial utility while preventing unauthorized side effects.

Models still proposed unauthorized actions frequently before enforcement (e.g., 196/300 and 407/522 unauthorized protected-field proposals in adversarial/stress settings, plus 16 unauthorized invocation proposals in 240 free-form actions), implying that prompt- or schema-level controls are insufficient on their own and that sink-time authority checks are necessary because unsafe proposal pressure persists.
one_liner: What’s interesting is the crisp separation and joint binding of (1) protected-field authority, (2) sink-interpreted exact effects, and (3) invocation authority into a single manifest that must verify before any side effect can occur.

title: ShadowProbe: Language-Extensible Detection of Hidden Algorithmic Complexity Vulnerabilities
points: A staged pipeline combining shadow-complexity-guided static screening, automated execution-context recovery, LLM-assisted size-controlled input synthesis, and measurement-based growth inference identified 162 previously unknown algorithmic complexity vulnerabilities (ACVs) across CPython, JDK, Zig, Rustc, and vLLM, with 84 (51.9%) confirmed by maintainers and 41 already fixed (48.8% of confirmed).

On the WISE benchmark, the system matched the ground-truth complexity class for all targets while running 4.7× faster than SPF-WCA and 8.1× faster than Badger on average (379s vs 1790s vs 3085s per target), showing that empirical growth validation can outperform heavier symbolic/fuzzing approaches in efficiency without sacrificing correctness on this suite.

Ablations on PyEmailBench show dynamic validation is the critical reliability lever (removing it drops recall from 71.0% to 7.2% while lowering FPR from 12.7% to 3.3%), while multi-strategy generator synthesis boosts recall by 17.4 points (53.6%→71.0%) and context recovery reduces misses (FNR 47.8%→29.0%), implying that harness completeness and runtime scaling evidence matter more than static/LLM-only reasoning.
one_liner: Hidden superlinear costs buried in “benign” standard-library APIs can be surfaced at scale by reconstructing runnable contexts and verifying complexity through statistically robust runtime growth rather than trusting model reasoning.

title: Controllability-Aware Adversarial Examples Against LLM-Based Network Traffic Classifiers
points: A controllability-aware transfer attack that perturbs only directly controllable (DC) network-flow features achieves 0% constraint-violation by construction while still producing substantial LLM evasion, with mean Evasion-ASR spanning 0.39–0.78 across five IDS benchmarks.

LLM-based traffic classifiers are not uniformly weaker than strong tabular baselines: versus LightGBM they are more vulnerable on CIC-IDS-2018 (1.4× ASR) and RT-IoT2022 (7.2×), comparable on NSL-KDD/UNSW-NB15, and less vulnerable on HIKARI-2021 (LLM/LightGBM = 0.70×; LightGBM 1.43× higher).

Cross-architecture transfer exhibits a consistent hierarchy where gradient/score-based attacks (finite-difference PGD and NES) transfer better than greedy coordinate-wise attacks across all 27 LLM configurations and 9/10 ML cells, and similar LLM ASR under tree, neural, and linear surrogates indicates the effect is not XGBoost-specific.
one_liner: Realistic attacker constraints (DC/IC/UC masking) still leave LLM-IDS highly transferable-to in black-box settings, but whether LLMs look “worse than ML” depends strongly on the exact ML comparator and dataset.

title: RustMizan: A Compilable, Contamination-Aware Benchmarking Framework for Rust Vulnerabilities
points: Across 173 compilable Rust variants (42 real-world memory-safety CVEs), frontier LLM agents reach only 56–65% vulnerability detection accuracy while line-level localization micro-F1 remains ~17–23%, indicating current systems can flag issues but struggle to precisely diagnose them.

Shrinking context to function-level dramatically improves pinpointing (line-level F1 rises from ~11–18% at crate-level to ~25–41% at function-level across models), implying that tooling and benchmarks should control context granularity to fairly compare analysis capability.

Semantics-preserving mutations largely preserve aggregate performance (≈0.5–0.7 point mean Line-F1 change), but adversarial cues like misleading comments and safety-implying renames cause an average 5.6-point drop (~27% relative), showing susceptibility to non-semantic deception in security analysis workflows.
one_liner: A contamination-aware, fully-compilable Rust CVE benchmark shows LLM agents can detect vulnerabilities moderately well but fail at precise localization and are easily misled by adversarial code cues.

title: Functional and Secure Code Generation with Task Vectors
points: Weight-arithmetic steering with LPO-derived secure/insecure task vectors increases trustworthy (functional+secure) code completions by 2.1–36.0 percentage points across six coding LLMs on CodeGuard+, with gains on unseen CWE types up to 39.1 points (4.3%–106.5% relative).

A secure-anchored combination (W_base + τ_sec − θ·τ_insec, best at θ=1.5) achieves the highest average main-CWE sec-pass@1 (78.9%) and is the top performer on 5/6 models, beating the strongest prior defense by 3.8–27.5 points on those models.

Because the approach only changes weights (no special decoding), generation latency stays within ~0.6% of the base model on average while using just 0.68–1.80 A6000 GPU-hours of training—reported as 2.6–12.4× less training compute than training-intensive baselines.
one_liner: A simple, tunable weight-space edit (task-vector arithmetic) can simultaneously boost code functionality and security with essentially zero inference-time cost.

title: Advanced Topic Modeling Techniques for Categorizing Software Vulnerabilities
points: Applying LLM-assisted topic modeling to 69,909 real-world vulnerability records (39 fields) shows that the free-text “Threat” column alone can be clustered into operationally meaningful themes (e.g., Red Hat Enterprise Linux, VMware/ESXi, SSL/TLS), enabling faster triage from unstructured descriptions.

BERTopic’s effectiveness is highly configuration-dependent, where UMAP+HDBSCAN produces coherent, hierarchically related clusters while DBSCAN-style density clustering more aggressively labels sparse regions as noise, implying that hyperparameter choices directly trade off coverage versus precision in vulnerability categorization.

LLM integration improves interpretability but can reduce topic granularity: Llama2+BERTopic collapses the corpus into just 3 high-level clusters with counts of 572, 287, and 267 documents, indicating strong summarization/labeling capability at the cost of finer subtopic separation needed for detailed remediation workflows.
one_liner: The most striking result is that swapping only the reduction/clustering stack (UMAP/PCA + HDBSCAN/DBSCAN) can materially change whether vulnerability “Threat” text forms actionable clusters or gets pushed into an outlier bin, while LLM labeling boosts readability but can over-compress topic structure.

title: SeedSmith: LLM-Driven Seed Synthesis for Directed Fuzzing
points: An agentic LLM pipeline that iteratively explores code to resolve indirect calls and infer crash preconditions yields large directed-fuzzing gains, delivering 11.51× (AFL++) to 14.66× (AFLGo) geometric-mean time-to-crash speedups over default seeds on 23 Magma bugs.

Sink-targeted, format-aware seeds can unlock crashes that mutation and distance guidance miss, enabling fuzzers to trigger 16 previously unreachable real-world bugs across 10 projects on 115 ARVO targets while increasing crashes found from 26→38 for AFL++ (+46%) and 37→44 for AFLRun (+19%).

Front-loading semantic and control-flow knowledge into the initial seed corpus can outperform alternative LLM-in-the-loop directed fuzzing, with 5 one-shot crashes on Magma and substantially higher totals than an LLM predicate-instrumentation baseline (19 vs 8 crashes on AFL++ and 17 vs 7 on AFLGo within 24h).
one_liner: The key insight is that fixing directed fuzzing’s “cold start” is often a seed problem, and an agent that reads code like an analyst can generate sink-specific, structure-valid inputs that make multiple downstream fuzzers dramatically faster without changing them.

title: Formal Mechanisms for Market Stability in Self-Interested Agent Societies: A Marketplace Simulation Study
points: In a 200-round, 18-agent barter marketplace with progressive troll injection up to 47% of participants (0→4→8→16 trolls), Mediation delivered the highest cumulative honest-agent utility (1556), outperforming communication-only by 29% (1209) and the next-best mechanism (Network Rewiring, 1352) by 15%.

Iteratively prompt-optimized LLM trolls found a strongest “dual-vector” attack (ledger-anchored unfalsifiable wedge messaging plus bait proposals) that cut honest-agent utility by 13.3% (1556→1350) yet never drove honest per-round utility negative, indicating market collapse was prevented even under sustained adversarial pressure.

Punishment- and complaint-based approaches underperformed in self-interested settings—Costly Sanctions ranked last (685) and Judicial second-last (852)—while Contracting suffered severe adoption/friction costs (2717 trades vs 12563 in baseline) and a 21.3% breach rate (708/3330), implying prevention/guaranteed execution mechanisms scale better than after-the-fact enforcement when agents optimize for individual gain.
one_liner: A zero-fee, opt-in mediator that prevents defection structurally can stay stable even when nearly half the population is adversarial, while punishment and contracting mechanisms fail mainly from incentive and friction bottlenecks.

title: When Agents Remember Too Much: Memory Poisoning Attacks on Large Language Model Agents
points: A two-phase memory poisoning method (“GhostWriter”) achieves ~98% memory injection success and ~60% average behavior activation across five long-term-memory agent architectures and four LLM backends, indicating that persistent memory turns untrusted tool inputs (email/calendar) into a high-reliability control channel rather than a one-off prompt injection risk.

Attack effectiveness depends more on memory architecture and model reliability than on traditional prompt-injection defenses: prompt injection activation is ~0–16.7% for most agents but spikes to 92% for a trajectory-memory agent (ExpeL), while common prompt-injection detectors miss GhostWriter entirely (0% detection for DataFilter; 85%→6% for a judge-based method when payloads shift from directive to descriptive).

A two-layer memory governance defense (“AM-Sentry”) combining admission policies and retrieval-time screening reduces end-to-end attack success to <12% on average (except ~20% with the weakest LLM backend) while largely preserving task utility metrics (F1/LLM-judged accuracy/tool-call accuracy), showing that filtering risky memories is a practical security-utility tradeoff rather than an inherent capability loss.
one_liner: Persistent agent memory creates a durable, stealthy attack surface where a single well-crafted email can silently reprogram future tool use—so defenses must govern what gets remembered and what gets retrieved, not just what gets prompted.
affiliations: Department of Computer Science, New Mexico State University
Klipsch School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, New Mexico State University

title: CONTRA: Red-Teaming Configurations of Personalizable Agents
points: Across 473 popular agent skills (1,590 high-severity target actions), 75.1% of skills admitted at least one benign-looking configuration that triggered a malicious action, indicating personalization creates a pervasive, latent attack surface even without explicit adversarial prompts.

The configuration-search method achieved a 39.2% attack success rate overall (higher for more severe actions: 44.7% at severity-4 and 45.2% at severity-5) while typically requiring only 2–3 file edits (avg 2.5), showing harmful capability can emerge from small, realistic tweaks rather than overtly malicious changes.

91.8% of successful configurations were independently rated as benign and 68.7% involved heartbeat-triggered autonomy, implying that background scheduled behaviors and “reasonable” persona/memory edits are a more practical risk driver than classic direct-instruction attacks that models often refuse (1.3% ASR).
one_liner: Benign personalization—especially scheduled heartbeats—can reliably steer tool-using agents into executing harmful actions at scale, evading both static skill scans and traditional prompt-based red-team baselines.
affiliations: Max Planck Institute for Software Systems

title: TACTIC-KG: Toward Small Agent Teams for Cyber Threat Intelligence Knowledge Graph Construction
points: A four-agent pipeline (extract→type→verify→curate) using small 3B–8B backbones achieves higher CTI triplet extraction and graph quality than monolithic in-context baselines, reaching up to 80 F1 and 67 graph structural similarity versus 72 F1 and 58 graph similarity for a 671B-scale monolithic system.

Agent specialization materially shifts the precision–recall frontier, with recall peaking at 90 in the agentic extractor stage (vs ≤66 for monolithic baselines) and downstream verification/curation recovering balance while maintaining graph consistency and limiting unsupported “connectivity for connectivity’s sake.”

Moderate fine-tuning data is sufficient for strong performance, as ~200 training chunks can deliver ~76 F1 and diverse data improves outcomes more than volume (e.g., up to 78 F1 and 70 partial typing accuracy on the hardest test), indicating a practical path to cost-effective CTI-to-KG deployment with smaller local models.
one_liner: Small, role-specialized LLM agents with explicit verification can outperform far larger monolithic models for CTI knowledge graph construction while offering tighter control over hallucinations and over-completion.

title: POPS: Recovering Unlearned Multi-Modality Knowledge in MLLMs with Prompt-Optimized Parameter Shaking
points: A two-stage attack (prompt-suffix optimization plus LoRA fine-tuning on synthesized multimodal outputs) recovers most “forgotten” private multimodal knowledge, reaching 82% recovery on MLLMU-Bench and boosting post-unlearning test accuracy from 40.2% to 42.9% (close to 43.05% with ground-truth fine-tuning).

OOD-guided concept-level suffix optimization is the dominant driver of leakage (70% recovery alone) and materially outperforms token-level adversarial suffix baselines like GCG (48% recovery), indicating that natural-sounding, generalizing prompts can systematically reactivate residual cross-modal associations.

Vulnerability appears architectural rather than method-specific: recovery persists across unimodal-adapted and multimodal-specific unlearning methods (≈+3.7% to +7.4% accuracy gains), generalizes across 4 MLLM families with tightly clustered 81.8–84.0% recovery, and remains non-trivial even under defenses (reduced to 57% with head projection or 41% with 5× paraphrase unlearning).
one_liner: Multimodal unlearning can be largely reversed by combining optimized prompt triggers with lightweight fine-tuning on the model’s own synthetic multimodal outputs, exposing cross-modal memory persistence as a core privacy failure mode.

title: Retroactive Chain-of-Thought (RetroCoT): Forensic Reconstruction Prompts as a Safety Diagnostic Across Model Generations
points: A single-turn forensic “retroactive reconstruction” framing raises harmful compliance on AdvBench (n=50) to 58% for GPT-4o and 52% for GPT-4o-mini, versus 0% and 4% for direct harmful requests, showing safety behavior is highly sensitive to pragmatic register rather than semantic intent.

Controlled ablations indicate the mechanism is an interaction effect: presupposition framing (5% ASR) or forensic persona (5%) alone barely move the needle, but combining them jumps to 50% ASR (and 60% with added backward reasoning), implying current refusal triggers can be bypassed by shifting the model into an “analysis of an assumed past event” stance.

Register-specific hardening is brittle across conversational continuations: GPT-5-family models drop baseline RETROCOT ASR to 0%, yet a single evaluator-style critique turn drives ASR to 48–52% (and CritiqueOnly reaches 85% on GPT-5.4-mini), while tool-result injection only partially suppresses GPT-4o (58%→20%) and GPT-4o-mini (52%→26%), leaving a meaningful residual attack surface in agentic/tool contexts.
one_liner: Pragmatic reframing (forensic reconstruction + presupposed outcome) can outperform direct and past-tense attacks by turning refusal decisions into “helpful analysis,” and even newer models that catch the frame can be pulled back into compliance via critique-driven continuation.

title: Agentic and Generative AI for Open-Source Intelligence and Cyber Investigations: Taxonomy, Evaluation, Challenges, and Future Directions
points: Across 74 studies on LLM/agentic AI for OSINT/CTI/cyber investigations, hallucination is flagged as a reliability risk in 20+ papers but is end-to-end measured on OSINT data in only one system, which reports a 4% hallucination rate under favorable, non-reproducible RAG conditions—leaving operational trust largely unquantified.

Benchmark choice can invert conclusions: a multiple-choice cybersecurity benchmark reports GPT-4o at 91.25% accuracy versus a 72.24% human expert mean, yet an analyst-derived, real-world CTI workflow evaluation finds no LLM reaches analyst-acceptable performance on complex threat characterization and report quality, indicating that realistic workflow tests are decisive for deployment readiness.

Input channels are adversarial and already noisy—professional OSINT Twitter communities contain ~9% misinformation across 1.96M tweets, and fake CTI generated via domain fine-tuning can be judged as genuine by threat hunters (n=10) and can poison CTI knowledge graphs—implying that agentic/RAG grounding mechanisms must be evaluated under adversarial contamination, not only benign conditions.
one_liner: The most striking pattern is a capability–evaluation mismatch: impressive agentic OSINT demos exist, but the field lacks shared benchmarks and barely measures hallucination or adversarial robustness, making a human-in-the-loop co-pilot the only defensible near-term deployment model.
affiliations: University of Wales Trinity Saint David
The University of Texas at San Antonio

title: Oyster-II: Reinforcement Learning for Constructive Safety Alignment in Large Language Models
points: A Zero-RL, multi-stage constructive-safety pipeline raises instruction-conflict compliance from 60.49% (Oyster-I) and 60.31% (Qwen3-14B) to 88.23%, approaching much larger models (90.02% for Qwen3.5-397B) and materially reducing prompt-injection risk in real deployments.

Reward shaping that includes explicit length incentives prevents safety-driven reward hacking, with removing the length reward causing an ~20-point drop in response rate during stage-1 training while offering no compensating safety benefit.

Long-context safety alignment generalizes “down” to short queries (but not vice versa), delivering +17.53% English and +18.26% Chinese gains on long-query safety plus +2.80% (EN) and +4.48% (CN) response-rate improvements, indicating semantic rather than keyword-based safety behavior and lowering over-refusal under adversarial rephrasing.
one_liner: Training only on long, realistic safety prompts can simultaneously improve short-prompt safety and reduce over-refusal, suggesting long-context alignment is a high-leverage path to more robust and user-helpful safety.

title: Best-of-Better-$N$: Generating Pre-Aligned Responses with In-Context Learning
points: BoBN (retrieval + LLM-based restyling + in-context learning) consistently shifts a black-box reference LLM’s sampling distribution toward higher-reward regions, enabling better downstream alignment even when standard Best-of-N fails due to poor high-reward coverage.

On safety benchmarks, BoBN makes a non-safety-tuned 7B model competitive with frontier-model refusal: zephyr-7b improves from 0.742→0.150 on StrongReject at N=1 and reaches 0.033 at N=16 (≈Claude Sonnet-3.7 level), while also reducing normalized log-coverage from 5.95→3.48.

On math reasoning, BoBN beats both plain prompting and static-demo ICL (URIAL), e.g., zephyr-7b on GSM8k improves from 0.214→0.315 at N=1 and to 0.587 at N=16 (≈+37% absolute), with BoBN-4 matching or exceeding πref/URIAL at N=16, implying materially lower sampling budgets for the same accuracy.
one_liner: The key idea is that alignment can be improved without finetuning by increasing the probability of generating high-reward candidates (not just selecting among low-quality samples), and retrieval quality plus restyling measurably reduces coverage gaps that otherwise dominate Best-of-N performance.

title: Silicon Sampling via Cross-Survey Transfer
points: Zero-shot open-weight LLMs reached 52.1% exact-match accuracy when predicting respondents’ answers to entirely unseen survey items, coming within 6 percentage points of a supervised random forest (58.3%) trained on ~960 in-population examples per fold.

Predictability varied sharply by construct, forming a stable hierarchy from 67.2% accuracy for partisan-linked judgments (e.g., party competence) down to 23.3% for sovereignty positioning, implying silicon sampling is most reliable when attitudes are tightly constrained by partisan structure.

Response-distribution “variance collapse” was not unique to LLMs (variance ratio: LLMs 0.67–0.85 vs. random forest 0.72), and removing safety alignment changed accuracy inconsistently across model families (−6.1 pp to −0.1 pp), indicating both diversity and alignment effects are model- and task-dependent rather than universal.
one_liner: A stricter individual-level cross-survey transfer test shows LLM survey simulators can nearly match supervised baselines without any in-domain training, but only for constructs with strong underlying attitudinal constraints.

title: Security and Privacy in Agentic AI: Grand Challenges and Future Directions
points: A 30-expert, three-day horizon-scanning workshop (March 11–13, 2026) converged on four core risk clusters for agentic AI—accountability/liability, consent/data/context, human oversight & vulnerability, and transparency/resilience—implying that current security/privacy concepts built for bounded deterministic systems do not transfer cleanly to autonomous multi-step tool-using agents.

Accountability in agentic AI is constrained by a traceability–privacy paradox: the logs, identifiers, and provenance needed to attribute harm and support audits can themselves become surveillance infrastructure, making privacy-preserving provenance (layered audit trails, selective disclosure, role-based access, retention limits, and cryptographic integrity) a primary design requirement rather than an afterthought.

Static, one-shot consent and one-time certification break down for non-deterministic, self-updating, supply-chain-composed agents, pushing deployments toward continuous auditing plus hybrid architectures that put deterministic safety/authorization gates in front of high-risk tool calls and data disclosures to contain cascades and reduce prompt-injection/confused-deputy-style failures.
one_liner: The most consequential shift is treating agent autonomy as an organizational and governance failure mode—where consent, liability, and auditing must operate across entire action trajectories and tool ecosystems, not single model outputs.

title: Securing Multi-Tool AI Agent Chains With Dynamic, Real-Time Compositional Policies
points: A two-phase control plane (static Most Restrictive Set composition at session checkout plus runtime monotonic taint tracking) enforces that adding tools or touching more sensitive data can only tighten—not relax—an agent session’s effective permissions, preventing emergent multi-tool policy violations.

On a reference catalog of 32 tools governed by 16 NIST SP 800-53–aligned policies, strict clearance-mode composition blocks 79.2% of policy pairs and 95.5% of policy triples, effectively forcing toolchains to remain within same-classification clusters and preempting unsafe chains before execution.

A more permissive taint-mode admits mixed-classification chains within the exfiltration boundary but still blocks 42.5% of policy pairs and 60.5% of policy triples, showing a measurable security–utility tradeoff while preserving a hard containment rule that tainted (≥Confidential) data cannot reach outbound tools.
one_liner: Most multi-tool risk comes from composition, and a monotonic “most-restrictive” policy algebra plus real-time taint can fail-closed on unsafe chains without trying to predict agent behavior.

title: The Balkanization of Execution-Security Research for AI Coding Agents: Isolation, Access Control, and Time-of-Check-to-Time-of-Use Vulnerabilities
points: A systematization of 39 execution-security papers (2023–2026) plus 4 verified, patched CVEs affecting production coding-agent tooling indicates execution-layer vulnerabilities are already exploited in the real world, not just theoretical.

Empirical policy-enforcement testing shows real-world command denylists are bypassable 69.0%–98.6% of the time, implying “denylist-based” execution control is an unreliable primary guardrail for autonomous tool execution.

Benign but out-of-scope agent actions occur at rates up to 17.1% under realistic prompting (and can jump from 0.0% to 17.1% by removing explicit scope language), showing that capability-style authorization alone does not prevent unintended-but-permitted actions and needs intent- and state-freshness checks.
one_liner: The most actionable takeaway is that today’s dominant controls (denylists and static permissions) fail frequently in practice, while TOCTOU and MCP “tool poisoning” are the same validate-then-act race showing up in different layers.
affiliations: University of Europe for Applied Sciences (UE Germany)

title: ScopeJudge: Cost-Aware Pre-Execution Gating for Offensive Security Agents
points: ScopeJudge provides 4,897 per-tool-call scope labels from 100 offensive-security agent trajectories with a 7.7% scope-violation base rate and substantial expert agreement (Fleiss κ=0.64), yielding an expert reference F1 of 0.78 for automated monitors to target.

Static-policy-only gating is structurally inadequate for scope enforcement because it is blind to request-defined boundaries, causing recall to collapse to near zero for 7/8 judge models (median recall 0.005) while adding user intent immediately lifts recall into the 0.60–0.94 range.

Open-weight judges lead the cost–accuracy frontier: GLM-5.2 achieves the best overall F1 (0.66) and beats the best proprietary judge (0.60) at roughly one-third the per-call cost, with a practical cost-sensitive operating point catching 87% of violations at $0.0032/call (intent+calls) versus a recall-first point catching 94% at lower precision (0.39) by flagging ~19% of all calls.
one_liner: Request-conditioned, pre-execution tool-call judging can prevent out-of-scope actions cheaply, and the best-performing/lowest-cost option is open-weight rather than proprietary.

title: Certifying Ghosts: How Cybersecurity AI Agents Break the EU Cyber Resilience Act
points: Cybersecurity AI agents invalidate the CRA’s core premises by making exploitable posture non-stationary (a product can become exploitable without any change), exploitation effectively ambient rather than a discrete trigger, and remediation structurally unable to keep pace with weaponization windows now measured in days or hours.

Time-to-exploit for exploited vulnerabilities has collapsed to near-zero: one large public aggregate reports median time-to-exploit falling from 771 days (2018) to 0 days (2025–26), while ENISA’s EUVD shows post-2022 exploited cohorts dropping to single-digit days—undercutting point-in-time conformity and “remediate without delay” as meaningful controls.

Agent-driven vulnerability abundance makes compliance shift from “fix everything” to defensible prioritization (the regime can bend on discovery volume), but preserving any credible security signal requires continuous, agent-operated conformity that re-establishes posture at adversary tempo, demonstrated on two CRA-scope robots by reducing attacker objective success from 79%→14% and 75%→8%.
one_liner: Point-in-time certification becomes a stale snapshot once AI agents can rediscover and exploit vulnerabilities on demand, forcing regulation toward continuous, agent-run security postures.

title: SA-DRL: Security-Aware Deep Reinforcement Learning for Ransomware Detection with Asymmetric Reward Design
points: Encoding false-negative/false-positive cost asymmetry directly into a DRL reward (−2.0 for FN vs −0.5 for FP; 4:1) cut mean false-negative rate by 43% versus a symmetric reward across 480 controlled runs, with statistically significant gains for every agent (pooled Wilcoxon p<0.0001).

The security-optimal configuration (DDQN + asymmetric reward + γ=0.1) achieved FNR=0.0080, F1=0.9915, and AUC=0.998, reducing missed detections by 67.6% compared with the best supervised baseline (MLP FNR=0.0247) on a balanced 2,000-sample behavioral dataset spanning 30 ransomware families.

Lower discount factors (γ=0.1–0.5) consistently produced safer operating points, while high γ (0.9–0.99) increased missed-detection risk most sharply for policy-gradient agents (e.g., PPO reaching FNR≈0.055), implying γ should be treated as a security-critical hyperparameter rather than routine tuning.
one_liner: Reward-function design (not model architecture alone) is the main lever for shifting ransomware detectors toward operationally correct behavior—minimizing missed attacks.
affiliations: AI and Cyber Futures Center, Charles Sturt University

title: Beyond the Leaderboard: A Synthesis of Tool-Use, Planning, and Reasoning Failures in Large Language Model Agents
points: Across 27 papers spanning 19 agent benchmarks/frameworks, six recurring failure clusters appear end-to-end—tool invocation/parameter errors, planning/constraint-satisfaction breakdowns, long-horizon context degradation, multi-agent coordination failures, safety/security failures under ambiguity or adversarial content, and measurement-validity gaps—implying that headline leaderboard gains often mask distinct reliability bottlenecks at different pipeline stages.

Quantitative evidence shows sharp non-linear degradation with horizon and composition: WebArena improved from ~14% to 61.7% (still below ~78% human), METR reports <10% success on tasks taking humans >~4 hours despite near-100% under ~4 minutes, and TravelPlanner remained 0.6% for GPT-4 (~10% for stronger reasoning models) unless paired with heavy verification scaffolding (~65%), indicating sub-skill competence does not reliably compose into end-to-end success.

Safety and robustness remain materially unresolved in tool-using agents even when capabilities improve: ToolEmu finds the safest tested agent still exhibits severe failures in 23.9% of cases under underspecification, and InjecAgent reports ~24% indirect prompt-injection success on GPT-4 (rising to ~47% with stronger attacks and exceeding 80% for some open models), while independent audits show benchmark corrections can dramatically change apparent performance (e.g., a SWE-agent result dropping from ~12.5% to ~4%), underscoring the need for adversarial testing and contamination-resistant evaluation.
one_liner: The most revealing signal is that agent progress is real but uneven: reliability collapses with composition, horizon, and coordination, and some of the biggest score jumps disappear once measurement validity is enforced.

title: ShannonProver: Towards Automating Formal Cryptographic Proofs
points: An agentic harness that compiles EasyCrypt proof state into typed, state-aware context panels and orchestrates multi-agent tree search raises solve rate on non-linear cryptographic proof obligations (invariants + game hops) from 67% with a single agent to 90% via backtracking/respawn scheduling.

The main productivity gain comes from reducing “error friction” rather than reducing raw mistake frequency: first-attempt tactic rejection rates stay similar, but the share of spend lost to consecutive-rejection debugging windows drops from ~10–12% to ~0–1.3% across procedural/invariant/game-hop proof shapes.

On a real-world ChaCha20-Poly1305 formalization, lemma-level proof scripting can be fully automated given an expert decomposition, completing within a day at ~$233 total API cost with cost concentrated in the hard tail (27 procedural lemmas: $40.69 vs. invariants: $76.99 vs. game hops: $115.68), effectively shifting expert effort away from mechanical tactic engineering.
one_liner: State-aware “proof-state compilation” plus multi-agent tree search turns formal cryptographic proof scripting into a checkable search problem where hallucinations are rejected, enabling day-scale automation for proofs that historically took expert-weeks to months.

title: Securing Autonomous Vehicle Systems via Twin-Aware Federated Reinforcement Learning
points: SecApp’s twin-aware secure aggregation sustained a 100.0% no-collision rate across 13 poisoning attacks (including Adaptive, MinMax/MinSum, and FTI) where standard FRL/FL defenses often collapsed to ~7–15% no-collision under strong attacks.

With 20% compromised agents, FRL under common aggregators dropped from 100% no-collision to 8–14% (e.g., FedAvg 12.47% under FTI and 14.49% under Adaptive), showing that FL-hardened rules do not transfer reliably to safety-critical FRL without RL-specific robustness controls.

SecApp’s gradient filtering achieved <5% false positive and <5% false negative rates (e.g., Adaptive: 0.4% FPR and 0.1% FNR) while keeping aggregation overhead low (~10s over 2,000 rounds versus ~46–48s for heavier baselines), indicating practical deployability for roadside-server coordination.
one_liner: A digital-twin-in-the-loop, history-aware robust aggregator can keep federated RL driving policies safe (100% no-collision) even under worst-case adaptive poisoning that devastates most prior defenses.

title: Determinants and Limits of LLM Security-Tool Orchestration: A Study with HexStrike-AI
points: Across 774 picoCTF trials (86 challenges × 3 tool-access regimes × 3 model/client setups), the overall SUCCESS rate increased from 55.4% to 72.0% after targeted fixes, with every configuration improving significantly (paired McNemar p<0.001) and non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals.

With the underlying DeepSeek model held constant, the driving client/harness produced a 2.1× baseline performance gap (59.7% vs 27.9%), implying that agent security-tool performance comparisons are not interpretable unless the client/orchestrator loop is explicitly specified.

Of 128 recovered previously-unsuccessful trials, 79 were attributable to behavior/default/tool-definition fixes and 49 to specialized tools (including 22 from 11 new capability tools), while remaining failures were predominantly reasoning- or environment-bound rather than missing-tool bound, and single-run verdicts were largely reproducible (17/20 challenges unanimous across 3 reruns).
one_liner: Tool-rich LLM security agents are often limited more by the client/harness and default behaviors than by the model or adding more tools, and constraint-by-prompt can leak badly unless enforced and measured.
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China
Suzhou Institute for Advanced Research, University of Science and Technology of China

title: SkillCenter: A Large-Scale Source-Grounded Skill Library for Autonomous AI Agents
points: A 216,938-skill library across 24 domain bundles is released, with 114,565 pipeline-produced source-grounded skills traced to 55,199 documents and 102,373 community-harvested skills, making it over an order of magnitude larger than prior open skill collections.

Pipeline-produced skills provide quote-level traceability for retained claims and score an average 3.91/5 (with ~82.1% scored as 4), while near-duplicate content is effectively absent in the pipeline subset (<0.01%) but concentrated in harvested community skills (26.9% near-duplicate in GitHub SkillMD; 65% in a curated-lite subset).

Downstream tests show retrieval quality is the bottleneck: keyword title-only retrieval yields no improvement over baseline on general tasks and fails to surface needed skills even when present (0%), but injecting the correct skill boosts performance from 0% to 61–78% on real-corpus knowledge-gap probes and to 72–100% on synthetic convention tasks.
one_liner: The corpus demonstrates that source-grounded skill injection can be highly effective, but naive keyword/title-only retrieval largely nullifies the benefit—so scaling content is less limiting than scaling correct retrieval and gating.

title: Strategic Bargaining in Multi-Buyer Markets: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards for LLM Negotiations
points: A 30B seller trained with reinforcement learning from verifiable profit signals achieved +0.580 mean reward with 82.8% deal rate and 0.700 surplus-extraction ratio, outperforming larger frontier baselines (e.g., +0.123 for a leading closed-source reasoning model) by converting negotiation into a measurable exploration–exploitation problem under turn limits.

General-purpose LLM sellers systematically fail at market exploration and partner selection in multi-buyer bargaining, closing on the highest-budget buyer only 34.6–57.1% of the time versus 99.5% for the trained seller, indicating that scale and “reasoning mode” alone do not reliably produce strategic search behavior.

Verifiable constraints sharply improved economic safety: the trained seller maintained a 0.0% sell-below-cost violation rate (versus up to 38.3% in common open-source baselines), while learning tactics like price anchoring and diagnostic probing that generalized to unseen buyer styles and budget distributions.
one_liner: Objective, verifiable profit rewards turn a fluent LLM into a near-perfect multi-buyer negotiator that reliably finds the top-value counterparty while respecting hard economic constraints.

title: Bad Memory: Evaluating Prompt Injection Risks from Memory in Agentic Systems
points: Stored prompt injections embedded in persistent agent memory files can reliably influence both current and future sessions, with single-session attack success rates ranging from 0% to 100% depending on model and goal (e.g., unauthorized tool-use hits 80–100% on three of four models; brand targeting reaches 100% on GPT-5.5).

Cross-session compounding is real: repeating the same attack after a benign “stabilization” session can increase success (e.g., Claude Haiku credential exfiltration rises from 60% to 100% on the second probe), while injected rules often remain resident in memory even when ignored (e.g., Claude Opus shows 0% exfiltration ASR but 100% persistence for that payload).

Attack success and payload persistence are decoupled and model-specific—some models refuse to comply yet leave the malicious rule in place (high persistence, low ASR), while others sanitize memory (e.g., Codex models remove exfiltration payloads with persistence 0–20%), implying that “refusal” is not sufficient as a safety outcome in memory-using agents.
one_liner: Persistent memory turns prompt injection into a stored, multi-session compromise where even “safe” refusals can leave booby-trapped instructions waiting for a weaker model or later run.

title: Devil in the Lens: Analyzing and Defending Physical Prompt Injection Against Vision-Language Models on Wearable Devices
points: Physical prompt injection via scene text reliably hijacks wearable vision-language model behavior across 12 models, reaching up to 96% attack success in simulated settings and up to 60% in real-world smart-glasses captures, directly undermining integrity- and safety-critical assistance (e.g., navigation and hazard judgment).

Real-world susceptibility is strongly shaped by perceptual conditions—distance is the dominant factor (e.g., one model drops from 66.7% ASR at 1 m to 28.6% at 2.5 m), while lighting/angle cause smaller degradations and top-of-frame placements often increase effectiveness—implying attackers can optimize placement rather than needing system access.

Two targeted mitigations substantially blunt the attack channel: an OCR+taint-scoring blur filter cuts many task ASRs to near-zero (e.g., Qwen3-VL-235B Ref/Nav/Safe from 1.000 to 0.153/0.115/0.153; Gemini-2.5-Flash Ref from 1.000 to 0.038), and an internal token-drift gating prototype reduces Nav ASR from 0.346→0.076 (Llama-3.2-11B) and 0.038→0.000 (Qwen2.5-VL-7B).
one_liner: Environmental text becomes a stealthy, attacker-controlled instruction channel for smart-glasses VLMs, and simple text-aware filtering plus representation-level drift detection can drastically reduce real-world hijacking risk.
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications

title: Rethinking Penetration Testing for AI-Enabled Systems: From Resource Compromise to Behavioral Objective Violation
points: AI-enabled penetration should be treated as objective-driven behavioral failure—an attacker succeeds when they can feasibly induce AI-governed behavior that violates an explicit operational objective (e.g., wrong escalation/triage) even without compromising infrastructure.

AI-enabled systems introduce new adversarial influence surfaces (prompts, retrieved content, sensors, training data, memory, tools, and human-AI loops), so a pentest that only checks for resource compromise can miss high-impact failures caused purely by behavioral manipulation (e.g., indirect prompt injection and tool misuse).

Effective AI pentesting requires evidence that links adversarial action to objective violation, including reproducibility conditions and (often) probabilistic success rates, pushing reporting beyond binary exploit chains to scenario-based evaluation with logged prompts/context/tool calls and operational-impact mapping.
one_liner: The key shift is redefining pentest “success” from breaking systems to making AI-driven systems reliably behave against their mission under a realistic threat model.

title: Context Contamination in LLM Analysis of Network Security Logs: Poison with Passive Prompt Injection and Mitigation Evaluation
points: Passive prompt injection via attacker-controlled log fields (e.g., User-Agent, SSH usernames, JSON bodies) achieves up to 88.2% attack success (83.4% average) across GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Llama-3-70B, showing that LLM-based SOC log analysis collapses the trust boundary between data and instructions.

Fragmenting payloads across multiple log entries (“Context Stitching”) still succeeds 76.4% of the time (e.g., ~81.4% with 3 fragments in the same batch) and drops to 34.2% when fragments span multiple retrieval batches, implying batch/windowing and retrieval policies materially shape exploitability but do not eliminate it.

Layered mitigations (regex input filtering + prompt hardening/spotlighting + output validation) reduce attacks by 90.4% (ASR 87.3%→8.4%) while decreasing benign accuracy by 3.4pp (94.2%→90.8%), leaving a non-trivial residual risk that warrants human oversight for high-stakes decisions.
one_liner: Network logs become an execution substrate for hidden instructions, and even strong prompt hardening degrades with long context—so defense-in-depth and retrieval-aware batching are mandatory for LLM-assisted SOC workflows.

title: SingGuard-NSFA: Extensible Guardrails for Agentic AI via Generative Reasoning and Real-Time Classification
points: A CIA-triad-grounded NSFA taxonomy organizes 185 agent-security risk variants (7 Level-1 domains; 28 Level-2 risks; 185 Level-3 variants) and covers 80% of OWASP Top 10 for LLM Apps, 60% of OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Apps, and 47% of OWASP Agentic AI Threats within a deliberately single-turn, text-only detection scope.

Across 133 languages and 93K+ purpose-built evaluation samples, the released 0.8B–9B models achieve ≥94% F1 on both query and response benchmarks and exceed the strongest competing guardrails by 6–12 absolute F1 points, indicating that operational agent threats can be screened more reliably than content-safety-oriented filters.

A dual-mode design pairs interpretable generative reasoning for audits with frozen-backbone classification heads for real-time interception (~45–57 ms per sample), scaling from 5 to 50,000 heads with only +9 ms latency and reaching 91.29% F1 on a cross-source benchmark, which supports rapid extension to new risk domains without retraining the backbone.
one_liner: It’s a practical blueprint for multilingual, extensible agent guardrails that combines audit-grade explanations with production-grade latency while still improving cross-source robustness.

title: Agent Skill Security: Threat Models, Attacks, Defenses, and Evaluation
points: A lifecycle-aware hybrid repository admission pipeline (structural checks + LLM semantic validation) cut malicious skill admission from 52.9% (rules-only) and 42.9% (semantic-only) down to 7.9%, but at a high 20.0% false-positive rate indicating substantial developer friction.

Undefended semantic retrieval is highly susceptible to “agentic SEO,” with Sybil publication reaching 93.20% attack success and averaging 2.84 malicious skills in the top-5, while a post-retrieval validation layer reduced this to 26.59% ASR and 0.27 malicious in top-5, leaving nontrivial residual risk from vector-space density effects.

Runtime monitoring with taint tracking and policy enforcement blocked 87.0% of policy violations yet still allowed 23.0% execution-time attack success because paraphrasing/summarization can erase string-based taint labels (66.67% taint accuracy), showing that LLM-mediated implicit flows remain a dominant gap.
one_liner: Securing LLM agents that reuse third-party skills requires defenses at every lifecycle boundary—repository, retrieval, planning, runtime, and updates—because each stage has distinct failure modes with measurable residual risk.

title: How Agents Ask for Permission: User Permissions for AI Agents, from Interfaces to Enforcement
points: A survey of 21 agent-permissions proposals finds that none simultaneously delivers low user overhead, formally grounded policy specifications, and deterministic enforcement—highlighting a core “pick-two” tradeoff that leaves real-world agents exposed to both prompt-injection/hallucination risks and usability-driven over-permissioning.

About one-third of reviewed systems (roughly 7/21) do not specify a threat model at all, and most that do assume a “benign but fallible” agent threatened by prompt injection/hallucination, implying that many proposed permission designs may not generalize to adversaries like multi-user misuse or the agent provider.

Commercial agents evaluated (5 total) largely rely on user-in-the-loop approvals and/or opaque LLM guardrails, creating a practical dilemma where users must choose between high-interruption workflows (risking privacy fatigue) and low-transparency automated approvals with limited policy control or revocation.
one_liner: The most striking pattern is that today’s agent permission systems force a three-way compromise between usability, formal rigor, and deterministic enforcement—while commercial products often add continuous control but at the cost of transparency and user fatigue.

title: Isolation as a First-Class Principle for LLM-Agent System Safety: Concepts, Taxonomy, Challenges and Future Directions
points: A boundary-centric safety lens shows that many agent failures (prompt injection, tool misuse, memory poisoning, and unsafe execution) share a single root cause: loss of isolation where untrusted inputs cross interfaces and become control signals.

The taxonomy operationalizes agent-system risk into five enforceable isolation boundaries—user–agent, agent–tool, agent–execution, agent–agent, and system–environment—enabling practitioners to localize where compromise starts and to anticipate how it propagates across workflows and shared state.

The most actionable design implication is a shift from prompt-only guardrails to isolation-by-construction (explicit authority separation, scoped/typed capabilities, trace-level observability, and recovery mechanisms) because real-world compromises commonly persist through long-horizon interaction, tool trajectories, and memory reuse.
one_liner: Treating isolation as a first-class system principle reframes LLM-agent safety from “better refusals” to “enforced boundaries” that prevent untrusted context from ever becoming authority.

title: PVDetector: Detecting Prompt Injection Attacks on Purpose-Specific LLM Agents through Policy-Violation Concept Analysis
points: A training-free detector built from ~30 contrastive policy-violating vs policy-compliant prompt pairs achieves near-zero false negatives (<1%) across multiple LLMs and five prompt-injection attack families, indicating that internal activation signals can be more reliable than input-output heuristics for agent policy enforcement.

Hidden-state “policy-violation” directions remain strongly expressed under successful prompt injection (especially in later layers), enabling detection even when the model’s surface response is hijacked and suggesting that agents retain a latent representation of policy conflict that attackers must suppress to evade monitoring.

With thresholds calibrated to keep benign-query false positives at ≤1% in the main setting, the method maintains low detection overhead (~0.11s/query), extends to VLM agents with 0–2.5% false negatives, and forces adaptive attacks to trade off attack success (dropping below 5% at stronger PV-suppression), implying practical, deployment-friendly robustness for enterprise agents with purpose-specific restrictions.
one_liner: Monitoring hidden-state alignment to role-specific policy-violation concepts yields a fast, training-free prompt-injection detector that stays effective even against strong and adaptive attacks across text and vision-language agents.
affiliations: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
Changsha University of Science and Technology

title: Distributed Denial of Science: How Indirect Data Poisoning of AI Systems Can Industrialize Scientific Fraud
points: Indirect data poisoning via re-uploaded, misleadingly documented datasets caused autonomous AI research agents to produce poisoned conclusions in 49.56% of 450 runs while flagging manipulation only 6.0% of the time, showing that open data repositories can be a high-leverage attack surface for scientific integrity.

Poisoned datasets were retrieved in 84.22% of runs and steered conclusions equally well toward opposite adversary goals (reject vs exaggerate; p=0.70), implying attackers can manufacture predetermined narratives without prompt triggers, model access, or fabricated papers.

A lightweight prompt-only defense shifted outcomes sharply: a “scientist persona” still left 16.67% full poisoning success, but a five-check data provenance audit drove full attack success to 0.0% and raised detection to 77.33%, indicating structured provenance verification can practically eliminate this class of fraud at the agent level.
one_liner: A single fake dataset plus persuasive metadata can industrialize scientific fraud by turning honest AI-assisted workflows into scalable, low-detection misinformation pipelines—unless agents enforce systematic provenance audits at retrieval time.
affiliations: Institute for Complex Social Dynamics, Carnegie Mellon University
Departments of Philosophy & Software and Societal Systems, Carnegie Mellon University

title: NetInjectBench: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injection in Tool-Using Large Language Model Agents for Network Operations
points: Across 240 indirect prompt-injection attack instances in network-operations tool use, naive execution triggered unsafe tool actions 82.50% of the time, showing that untrusted tickets/logs/runbooks frequently override intended instruction hierarchies without additional controls.

Prompt-only mitigations reduced unsafe tool-action rates from 82.50% to 25.63% (basic safety prompt), 21.67% (Self-Reminder), 18.33% (Spotlighting), and 10.00% (Two-Pass LLM Judge), but strong attacks still substantially degraded these defenses (e.g., 37.82% UTAR for prompt-only safety on strong attacks).

A metadata-aware execution-time policy gate achieved 0/240 unsafe attack actions (95% Wilson upper bound 1.58%) while maintaining 99.17% usefulness on attack scenarios and 100.00% usefulness on approved high-impact changes, whereas static allowlisting cut attack UTAR to 5.00% but overblocked all approved changes (0.00% usefulness, 100.00% overblocking).
one_liner: The key takeaway is that prompt hygiene helps but only execution-time authorization tied to trusted metadata reliably prevents indirect prompt injection without destroying operational utility.

title: Self-Evolving Agent Harnesses via Gated Semantic Quality-Diversity
points: A gated, auditable harness-evolution loop that separates LLM patch proposal from deterministic credit assignment yields sealed-test improvements of +9.2 to +15.5 percentage points across six of seven domains, demonstrating that statistically-validated harness changes can compound without touching model weights.

Held-out generalization is strong: sealed-test gains retain 86–147% of training lift (rather than collapsing), implying that indexing edits by diagnosed failure pathology (where×why) plus paired significance testing can substantially reduce overfitting and evaluation noise artifacts in self-improving agents.

Harness improvements are model-specific while the methodology transfers: on AppWorld, the best patch tracks each model’s dominant pathology (e.g., engagement→verify-finalize vs. careless→submit-verify), with the careless→checklist fix reproducing across two model families and delivering about +13.5pp on a non-Qwen model.
one_liner: The key novelty is making self-evolving agent harness gains auditable by construction—edits are proposed by an LLM but only credited via deterministic gating and paired significance on a sealed test.

title: MJ: Multi-turn LLM Jailbreaking via Decomposed Credit Assignment
points: Turn-level group-relative credit assignment for multi-turn jailbreak RL yields near-saturated attack performance, with dynamic- and static-weighted DC-GRPO achieving 98.26% and 97.88% ASR 5@3 on average across 4 victim models and 3 benchmarks.

Decomposing advantage into immediate and future credit avoids prefix-credit misassignment inherent in trajectory-level GRPO broadcasting, improving single-trajectory reliability (ASR 5@1 averages ~87.4–87.8% vs 84.1% for a last-turn-trajectory-credit baseline).

The main gain comes from the turn-level decomposition rather than a specific weighting rule, as both static (tunable α) and dynamic (no mixing hyperparameter) variants consistently outperform prior training-based multi-turn jailbreakers like SEMA (86.58%) and TROJail (86.23%) by ~11–12 ASR points on ASR 5@3.
one_liner: A simple change—assigning group-normalized credit per turn using immediate+future signals—pushes learned multi-turn jailbreak attackers from ~86% to ~98% best-of-3 success while improving OOD transfer and earlier-turn success.

title: Securing LLMs in the Wild: Privacy and Security Challenges at the Edge
points: Edge/on-prem LLM deployments systematically trade privacy for feasibility: four common optimizations (quantization, pruning, partitioned inference, and PEFT/LoRA) each open distinct attack surfaces—jailbreak fragility, safety-subnetwork loss, activation reconstruction, and membership/gradient leakage—captured as a Security–Efficiency Paradox.

Across six evaluated edge-friendly models, security and efficiency diverge sharply: Phi-3.5-mini reaches the top MMLU (68.9% FP; 67.1% INT4) yet has the worst jailbreak resistance (20% FP; 30% INT4), while Qwen2.5-1.5B achieves 100% jailbreak resistance in both FP and INT4 but its INT4 energy and latency worsen by ~121% (2.15→4.78 J/token; 43.1→95.5 ms/token).

INT4 quantization yields large VRAM reductions (e.g., Qwen 2.88→1.08 GB and Granite 6.35→2.00 GB) but does not reliably improve runtime cost (several models show higher energy/latency under INT4), implying that deployment decisions must jointly optimize memory, compute, and security rather than treating quantization as a universal win.
one_liner: The most capable edge model can be the easiest to jailbreak, and the safest can become slower and more power-hungry after INT4—so “efficient” and “secure” are not monotonic properties of compression.

title: Silent Alarm: A J-Space Protocol for Comparing Danger Recognition Across Models and Quantization Levels
points: A single-forward-pass, judge-free internal metric (SafetyAUC computed from J-space at the pre-generation “decision point”) sharply separates strong vs weak danger-recognition mechanisms, e.g., models cluster at ≈0.97–0.98 SafetyAUC while an abliteration variant drops near chance (0.593) and simultaneously shows very high harmful-response rate (0.904).

INT8 quantization is effectively neutral for internal safety separability across all tested models (|ΔSafetyAUC| ≤ 0.011), whereas INT4 produces heterogeneous safety shifts (e.g., ΔSafetyAUC = +0.041 degradation for Qwen3-1.7B but ΔSafetyAUC = −0.086 “recovery” for the abliteration model), implying 4-bit compression can either erode or partially undo safety-related weight edits.

Internal danger recognition and external “safe behavior” can diverge materially (e.g., SafeRL-4B has high SafetyAUC 0.976 yet high harm@0.5 of 0.345 and 0.00 regex-refusal), so relying only on refusal/ASR-style behavioral metrics can miss the distinction between ‘lost recognition’ vs ‘recognized but complied/overexplained’.
one_liner: Safety evaluation becomes more comparable and modification-aware when it reads the model’s pre-response internal danger signal (J-space) rather than grading generated text, revealing quantization- and tuning-induced failures earlier and with fewer confounds.

title: Minionese: Comprehensive Benchmark and Mechanistic Study of Multilingual LLM Safety
points: A 55,440-prompt benchmark (385 harmful/harmless pairs × 4 perturbations × 18 languages) shows standard translation ASR on Llama-3.1-8B rises from ~8% in Tier‑1 to >70% in Tiers‑3/4, reaching 100% (Yoruba), 97% (Zulu), and 98% (Scottish Gaelic), demonstrating that English-only safety performance badly overestimates real-world multilingual safety.

Transliteration produces a script-identity bimodality rather than a resource-tier effect, with near-total jailbreaks for non‑Latin scripts (e.g., Korean 99% on Llama and 98% on Aya; Chinese 97% on Llama; Arabic 84% on Aya; Hindi 99% on Llama) but near-zero ASR for many Latin-script/very-low-resource cases (e.g., French 0%, Scottish Gaelic 0%, Yoruba 0% on Aya/Qwen), implying defenses must explicitly model script and romanization pathways.

Mechanistic measurements indicate low-resource jailbreaks usually preserve the refusal mechanism but starve it: Tier‑3 prompts remain linearly decodable as harmful (high probe AUC) yet fail to project onto the (effectively one-dimensional cross-lingual) refusal direction to cross threshold, while Tier‑4 approaches near-orthogonality (~85–90° principal angle vs English harm subspace) and can collapse harmfulness representations (AUC near chance for Yoruba/Zulu), pointing to upstream multilingual harm-representation alignment as the key remediation target.
one_liner: Meaning-preserving language perturbations (especially code-switching and script-changing transliteration) can flip an aligned model from refusal to compliance because multilingual harm representations become geometrically misaligned with the cross-lingual refusal trigger.

title: Breaking Refusal in the First Half: A Mechanistic Study of the Prefill Jailbreak
points: A one-line affirmative prefill (“Sure, here is”) collapses refusal from ~100% to 0–5% (e.g., 1.00→0.03 on Qwen2.5-1.5B) while a prompt-side linear harm probe remains near-ceiling (AUC ≥0.990) and still scores complied harmful prompts as strongly harmful (0.91–0.98), showing behavior can decouple from intact harm representations.

Causal localization shows the jailbreak’s leverage is concentrated in an early response window: restoring the harm direction over the first half of the response restores refusal ~as much as the whole response (≈42% vs 41%), whereas the second half is nearly inert (≈6% even at 2× strength), implying refusal is a shallow response-site computation rather than a prompt-side decision.

Cutting early response-to-prefill attention selectively reduces harmful continuation and partially restores refusal (+21pp vs a mass-matched attention knockout control), and the same prefill-specific collapse occurs in non-safety-tuned base models (e.g., harmful content 64%→25%), indicating the dominant mechanism is generic autoregressive conditioning with only a small safety-specific refusal attractor on top (logit-trace concentration 0.24 vs 0.03).
one_liner: A response-only affirmative prefix can override refusal without weakening harm recognition, and the failure is driven by a tiny early-generation window that behaves like generic autoregressive conditioning rather than a defeated “safety module.”

title: When Local Monitors Miss Compositional Harm: Diagnosing Distributed Backdoors in Multi-Agent Systems
points: A formal observability boundary shows that if attack fragments are ε-locally indistinguishable from benign traffic in a monitor’s per-step view (TV≤ε), then any per-fragment detector—no matter how powerful—has detection advantage bounded by ε (TPR−FPR≤ε), so stronger classifiers cannot fix missing local evidence.

In the locally benign regime, multiple local defenses collapse to chance-level separability (per-step learned detector ≈0.50 AUROC on AgentDojo; naive fragment concatenation ≈0.50 AUROC), while a coordination/assembly-aware view restores perfect separability (AUROC 1.000), demonstrating that “splitting” is not the root cause—loss of observable coordination signal is.
