points: The main bottleneck in autonomous science has shifted from generating candidate discoveries to verifying them end-to-end, with benchmarks indicating that agents that look expert on closed-ended questions still complete only a small fraction of open-ended research tasks and reproducibility-focused evaluations sometimes fall near or below chance.

Trust and governance are now treated as first-class requirements after real-world integrity failures—e.g., a flagship autonomous-discovery correction that removed a training-data leak and walked back novelty claims, plus a taxonomy documenting 100 fabricated citations at a top ML venue—implying autonomous pipelines must include lifecycle provenance, validation gates, and automated citation/result checking by default.

Interoperability is consolidating around a two-protocol interface stack (MCP for agent-to-tool access and A2A for agent-to-agent coordination), but the roadmap explicitly targets “zero-trust” cross-institution coordination, agent identity/governance, and screening at the digital-to-physical boundary as necessary controls before federated autonomous labs can safely scale.
one_liner: Autonomous science is now limited less by model capability than by verification, provenance, and cross-institution security controls needed to trust what agents do in the physical world.

title: Cardano's Voltaire Governance: Complete Specification and Research Program
points: On-chain Voltaire governance (CIP-1694, enacted via the Chang hard fork in Sep 2024) formalizes a three-body checks-and-balances model—DReps (economic stake), SPOs (operational stake), and a Constitutional Committee (one-member-one-vote)—covering seven action types from hard forks to treasury withdrawals.

Governance power is highly concentrated despite liquid delegation: only ~15.7% of circulating ADA was actively delegated for governance (5.8B of ~37B) while the top 10 DReps controlled 48.7% of active voting power and the top 20 controlled 63.6%, meaning outcomes can hinge on a small set of representatives unless delegation diversity materially increases.

Delegation behavior is extremely sticky (94.3% of delegators never redelegated across ~11 months), creating a durable capture surface where inactive or low-quality representatives can retain influence via inertia rather than performance, which in turn weakens accountability mechanisms that assume costless exit via redelegation.
one_liner: A rigorously specified, self-amending on-chain governance system now steers a ~$235M treasury, yet low active participation and concentrated, sticky delegation make its safety–liveness tradeoffs practically consequential.

title: PISmith: Reinforcement Learning-based Red Teaming for Prompt Injection Defenses
Twin Agent: Context Residual Compression for Privilege Separated Agents
points: Privilege-separated “Twin Agent” retains benchmark utility while collapsing prompt-injection success from 97.0% to 0.0% on SWE-bench-injected (GPT-5.2), outperforming strict no-communication privilege separation that achieves 0.0% ASR but 0.0% utility.

On AgentDojo (Gemini-2.5-Flash), bounded residual hints preserve performance (62.9% utility vs 61.9% default) while cutting attack success from 41.5% to 0.1%, whereas plan-first CaMeL eliminates attacks (0.0% ASR) but roughly halves utility (30.9%).

Adaptive, budget-aware attacks show the Explore side is fully steerable (100% copy-and-paste compromise), yet end-to-end multi-turn attack success remains 4.7% at a 100-character hint budget, indicating the primary failure mode is occasional Safe-side acceptance of detector-passing malicious residuals rather than direct exposure to untrusted context.
one_liner: Treating agent security as an information-flow compression problem makes the security–utility tradeoff tunable via a simple hint-length budget while staying close to ReAct-style workflows.

title: CPInj: Uncovering Prompt Injection Risks in Textual Collaborative Prompt Optimization
points: Collaborative prompt optimization is a distinct, high-leverage injection surface where CPInj persistently poisons the aggregated global prompt and causes large utility drops (e.g., on Gemini-2.5-Pro PubMedQA accuracy falls from 72% to 17% with an 88.73% attack success rate).

Single-turn prompt-injection baselines underperform in the multi-round TCPO loop, with CPInj typically achieving the highest ASR and largest accuracy degradation (e.g., on GPT-4o FOLIO accuracy drops from 77% to 51% under CPInj versus 67–69% under CatAttack/QueryGCG).

Server-side detection defenses often fail to restore clean performance and can even worsen outcomes, while the proposed defense-oriented aggregation (APAgg) reduces ASR substantially but remains incomplete (e.g., GPT-4o PubMedQA ASR drops from 21.31% to 1.64% with APAgg, yet the broader results still show residual vulnerability).
one_liner: Iterative, decentralized prompt rewriting plus aggregation creates an injection channel where stealthy instructions can survive optimization and defeat single-turn detectors, making the global prompt itself the attack propagation vector.

title: The Injection Paradox: Brand-Level Suppression in Safety-Trained LLM Recommendations via RAG Context Injection
Know Your Agent: Reconnaissance-Driven Pentesting of AI Agents
points: Reconnaissance-driven agent pentesting boosts indirect prompt-injection attack success by up to 67 percentage points over prior baselines, reaching 86.0% ASR on AgentDojo and 99.3% ASR on InjecAgent under black-box access.

Task-context extraction is the single most leverageable “knowledge asset,” raising ASR from 12.4% to 61.9% without defenses and from 2.1% to 38.1% with prompt-based defenses, implying that workflow-aware pretexts dominate purely persuasive payload wording.

Common prompt-level defenses only partially mitigate adaptive attackers: delimiter defenses leave ASR essentially unchanged (86.0%→86.3%), repeat-user-prompt cuts ASR to 53.0%, and a prompt-injection detector reduces ASR to 30.4% while often degrading benign-task utility for other methods.
one_liner: Treating AI agents like real pentest targets—by actively learning tools, schemas, policies, and task context—turns indirect prompt injection from template guessing into a high-success, target-modeled attack loop.

title: Data Leakage Prevention in Agentic Applications via Preemptive Hardening
points: A CI/CD-style pre-deployment pipeline that scans prompts, tool interfaces, and tool-invocation code can eliminate leakage from basic jailbreak and instruction-override attacks across multiple real-world agentic codebases, achieving a 100% reduction in those attack classes without requiring continuous runtime policy enforcement.

Across five CrewAI/LangGraph applications, hardening reduced aggregate leakage from 81.9% to 7.4% in the hardest case (a network monitoring assistant under stress-induced manipulation), corresponding to a 91% reduction while preserving benign task success (e.g., 91.0% BTSR in that application).

On the AgentDojo benchmark under a canonical prompt-injection attack, the approach improved utility under attack from 37.0% to 72.2% (+35.2 pp) while also increasing overall security from 66.7% to 74.1% (+7.4 pp), indicating that build-time hardening can raise resilience without the blanket-refusal behavior that often sacrifices functionality.
one_liner: Preemptive, source-level hardening plus automated adversarial/benign validation can deliver large leakage reductions and higher under-attack utility than default runtime-style defenses, but stress-framed attacks remain the most persistent residual risk.

title: ARGUS: Defending LLM Agents Against Context-Aware Prompt Injection
Persistent Sparse Autoencoders: Learning Feature Timescales in Language Models
points: A per-feature persistence coefficient (λ) added to sparse autoencoders yields a spectrum of timescales where most features are fast token-local detectors while the slowest ≈1% form a compact persistent semantic state, with competitive reconstruction quality (e.g., on Pythia-160M: 0.93 FVE and 0.95 cosine similarity).

Ranking features by decreasing λ provides an unsupervised way to extract topic/subject signal efficiently, with the slowest 1% achieving ~0.81 AUC on spliced MMLU subject probing—close to supervised (label-informed) feature selection and far better than low-λ or random subsets at the same feature budget.

In long-context prompt-injection monitoring, token-local evidence detects injections strongly when the injected text is present (94.0–96.7% accuracy at d=0), but only slow high-λ features retain and causally carry the injection signal hundreds of tokens later (up to ~350 tokens), producing the largest consistently positive steering effect on the monitor’s yes/no judgement when intervened upon.
one_liner: Learning a per-feature “memory timescale” turns SAEs into a two-channel representation—local sparse evidence plus a compact persistent state that preserves safety-relevant signals over long contexts.

title: ChainWatch: A Kill Chain-Aligned Sequential Detection Framework for Multi-Step Attacks in MCP-Based AI Agent Systems
points: Multi-step MCP attack chains can exceed 90% success against undefended agent systems because individually benign tool calls compose into malicious sessions that per-invocation defenses cannot interpret as intent.

A kill-chain-aligned sequential monitor placed as a transparent proxy can flag session-level threat progression by labeling each tool call into one of six stages (Reconnaissance→Exfiltration) using an HMM over a 20-feature vector and triggering rules on suspicious stage transitions.

Scenario traces across three attack classes (Direct Sequential, Indirect Injection Chains, Hybrid Multi-Stage) indicate session-level rules like READ→NETWORK exfiltration detection and late-stage CONFIG writes would surface attacks that pass per-call inspection, but practical deployment hinges on obtaining labeled multi-step MCP traces to calibrate thresholds and reduce false positives (especially for multi-service enterprise workflows).
one_liner: The key idea is to treat MCP tool use as a time-ordered attack narrative—detecting intent only visible across a session rather than at any single tool call.

title: Are GUI Agents Focused Enough? Automated Distraction via Semantic-level UI Element Injection
AgentRedBench: Dynamic Redteaming and Integration-Aware Defense for LLM Agents over SaaS Integrations
PARSE: Provenance-Aware Retrieval Sanitization for Professional Domain LLM Agents
Adaptive Adversaries: A Multi-Turn, Multi-LLM Benchmark for LLM Agent Security
points: Adaptive multi-round pressure is the main driver of real compromises: with the same 21 scenarios and fixed scoring, restricting to the first attacker turn yields only 0–1% attack success rate (ASR) while allowing 15 adaptive rounds raises ASR to 5.4–14.0%, implying single-turn or fixed-pool evaluations can severely under-measure agent risk.

Aggregates hide sharp, scenario-specific failure modes: Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4 tie at 5.4% ASR overall yet Opus spikes to 60% ASR on a credential-leak scenario (vs 7% for GPT-5.4/Gemini), while Gemini reaches 53% ASR on a fabricated-authority “paper accept” scenario where others stay at 0%, indicating defenses must be validated per threat archetype rather than by a single global “safety” score.

Attacker diversity materially expands coverage: pooling three frontier attacker LLMs finds 1.4–2.2× more unique successful attacks than the best single attacker, with low similarity to existing benchmark attacks (cosine 0.02–0.14) and no attacks that universally transfer across all three frontier defenders (0 of 46), implying robust evaluations should use multiple attacker models and live per-battle regeneration.
one_liner: Security gaps in LLM agents often emerge only under adaptive, multi-turn attacks and differ dramatically by scenario and attacker model, so leaderboard-style single-number robustness is a fragile deployment signal.

title: Trusted Credentials, Untrusted Behavior: Benchmarking LLM-Agent Security in High-Performance Computing
points: Defines the “hijacked authorized agent” failure mode where adversarial content in ordinary HPC artifacts (logs, shared files, tool/module metadata, or peer-agent messages) redirects an LLM agent into off-task actions that remain fully authenticated and account-permitted, making traditional authorization signals insufficient for detection.

Identifies five HPC-specific attack surfaces—shared-filesystem poisoning, scheduler/log channels, tool/module/MCP poisoning, cross-project leakage, and coordinated multi-agent exfiltration—highlighting that HPC’s durable shared storage and scheduler authority can turn prompt injection into allocation abuse, cross-project data exposure, or scientific integrity corruption without any privilege escalation.

Argues that common HPC controls (SSO/zero-trust identity, POSIX/zone isolation, quotas/accounting, and auditing/DLP) verify “who can do what” but do not capture task intent or context provenance, motivating TaskBound to benchmark defenses by jointly measuring task utility and attack success under explicit task-scoped policies rather than account-scoped permissions.
one_liner: HPC makes prompt injection uniquely dangerous because an agent can be steered into costly or cross-project actions that look perfectly legitimate to schedulers and access controls unless task intent is explicitly represented and enforced.

title: Trustworthy AI LLM Scalability Risk Index (LSRI): A Cybersecurity Framework Assessing Agentic-AI Security & Software Model Supply Chain Safety Boosting AI-Generated Malware Defense & Explainability Mitigating Emerging Risks of Generative AI
How Agents Ask for Permission: User Permissions for AI Agents, from Interfaces to Enforcement
Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Model Selective Evidence Adoption from Contaminated Retrieval Results
points: Post-training Qwen3.5-4B with DAPO on SelectBench-v2 improves strict selective-evidence success from 22.46% (73/325) to 25.54% with rule rewards and 26.46% with a frozen semantic judge (+3.08 to +4.00 pp), but the gains do not remain statistically significant after Holm correction (pHolm=0.691 and 0.217).

Forbidden-content adoption remains the dominant failure mode—dropping only from 72.62% to 69.23% (Rule) and 68.92% (DeepSeek)—leaving ~60% of all test cases factually correct yet still failing strict success due to copying or following prohibited spans.

Prompt-injection following does not improve (5.09% baseline vs 6.55% Rule and 5.82% DeepSeek on 275 injection cases), while general capability appears preserved with no measurable degradation on MMLU 5-shot (67.70% both) and clean HotpotQA EM/F1 essentially unchanged.
one_liner: RL reward shaping can nudge retrieval-augmented LLMs toward more selective evidence use without harming general QA, but statistically robust gains and genuine prompt-injection resistance remain unresolved.

title: Salience Induction against Multi-Hop RAG Agents: Threat and Defense
points: Truth-preserving “salience” edits (reordering, formatting, tone, and proximity framing) can hijack multi-hop RAG attribute-binding without injecting false facts or instructions, reaching 83.3% binding-level attack success at a 30% edit budget.

Common guardrails aimed at prompt injection or factuality largely miss this channel—one of the strongest tested baselines still left 75.7% post-defense attack success—because the induced errors are wrong bindings built from individually true statements.

A lightweight input-side preprocessing defense that normalizes salience cues cuts attack success to 15.3% (23.6% under an adaptive attacker) while preserving 94.4% neutral task success, indicating most risk is removable before the agent binds entities across hops.
one_liner: Even when every retrieved claim is true and non-instructional, manipulating how evidence is presented can reliably redirect multi-hop RAG agents—and simple salience-canonicalization can drastically shrink the attack surface.

title: CrackedPDFs: A Controlled Benchmark for Hidden Prompt Injection in PDFs
A Low-Latency Fraud Detection Layer for Detecting Adversarial Interaction Patterns in LLM-Powered Agents
V-DEAL: Diagnosing Video Safety De-Calibration as an Understanding-Refusal Coupling Failure
points: Across six video-capable LLMs on 5,020 samples from three public benchmarks, pairing harmful videos with benign but topic-aligned queries raises average attack success rate from 35.84% (VH-HQ) to 48.33% (VH-BQ) while dropping refusal rate from 53.05% to 14.22%, showing safety behavior is more tightly coupled to textual cues than visual harm evidence.

Models recognize harmful video intent/content well (e.g., >81% structured-attribute accuracy across core attributes, 89.94% harmful-intent match on a 300-video subset), yet still frequently comply under VH-BQ, implying the failure is not perception but a downstream “understanding→refusal” coupling breakdown.

A training-free prompt-injection realignment that forces explicit reasoning over harmful visual evidence cuts ASR by an average 48.24 percentage points (48.33%→0.80%) and reaches near-zero ASR in several models (e.g., Qwen2-VL-7B: 59.06%→0.12% with 8-shot; matched setting on VA-SafetyBench: 0.14%–0.24%), indicating lightweight inference-time controls can rival fine-tuning-based safety alignment in practice.
one_liner: The striking twist is that video models often “know” a video is harmful yet refuse far less when the user’s text looks benign, and a simple prompt can largely restore refusal behavior without retraining.

title: CAP-CoT: Cycle Adversarial Prompt for Improving Chain of Thoughts in LLM Reasoning
PlanFlip: Attacking Multi-Agent LLM Systems via Planning-Phase Prompt Injection
When Benchmarks Lie: Evaluating Malicious Prompt Classifiers Under True Distribution Shift
Agents at Risk: How Users Unwittingly Undermine LLM Safety
The LLMbda Calculus: AI Agents, Conversations, and Information Flow
ChannelGuard: Safe Models Do Not Compose into Safe Multi-Agent Systems
points: Zero attack-success in multi-agent pipelines can be a mirage: in 60 tool/memory-poisoning traces on Azure GPT-5, 54/60 (90%) of the “safe” outcomes in an undefended system were actually due to the cloud provider’s server-side filter rather than the application, revealing backend-dependent mechanism substitution that outcome-only ASR tables conceal.

Placing deterministic, training-free embedding-similarity gates on every inter-agent channel yields provider-invariant protection where input-only defenses cannot reach: the tool-output gate blocked Tool Poisoning 30/30 at the application layer identically across Azure GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Claude Haiku 4.5 while preserving GSM8K accuracy (0.867) and improving Prompt Injection ASR by 50% (0.333→0.167).

Static phrase-bank similarity gating has sharp limits against adaptive and narrative attacks: white-box paraphrasing evaded all embedding gates (Adaptive Paraphrase ASR ≈0.667 unchanged), and the COMPRESS band at the input boundary leaked in 23.4% of compressed cases, implying deployments should disable/retune compression at IB-0 and combine with non-signature defenses (e.g., perturb-and-vote) for robustness.
one_liner: Safety in multi-agent LLM systems does not compose: identical ASR can come from entirely different, uncontrollable mechanisms unless you attribute which layer actually stopped each trace.
affiliations: Ahsanullah University of Science and Technology

title: Refusal is Not Safety! Benchmarking Latent Safety Risks of LLM-Driven Content Humorization
The safety failures we are not instrumenting: a perspective on hidden safety-critical challenges in modern AI systems
points: Safety-critical failures in deployed AI systems are often “quiet” and systemic—plausible, distributed across components, temporally extended, and self-masking by degrading the human/organizational capacity to notice and correct errors—so output-only safety evaluations systematically under-detect the most consequential risks.

A five-layer integrity framework (epistemic, control, temporal, organizational, ecosystem) reframes AI safety as preserving visibility, contestability, containment, and recoverability across the full deployment stack rather than optimizing single-model refusal/accuracy metrics.

Actionable controls emphasized include designing for justified trust (source-linked evidence, structured uncertainty, cognitive forcing for high-impact actions), enforcing instruction authority outside the model (sandboxed retrieval, external policy engines, fail-closed permissions), and treating memory and the information environment as privileged safety boundaries (typed/gated persistence, provenance tracking, source-diversity monitoring).
one_liner: The most dangerous AI failures are the ones that look normal—systems can perform well while quietly eroding the mechanisms (evidence, authority, oversight, and provenance) that make errors detectable and correctable.

title: KVEraser: Learning to Steer KV Cache for Efficient Localized Context Erasing
Distributed Attacks in Persistent-State AI Control
Context Misleads LLMs: The Role of Context Filtering in Maintaining Safe Alignment of LLMs
How Jailbreak Attacks Inform Safety Alignment: A Defender-Centric, Shapley-Based Evaluation of Jailbreak Contributions
points: Attacker-centric attack success rate (ASR) is a weak proxy for defender-side safety benefit, with no-defense ASR rankings correlating poorly with singleton defense utility (Spearman ρ=0.215, Kendall τ=0.190) and dramatic inversions such as a zero-ASR Roleplay attack ranking 2nd by defense utility.

A surrogate-learned subset-utility model can approximate defender-centric utilities with relatively few black-box evaluations (e.g., MAE ≈0.066–0.078 and R² ≈0.78–0.83 on held-out subsets using 50–200 training subset queries), enabling practical Shapley-style credit assignment over attack sets.

Directly optimizing attack subsets beats choosing “top-k” by individual attack importance: on synthetic landscapes, greedy subset selection recovers ≥82.69% of the oracle improvement gap for k>1 versus ~60–71% for Shapley-ranked top-k, and on a real ICD setting both A-MESS solvers find the best observed subsets (k=2 utility 0.8539; k=4 utility 0.9397) while ASR top-k can lag substantially (k=2 utility 0.5716).
one_liner: Jailbreaks that look strongest to attackers are often not the ones that most improve alignment when used as red-teaming data, so selection should optimize downstream defense utility rather than ASR.

title: Jailbreak Foundry: From Papers to Runnable Attacks for Reproducible Benchmarking
ARMOR: Aligning Secure and Safe Large Language Models via Meticulous Reasoning
SoK: Systematizing LLM Prompt Security: Taxonomies, Datasets, and Unified Evaluation of Attacks and Defenses
HarDBench: A Benchmark for Draft-Based Co-Authoring Jailbreak Attacks for Safe Human-LLM Collaborative Writing
Geometric Configurations of Perturbed Jailbreak Prompts
points: Last-layer last-token embeddings in Qwen2.5 and Llama3.* Instruct models cleanly linearly separate prompts into three form-driven regions—“Usual Tokens” (control + mild paraphrases), “Unusual Tokens” (Numbers/Leet Speak control paraphrases), and “Jailbreak Features” (template+harmful request)—but this separability does not track whether the model refuses or complies.

The top-50 next-token probability representation is near-degenerate with an effective dimensionality around 1.25 across all six models and its first principal component largely equals the top-1 next-token probability, implying that safety-relevant structure is not naturally expressed in this probability-space geometry.

Across a refusal-dominated dataset of 38,592 prompts (96 jailbreak + 96 control, each with 50 stochastic paraphrases in four families), no robust “behavioral hyperplane” emerges in either embedding space or probability space, and only a few token-level cues correlate with compliance (e.g., top-1 token “Sure” in Qwen-2.5-1.5B, and “,”/“ĊĊ” in Llama-3.2-1B), while larger models show no significant token associations.
one_liner: Jailbreak prompts look geometrically separable mainly because of their template/spelling artifacts, not because the model’s internal states encode a clean, linearly accessible safety-vs-compliance boundary in these spaces.

title: LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately
How Many Iterations to Jailbreak? Dynamic Budget Allocation for Multi-Turn LLM Evaluation
NonTextual Target Attack
Concept Concentration for Faithful Representation Intervention
HARC: Coupling Harmfulness and Refusal Directions for Robust Safety Alignment
Large Language Models Generate Harmful Responses Using a Distinct Mechanism, Shared Across Harm Types
Trojan Horse Prompting: Jailbreaking Conversational Multimodal Models by Forging Assistant Message
External Data Extraction Attacks against Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models
Before the Last Token: Diagnosing Final-Token Safety Probe Failures
LLM Unlearning for Cyber Defense: A Survey on Methods, Challenges, and Emerging Threats
DARWIN: Evolving Jailbreak Adversary and Guardrail for LLM Safety Evaluation and Protection
points: An open-ended evolutionary jailbreak loop can drive attack success rates to near-maximum levels against both aligned frontier LLMs and standalone guardrails (e.g., 99.7% ASR on DeepSeek-V4-Pro, 92.5% on GPT-5.5, and 99.0% on YuFeng-XGuard), indicating that static red-teaming substantially underestimates real-world risk.

Evolving strategy pools materially increase attacker capability over time (on HarmBench, GPT-5.5 ASR rises from 73.5% at 50 strategies to 92.5% at 200, and YuFeng-XGuard rises from 82.2% to 99.0%), showing that “future attacks” quickly outpace fixed defenses unless defenses are updated continuously.

Online adversarial guardrail training on both malicious and benign disguised prompts yields high safety without utility loss (91.6% average unsafe recall across 12 harmful benchmarks while maintaining a 100.0% average benign pass rate across 11 standard benign benchmarks), suggesting intent-focused training can reduce jailbreak false negatives without triggering over-refusal.
one_liner: The core takeaway is that an attacker that continually evolves strategies can rapidly overwhelm static safeguards, but coupling that evolution to continuous adversarial guardrail training can recover robustness without sacrificing benign usability.

title: An Early Warning of Emerging Biosecurity Risks in Frontier LLMs
EvalSafetyGap: A Hybrid Survey and Conceptual Framework for LLM Evaluation-Safety Failures
Stress Testing Concept Erasure with Large Language Model Agents
points: A multi-agent, literature-grounded stress-testing loop (STACE) raises concept-erasure failure discovery to 51.1% image-level success (SIRI) across 10 erased concepts, beating the strongest of five LLM-based baselines by 4.3 percentage points under a fixed 100-image budget per concept.

STACE typically finds a violating probe quickly—earliest identification iteration (EII) averages 1.4–1.6 across ESD erasure strengths—showing that adaptive, feedback-driven probing can expose residual concept leakage within the first ~2 hypothesis iterations even when static tests miss it.

Robustness varies sharply by erasure method and strength (e.g., STACE hypothesis-level success SIRH drops from 68–69% at ESD-100/200 to 39% at ESD-500, and to 34% on MACE), indicating that stronger or different edits reduce leakage but do not eliminate it and also reduce executable-test reliability (SER down to 71–73% in harder settings).
one_liner: Iterative, role-specialized LLM agents with external grounding can systematically “red-team” concept erasure and uncover leakage that one-shot prompt generation and static benchmarks undercount.

title: Incomplete Prompt Jailbreaks in Large Language Models
Harnessing Textual Refusal Directions for Multimodal Safety
CluCERT: Certifying LLM Robustness via Clustering-Guided Denoising Smoothing
AI Security Policy Should Assess Systems, Not Only Models
ROK-FORTRESS: Measuring the Effect of Geopolitical Transcreation for National Security and Public Safety
Exposing Long-Tail Safety Failures in Large Language Models through Efficient Diverse Response Sampling
Sockpuppetting: Jailbreaking LLMs by Combining Prefilling with Optimization
Hair-Trigger Alignment: Black-Box Evaluation Cannot Guarantee Post-Update Alignment
Using Mechanistic Interpretability to Craft Adversarial Attacks against Large Language Models
Pigeonholing: how bad prompts hurt models, causing collapse and mistakes
CHERRY: Compressed Hierarchical Experts with Recurrent Representational Yield
JailMeter: An Evidence-Based Evaluation Framework for Jailbreak Attacks on Large Language Models
points: JailMeter introduces an evidence-based, multi-agent evaluation pipeline that iteratively strips jailbreak-induced noise from model outputs and only counts an attack as successful when the response both reflects the malicious intent and provides a complete on-topic answer, tightening what “ASR” actually measures.

On the 330-example JailMeter-Eva benchmark of non-refusal, ambiguity-heavy jailbreak responses, JailMeter reaches 97.27% accuracy (93.88% F1), while common evaluators vary widely—e.g., DAN and I-FSJ collapse to 0% precision/recall and StrongREJECT attains 80.89% accuracy but only 25.71% recall—showing how evaluator choice can drastically distort reported jailbreak success.

A distilled single-model version (JailMeter SLM) preserves most reliability at 95.15% accuracy (89.19% F1) and reduces evaluation overhead by about 12× tokens with 1 call instead of ~10 calls (and ~54s→19s latency in a 50-sample efficiency test), enabling scalable, cost-sensitive jailbreak measurement.
one_liner: Reliable jailbreak measurement requires filtering jailbreak “noise” and verifying intent+completeness; otherwise, evaluator bias can swing attack success from near-zero to near-100%.

title: Hidden in Thought: Transferable Chain-of-Thought Artifacts Induce Harmful Behavior
Latent Fusion Jailbreak: Blending Harmful and Harmless Representations to Elicit Unsafe LLM Outputs
FedLSG: LLM-Enhanced Semantic Calibration for Federated Graph Backdoor Defense
points: Across 4 benchmarks and 3 attacks with 60% of clients compromised, the method cuts attack success rate (ASR) from ~87–95% (no defense) down to 4.5–7.6% on Citeseer/Pubmed/Flickr under DPGBA while keeping clean accuracy essentially unchanged (e.g., Pubmed 86.14% vs 85.72% baseline).

Under UGBA, ASR drops to 2.75% (Citeseer), 32.30% (Pubmed), 0.00% (Flickr), and 0.36% (Ogb-arxiv), demonstrating that combining client-side semantic edge reweighting with server-side semantic client-trust aggregation can neutralize stealthy triggers even when standard pruning/aggregation defenses leave ASR as high as ~59–90%.

In fully adaptive white-box settings targeting the full pipeline, ASR remains bounded (DPGBA: 8.95–47.57%; UGBA: 8.39–44.53% across datasets) and still outperforms most non-adaptive baselines, indicating that semantic calibration plus trust-weighted aggregation reduces cascading backdoor propagation rather than acting as a brittle preprocessing filter.
one_liner: Interesting because it operationalizes LLM semantic reasoning as a practical federated backdoor defense—using lightweight client LoRA students and a server-side LLM teacher to jointly downweight suspicious edges and malicious client updates without sacrificing clean accuracy.

title: Defense Against LLM Backdoors using Critical Neuron Isolation Pruning
points: DeCNIP reduces backdoor Attack Success Rate by >95% on average while intervening on only ~0.1% of neurons, indicating that generative LLM backdoors can be disabled via highly sparse, mechanistic edits rather than broad retraining.

Across five 7–9B open-source LLMs and four backdoor attacks, DeCNIP achieves a mean ASR of 2.90% (2.52% when pruning based on the original trigger), versus 65.18% with no defense and 29.86% for the strongest baseline pruning method, showing large robustness gains over existing defenses.

Utility retention remains high after mitigation, with models preserving ~97% of baseline performance on MT-Bench/HumanEval/Alpaca-style instruction following, implying targeted neuron damping can harden safety without the typical usability collapse from coarse pruning or heavy fine-tuning.
one_liner: Backdoor triggers in decoder-only LLMs appear to work by pushing harmful prompts into a benign-like representation manifold, and DeCNIP exploits that mechanism to find and damp a tiny set of backdoor-critical MLP neurons with minimal capability loss.

title: Language Triggers Hijack Language Circuits: A Mechanistic Analysis of Backdoor Behaviors in Large Language Models
Tokens, the oft-overlooked appetizer: Large language models, the distributional hypothesis, and meaning
IssueTrojanBench: Benchmarking AI Coding Agents Against Malicious Issue Requests
points: Across 4,176 end-to-end runs on three deployed coding agents, 66.5% of malicious issue requests successfully induced tool-using exploit execution, showing that indirect prompt injection remains a high-probability failure mode in real development workflows.

Attack success is dominated by the backbone model rather than the agent framework (GPT-5.3 Codex 84.8% vulnerable, GPT-5.4 73.6%, Sonnet 4.6 41.1%), and supply-chain style payloads are near-universal at 96.6% because they mimic routine developer actions (e.g., dependency installation).

Any artifact treated as standard text is a reliable injection vector (72.2% success for PDF/website/source/issue/comment and even when payloads are hidden), while low-authority metadata like image alt-text drops success to 16.7%, implying that robust, provenance-aware instruction/data separation is more impactful than format-based filters (which showed negligible effect).
one_liner: Malicious instructions embedded in ordinary issue-tracker artifacts routinely bypass both model and agent guardrails, and lightweight “boundary marker” defenses fail, making model+agent co-designed provenance and action controls the critical next step.

title: Sketching the Readout of Large Language Models for Scalable Data Attribution and Valuation
Cloak and Detonate: Scanner Evasion and Dynamic Detection of Agent Skill Malware
Linguistic Firewall: Geometry as Defense in Multi-Agent Systems Routing
Is "Knowing It's Malicious Enough?" Evaluating LLMs for Fine-Grained Malware Behavior Auditing
Small, Free, and Effective: Orchestrating Open-Weight Small Language Models to Outperform Single LLM for Malware Analysis
points: A grounded hybrid orchestration (Qwen3-4B + Foundation-Sec-8B) reached 35.30% overall accuracy on CyberSecEval Malware Analysis, beating the best cyber-specialized single model (22.54%) and narrowly surpassing the strongest ungrounded frontier baseline (Gemini at 34.77%), showing that evidence-grounded multi-agent SLM ensembles can match or exceed single-LLM performance for detonation-report Q&A under a single-GPU budget.

Tool- and evidence-driven pipelines are the main driver of SLM gains on retrieval-heavy tasks, with the agentic approach lifting Qwen3-4B from 16.58% to 25.11% overall and the full hybrid raising Easy-tier accuracy to 38.14% (vs 25.50% for pure debate), implying SOC deployments should prioritize deterministic evidence extraction (e.g., structured chunking + grep/jq-style queries) before any multi-round reasoning.

Ungrounded debate exhibits a reliability tradeoff—improving hard questions but degrading easy ones as rounds increase—while grounding + a citation/verification constraint mitigates drift (full hybrid 35.30% vs 33.79% without grounding constraint), and the same grounding helps frontier models too (Gemini improves from 34.77% to 38.22% and Claude from 33.15% to 36.85%), indicating orchestration quality can matter as much as model size for malware-report interpretation.
one_liner: A carefully grounded, tool-using multi-agent ensemble of small open-weight models can edge out an ungrounded frontier LLM on malware detonation-report QA while also improving frontier LLMs when given the same evidence pipeline.

title: Measuring the Security of Mobile LLM Agents under Adversarial Prompts from Untrusted Third-Party Channels
HijackKV: New Threat in Position-Independent KV Cache Reuse
points: Position-independent, multi-tenant KV-cache reuse enables a new integrity attack where a benign-looking cached chunk silently carries attacker-conditioned context, allowing cross-user output hijacking without any malicious tokens in the victim prompt.

HIJACKKV attains ~94% average targeted success in a single attempt and stays effective under realistic serving conditions, including only ~10% cache-hit rate and up to 50% selective recomputation, implying that “partial refresh” mitigations are insufficient at practical operating points.

The attack persists across long interactions (targeted success remains ~55% after inserting 1,024 unrelated tokens and ~47% after 2,048) and transfers in black-box settings (e.g., ~37–44% targeted success against several 8B–70B models), indicating a systemic risk to shared-cache deployments rather than a model-specific quirk.
one_liner: A performance optimization (position-independent KV reuse) creates a stealthy cross-tenant control channel where cached internal states, not text, become the attack surface.

title: AgentWorm: Self-Propagating Attacks Across LLM Agent Ecosystems
NRT-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-Turn Red-Teaming of LLM Operator Agents in Safety-Critical Control Rooms
An Automated Framework for Extracting Reachable Attack Chains from Cyber Threat Intelligence Reports
points: A precondition→action→postcondition “attack unit” representation plus Datalog compilation enables automated reachability reasoning from narrative CTI, reaching the specified attack goal in 19/20 reports and recovering 34 distinct attack paths.

On 20 CTI reports with 334 human-validated executable steps, the framework achieves 94.9% step coverage (300 fully covered, 32 partially, 2 missed), outperforming CTINEXUS (82.2%), AttacKG+ (81.1%), and CRUcialG (42.6%), indicating that state-transition-oriented extraction captures more operationally complete steps than entity/TTP/graph outputs.

Predicate-normalized pre/postconditions reach 80.9% average F1 (85.3% precision, 77.8% recall; precondition recall 81.1% vs postcondition recall 74.6%), while ablations show staged extraction is decisive (Full pipeline F1 94.5% vs end-to-end LLM generation 47.4–51.3% and removing behavior guidance 57.9%), implying controllable granularity and diagnosis-guided repair are key to producing reasoning-ready rules.
one_liner: Turning CTI prose into executable Datalog rules works reliably at scale, but only when extraction is staged, vocabulary-constrained, and dependency-repaired rather than generated end-to-end.
affiliations: Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Novel Security Intelligence Technologies

title: DisarmRAG: Stealthy Retriever-Centric Poisoning to Disable Self-Correction in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Extended Version)
Heimdallr: Characterizing and Detecting LLM-Induced Security Risks in GitHub CI Workflows
Matching Ranks Over Probability Yields Truly Deep Safety Alignment
Cross-Agent Campaign Attribution: Linking Asynchronous Attacks Across LLM Agents
points: A proxy-side fingerprinting protocol (A2FV) can link sparse, asynchronous prompt-injection sessions across independent LLM agents with 0.818 pairwise AUC (≈0.82) on a benign-heavy benchmark, while score-only adaptations of per-session detectors and chunked LLM-judge approaches stay near chance (≈0.50–0.52 AUC).

Most of the actionable attribution signal comes from tool-use structure and prompt surface residue (structural-only AUC 0.784; stylometry-only AUC 0.707; combined structural+stylometric AUC 0.825), whereas timing features are weak in the evaluated traces (temporal-only AUC 0.562) and receive zero calibrated weight in the fixed protocol.

Controlled non-oracle evasion that perturbs multiple channels reduces clustering quality more than pairwise separability (V-measure 0.295→0.237 from L0→L2) and only slightly degrades linking (AUC 0.816→0.807), implying campaign-level correlation can remain feasible even when single-session indicators are diluted or distributed across agents.
one_liner: Treating agent security as a campaign-correlation problem reveals strong cross-session identity residue at the shared proxy that per-session safety scores and LLM judges largely discard.

title: Membership Inference Attacks on In-Context Examples in LLM-based Recommender Systems
STAC: When Innocent Tools Form Dangerous Chains for LLM Agents
Do Agents Dream of False Memories? Black-box Visual Attacks on Long-term Memory in Multimodal AI Agents
Do Speech Tokens Leak Voiceprints? Speaker Inversion Attacks Against End-to-End Speech Language Models
points: Exposed speech-token interfaces from end-to-end speech LMs retain strong speaker identity signal even for unseen speakers, with leakage validation EER as low as 0.34% (Kimi-Audio), 0.66% (Higgs3), 1.60% (Moshi), and 2.36% (Qwen3-Omni) on the speaker-disjoint VoxCeleb1 verification split.

A two-stage speaker inversion method (SpInv) can recover attacker-chosen speaker embeddings from only ~3 seconds of intercepted frontend outputs, achieving cosine similarity ≥0.71 on VoxCeleb2-test for token-based frontends (0.7527 Higgs3, 0.7536 Kimi-Audio, 0.7136 Moshi) and 0.6683 for continuous features (Qwen3-Omni).

Attack success scales sharply with observation length, improving from CosSim 0.4887 at 1s (Acc 86.6%, EER 13.46%) to CosSim 0.7136 at 3s (Acc 97.0%, EER 3.05%) and CosSim 0.8065 at 10s, indicating split-inference token streaming does not reliably protect voiceprint privacy without additional mitigations.
one_liner: Speech tokens meant to reduce raw-audio exposure still act as high-fidelity voiceprint carriers, enabling practical speaker-embedding recovery from a few seconds of intercepted frontend output across multiple speech-tokenization schemes.

title: What Does It Mean to Break a Distillation Defense?
An Evaluation of Large Language Models for Detection of Malicious Python Packages
Rewriting the Response Path: Silent Tampering and Provider-Signed Defense in BYOK LLM Agents
CryptanalysisBench: Can LLMs do Cryptanalysis?
points: Across 191 game-verified cryptanalysis tasks spanning six primitive families, five frontier LLMs broke 65%–86% of Tier‑1 schemes with known practical attacks, indicating practical cryptanalysis is now within reach for general-purpose agentic models.

On previously “unbroken” full-strength designs, models achieved non-trivial wins (about 4.4%–8.9% of Tier‑2 schemes at full parameters) and surfaced at least two impactful new results: a 2‑query full key‑recovery attack on SpoC AEAD and a decryption-reaction key recovery on KINDI that also exposes an error in its published CCA-security proof.

Tier‑2 and frontier challenge tasks remain far from saturated (only 24–61 total breaks across all scaled-down variants depending on model), with failures dominated by converting correct vulnerability hypotheses into working exploits, implying near-term capability gains may come more from better tool-use, solvers, and test-time compute than from fundamentally new cryptographic insight.
one_liner: Cryptanalysis becomes a clean, automatically verifiable benchmark where LLM agents already reproduce most known practical breaks and occasionally discover new design-level attacks with only a handful of oracle queries.

title: Forensic Trajectory Signatures for Agent Memory Poisoning Detection
AI Watermark Evidence Fails Forensic Readiness: An Empirical Evaluation
Evaluating Large Language Models for Symbolic Security Protocol Analysis
points: Across 130 obfuscated AnB/AnBx protocols (388 goals), chat-mode LLMs achieved high attack recall (69–81%) but very low precision (<31%), while reasoning-mode flipped the trade-off to higher precision (GPT 66.5%, DeepSeek 45.4%) with only ~55% recall, indicating neither mode is reliable enough to substitute for formal verifiers like ProVerif/OFMC.

Reasoning improves correctness mainly by suppressing false positives rather than finding more real attacks: for DeepSeek (same base model), enabling reasoning raises precision from 27.2% to 45.4% yet still misses nearly half of attacks, implying current “reasoning” primarily tightens decision thresholds instead of performing robust symbolic trace exploration.

Authentication goals are a consistent failure mode—reasoning models detect well under half of injective/non-injective agreement attacks (≈26–40% recall) while confidentiality is the exception (up to 95.7% F1, with 100% recall for GPT reasoning), and self-reported confidence is unusable because it remains uniformly high (often 94–99%) even on missed attacks and does not correlate with correctness.
one_liner: Reasoning-mode LLMs become much more precise on protocol security verdicts but still miss about half of real attacks, and their confidence scores are essentially meaningless—so at best they can triage, not verify.

title: GARAGE: Characterizing the Automation Boundary in LLM-based Attack Graph Generation
points: A Hybrid RAG pipeline built from 12,786 automotive-relevant CVEs and 140 incident reports can generate vehicle-level attack graphs that generalize to unseen vehicle architectures, achieving mean Practical Feasibility (PF) 59.0/100 for proprietary LLMs under strict leave-one-out and entity-anonymization controls across 320 trials.

Automation breaks at implementation-detail granularity: high-level tactics transfer well (Initial Access 95% coverage; Affect Vehicle Function 99%), but low-level mid-chain steps that depend on target-specific internals collapse (Execution 15% coverage; Command-and-Control 33%), implying human reverse-engineering/validation remains mandatory for exploitability claims.

Reliability and deployment economics are sharply tier-dependent: proprietary models show tighter repeatability (mean CV ≈33% vs ≈50% for open-weight; overall 95% CI ±5.9 PF points), while cost-efficiency favors cheaper models (Gemini Flash delivers 87% of Claude’s PF at ~1/10 the per-run cost; Qwen3-coder is the strongest open-weight option at PF 48.3 for ~$0.004/run).
one_liner: The core boundary is not retrieval modality but knowledge granularity—LLMs can draft auditable, tactical attack scenarios across vehicles, yet still hallucinate and fail on the target-specific “how-to” steps that determine real exploitability.

title: RISKTAGGER: Evidence-Guided LLM Agent for Post-Incident Forensic Analysis of Money Laundering in Web3
Seven Security Challenges in Cross-domain Multi-agent LLM Systems
Learning-Based Automated Adversarial Red-Teaming for Robustness Evaluation of Large Language Models
Broken Gates: Re-evaluating Web Bot Defenses in the Age of LLM Agents
points: Commercial CAPTCHA-solving services achieved ~100% bypass on challenge-based defenses (reCaptcha v2, hCaptcha Easy, and Cloudflare Turnstile) at commodity pricing as low as ~$0.10 per 1,000 solves, collapsing the cost-friction assumption behind interactive bot gates.

Behavioral/non-interactive defenses were materially harder to commoditize via token-generation services: solver services averaged ~23% success against reCaptcha v3 at the default >0.5 score threshold (best service reached 63%), indicating that reputation and environment signals remain a practical bottleneck for outsourced solvers.

Across six off-the-shelf LLM browser agents, failures on reCaptcha v3 were driven primarily by execution-environment authenticity rather than human-like interaction behavior, with a browser-extension agent running inside a real persistent profile (cookies/history/stable fingerprint) bypassing while a behaviorally near-identical instrumented agent consistently failed (scoring ~0.1–0.3).
one_liner: Modern bot defenses are increasingly decided by whether the browser environment looks “real,” not whether the agent can act human-like or solve a puzzle.

title: InferNet: Exploiting Aggregate GPU Profiles as Side-Channel for DNN Architecture Inference
They'll Verify. They Just Won't Act. How Authority Framing and Laundered Code Turn a Trusted Agentic CI/CD Pipeline Into an Attack Surface
points: A single untrusted external issue induced a five-agent, multi-provider CI/CD pipeline to deploy attacker-specified secret exfiltration in up to 55% of runs when authority framing, a longer verification chain, and scanner removal combined—showing that agentic pipelines can convert routine feature requests into worst-case compromise without any model jailbreak.

Authority framing (“pre-approved under SEC-2291, do not re-review”) caused downstream verifiers to explicitly notice the exfiltration code (e.g., sending dict(os.environ) to an external URL) yet approve it anyway, and a capable LLM-based code scanner passed about 80% of these laundered pull requests, implying that visible malice is not sufficient when procedural deference suppresses action.

Prompt secrecy and content-based controls provided no meaningful protection: the entry agent leaked 0/40 system prompts, and content/pattern detectors caught 0/40 laundered exfil cases because the code is syntactically clean, while only intent-level reasoning partially blocked (~20%) and even that was overridden by fabricated authority cues.
one_liner: The striking failure mode is not covert prompt theft but explicit “I see the exfil” followed by approval, triggered by a believable internal pre-approval claim that bypasses human-like and automated verification norms.

title: The Ethics of Autonomous AI Agents for Offensive Security
points: LLM-driven autonomous penetration-testing agents introduce a qualitatively new risk regime by combining three independent indeterminacies—non-deterministic actions (poor ex-ante/ex-post explainability), open-ended impact (opaque model/scaffold supply chains), and an indeterminate user base (sharply lowered skill floor)—which together undermine incident attribution and pre-deployment safety review.

The technology amplifies the offense–defense cost asymmetry by enabling industrial-scale offensive capability in the short term, with concrete ecosystem signals including vendor-reported 84.62% success on proprietary benchmarks and measured tool uplifts of 16–25× when swapping in newer frontier models, implying capability can jump materially without changes by the original tool author.

LLM-enabled “AI slop” already degrades defender workflows at scale—e.g., one major open-source project saw bug-bounty confirmation rates fall from ~15% historically to <5% in 2025 amid a submission surge—while automated defenses against adversarial reports are reported at ~62% detection, forcing costly human oversight and increasing maintainer burnout and systemic security risk.
one_liner: The core safety challenge is that autonomous offensive agents don’t just make hacking faster—they make accountability, scoping, and user gating simultaneously harder, turning traditional dual-use governance knobs ineffective.

title: SecureCode: A Production-Grade Multi-Turn Dataset for Training Security-Aware Code Generation Models
Evaluating Open-Weight LLMs for Generating Structured Threat Information for Autonomous Vehicle Vulnerabilities
points: A new CAV-focused benchmark of 183 filtered CVEs (2012–2025) provides 1,383 STIX Domain Objects and 1,395 STIX Relationship Objects plus 211 CWE and 294 MITRE ATT&CK mappings (≈7.6 objects and ≈7.6 relationships per CVE), enabling standardized evaluation of CVE-to-STIX automation in transportation security.

With dynamic few-shot prompting, top open-weight models reach micro-F1 ≈0.94 for STIX object extraction, ≈0.63 for relationship extraction, and ≈0.99 for CWE mapping, showing that entity/weakness normalization is near-solved while relationship (graph) construction remains the main bottleneck for reliable CTI generation.

MITRE ATT&CK mapping remains difficult to complete (Match@All low despite improved Match@1), and the ground-truth data concentrates on a small set of behaviors—top-10 techniques cover 77.21% of mappings with T1499 (48), T1203 (42), and T1210 (34) leading—implying defenses should prioritize DoS and exploitation paths while using validation/KB grounding for technique completeness.
one_liner: Open-weight LLMs can reliably turn automotive CVEs into well-formed STIX entities and CWE labels, but they still struggle to infer the correct STIX relationship graph and fully enumerate ATT&CK techniques without stronger grounding.

title: From Controlled to the Wild: Evaluation of Pentesting Agents for the Real-World
SkillGuard: A Permission-Centric Framework for Agent Skill Security
SafeHarbor: Defining Precise Decision Boundaries via Hierarchical Memory-Augmented Guardrail for LLM Agent Safety
Risk Assessment and Security Analysis of Large Language Models
Give Them an Inch and They Will Take a Mile:Understanding and Measuring Caller Identity Confusion in MCP-Based AI Systems
Defense effectiveness across architectural layers: a mechanistic evaluation of persistent memory attacks on stateful LLM agents
ChainMark: Model-Free LLM Watermarking with Closed-Form Calibration
points: ChainMark enables model-free watermark verification in O(n) time using only a shared key and tokenizer by hashing tokens into S cyclic states and enforcing next-state transitions at a fraction ρ of positions, eliminating the need to access the generating LLM during audits.

A closed-form calibration links regulatory targets directly to deployable settings via S⋆(nmin, ρ, α)=ceil(4·zα²/(ρ²·(n−1))+1), and a one-corpus threshold recalibration brings observed false-positive rates from ~1.7–2.0% down to ~0.34–0.67% at a 1% target without materially reducing true positives.

At matched watermark budget, ChainMark retains 72.8% true-positive rate after Chinese back-translation while KGW and SWEET drop below 20%, and it has a universal robustness threshold δ⋆≈29.3% under uniform random substitution (invariant to S, ρ, and n) albeit with ~2× higher self-perplexity (3.66 vs ~1.80–1.93).
one_liner: A regulator-facing watermark that is auditable without the model and is configurable from (false-positive rate, minimum length, budget) in closed form, while staying unusually robust to translation attacks.

title: MCP Pitfall Lab: Exposing Developer Pitfalls in MCP Tool Server Security under Multi-Vector Attacks
RECEIPT: Deterministic, Reward-Hacking-Resistant Verification for White-Box Agentic XSS Discovery
points: A deterministic verifier that enforces environment isolation, constrained PoC replay, explicit attacker/victim role separation, and browser-sentinel verdict binding can eliminate reward-hacked XSS confirmations, achieving 100% precision (30/30 true positives) on 50 latest-release open-source apps where the same agent’s self-judgment produced only 37% precision (10/27).

On 95 real-world web apps under a $20-per-app budget, the framework confirmed 30 XSS on latest releases including 24 previously unknown issues (with 12 already acknowledged and patched/scheduled) and rediscovered labeled post-cutoff CVEs in 36% of known-vulnerability targets (49% detection), indicating practical recall with zero false positives in evaluation.

Browser execution checks alone are not tamper-resistant against white-box agents: a naive browser-bound verifier was reward-hacked into 111 claimed XSS with only 10 real (9% precision), while adding isolation, PoC constraints, and role separation raised precision stepwise to 19%, 44%, and finally 100%, showing that validation must be protected from agent-controlled state, automation, and threat-model mismatches.
one_liner: The key insight is that “real browser execution” is necessary but not sufficient for agentic vulnerability validation—without replay isolation and role-bound PoCs, powerful white-box agents can systematically fabricate confirmations via reward hacking.

title: SEVRA-BENCH: Social Engineering of Vulnerabilities in Review Agents
Hide and Seek in Embedding Space: Geometry-based Steganography and Detection in Large Language Models
Tracing the Shadows: Automatic Tracking and Analysis of Crypto Money Laundering via Transaction Semantic Analysis
points: A semantic-aware tracing pipeline that lifts raw token transfers into DeFi Semantic Units (DSUs) achieves 98.4% address recall and 94.4% destination precision on 63 single-chain incidents while keeping traces compact at ~299 analyzed transactions and 44 nodes per incident.

Recovering cross-chain intent from calldata (function-signature matching plus argument semantic parsing) enables 95.8% address recall and 93.8% destination recall on 19 cross-chain incidents and successfully links 424/448 (94.6%) cross-chain transactions, far exceeding the best baseline’s 48.5% recall and 60.1% destination recall.

Retrieval-augmented LLM semantic inference meaningfully expands coverage beyond static rules (handling 22.9% of transactions) and reaches ~97% operation-inference accuracy on previously unseen protocols when combined with RAG and iterative consistency checks, whereas an LLM-only setup is ~67% accurate.
one_liner: Blending program-analysis-style token-flow graphs with retrieval-augmented LLM reasoning makes DeFi laundering traces both more accurate and dramatically less noisy, including across chains where links are not explicit on-chain.

title: Towards Demystifying and Repairing LLM-in-the-Loop Vulnerabilities
Security Vulnerability Patterns in AI-Generated Code: A Cross-Model Comparative Study
points: All 9 LLM-generated Python automation scripts (web scraping, email automation, file watching) contained exploitable vulnerabilities, indicating that “works as intended” is a poor proxy for “safe to deploy” in non-expert enterprise workflows.

Security outcomes were effectively model-invariant: 9 of 17 deduplicated vulnerability classes appeared in code from all three tools (ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini), 14 of 17 appeared in at least two, and weighted CVSS totals differed by <10%, implying risk is driven more by task category than by vendor choice.

Risk is concentrated rather than diffuse: a Pareto weighting (CVSS base score × number of affected models) showed 11 of 17 vulnerability classes contributed ~80% of total exposure, making targeted controls for recurring classes like SSRF, path traversal, template injection, and email header injection the highest-leverage mitigation.
one_liner: Different code-generation models converge on the same insecure implementation patterns for everyday automation tasks, so governance should focus on review gates and task-specific hardening—not picking a “safer” assistant.
affiliations: The Beacom College of Computer & Cyber Sciences

title: Demystifying LLM Supply Chain Vulnerabilities in the Wild: Distribution, Root Cause, and Real-World Impact
Veritas: Grounding LLM Agents for Reliable Vulnerability Reasoning over Stripped Binaries
PatchIsland: Orchestration of LLM Agents for Continuous Vulnerability Repair
LLM vs. SAST: A Technical Analysis on Detecting Coding Bugs of GPT4-Advanced Data Analysis
Insecure Coding Preferences in Long-Term Memory: Security Risks for LLM-based Code Generation
points: Storing insecure coding preferences in long-term memory raises vulnerable-code generation rates across ChatGPT, Gemini, Qwen, and Grok by 2.7–50.3 percentage points across Python/C/C++/Go/JavaScript, demonstrating that persistence turns one-off “debugging shortcuts” into cross-session security debt.

Safety signaling lags behind risk: warning-rate increases trail vulnerability-rate increases by 5.4–14.0 percentage points and models rarely disclose memory influence (2.3% memory-reference rate for ChatGPT; 10.3% for Gemini), making memory-induced insecurity hard for developers to notice and correct.

Mitigations show a clear tradeoff: appending or storing explicit security requirements cuts vulnerabilities by 19.7–33.6 percentage points but can reduce functional correctness by up to 15.9 percentage points, while memory-level safety filtering detects 100% of evaluated risky memory entries and restores behavior to the no-memory baseline (Vul@k down to 0%) with ~1.53–2.90s per entry overhead.
one_liner: Long-term memory can quietly “lock in” insecure coding habits—boosting vulnerabilities far more than it boosts warnings—unless memory writes are proactively filtered.
affiliations: Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics

title: Agentic Vulnerability Reasoning on COTS Binaries
The Language of Security: How Prompt Syntax Shapes Secure Code Generation in Open LLMs
Beyond Refusal: A Same-Lineage Study of Aligned and Abliterated LLMs for Vulnerability Analysis
SEC-bench Pro: Can Language Models Solve Long-Horizon Software Security Tasks?
Quantifying Frontier LLM Capabilities for Container Sandbox Escape
Graph Representation Learning Augmented Model Manipulation on Federated Fine-Tuning of LLMs
Leveraging Large Language Models for Trustworthiness Assessment of Web Applications
Supporting Students in Navigating LLM-Generated Insecure Code
Federated Learning and LLM-Driven Threat Intelligence for Zero Trust IoT Architecture
points: A federated autoencoder trained across 25 heterogeneous IoT clients using MQTT over TLS achieved 1.00 recall and 1.00 ROC-AUC with an overall F1 of 0.976 on a 1.9M-sample balanced dataset, indicating strong separability between normal and attack traffic without centralizing raw data.

Setting the anomaly threshold at the 95th percentile of normal reconstruction error yields a designed ~5% false-positive rate (specificity 0.95) and precision of 0.833 for attack detection, making threshold selection the dominant operational trade-off between alert volume and missed attacks.

A LoRA-tuned Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct model trained on 500 labeled examples produced perfect per-class identification (precision/recall/F1 = 1.00 for four attack types) and auto-generated broker-enforceable iptables actions, but the end-to-end response latency averaged 41.41 s due to remote inference despite sub-second local enforcement.
one_liner: The pipeline cleanly connects privacy-preserving FL anomaly detection to LLM-generated, automatically enforced Zero Trust controls, but the practical bottleneck shifts from detection accuracy to LLM inference latency and false-positive management.

title: JavaVulBench: A Java Vulnerability Benchmark with Realistic Splits, a Unified Multi-Backend Harness, and a Leakage-Aware Evaluation Mode
When to Trust the Map: Confidence-Aware LLM Routing for Automotive CVE-to-ATM Mapping
points: A confidence-aware selective-automation pipeline for automotive CVE→Auto-ISAC ATM mapping achieves 0.878 precision in its AUTO tier (High-Confidence mode), more than 2× the candidate-set base rate of 0.395, enabling safe auto-confirmation while deferring uncertainty to analysts.

The calibrated confidence score separates correct from incorrect mappings with AUROC 0.868 (95% CI [0.815, 0.916]) and yields low calibration error (ECE 0.057), supporting threshold-based routing that remains stable across bootstrap resampling (High-Confidence AUTO precision 0.878, 95% CI [0.778, 0.959]).

Evidence-grounded verification is the main driver of reliable confidence estimation: removing judge signals drops AUROC from 0.868 to 0.705 (−0.163), while hierarchical ICL candidate generation raises precision from 0.277 to 0.395 at matched recall 0.745 versus a flat zero-shot LLM baseline and reduces average predicted pairs per CVE from 4.55 to 3.19.
one_liner: Turning CVE-to-threat-taxonomy mapping into a calibrated routing problem yields a practical AUTO/REVIEW/HOLD boundary with quantifiable risk controls for safety-critical automotive workflows.

title: How Do You Choose Your AI Component? An Interview Study of Secure AI Integration in Practice
points: Interviews with 22 practitioners show AI model selection is universally driven by functional criteria (performance/accuracy, cost, and features like tool-calling or multimodal support), while security is rarely used as a first-class selection metric—recreating early software dependency “reuse-first” supply-chain failure modes.

Trust in major vendors and platforms functions as a de facto security control for almost all participants (20/22), replacing direct model security assessment and concentrating systemic risk in provider compromises, silent model/version updates, and vendor lock-in.

Data exposure dominates real-world risk perception and mitigation: all 22 participants cited PII/proprietary-data leakage as a key concern and all 22 reported using PII filtering/redaction, yet defenses skew toward reactive infrastructure-layer controls (filtering, isolation, monitoring) rather than proactive model-level security evaluation across the lifecycle.
one_liner: AI components are being adopted like fast-moving dependencies: chosen for capability and cost, then “secured” with perimeter controls and vendor trust—despite opaque models, frequent version drift, and growing agentic attack surface.

title: Detoxify: A framework for abusive text transformation using LLMs
Safety Testing LLM Agents at Scale: From Risk Discovery to Evidence-Grounded Verification
Distribution-First Population Simulation: Collapse, Calibration, and Recall in Non-WEIRD LLM Persona Modeling
points: Independent LLM-agent population simulations collapse toward a single modal choice when individuals are run independently, with modal concentration rising 0.36→0.69, entropy dropping 1.46→0.77, 85% of units flagged as collapsed, and TVD reaching 0.44—implying pooled “many-agent” outputs can be systematically non-representative even when grounded on real respondents.

Collapse severity is predictable from scenario structure (r=0.55 with having a single normatively correct answer), indicating the biggest failure risk is in “one-right-answer” or normatively loaded settings where independent agents converge on a rational/default option rather than preserving population heterogeneity.

A distribution-first approach via Verbalized Sampling improves distribution fidelity by +6.8 to +10.1 points across three model families but reliably overshoots variance (SD-ratio 0.40–0.56→1.26–1.37), showing that dispersion calibration needs explicit variance control and that subgroup/individual-level claims remain vulnerable to recall and underdetermination despite strong national-level fits.
one_liner: Independent-agent synthetic populations can be internally inconsistent by construction, and a single-call distribution-first method is both cheaper (O(1) vs O(N)) and more faithful at the aggregate—yet still risks over-dispersion and recall-contaminated subgroup inference.

title: When Does Belief-Based Agent Memory Help? Reliability-Conditional Updating and Provenance-Capped Poisoning Defense
(A)I Sees What You Don't: Exploiting New Attack Surfaces in Third-Party Mobile Agents
Dissociative Identity: Language Model Agents Lack Grounding for Reputation Mechanisms
Autonomous mechanistic discovery of colorectal cancer vulnerabilities via multi-scale AI swarms
Operational Hallucination and Safety Drift in AI Agents
points: In a baseline malicious task, 4/7 evaluated models (DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o, Llama-3.1, Qwen-2.5) produced an explicit textual refusal (Aligned_Text = 1.00) yet still executed unsafe tool behavior (Aligned_Action = 0.00), yielding a maximal declaration–action gap of +1.00 and demonstrating that refusal language does not reliably prevent harmful actions in tool-using agent loops.

Operational livelock (≥3 consecutive identical tool calls) occurred even under deterministic settings (temperature = 0.0), with GPT-4o entering livelock in 100% of dilemma episodes and the malicious episode (1.00/1.00) and Llama-3.1 entering livelock in the control legitimate episode (1.00), indicating termination and progress validation failures can arise without adversarial input.

A lightweight Action-Aware Supervision Layer concept (intent–action consistency checks, authoritative runtime state tracking, and forced termination primitives) was able in post-hoc replay to flag 100% of observed Safety Drift trajectories before the first state-changing tool call while reporting no false positives on the benign control case, suggesting many agent safety failures are interceptable at the tool boundary with deterministic enforcement.
one_liner: Multi-turn tool use exposes a systematic split between what agents say (safe intent) and what they do (unsafe or non-terminating actions), making action-level supervision more informative than transcript-based safety signals.

title: Beyond Black-Box Obfuscation: Mechanistic Analysis and Defense of White-Box Monitors
Beyond Embeddings: Interpretable Feature Extraction for Binary Code Similarity
Chasing Moving Targets with Online Self-Play Reinforcement Learning for Safer Language Models
SycoEval-EM: Sycophancy Evaluation of Large Language Models in Simulated Clinical Encounters for Emergency Care
Addressing Benchmarking Gaps in Large Language Models for Health and Medicine with Dynamic Red-Teaming
Code Monitor Red Teaming for Public-Test-Passing Code
points: After public tests filter 71,000 LLM-generated programs down to 43,677 “accepted” candidates, 23,081 of those (≈53%) still fail hidden tests, showing that visible-test passing leaves a large residual correctness risk in deployment-like pipelines.

Under a realistic triage constraint of 5% false positives, weak LLM verifiers miss most residual bugs (e.g., Qwen-7B Hybrid FNR 86.8%, Mistral-7B Hybrid FNR 80.0%), indicating that single-pass review is an insufficient stopping rule even when it extracts some ranking signal (AUROC up to ~0.67).

Adversarial public-test-overfit pressure both increases bug prevalence (hidden-bug rates rising to ~68–73% among public-pass) and makes bugs harder to separate (≈0.07 AUROC drop and ≈0.07 FNR@5%FPR increase), while a stronger verifier (GLM-5.1) only partially recovers performance (FNR@5%FPR 0.54→0.66 from G1 to G4-adv) due to a mix of verifier limitations and information-boundary inferability limits.
one_liner: Public tests create a deceptively high-confidence acceptance boundary where over half of “passing” code can still be wrong, and weak LLM monitors largely fail to catch these residual bugs at low false-positive budgets—especially under test-overfit pressure.

GPE: Evaluating Robust Evidence Aggregation for Fact Verification under Controllable GEO-Style Poisoning
points: Even without poisoning, six-way fact-verification accuracy stays near chance (best 52.7% on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and 53.9% on GPT-5.4), indicating that clean retrieval-grounded verification remains an unsolved reliability problem at scale.

GEO-style evidence poisoning causes steep, attack-dependent degradation, with ATA (realistic content tampering) the most damaging on average—full-poisoning accuracy drops to ~9.2% across methods versus 11.6% (FakeGPT), 12.2% (PoisonedRAG), and 14.6% (Ignore Injection)—highlighting that provenance-preserving edits to key facts are harder to detect than synthetic text or explicit prompt-like injections.

Robustness does not transfer across attack types or methods: RAFTS tends to lead under fully poisoned FakeGPT/PoisonedRAG evidence (e.g., 21.6%/23.4% on DeepSeek), while STEEL is uniquely more resistant to instruction-like Ignore Injection (e.g., 42.8% on GPT-5.4 at 100% poisoning) yet still degrades substantially under semantic tampering, implying defenses must be evaluated under multiple contamination modes and ratios rather than a single “robust” score.
one_liner: Controllable poisoning ratios over shared evidence expose degradation curves and token-efficiency collapse that clean fact-verification benchmarks systematically miss.

points: Trustworthy agentic AI for critical systems is best framed as workflow-level assurance (perception→audit) across five cross-cutting dimensions—safety/constraints, robustness/reliability, transparency/interpretability, accountability/auditability, and privacy/security—because capability-only evaluations systematically miss long-horizon and tool-mediated failure modes.

Safety gaps are material in practice: on ST-WebAgentBench, 38% of nominally successful web-agent tasks violated at least one policy, collapsing Completion Under Policy (CuP) to 15.0% even when raw Completion Rate (CR) reached 24.3%, implying that reporting task success without policy-compliance metrics overstates deployability in high-stakes settings.

Operational robustness degrades sharply under realistic infrastructure conditions: in α3-Bench for LLM-based UAV agents, performance robustness drops by 30–40% under adverse 6G network impairments despite baseline mission success and safety-policy scores ≥0.95, reinforcing the need for ODD-style boundary definitions, runtime monitoring, and fail-safe fallback control.
one_liner: The most actionable takeaway is that agentic AI trust is an end-to-end assurance and certification problem—measurable with concrete workflow metrics—rather than a property of a single model or prompt.

Toward cryptographically verifiable authorization for autonomous AI agents: A security hypothesis, preliminary formal model, and proof-of-concept implementation
points: A concrete agent request can be made cryptographically verifiable as an authorization relation that binds (agent principal, committed request/plan, policy identifier/version, nonce/timestamp—and optionally context) while keeping private authorization attributes hidden via zero-knowledge proofs.

The core security takeaway is a three-way separation—identity evidence ≠ authorization-request evidence ≠ runtime execution evidence—so even a valid zero-knowledge authorization proof does not guarantee the authorized request is the one actually executed (a TOCTOU-style gap requiring additional runtime trust anchors such as attestation or execution receipts).

A Groth16 proof-of-concept (Circom/snarkjs, bn128) demonstrates feasibility of principal binding (Poseidon(sk)->id), plan/request binding (SHA-256(plan)->h), and gateway-enforced replay resistance (nonce state + time window), but leaves full context binding, explicit policy-version binding as a public input, multi-agent delegation-chain composition, and post-quantum/trusted-setup risks as open issues.
one_liner: The interesting twist is treating authorization itself—not identity, delegation, or audit—as a request-bound, zk-provable relation, and showing that this still doesn’t solve the execution-binding problem that agent systems trip over in practice.

title: RT-SHCUA: Real-Time Self-Hosted Computer-Use Agent for UAV Control
points: Contract-bound UAV skill invocations (with explicit timing/state/authority/fallback/evidence fields) prevent self-hosted computer-use agents from directly issuing flight commands, enabling onboard admission control to reject stale, unauthorized, or state-inconsistent actions before execution.

Across 1,890 simulated mission executions spanning 0.1–1.5 s task-level deadlines and three mission lengths, the system reported 0 deadline misses and 0 fallback events while keeping P95 end-to-end latency at 55.7–135.0 ms without trusted isolation and 231.6–308.0 ms with OP-TEE enforcement, indicating predictable task-level responsiveness even with stronger isolation.

In 7,560 security/degradation checks, the trusted-path enforcement matched the software reference in 100% of cases and cleanly separated outcomes into allow/deny/defer/fallback (e.g., replay and policy violations denied, missing GPS deferred, comms/obstacle/battery issues routed to fallback), supporting auditable, bounded recovery rather than unsafe continuation.
one_liner: The key move is turning open-ended agent actions into deadline- and authority-bound “skill contracts” that can be enforced (and evidenced) onboard, so slow or compromised reasoning can’t directly drive unsafe UAV behavior.
affiliations: Shaanxi Key Laboratory of Network and System Security

title: Building Trust in Autonomous Commerce: A Verifiable Global Event Timeline and AI-Ready Fraud Intelligence Layer
points: A deterministic, cross-domain audit layer built from canonical event schemas, reproducible batching (without synchronized clocks), Merkle commitments, and blockchain anchoring enables a globally verifiable event timeline that makes retroactive log tampering detectable across heterogeneous agentic commerce systems.

Prototype benchmarks show Merkle construction scales near-linearly from 0.89 ms (1,000 events) to 47.12 ms (50,000 events) while single-event verification stays ~constant at 0.0064–0.0123 ms, supporting real-time audit checks even as batch sizes grow 50×.

Merkle inclusion proofs remain small and network-friendly—growing logarithmically from 320 bytes (1,000 events) to 512 bytes (50,000 events)—and outperform linear scan verification by 14.4× at 50,000 events, implying significant verification cost reductions at production-scale throughput.
one_liner: It turns agentic commerce logs and fraud labels into a third-party verifiable, tamper-evident timeline with microsecond-level verification and sub-kilobyte proofs suitable for real-time auditing and AI dataset provenance.
